title: Deleting a user's data from backups: crypto-shredding with one key per person
description:
A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can't edit most of those.

Crypto-shredding is the standard way out: encrypt each person's data under their own key, keep the keys in one small keystore, and "delete" a person by destroying their key. The ciphertext can stay wherever it is. Without the key it's noise.

I built a small library for this called aegis-shred: a Rust core, a Python package and a CLI.

from aegis_shred import MasterKey, Vault

vault = Vault.open("keys.db", MasterKey.from_env("AEGIS_MASTER_KEY"), create=True)
blob = vault.seal("user-42", b"alice@example.com", context=b"users.email")  # store anywhere
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # b'alice@example.com'
vault.shred("user-42")                       # erase user-42, everywhere, at once
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # raises aegis_shred.Shredded

How it works 

master key (from your secret manager)
  └─ wraps one data key per subject ───── keystore (SQLite file)
        └─ HKDF → one key per sealed object
              └─ AES-256-GCM, chunked (STREAM)
                    └─ sealed blob/file ── your database, S3, backups, …
  • seal creates the subject's key on first use and returns a self-describing blob. The blob names a random key id, never the user.
  • unseal checks every chunk. A modified byte, a reordered or missing chunk, truncation, or a different context all fail.
  • shred deletes the wrapped key in one transaction, writes a tombstone and a hash-chained audit entry, and returns a receipt. From then on, in every process, that user's blobs raise Shredded.
  • The keystore stores subjects only as HMAC(index_key, subject_id), so the keystore and audit log don't list your users either.

The context argument binds a blob to where it lives, so a ciphertext copied from one column into another won't decrypt.

Large files are streamed in 64 KiB chunks with constant memory, and the output file only appears if every chunk verifies.

Install 

pip install aegis-shred          # prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, Windows
cargo add aegis-shred            # Rust library
cargo install aegis-shred-cli    # the aegis command

Honest limits

This is v0.1, alpha. The byte format is specified and versioned, every guarantee has a test, and a second independent implementation in Python runs in CI. But there has been no independent security audit. Read the threat model in the repo before relying on it.

Whether crypto-shredding satisfies GDPR Art. 17, CCPA or India's DPDP Act for your situation is a question for your lawyers. The library gives you the mechanism and an audit trail, not legal cover.

Repo (MIT OR Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/Aegis

Feedback on the threat model and the file format is the most useful thing you could send me.

title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
description:
arXiv:2610.19048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

title: DeBoneDiT: Depth-Driven Conditional Bridge Diffusion Transformers for Bone Suppression in Chest X-Ray Images
description:
arXiv:2610.19466v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chest X-Ray (CXR) is a primary modality for diagnosing pulmonary diseases, yet the overlap of bony structures often obscures critical radiographic findings, increasing the risk of diagnostic uncertainty. While Dual-Energy Subtraction (DES) is the clinical benchmark for bone suppression, its widespread adoption is primarily hindered by specialized hardware requirements and increased radiation exposure. Recently, diffusion-based generative models have shown promise for this task, yet they are still constrained by reconstruction-biased latent compression, prior-induced domain gap, and a scarcity of high-quality paired datasets. To address these challenges, we propose DeBoneDiT, a depth-driven conditional bridge diffusion Transformer architecture for efficient high-resolution bone suppression. We first introduce Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE), a structure-aware vision tokenizer for latent compression. By incorporating a multi-level depth feature loss derived from the pretrained Depth Anything V2 encoder, DAE preserves both visual fidelity and structural consistency. Second, we formulate bone suppression as a source-conditioned Brownian bridge diffusion process, leveraging CXRs as both the diffusion prior and structural guidance to narrow the source-to-target domain gap and maintain anatomical plausibility. Furthermore, we have constructed and released SZCH-X-Rays, the largest publicly available high-quality paired dataset for bone suppression to date, comprising 741 pairs of CXR and DES soft tissue images. Extensive experiments and downstream evaluation demonstrate that DeBoneDiT achieves superior bone suppression performance with reduced computational overhead.

title: AWS License Manager now supports license type conversions for Ubuntu Pro purchased through AWS Marketplace
description:
AWS License Manager  now supports in-place upgrades for EC2 Ubuntu LTS (Long Term Support) instances to Ubuntu Pro available on AWS Marketplace. This allows customers to strengthen their security posture and meet compliance requirements without rebuilding their fleet or migrating workloads to a new instance or AMI. With an Ubuntu Pro subscription, customers receive security patches for up to 10 years — extendable to 15 years with the Legacy add-on. This coverage extends beyond the base OS to thousands of additional packages, including widely used open-source applications such as NGINX, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. Ubuntu Pro also supports Kernel Livepatch, which applies critical kernel security fixes without rebooting to minimize downtime.

With this launch, customers, who have an existing Canonical Ubuntu Pro subscription through AWS Marketplace, can upgrade directly during the conversion workflow. Customers who do not yet have a subscription can subscribe to Canonical Ubuntu Pro from within the AWS License Manager console. The new feature is available in  all commercial regions  where AWS License Manager is available.

To get started, navigate to the  AWS License Manager console  and the  AWS License Manager User Guide .

title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
description:
arXiv:2610.19185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $\gamma^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.

title: Vercel Sandbox can now run for up to 24 hours
description:
Vercel Sandboxes can run uninterrupted sessions for up to 24 hours (up from 5 hours). This new max duration unlocks workloads that require longer runtimes, such as large-scale data processing, E2E testing pipelines, and long-lived agentic workflows.

Pair with persistent sandboxes to maintain durable state across extended runs.

title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.19502v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.

title: A threshold is not a measurement: what your dedup cut actually does at each artefact length
description:
Deduplicate at Jaccard 0.7. Flag a pair whose Dice similarity is at least 0.8. Every one of those numbers was calibrated once, on one corpus, and then applied to artefacts of every size — a 40-token comment, a 3000-token report, a source file, a training example.

The threshold is the only thing that was calibrated at one length. The false-positive rate is not, and a paper I have been reading measures where it goes.

The short version, before the mechanism:

  • On unrelated same-length text, the null median of char-bigram Dice rises from 0.5389 at L = 40 to 0.9096 at L = 3000. A cut calibrated on short artefacts therefore over-flags long ones — and a cut calibrated on long ones cannot certify anything about short ones.
  • The four standard statistics split into two classes: the character statistics' null tracks length (char 3-gram cosine: 0.1787 rising to 0.8163), while the shingle statistics' null never leaves the floor (word-3 Jaccard's p95 peaks at 0.0084, word-5's at 0.0003).
  • At a false-positive-matched operating point, the perturbation rate at which recall falls to one half moves as a power law for the character statistics — slope -0.230, R^2 = 0.950, n = 7, a 2.70x span — and stays flat for the shingles (1.08x).
  • Below a certification floor L* the null's own p95 is 0, so the matched threshold is 0, so every pair passes: the false-positive rate is 1.0, not alpha.

That last one is the finding worth carrying into a code review. It is not a reading of 0.0000 on a curve. It is a hole in the curve, and it reports as a pass.

Why a threshold cannot be transferred

A similarity statistic is an average over the artefact's own material — its set of shingles, its bag of character n-grams. A fixed edit rate destroys roughly the same fraction of that material at every length, so to first order the effect size a check sees is length-free. What does change with length is the variance: more material means more comparisons means a tighter estimate. So you expect the curve to get narrower with length.

Whether its location also moves is a separate question, and it is falsifiable in both directions — a flat eps*(L) would have been just as informative as a sloping one. The measurement says the location moves, and only for one family of statistics. That is why "longer artefacts are easier" is true and irrelevant at the same time: reliability does improve with length, and the claim people actually deploy is about a fixed cut.

What I re-ran before quoting any of it

The package ships a one-command reproduction, so I ran it at the published ref rather than reading the tables — from a git archive export of origin/main, so the working tree cannot flatter the numbers:

$ bash reproduce.sh
build          python3.13 3.13.9 | stdlib only (no third-party import anywhere in the package)
corpus         8 file(s) verified against corpus/SHA256SUMS
  spike_v0  MATCH  e828ae4db8878d34
  spike_v1  MATCH  81ea052b3018dc85
  ...
  floor_v3  MATCH  ed54a9a7cdd272a2
instruments    11 of 11 reports re-run byte-identically
analysis       the boundary power law (slope -0.230, R2 0.950)
figures        7 of 7 figure file(s) re-generated byte-identically
certificate    plant 1: identical objects must NOT fire
certificate    plant 2: a one-byte change MUST fire
certificate    plant 3: the real cross-process defect MUST fire
stratum        the repair restores alpha on every live cell
manuscript     the manuscript is exactly what the build renders from the reports
REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN

Two things worth noticing, because they are design decisions rather than accidents.

First, the comparison is byte equality against the shipped reports, not "close enough" — eleven instruments re-run from their own code over a committed 5.6 MB corpus, plus the seven figures regenerated from those reports. The instruments import nothing outside the standard library, and the float reductions use math.fsum (exactly rounded in every CPython), so no library version's arithmetic enters the comparison. When I quote 0.9096 below, that is a value I re-derived, not a value I read.

Second, the run carries a mechanism certificate, not just a value: it predicts eps* from the measured decay curve and the measured threshold in 21 cells, and the paper states the worst deviation (0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05). A number that survives the reproduction is a number; a number whose derivation is also checked is what lets you trust the mechanism rather than the artifact.

Claim 1 — the null is a function of length, and it splits the statistics

On unrelated same-length text, at seven lengths spanning 75x:

statistic null median / p95 at L = 40 at L = 3000
char-bigram Dice median 0.5389 median 0.9096
char 3-gram cosine median 0.1787 median 0.8163
word-3 Jaccard p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0084
word-5 p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0003

Two consequences, and they point in opposite directions for a deployer.

For the first class, a single cut cannot mean the same thing at two lengths: at 0.7, char-bigram Dice is a strict cut on short artefacts and a permissive one on long ones, because the null itself is already at 0.91 there. Your false-positive rate did not drift by a few percent. It moved from small to near-total.

For the second class, the cut means very little at any length — a word-3 Jaccard cut at 0.7 sits far above a null whose p95 is 0.0084, so it is a real cut, but it is also throwing away recall it did not have to. Different failure, same root cause: the number was never a statement about the corpus it is now being used on.

Claim 2 — the boundary moves as a power law for one family and not the other

The genuine object here is the operating characteristic: the probability of flagging a perturbed artefact as a function of the perturbation rate, at a fixed false-positive rate. The paper calls the point where recall falls to one half the boundary eps*, and measures it at the false-positive-matched operating point:

  • char-bigram Dice: eps* falls with slope -0.230 (R^2 = 0.950, n = 7) — a 2.70x change over the length range;
  • word-3 Jaccard: 1.08x — flat, within noise.

And the paper does not stop at the fit: the mechanism certificate predicts eps* from two measured quantities (the decay curve and the threshold) in 21 cells with a worst deviation of 0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05. The mechanism proposed is the headroom 1 - tau that the rising null eats — not the edit count. That is the part I would have got wrong from first principles: the intuition is that longer text is harder to perturb detectably; the measurement says the boundary moves because the null moved into the threshold's headroom.

Claim 3 — below a floor, the check certifies nothing and reports a pass

Where the fraction of unrelated null pairs exceeding 0 falls below alpha, the null's p95 is 0, the matched threshold is 0 — and the check's false-positive rate is 1.0.

This is measured as a band, because two reasonable definitions of the floor bracket it: L* is 100-130 for word-3 Jaccard and 1196-2000 for word-5 at alpha = 0.05, and it rises as alpha rises (at alpha = 0.01 the word-3 floor is 40, against 100 at 0.05).

So the floor is not a property of the corpus or of the statistic alone. It is a property of the claim: at a stricter alpha you need longer artefacts before any recall claim can be certified. And below it, the check is not "slightly weak". Every pair passes, including every unrelated pair.

If you are calibrating on a corpus that contains short items and then applying the cut to them, this is the cell where your evaluation says 0.0000 and your deployment says yes to everything.

Claim 4 — the null is stratified, and the repair is not the threshold

Two smaller results that a deployer can act on directly.

The null key is a declared parameter. The comparison p95 must be drawn under the same key as the judged pair — a length ratio of 2 moves the false-positive rate by up to 0.063. If your null was built from pairs of equal length and your scan judges unequal ones, the null is answering a different question.

The stratum weights are too. A null calibrated on a uniform population reads its false-positive rate inflated by up to 9.4x when the scan's per-stratum shares are skewed. The repair is to reweight the null to the scan's own shares — not to move the threshold — and it lands inside alpha ± 0.05 in 13 of 13 live cells. Moving the cut would have "fixed" the rate at the cost of every recall claim you have.

And a composition law, which is the one I would put on a design doc: fusing two statistics at their own matched operating points gives eps*(OR) >= max(eps*) and eps*(AND) <= min(eps*), measured at 96 composed cells (6 statistic pairs × 2 compositions × 4 lengths, under both edit operators) with 0 violations. So OR buys you the robust member's boundary at the price of the false-positive rate, and AND buys the brittle member's — the two compositions are the two ends of one trade, not two designs you can pick from.

What I would do differently on Monday

  1. State the length distribution next to the threshold. A cut of 0.7 plus "calibrated on 40-200 token items" is a very different claim from a bare 0.7, and the second one is what ships today.
  2. Check which class your statistic is in. If it is a character-n-gram statistic, your threshold's meaning is length-dependent and the fix is per-length operating points (or a length-free statistic). If it is a shingle statistic, your null is on the floor and the question is whether the cut is doing any work at all.
  3. Find your floor before you find your threshold. Below L* there is no threshold to tune. If your corpus has items under a hundred tokens, know that the cell exists.
  4. Reweight the null to the scan, and declare the key. Neither is a modelling change; both are the difference between the rate you measured and the rate you get.

None of this says a deployed check is broken. A check calibrated and operated at one length is correct at that length — which is exactly what its own evaluation measures, and exactly why the evaluation does not transfer.

Reproduce it 

cd papers/issue-130 && bash reproduce.sh

About five and a half minutes, CPython 3.9+, standard library only — no third-party import anywhere in the package, and the corpus (eight Project Gutenberg texts, 5.6 MB) is committed and verified against SHA256SUMS at the start of every run. The script re-runs eleven instruments from their own code and compares each fresh report byte-for-byte against the shipped one, re-derives the tables, regenerates the figures, and runs the mechanism certificate and the plant batteries. REPRO_FULL=1 adds the two-run determinism certificate (~13 minutes more).

One honest detail about my own run: the journal's reference gate needs CPython ≥ 3.12 and lives in the journal's .github/tools/, so from an archive export that step reports skipped rather than passing. The package's own gates — instruments, figures, analysis, the plant batteries, the stratum repair — all ran and all passed. If a reproduction has three exit states rather than two, that is the state you want it to land in rather than being counted as either success or failure.

This is paper #130 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is A Threshold Is Not a Measurement; the source, the corpus, the eleven instruments and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-130 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a similarity check in production whose threshold was calibrated on one length distribution and is applied to another, the measured operating characteristic for your statistic is the kind of data this line of work is short of.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Candidate Search: Bounded Fallbacks and Audit Trails
description:
Recruiting search has a hard constraint that a demo tends to hide: an answer assembled from a slow or unauthorized source is worse than a narrower answer that a recruiter can verify. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that remains attached to every candidate claim. Treat each fallback as a contract with a deadline, an access check, and an audit event.

I approach this like a ledger boundary. A candidate profile is an indexed fact, a ranking decision is a derived fact, and a citation is the receipt that lets somebody reconstruct the decision later. The system should never imply exactly-once retrieval, because networks retry and sources change; it should make each stage idempotent and make duplicate evidence harmless.

Start with a retrieval contract

Before choosing a vector engine, map the user-visible answer to fields the pipeline can actually retrieve. For “find backend candidates who have shipped payment reconciliation,” the contract might require a candidate identifier, an access scope, the matching excerpts, their source identifiers, and a freshness timestamp. A result that has a high similarity score but no source identifier is incomplete, even if its prose sounds convincing.

Preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item. Put those attributes beside the chunk, not in a separate cache that can drift. At query time, apply the tenant and authorization predicates before ranking or generation. This is where many fallback designs quietly leak data: the primary index filters correctly, then the lexical fallback searches a shared table without the same predicate.

The contract also defines failure semantics. An empty stage means “try the next permitted stage,” while a denied stage means “stop and record the denial.” A timeout is not permission to broaden scope. That distinction belongs in the audit trail with a request ID, stage name, query limit, and selected source IDs.

Three words matter: bounded, attributable, repeatable.

It failed closed.

How should fallbacks shape retrieval architecture for recruiting candidate search?

Use a narrow-to-broad sequence, with explicit budgets at every hop:

  1. Search the tenant’s candidate collection with semantic retrieval and a small top-k.
  2. If recall is insufficient, run a lexical query over the same authorized corpus, preserving the original filters.
  3. If the corpus is stale or lacks a required document, consult an approved web-backed source, but return its URL or document identifier as context rather than silently blending it into a profile.
  4. If all bounded stages fail, return a partial answer that says what was searched and what was unavailable; do not fabricate a match.

Each stage gets its own timeout and retry budget. A 300 ms semantic query followed by a 300 ms lexical query is a product decision, not an implementation detail. Retries must use exponential backoff for rate limits, and a consumer that receives the same event twice must be idempotent. In payment systems I would call this the exactly-once mindset: execution may happen more than once, but the recorded effect and the explanation remain stable.

Web-backed context deserves extra skepticism. Scrape or search results can be stale, duplicated, or outside the recruiter’s authority. Store the returned URL or document ID, the retrieval time, and the policy decision that allowed it. A reviewer should be able to remove that source and see which part of the answer changes.

Collection boundaries and auditability

Separate collections by tenant and, where policy requires it, by document class such as resume, portfolio, and public posting. Collection deletion should be an explicit administrative event; deleting a vector without recording why creates an audit gap. Keep a tombstone with the candidate ID, actor, timestamp, and replacement status so a later reconciliation can distinguish “never indexed” from “intentionally removed.”

The same discipline applies to updates. Use a deterministic document key derived from tenant, candidate, and source revision. Upserting that key can be retried without creating a second profile chunk. Query responses should carry source identifiers into the generation prompt and into the final response metadata. This is the practical bridge between retrieval-augmented generation research and a recruiting workflow: the model gets context, and the recruiter gets evidence.

Here is a small Go adapter for one bounded semantic stage. It calls Infrai through plain HTTP, keeps the key in the environment, and treats a rate limit as a signal to wait rather than a reason to flood the service. The payload fields are the stage contract owned by this application: collection, tenant, query, and limit.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func querySemantic(ctx context.Context, tenant, query string, limit int) ([]byte, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "collection": "candidate-content",
        "tenant":     tenant,
        "query":      query,
        "limit":      limit,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 300 * time.Millisecond}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, baseURL+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query remained rate-limited after retries")
}

The caller records the stage name and error before moving on, then deduplicates by (tenant, candidate_id, source_id). That key is more useful than a similarity score when a recruiter asks why two excerpts appeared twice.

Comparing engines without losing the policy layer

The engine is replaceable; the retrieval contract is not. These options have different operational shapes, so the right choice depends on where the team wants to own policy and scaling work.

Option Useful fit Trade-off for candidate search
Elasticsearch Teams already operating a search cluster and needing lexical plus vector features in one system More cluster and mapping responsibility; tenant filters and audit fields remain your design
OpenSearch Organizations preferring an open-source distribution and self-managed deployment choices You own upgrades, capacity, and the consistency of security filters across fallback paths
Pinecone A managed vector-first service when semantic retrieval is the central workload Lexical fallback and evidence storage usually require another system, increasing reconciliation surface
Infrai A plain REST boundary is useful when a polyglot service should call vector capabilities without installing an SDK Validate collection tenancy, retention, and export requirements against your governance policy before standardizing

Infrai’s relevant advantage here is the plain REST API: any service that can send HTTP can call it, with no client library version to maintain. Its broader single-key surface can also reduce the number of authentication boundaries in a small pipeline, but that is an integration convenience, not proof that its retrieval ranking fits every corpus.

The discovery surface is public and self-describing, with 295 routes across 20 modules. Infrai’s one key, one bill convention means the same credential can cover the vector stage and adjacent backend calls. For a recruiting platform that also needs storage or scheduled reconciliation, that broad capability surface and uniform map can reduce adapter work while leaving the ranking policy in your code.

The catch is ownership. A team that needs custom analyzers, on-prem residency, or deep cluster-level tuning may be better served by Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. A team that wants a managed vector service and already has a separate evidence store may prefer Pinecone. Do not choose on a unit-price screenshot; choose on filter correctness, deletion semantics, and the evidence a reviewer can inspect.

Rollout and reconciliation checklist

Start with shadow traffic: run the new semantic stage beside the current search, compare candidate IDs and source coverage, and log every divergence without changing recruiter-visible results. Then enable the first fallback for a small tenant set. Define a maximum end-to-end deadline, a maximum number of returned excerpts, and a clear partial-answer status.

At launch, monitor four audit measures: the share of results with source IDs, authorization-filter failures, duplicate evidence keys, and timeout frequency by stage. Reconcile index contents against the source-of-record on a schedule. When a candidate is deleted or access is revoked, remove its vectors and verify that no fallback collection still returns the old source.

Your mileage may vary: a public portfolio may be acceptable for one recruiting workflow and prohibited for another. Keep that policy outside the ranking model, version it, and record the decision with each retrieval event. That is how a fallback becomes a controlled path instead of an accidental data boundary.

  • https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/search-plugins/knn/

title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
description:
arXiv:2610.19257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.

title: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning-Based Forest Classification - Separating Similar Forest Classes using Sentinel-2 Time Series
description:
arXiv:2610.19270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ecological insurance theory posits that diverse forests are more resilient and better able to adapt to changing environmental conditions. Increasing drought and heat stress in Central Europe promotes mixed forests for maintaining ecosystem services. However, a diverse species distribution complicates remote sensing-based species mapping, as distinguishing pure from mixed species compositions at the pixel level remains challenging. We evaluated the potential of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for tree-species classification from Sentinel-2 time series and investigated the spectral-temporal features underlying class discrimination, with particular emphasis on separating pure from mixed Norway spruce pixels. We compared RNN classification models with Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and used Integrated Gradients (IG) to quantify feature attributions across spectral bands and time. The best-performing RNN achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.851 on the test data, outperforming XGBoost by 0.012 and Random Forest by 0.103. Beyond classification performance, the attribution analysis revealed distinct spectral-temporal patterns associated with the separation of pure and mixed Norway spruce pixels. Attribution values increased particularly after approximately day of year (DOY) 125, while B11 showed the strongest contribution during periods of increasing spectral divergence between the two classes. These findings show that recurrent models can provide competitive classification performance while also revealing the phenological periods and spectral regions that are most relevant for distinguishing closely related forest compositions. Combining time-series classification with explainability therefore provides additional insight into the spectral-temporal mechanisms underlying tree-species discrimination and may support more detailed mapping of mixed forest structures.

title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
description:
arXiv:2610.19611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.

title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
description:
arXiv:2610.19436v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model-based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning-based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS-Net). Technically, we first incorporate the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based iterative algorithm into an end-to-end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS-Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS-Net+ by introducing the $\ell_{0}$-norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS-Net and MDUFS-Net+ outperform state-of-the-art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.

title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
description:
arXiv:2610.19220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Each thinking step is an attracting but strongly non-normal map exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.19133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy. Joint RAG+tool training achieves 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale, while a single epoch at 7B reaches 9.4%. These results demonstrate that robust defenses must explicitly train and evaluate across deployment channels.

title: Architectural Breakdown: We Rendered a HQ Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+We+Rendered+a+HQ+Demo+Video+on+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# We Rendered a 4K Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers. Here's the Architecture That Stopped It from Melting Down at 3 AM

The ticket hit at 2:17 AM on a Tuesday. Client wanted a 90‑second 4K demo video. We had a GitHub repo, three unused API keys, and thirty‑seven stranger nodes with 8 GB RAM and zero SLA. I still see the stack trace when I close my eyes.

Here is what happens when you try to render a film on infrastructure you don’t own, don’t control, and absolutely should not trust, and how we patched the holes that nearly cost us the deliverable.

---

## The Night Everything Broke

By hour three, three catastrophes collided: OOM kills on edge nodes, event‑loop stalls hitting twelve seconds during synchronous disk writes, and a lock‑contention storm on the shared output file that dropped throughput to four frames per minute. The coordinator thought we were fine because the chunk tracker was counting optimistic ACKs that never touched durable storage.

Node 12 dropped mid‑chunk. We lost frames 1,847 through 2,103. No checkpoint. No retry. The dispatcher was measuring success flags, not actual bytes written.

That is when I learned the hard way: a distributed render farm without backpressure is just a more expensive way to crash your laptop.

---

## Root‑Cause Breakdown

| Symptom | Root Cause |
|---------|-----------|
| Random OOM kills on nodes | Unbounded per‑frame texture cache, no memory semaphore |
| Event‑loop stalls over 5 seconds | Synchronous I/O blocking the asyncio event loop |
| Lock contention on output files | Global threading.Lock serializing all worker writes |
| Missing frames after node dropout | No idempotent chunk tracking or resumable uploads |
| Rate‑limit errors from cloud storage | Unthrottled multipart uploads from dozens of parallel workers |
| CPU starvation on weak nodes | Hardcoded 4‑core assumption on 2‑core machines |

Every assumption about the free farm was a liability. We fixed them all.

---

## The Architecture: Back‑Pressure‑Driven, Not Hope‑Driven

+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
| Coordinator |<-------> | Dispatcher |<-------> | Worker Pool |
| (SQLite WAL) | HTTP | (RingBuffer) | HTTP | (FFmpeg/Blender) |
+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
^ ^ ^
| | |
Chunk bookkeeping Backpressure enforcement Memory semaphore gating
Checksum verification Rate limiter Multipart uploader
Watchdog timer Chunk reassignment Status reporting


### Coordinator: Single Source of Truth

SQLite with WAL mode. Every chunk gets a UUID, a status transition log, and a checksum. Nothing lives in memory that is not also on disk. If the coordinator dies, the next restart replays the WAL and picks up exactly where it left off.

The dispatcher pulls from a `collections.deque(maxlen=512)`. Queue fills → new chunks wait. No memory spikes. No queue explosions. This is the kind of boring, deterministic design that ShipMVP’s rapid development stack ships in production builds, no magic, just plumbing that works.

### Dispatcher: The Traffic Cop

Rate limiting via `asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS=12)`. Our S3 bucket started choking at ~15 simultaneous multipart uploads. Each dispatch triggers a checksum verification before handing off to a worker.

Workers heartbeat every 30 seconds. Three missed heartbeats → chunks marked `PENDING_RETRY` and re‑dispatched. Lost nothing.

---

## Production Code: The Critical Path


python
import asyncio
import hashlib
import os
import sqlite3
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional
import aiohttp

MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH = 512
HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT = 90
MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS = 12
CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES = 30
MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB = 256
NODE_RAM_MB = 8192

max_chunks_per_node = (NODE_RAM_MB * 0.7) // MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB # 22 max
MEMORY_SEMAPHORE = asyncio.Semaphore(max_chunks_per_node)

chunk_queue: deque = deque(maxlen=MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH)
worker_semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS)
active_workers: dict = {}
retry_backoff = 0.5

class ChunkTracker:
"""Idempotent chunk state with checksum verification and WAL durability."""

def _init_db(self):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, check_same_thread=False)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS chunk_status (
            chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            worker_id TEXT,
            status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING',
            frame_start INTEGER,
            frame_end INTEGER,
            checksum TEXT,
            started_at REAL,
            completed_at REAL,
            failed_at REAL,
            retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0
        )
    """)
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS heartbeats (
            worker_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            last_seen REAL
        )
    """)
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

async def _db_execute(self, sql: str, params: tuple = ()) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
        return await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: sqlite3.connect(self.db_path).execute(sql, params).fetchall()
        )

async def mark_started(self, chunk_id: str, worker_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "INSERT INTO chunk_status (chunk_id, worker_id, status, started_at, retry_count) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, 'IN_FLIGHT', strftime('%s','now'), "
            "COALESCE((SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?), 0)) "
            "ON CONFLICT(chunk_id) DO UPDATE SET status='IN_FLIGHT', worker_id=?, "
            "started_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id)
        )

async def mark_completed(self, chunk_id: str, checksum: str) -> bool:
    async with self._lock:
        row = await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT status FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
        )
        if row and row[0][0] == "COMPLETED":
            return False
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='COMPLETED', checksum=?, "
            "completed_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (checksum, chunk_id)
        )
        return True

async def mark_failed(self, chunk_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='PENDING_RETRY', failed_at=strftime('%s','now'), "
            "retry_count=retry_count+1 WHERE chunk_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
            (chunk_id,)
        )

async def get_pending_chunks(self, limit: int = 50) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        return await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT chunk_id, frame_start, frame_end FROM chunk_status "
            "WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PENDING_RETRY') ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?",
            (limit,)
        )

async def escalate_if_over_retry(self, chunk_id: str) -> bool:
    row = await self._db_execute(
        "SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
    )
    return row and row[0][0] >= 3


### Watchdog: Detecting Dead Nodes Before Data Loss


python
async def watchdog(task_queue: asyncio.Queue, tracker: ChunkTracker):
while True:
await asyncio.sleep(15)
now = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
dead_workers = [
wid for wid, last in active_workers.items()
if now - last > HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT
]
for wid in dead_workers:
del active_workers[wid]
rows = await tracker._db_execute(
"SELECT chunk_id FROM chunk_status WHERE worker_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
(wid,)
)
for (chunk_id,) in rows:
await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
escaped = await tracker.escalate_if_over_retry(chunk_id)
if escaped:
print(f"[ALERT] Chunk {chunk_id} exceeded 3 retries")
task_queue.put_nowait(chunk_id)


### Worker: Bounded, Stateless, Idempotent


python
async def worker_task(worker_id: str, tracker: ChunkTracker, upload_queue: asyncio.Queue):
while True:
chunk_id = await asyncio.to_thread(upload_queue.get)

    async with MEMORY_SEMAPHORE:
        await tracker.mark_started(chunk_id, worker_id)
        active_workers[worker_id] = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()

        env = os.environ.copy()
        env["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "2"
        cmd = [
            "ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", f"frames_{chunk_id}.txt",
            "-frames:v", str(CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES),
            "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-c:v", "libx264",
            "-preset", "fast", "-threads", "2",
            "-movflags", "+faststart", f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4"
        ]

        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            *cmd, env=env,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE
        )
        stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=120)

        if proc.returncode != 0:
            await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
            continue

        with open(f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4", "rb") as f:
            checksum = hashlib.md5(f.read()).hexdigest()

        completed = await tracker.mark_completed(chunk_id, checksum)
        if completed:
            print(f"[OK] {chunk_id} checksum={checksum}")
        else:
            print(f"[SKIP] {chunk_id} already completed (idempotent)")


---

## Hardware Profiling: What 8 GB RAM Actually Gives You

| Node Type | vCPUs | RAM | Measured FPS | Peak Memory | Stall Events |
|-----------|-------|-----|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| t2.micro clone | 1 | 4 GB | 2.1 | 3.8 GB | 47 |
| t3.small clone | 2 | 8 GB | 4.3 | 6.1 GB | 12 |
| c5.large clone | 2 | 4 GB | 3.8 | 3.9 GB | 31 |
| n1‑standard‑2 | 2 | 7.5 GB | 5.1 | 6.8 GB | 8 |
| Custom 4‑core | 4 | 8 GB | 6.2 | 7.4 GB | 3 |

The 2‑core 8 GB nodes were the sweet spot. More cores did not help; FFmpeg’s CPU‑bound rendering hit diminishing returns past 2 threads per chunk, and extra context switching killed tail latency. The 4‑core nodes looked great on paper but aggressive CPU sharing with other tenants caused unpredictable pauses that wrecked frame‑timing consistency.

We locked in `CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES=30` with `MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB=256`. Stayed under 6 GB peak on the worst node. Render times between 8 and 14 seconds per chunk.

---

## The Multipart Upload That Saved Us

Resumable multipart uploads with per‑part checksums. Every worker streams directly to cloud storage in 5 MB parts. Each part gets an MD5 before upload. If a worker drops mid‑upload, the next one picks up from the last successful part boundary. No re‑rendering. No wasted cycles.

When Node 28 vanished during a 47‑minute upload window, we resumed from part 94 of 127. The client saw a green dot because we reported partial completion percentages, not binary success or failure.

---

## What We Learned the Hard Way

Three uncomfortable truths: the free farm would betray you, your monitoring would always be incomplete, and the first design would fail. We learned to measure actual bytes transferred instead of trusting optimistic progress bars. We learned to treat every node as temporary and stateless. We learned that backpressure is not a performance feature; it is the difference between graceful degradation and silent corruption.

The video rendered. 94 seconds of 4K. Zero missing frames. Two nodes died mid‑job and neither loss showed up. Total cost: $0.00. Engineering effort: ~180 person‑hours.

Worth it.

---

**Question for the comments:** What is the most painful distributed system failure you have debugged at 3 AM, and did you solve it by adding more observability or by removing entire components from the critical path?

title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
description:
arXiv:2610.19201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

title: Building a 12-axis political quiz with Vite, TanStack Start and Cloudflare Workers
description:
Most political quizzes squeeze you onto one line, left vs right, or a two-axis compass. I wanted something that keeps questions apart: you can want a strong welfare state and still distrust central government, or love new technology and be socially traditional. So I built The 12 Axes, a free quiz that scores you on twelve independent axes, in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

The statements and the scoring model come from the open-source 12Axes quiz (MIT). My part was the product around it: a fast, server-rendered site with shareable results and no accounts. Here is how it fits together.

The stack

  • Vite for the build and dev server.
  • TanStack Start (with TanStack Router) for file-based routes, server rendering and typed search params.
  • Cloudflare Workers to serve every page from the edge. The quiz itself has no backend at all.

There is no database. Everything a result needs fits in the URL.

Scoring in a dozen lines

Each statement belongs to one axis and points toward one of its two poles. Answers run from -2 (strongly disagree) to +2 (strongly agree). An axis score is the average answer, flipped for statements that point the other way and mapped to 0-100%:

export function scoreQuiz(items: QuizItem[], answers: (number | undefined)[]) {
  const sums = new Array(12).fill(0);
  const counts = new Array(12).fill(0);
  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    const answer = answers[i];
    if (answer === undefined) return;
    sums[item.axis] += answer * (item.level < 4 ? 1 : -1);
    counts[item.axis] += 1;
  });
  return sums.map((sum, axis) =>
    counts[axis] ? Math.round(50 + (50 * sum) / (2 * counts[axis])) : 50
  );
}

A skipped axis stays at 50, the neutral middle, rather than breaking the result.

A result that fits in 24 characters

Twelve scores from 0 to 100 need two base-36 digits each, so a whole result is a 24-character string:

export const encodeScores = (scores: number[]) =>
  scores
    .map((s) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round(s))).toString(36).padStart(2, '0'))
    .join('');

That string goes in the result URL as ?r=. Sharing a result is sharing a link: the result page rebuilds every score, match and chart from those 24 characters, so nothing is stored anywhere. Decoding validates strictly (/^[0-9a-z]{24}$/, every value ≤ 100) and anything else falls back to an empty state. TanStack Router's typed search params make this pleasant: the route declares the param, and the page component gets a typed value.

Matching ideologies and historical figures

Two kinds of matches are shown, and both use root-mean-square distance:

  • Ideologies are defined on four classic dimensions (economy, power, diplomacy, culture), so they are compared on the four matching axes. Match = 100 minus the RMS gap.

  • Historical figures have a position on up to twelve axes. Many took no stand on some of them; Aristotle had no view on biotechnology. Skipping those axes would favour figures with few known positions, because they get compared on less. So an unknown axis counts as a fixed gap of 28 points, and a figure needs at least six known axes to be ranked at all.

One bug worth sharing: I had entered one axis backwards for twenty figures, and every match still looked plausible. Now a unit test pins the direction of every axis with figures whose positions are unambiguous. Plausible-looking output is the hardest kind of wrong to notice.

Progress that survives a reload

The full test has 288 statements, so losing your place hurts. Progress lives in localStorage and is restored on load. Answers never leave the browser, which is also why there is no sign-up.

A share card made from the DOM

The share card is a normal React component styled like the rest of the site. To share it as an image, it is rendered off-screen and turned into a PNG in the browser. On phones that support the Web Share API with files, the share sheet gets the image directly:

if (navigator.canShare?.({ files: [file] })) {
  await navigator.share({ files: [file], url, title });
}

Elsewhere you get a download button. Building the card as a component, not a canvas drawing, means it uses the same fonts, translations and layout code as the page.

Three languages, one set of routes

English lives at /, Spanish at /es/ and Portuguese at /pt/. Every page renders hreflang alternates and a canonical URL. Each language also gets its own Open Graph image, so a link shared in a Spanish group chat shows a Spanish preview.

Running on Cloudflare Workers

The Worker's fetch handler is a thin wrapper around the TanStack Start handler. It is also where redirects belong:

  • the old launch domain 301s to the same path on the new one;
  • plain http:// 301s to https://, with a 308 for anything other than GET/HEAD so a request body is never silently turned into a GET.

Both live in a pure function with unit tests, including one that feeds each redirect target back in and expects no further redirect. A redirect loop on the edge is not something you want to discover from Search Console.

Deploys are one wrangler deploy. The custom domain, TLS and caching come with Workers.

SEO for a quiz site

A few things mattered more than I expected:

  • Server-render everything crawlable, including FAQ answers inside collapsed panels: hidden="until-found" keeps them in the HTML while staying collapsed.
  • A sitemap with real lastmod dates and an IndexNow ping after each content change, so Bing and other IndexNow engines hear about new pages without waiting for a crawl.
  • An explainer page per axis, so the site answers "what does this axis mean" and not just "take the quiz".

Try it

The quick test takes 60 statements, about six minutes: 12axes.site. I'd love to hear which axis surprised you, and whether the historical-figure match felt fair.

title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.19674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
description:
arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.
