title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.

title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
description:
arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

title: Explore Microsoft Azure: How to Get Started with Azure
description:
1. Introduction

  • Brief Overview of Microsoft Azure:

    • Microsoft Azure is a comprehensive cloud computing platform offered by Microsoft, providing a range of services including computing power, storage solutions, and networking capabilities. Azure is significant in the cloud computing industry because it allows businesses to build, deploy, and manage applications and services through Microsoft-managed data centers globally. With its extensive infrastructure and integration capabilities, Azure supports a wide variety of programming languages, tools, and frameworks, making it a versatile choice for developers and enterprises alike.
    • Azure is one of the most popular cloud platforms in the world, competing with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud. It is known for its extensive range of services, from basic virtual machines to complex artificial intelligence tools, and its ability to cater to businesses of all sizes, from startups to large enterprises.

  • Why Get Started with Azure?

    • Azure offers scalability, allowing businesses to adjust their resources according to their needs without upfront investments in physical hardware. This flexibility means you can scale up during high-demand periods and scale down when demand decreases, all within a cost-effective framework.
    • Azure’s pay-as-you-go pricing model, extensive support for open-source technologies, and seamless integration with Microsoft products like Office 365 and Dynamics 365 make it an attractive option for various industries, including healthcare, finance, and retail.
    • Professionals such as developers, system administrators, and data scientists can benefit from Azure by leveraging its tools to build, test, and deploy applications more efficiently.

2. Setting Up Your Azure Account

  • Creating a Microsoft Account:

    • If you don't already have a Microsoft account, visit account.microsoft.com and click "Create a Microsoft account." You can sign up using an existing email address or create a new one. Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the account creation process.

  • Signing Up for Azure:

    • Once you have a Microsoft account, go to azure.microsoft.com. Click on "Start for free" to begin the sign-up process. During sign-up, you'll need to provide some basic information and a payment method, even if you're using the free trial. Azure typically offers a 30-day free trial with $200 in credits, which you can use to explore various services.
    • After signing up, you'll be directed to the Azure Portal, where you can start managing your cloud resources.

  • Understanding the Azure Portal:

    • The Azure Portal is the central hub for managing all your Azure services. Upon logging in, you'll see a customizable dashboard where you can pin resources for quick access. The "All Services" section gives you access to all available Azure services, while "Cost Management" allows you to monitor your spending and set budgets to avoid unexpected costs.

3. Navigating the Azure Portal

  • Overview of the User Interface:

    • The Azure Portal interface is designed to be intuitive. The left-hand menu provides access to services, subscriptions, resource groups, and more. The top bar features a search function, notifications, and settings. Notifications will keep you updated on the status of your resources and any potential issues.

  • Creating Your First Resource:

    • For your first resource, let's create a Virtual Machine (VM). In the Azure Portal, click on "Create a resource" and select "Virtual Machine" from the options. Follow the guided steps to configure your VM, such as selecting an operating system, instance size, and region. Once configured, click "Review + Create" to finalize your VM setup.

4. Exploring Core Azure Services

  • Introduction to Key Services:

    • Compute: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) allow you to run applications in the cloud with your preferred operating system. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) helps you manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.
    • Storage: Azure Blob Storage is ideal for storing unstructured data, while File Storage and Disk Storage offer file-level and block-level storage solutions, respectively.
    • Networking: Azure Virtual Networks enable you to create isolated networks for your Azure resources, while Load Balancers and Azure DNS ensure high availability and optimized performance.
    • Database: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational database service, while Cosmos DB offers multi-model database capabilities for global distribution.

  • Use Cases and Examples:

    • Provide practical examples, such as hosting a website using Azure VMs, storing backups using Blob Storage, or setting up a scalable microservices architecture with AKS.

5. Managing and Monitoring Your Resources

  • Resource Management:

    • Group related resources using Resource Groups to manage them collectively. For instance, if you have a VM, storage account, and network all related to a single application, you can organize them under one Resource Group.
    • Use tagging to categorize resources by department, project, or environment, which helps with organization and cost management.

  • Monitoring and Alerts:

    • Azure Monitor offers insights into the performance and health of your resources. Set up alerts to notify you of potential issues, such as high CPU usage or low available memory, allowing you to respond proactively.

6. Learning and Certification

  • Azure Learning Resources:

    • Microsoft offers a wealth of learning resources, including free online courses through Microsoft Learn, extensive documentation, and hands-on labs. Consider exploring tutorials and joining Azure communities to stay updated on the latest features.
    • Engage with Azure blogs, podcasts, and forums to gain insights from other professionals and Azure experts.

  • Certification Pathways:

    • Starting with Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) is recommended for beginners. From there, you can pursue role-based certifications, such as Azure Administrator (AZ-104) or Azure Solutions Architect (AZ-305), to validate your skills and advance your career.

7. Conclusion

  • Recap of Getting Started:

    • In this guide, we walked through the essentials of getting started with Microsoft Azure, beginning with setting up an account and navigating the Azure Portal. We also explored creating your first resource, understanding core Azure services, and managing and monitoring your resources effectively. These initial steps are designed to provide a solid foundation for leveraging Azure's powerful cloud computing capabilities.

  • Call to Action:

    • Now that you have an overview of how to get started with Azure, it's time to take the first step. Create your Azure account today and start exploring the platform’s vast array of services. Whether you're deploying your first virtual machine or experimenting with Azure's AI tools, the possibilities are endless. Don't hesitate to dive in and discover how Azure can enhance your projects and business operations.
    • We encourage you to share your experiences or ask questions in the comments section below. Your insights and inquiries can help foster a supportive community where we can all learn and grow together in our Azure journeys.

title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
description:
arXiv:2610.14180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.

title: Turn a YouTube playlist into RAG-ready chunks with timestamp links
description:
If you build a RAG app, chatbot or search over video content, the first problem is getting clean text with timestamps so answers can link back to the exact moment. Here is a small recipe using the YouTube Transcript Extractor Actor on Apify. It costs $0.004 per transcript, and videos without captions are not charged.

Actor: https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch

What comes back

For each video you get the title, channel, duration, view count, language, whether the captions are auto-generated, the full text, and optionally timestamped segments. With chunkWords set, you also get chunks: pieces of roughly that many words, each with a start time. That is the part you want for embedding.

Fetch a playlist and write chunks with deep links 

import json
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=YOUR_PLAYLIST_ID"],
    "maxVideosPerUrl": 20,
    "chunkWords": 200,
    "includeAutoGenerated": True,
})

with open("chunks.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for v in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
        if v.get("status") != "OK":
            continue
        for c in v["chunks"]:
            f.write(json.dumps({
                "text": c["text"],
                "title": v["title"],
                "link": f'{v["url"]}&t={int(c["start"])}s',
            }) + "\n")

Each line of chunks.jsonl is ready to embed, and the link field opens the video at the start of that chunk, so your app can cite the exact spot.

Things worth knowing

  • status tells you why a video has no transcript (private video, captions disabled), so you can skip or retry those without the whole run failing.
  • languages lets you set preferred caption languages, and availableLanguages shows what else exists.
  • YouTube blocks datacenter IPs, so the Actor uses a residential proxy by default. My cost in tests was about $0.0009 per video, which is why it can be priced this low.
  • In my test batch, 11 of 12 videos returned a transcript. The one that did not was reported with a clear status.

If a video you care about fails, open an issue on the Actor page with the URL.

Xargaar Tools builds small, pay-per-use data tools.

title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
description:
arXiv:2610.19238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.

title: Why Your Connection Pool is Lying to You
description:
We hit a wall last month. Traffic was stable, CPU was idle, but p99 latency spiked to 2s. The PostgreSQL server looked healthy. The culprit wasn't the database; it was our Node.js connection pool configuration.

The Illusion of Saturation

Most teams set pool.max based on a static assumption: "We have 20 connections, so we can handle 20 concurrent requests." This fails because connections aren't just resources; they are locks. When you hold a connection for 50ms, you block 19 others. When you hold it for 500ms due to a slow downstream call or a complex join, you starve the queue.

The standard pg pool in Node behaves like a fixed-size barrier. If all max connections are in use, new queries wait in a FIFO queue. There is no fallback. There is no read replica offload. Just waiting.

The Bottleneck

Our logs showed queryQueueLength climbing steadily. We weren't seeing duplicate queries, but we were seeing long-held connections. Specifically, we had a service that called an external API inside a transaction. The transaction had idleInTransactionSessionTimeout set to 60s. The API was timing out at 5s, but the connection stayed open until the timeout or manual commit.

// The mistake: holding a connection during external I/O
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status'); // Blocks for 1-5s
  await client.query('UPDATE users SET last_synced = NOW() WHERE id = $1', [userId]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} finally {
  client.release(); // Too late, the queue was already backed up
}

The fix wasn't scaling out the postgres instance. It was architectural separation.

The Tradeoff

We split the lifecycle. We run the external API call outside the database transaction. Yes, this introduces a consistency window. If the API fails after we commit the intent, we have stale data. But in our case, eventual consistency was acceptable for sync status.

// Better: Short-lived transaction, external I/O separated
const updateResult = await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  ['pending', userId]
);

let finalStatus = 'failed';
try {
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status');
  finalStatus = response.ok ? 'success' : 'error';
} catch (e) {
  finalStatus = 'timeout';
}

await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  [finalStatus, userId]
);

The p99 dropped to 80ms. The queue depth flattened.

Edge Cases to Watch

  1. Nested Transactions: If your ORM supports savepoints, be careful. SAVEPOINT doesn't release the underlying connection, but it adds overhead. Avoid them in tight loops.
  2. Statement Caching: In Postgres 13+, prepared statements are cached per connection. If you have high-churn connection recycling, you might miss the cache benefits. node-postgres handles this, but custom drivers might not.
  3. Monitoring: Don't just watch active_connections. Watch backend_xact_start age. Long-running transactions are the real killers.

Connection pooling is not a silver bullet; it's a buffer against mismanagement. If your code holds DB connections while talking to other services, you're not pooling, you're hoarding.

How do you handle external I/O dependencies that logically require a DB transaction context? Do you use saga patterns, or do you rely on idempotency and eventual consistency?

title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19408v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Silent Installation Automation: A Practical Guide
description:
Installing GBase Database(GBase 8s) manually on multiple Linux servers is time-consuming and increases the risk of configuration inconsistencies. Automating silent installation and deployment verification helps database administrators streamline repetitive tasks and manage larger server environments more efficiently.

In this guide, we'll explore how to organize a batch deployment workflow for GBase Database(GBase 8s) using Bash, SSH, and installation response files.

1. Deployment Architecture

A simple deployment project can use the following structure:

gbase-deploy/
├── deploy_gbase.sh
├── bundle.properties
├── server_list.txt
├── verify_gbase.sh
└── logs/

Each file serves a specific purpose:

  • deploy_gbase.sh: Coordinates remote deployment tasks.
  • bundle.properties: Stores silent installation options supported by the installer.
  • server_list.txt: Defines the target servers.
  • verify_gbase.sh: Checks deployment status.
  • logs/: Stores execution logs for troubleshooting.

2. Prepare the Target Servers

Maintain a server inventory containing the connection details for each target machine.

# IP address SSH user SSH port
192.168.1.101 root 22
192.168.1.102 root 22
192.168.1.103 root 22

Before deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s), verify operating system compatibility, available disk space, network connectivity, and required system dependencies.

For unattended deployment, SSH key-based authentication is preferable to storing passwords in scripts.

3. Automate the Installation Workflow

The master script should coordinate the deployment process rather than hard-code every installation detail.

A typical workflow includes:

  1. Read and validate the target server list.
  2. Transfer the GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation package and configuration files.
  3. Execute the supported silent installation procedure remotely.
  4. Configure the database environment and initialize instances as required.
  5. Record execution results and identify failed deployments.

The exact response-file parameters, installation commands, and instance initialization procedures depend on the installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) release. Always validate them against the documentation accompanying your installation package.

For multi-server deployment, control parallel execution and maintain separate logs for each target. This makes failures easier to identify without interrupting unrelated deployment tasks.

4. Verify Deployment Results

Successful software installation does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for production.

Your verification workflow should check:

  • Whether the installation completed successfully.
  • Whether the database instance starts and reaches the expected state.
  • Whether the required network listener is available.
  • Whether database connections and basic queries work.
  • Whether locale settings and application connectivity meet requirements.

Tools such as onstat and dbaccess can help validate GBase Database(GBase 8s), provided they are used with the correct environment and permissions.

5. Production Best Practices

When extending GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment automation to more servers, keep these principles in mind:

  • Test first: Validate the workflow on a single server before scaling out.
  • Protect credentials: Use secure authentication and least-privilege access.
  • Keep deployments repeatable: Avoid duplicate configuration changes and unintended instance reinitialization.
  • Maintain logs: Record deployment status and errors for troubleshooting.
  • Plan recovery: Back up important data and prepare a rollback procedure before production changes.

Conclusion

Automating GBase Database(GBase 8s) silent installation can reduce repetitive administration work and improve deployment consistency across Linux servers.

A reliable automation workflow combines installation, environment configuration, instance initialization, and verification into clearly separated stages. By validating version-specific commands and monitoring every deployment, database teams can build a more maintainable process and prepare for future integration with CI/CD pipelines.

The key takeaway: Automate repetitive tasks, but keep version-specific installation logic and production validation explicit. That's the foundation of reliable GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment at scale.

title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
description:
Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha Chandrashekar

How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.

Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.

Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.

This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.

Why GPU reliability matters

Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners.

All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — -

  • Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on.
  • Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work.

Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too.

Why basic health checks are not enough

We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training.

The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time.

  • A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows.
  • A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss.
  • A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working.

Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break.

Our approach

We treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot:

1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine.

2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely.

3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine.

4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three.

The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working.

How the health checks work

Checks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector, runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work.

GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail.

  • Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool.
  • A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed.
  • Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines.
  • No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check.

Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automatically

When a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it.

Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users.

Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance.

One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window.

Validating a machine before it takes work

A machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service.

Letting long jobs survive machine loss

Even with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures.

Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL, the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause.

Measuring whether it works

We track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:

  • Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.
  • Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.
  • Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.

Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.

A closed remediation loop

These pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.

Sharing GPUs safely

Not every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.

Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.

Results

Moving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.

Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:

  • Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodes
  • Job success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%

What is next

We are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.

We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.

More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.

While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.

Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.

Closing

Hardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.

Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Five checks before turning an invoice CSV into a follow-up list
description:
An overdue-invoice view looks simple: read a CSV, compare due dates and sort. The awkward bugs live in the details. A worklist can send someone chasing the wrong amount even when its table looks correct.

We used these checks while building Cashflow Check at Xargaar Tools. The examples below are fictional.

1. Work in the smallest currency unit

For the current tool, amounts are plain positive decimals with no more than two decimal places. Convert them to integer cents before arithmetic. An invoice for 1,200.00 with 300.00 paid has 900.00 remaining, not 1,200.00 overdue.

Reject malformed amounts instead of quietly converting them to zero. Check that paid does not exceed the invoice total. Supporting every currency's decimal convention is a separate problem; this tool deliberately limits its input format.

2. Keep currencies separate

USD 900 and EUR 700 are two balances. They are not a meaningful total of 1,600 unless you explicitly choose exchange rates and a valuation date. Our review groups balances by the currency code supplied in the CSV. It does not convert currencies.

3. Validate calendar dates, not just date-shaped strings

A pattern matching YYYY-MM-DD is only the first check. Parse the date and round-trip it back to the same format to catch impossible dates. Use a chosen review date so that a saved worklist states when it was prepared.

An invoice due on the review date is due today, not already a day late. Keep that boundary explicit.

4. Reject duplicate invoice/customer pairs

A duplicate import row can double the amount a dashboard tells someone to chase. Make the key explicit and reject repeats with the input row number. Our current key is the invoice identifier plus customer name; if your source allows reused identifiers, define the right key for that source rather than copying this choice blindly.

5. Treat export as another input boundary

CSV quoting and spreadsheet formula handling solve different problems. Quote fields and double embedded quotes. Separately consider text beginning with formula-like characters such as =, +, - or @ before someone opens the export in a spreadsheet. Test the target spreadsheet's behavior rather than treating a single escape rule as a universal security guarantee.

The same caution applies to the worklist itself: imported payment data can be stale. Check payment records before contacting a customer. A local CSV tool cannot know that money arrived after the export.

Try the workflow

Cashflow Check's free sample runs in the browser without an account or invoice upload. It accepts up to 5,000 rows and a 5 MB CSV, shows remaining balances by customer and currency, and exports a follow-up worklist. It does not connect to a bank or send reminders.

Disclosure: this is our product. The optional one-time $19 review pack adds the offline download, editable review log and weekly workflow. The free tool stays available. It is one part of the Xargaar Tools collection.

title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
description:
arXiv:2610.14570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.

title: How to Choose the Right Trading Indicator: A Beginner’s Guide to Smarter Trades
description:
Every trader, whether new or experienced, eventually asks the same question: “Which indicator should I use?” With hundreds of options available, picking the wrong one can lead to confusion, late entries and avoidable losses. This guide explains what trading indicators do, which types matter most, and how to pick ones that fit your strategy.

What Is a Trading Indicator?

A trading indicator is a mathematical tool applied to price and volume data. It shows up as lines, bars or signals on your chart and helps you:

Identify the direction of a trend
Spot possible entry and exit points
Measure momentum and volatility
Confirm whether a move is strong or weak

Indicators don’t predict the future. They help you read what the market is doing right now, so your decisions are based on data rather than emotion.

The Main Types of Trading Indicators

  1. Trend Indicators
    These show the market’s overall direction. Moving Averages (SMA, EMA) and MACD are the most popular. They work best in markets that are clearly moving up or down.

  2. Momentum Indicators
    RSI and Stochastic measure the speed of price movement. They help you spot overbought or oversold conditions and possible reversals.

  3. Volatility Indicators
    Bollinger Bands and ATR show how much the price is moving. They are useful for setting stop-loss levels and sizing positions.

  4. Volume Indicators
    OBV and Volume Profile show how many traders are behind a move. A breakout on high volume is generally more reliable than one on low volume.

5 Tips for Choosing the Right Indicator
Match it to your trading style. Scalpers, day traders and swing traders need different settings and timeframes.
Don’t overload your chart. Two to four indicators that complement each other are plenty.
Combine different types. Pair one trend indicator with one momentum indicator for better confirmation.
Backtest before using real money. Test any indicator on historical data first.
Use proper risk management. No indicator is 100% accurate, so always use a stop-loss.
Ready-Made Indicators vs. Free Indicators

Free indicators are fine for learning, but many traders prefer professionally built, tested and optimized indicators. These usually offer cleaner signals, custom alerts, better visuals and less lag, which saves time and helps you trade with more confidence.

If you’re looking for reliable trading indicators built for serious traders, you can explore the collection at [Bolts – Trading Indicators](https://bolts.xo.je/

Final Thoughts

The best indicator is not the one with the most features. It is the one you understand, have tested, and can use consistently. Start simple, test carefully, manage your risk, and build your strategy step by step.

title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14136v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

description:
arXiv:2610.19497v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing. Our approach identifies rhetorical relations between sentence pairs and extracts key phrases, which are then replaced with semantically coherent but topically shifted content while preserving the original discourse structure. Experimental results on text summarization and question answering show that the proposed augmented data provides complementary supervision and improves combined-data training across the evaluated tasks. Comparisons with a standard RST parser and controlled ablations further support the proposed discourse representation.

title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
description:
arXiv:2610.19294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
description:
arXiv:2610.14727v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

title: Same config.json, different serve command: what to check before serving AREX-2
description:
When a fine-tune declares the same architecture class as a model you already serve (run behind an API on your own GPU), the tempting move is to swap --model-path and restart. BAAI's AREX-2 is a good test of that habit. It is a 27B model trained to work on a problem in rounds (propose, measure, reflect, revise), released on 29 September under Apache 2.0, not gated, and its config.json opens with Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, the same class as Qwen3.8-27B from the Qwen team.

We had been serving base Qwen3.8-27B with sglang, an open-source inference server, so we diffed the two configs. One caveat first: we have not run AREX-2. Every speed below is from the base model. Tables, command and sources are in the full AREX-2 serving analysis on inferencekey.com.

The diff that says "drop-in"

BAAI shipped a clean release: layer layout, head counts, context length, vocab and vision tower all match Qwen3.8-27B. The config differs only in transformers_version and two redundant top-level keys, and chat_template.jinja, the file that formats the conversation and tool calls, is byte-identical.

Stop reading there and you ship the old command.

Check the weights, not the config

The base model carries a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, a small extra layer that guesses a few tokens ahead so the server can emit several per step. AREX-2's config still declares it. Its weight files do not contain it.

config.json                    "mtp_num_hidden_layers": 1
safetensors index (AREX-2)     0 mtp tensors
safetensors index (Qwen3.8)    15 mtp tensors

The safetensors index lists every weight tensor in the release, so it is the honest inventory. A config field is a promise; check that something actually backs it.

The second quiet change is in tokenizer_config.json, which controls how text is cut into tokens. A community repack reports that the pre-tokenizer and decoder settings differ from Qwen3.8. Likely harmless. Also what surfaces as a garbled tool call hours into an agent run.

Flags that were right for the base model

Our quickest base-model setup ran on an RTX PRO 5000 in a CUDA 13 pod, with RadixArk's NVFP4 quant (weights compressed to 4-bit floats) and the z-lab DFlash2 drafter. It decoded (wrote output) at 115 to 136 tok/s. Little of that survives the swap:

  • No NVFP4 build of AREX-2 exists yet. Today you pick from BAAI's BF16 original (54.7 GB), prithivMLmods' FP8 (35.9 GB), cyankiwi's AWQ INT4 (20.2 GB) or numsu's INT4 W4A16 (18.6 GB).
  • The drafter was trained against another model. Speculative decoding has a small drafter propose tokens that the big model then verifies in one pass; it only pays off when most guesses are accepted. z-lab's DFlash2 drafter targets base Qwen3.8-27B, and a fine-tune changes which tokens the model favors, so nobody knows its hit rate on AREX-2. numsu's INT4 card does publish speeds with a DFlash2 drafter on two RTX 3090s, but without an acceptance length.
  • mamba_ssm_dtype. AREX-2 asks for float32. Our base command forced bfloat16, fine on Qwen3.8, untried on a model tuned for long reflective runs.
  • Parsers are a guess. These sglang options turn raw model text into separate reasoning and tool-call fields. qwen3 and qwen3_coder ought to work since the template matches. No sglang run of AREX-2 has been published.
  • Pick long context or speculation. The base model's 1M context is a YARN override that stretches its native 262,144 positions, and DFlash2 would not run with it. So: 1M without a drafter, or 256K with one.

FP8 on Ampere is the expensive mistake

The RTX A6000 is Ampere and has no FP8 hardware, so sglang keeps the weights in FP8 and unpacks them on the fly through Marlin kernels. Base Qwen3.8-27B decoded there at 24 tok/s. RedHatAI's INT4 W4A16 quant, same card, same 1M context: 41 tok/s. prithivMLmods' AREX-2 FP8 card agrees that full speed needs Ada, Hopper or later. An A100 is Ampere too, so reach for INT4 there.

Weights are not the whole bill. In our base-model INT4 run at 1M context, sglang took about 46 GB, of which only 17.8 GB was weights. Another 11.5 GB held state for the linear attention layers, and 12.8 GB went to the KV cache, the per-token memory the model keeps so it does not reread the whole context on every step. The per-GPU sizing for AREX-2 goes card by card from 80 GB to 24 GB, as estimates.

What to measure on the first run

Start dull: BF16 on an 80 GB card, the native 256K context, no speculative flags, the same parsers, one long agent task. Then change a single thing per run, like a soundcheck that starts with the kick drum. Watch:

  • tool calls parsing cleanly late in a long session, given the tokenizer change
  • decode tok/s against the base model on the same card, which the shared architecture says should match
  • acceptance length if you add a drafter, the number nobody has published
  • GPU hours per task, since the benchmark protocol allows up to 1,500 model calls and 24 hours per case

That last item drives the economics. AREX-2's self-reported 70.7 on Frontier-CS and 84.0 on BrowseComp come from that long protocol in BAAI's evaluation repo, with no independent reproduction we could find. Renting a GPU by the hour beats per-token pricing only while the card has work queued, for instance several cases side by side. For the rest of a single-GPU agent setup, see our earlier post on an 80B coding model on one rented A100 driven by Claude Code.

This is a plausible one-card project thanks to BAAI and the Qwen team for the models, prithivMLmods, cyankiwi, numsu, RedHatAI and RadixArk for the quants, z-lab for DFlash2, numsu again for an experimental MTP head trained on AREX-2 outputs, AI Search for flagging the release, and the sglang and vLLM projects. The config tables, the base-model command verbatim, the worker settings for slow warmups and the full limits list are in the complete AREX-2 on one GPU write-up.
