title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.19323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

title: When POST becomes GET: a redirect bug in a Node.js fetch wrapper
description:
A POST followed a 302 redirect and became a GET. Its body disappeared, but its Content-Type header stayed behind.

That showed up while extending the client comparisons in ssrf-lab, a testing harness I maintain. The affected package was @tak-ps/node-safeurl@1.8.0, a Node.js fetch wrapper that checks URLs and redirect destinations.

This is a functional redirect-conformance bug. The proposed fix is upstream PR #4, submitted and awaiting review as of October 14, 2026. These tests do not demonstrate an SSRF bypass.

The response looked fine. The request told the story.

The comparison uses a small HTTP server on 127.0.0.1. One route returns a redirect; the destination echoes the method, body, and headers it actually receives. That exact local origin is explicitly allowed in the wrapper's configuration.

Both native fetch and the wrapper successfully completed this request:

{
  method: 'POST',
  body: 'hello',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }
}

After a 302 redirect, the destination observed:

Client Method Body Content-Type
Native fetch GET empty absent
node-safeurl 1.8.0 GET empty text/plain

The same difference appeared for 301 POST and 303 PUT. Checking only the final status or whether the fetch promise resolved would miss it.

The Fetch redirect algorithm changes POST to GET for 301/302, and changes methods other than GET/HEAD to GET for 303. When it discards the body, it also removes the request-body headers: Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Location, and Content-Type.

The wrapper already handled the method and body changes. It was missing the corresponding header cleanup.

The fix belongs in the method-rewrite branch

The patch adds Headers to the existing Undici import, then extends the existing switchToGet branch:

if (switchToGet) {
  fetchInit.method = 'GET';
  fetchInit.body = undefined;

  const headers = new Headers(fetchInit.headers);
  for (const name of [
    'content-encoding',
    'content-language',
    'content-location',
    'content-type',
    'content-length',
  ]) {
    headers.delete(name);
  }
  fetchInit.headers = headers;
}

Content-Length is removed as well, because caller-supplied framing for the discarded body should not carry into the GET. It is separate from the standard's four named request-body headers.

Copying through Headers supports object, tuple-array, and Headers inputs without changing the caller's original headers. Unrelated headers survive. The URL validation logic is unchanged.

The condition matters: a 307 or 308 should preserve the method and body, so stripping these headers on every redirect would introduce another bug.

Prove both the fix and the unchanged cases

The upstream regression test records actual incoming requests and checks seven cases:

Redirect cases Before patch After patch
301 POST, 302 POST, 303 PUT All three fail All three pass
307 POST, 308 POST, 301 PUT, 302 PUT All four pass All four pass

It also checks that an unrelated header is preserved and the caller's headers are not mutated. The full patched upstream suite passes 198 tests on each of Node 22.23.3 and 24.21.0, alongside lint and build.

The recorded evidence includes the original failures, fixed tests, full-suite logs, and published-package comparison.

Run the comparison

With Node 22.19 or newer and npm:

git clone https://github.com/roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.git
cd ssrf-lab
git checkout 41659cda6825b2f7e324294d7242ef1b076b6cce
npm ci --ignore-scripts --prefix integrations/community
node integrations/community/check-redirects.mjs

This prints JSON for native fetch and the unmodified published package across five redirect cases. The HTTP comparison stays on the explicitly allowed loopback origin. The broader SSRF suite has separate network-isolation requirements.

The practical testing lesson is to assert what reached the destination: method, body, and headers. A successful response alone cannot establish that a wrapper preserved fetch semantics.

The harness, adapters, and reproduction are in ssrf-lab. Which redirect or URL-handling edge case would you add to this coverage?

AI disclosure: Codex assisted with the investigation, implementation, and test execution, and drafted this article from the linked code and recorded results.

title: PCAD-31-02 in Code: Validation Checks and Safe sqlite3 Queries Behind 30 of the 48 Items
description:
The Python Institute PCAD-31-02 exam has 48 items, and 30 of them come from two syllabus blocks: Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing (14) and Programming and Database Skills (16). If you can clean a messy file, validate it, move it into a database with safe queries and read the result back into pandas, you have practised the skills behind 62.5% of the exam.

This post does all of that in one small script you can run. Every output shown below was produced by running it with Python 3.12 and pandas 3.0.6, using only sqlite3 from the standard library for the database part.

What does the PCAD-31-02 exam look like?

PCAD (Certified Associate Data Analyst with Python) is the associate-level data exam of the OpenEDG Python Institute. The figures below come from the official PCAD certification page, read on 15 October 2026.

Item Value
Exam code PCAD-31-02, active since July 15, 2025 (PCAD-31-01 retired July 14, 2025)
Questions 48 single-select and multiple-select items, some scenario-based
Time 60 minutes, plus the NDA screen
Passing score 75%
Price Exam from $195; exam with retake from $225; practice test $49
Delivery Online through OpenEDG Testing Service (TestNow)
Prerequisites None formal; PCAP and PCED (or equivalent) recommended
Validity 6 years

How are the 48 items split across the five blocks?

The Python Institute publishes the split in the PCAD-31-02 exam syllabus, last updated July 15, 2025. Each item is worth up to one point, and the raw score is normalized to a percentage.

Block Items Weight
1. Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing 14 29.2%
2. Programming and Database Skills 16 33.3%
3. Statistical Analysis 4 8.3%
4. Data Analysis and Modeling 9 18.8%
5. Data Communication and Visualization 5 10.4%

Note what that means for your study plan. Blocks 1 and 2 are the bulk, but 30 of 48 is still below the 75% pass mark, so the statistics, pandas and charting blocks cannot be skipped. The script below covers the large blocks; it also touches objective 4.1.1 (cleaning with pandas) on the way.

Why load every column as text first?

Objective 1.2.2 asks you to identify erroneous data before you fix it. If pandas guesses types on load, a bad value can silently change a whole column's type, and you lose the chance to see which rows were wrong. Loading with dtype=str keeps the raw values so the cleaning step decides what each one means.

Here is a small order file with the problems the syllabus lists by name: stray spaces, mixed case, a thousands separator, a missing value written as text, a negative amount, a duplicate row, a date in the wrong format and five spellings of yes and no.

import io
import sqlite3

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 120, "display.max_columns", 10)   # print tables in full

RAW = """order_id,customer,country,amount,paid,order_date,ship_date
1001,  Ana Lima ,BR,120.50,yes,2026-09-01,2026-09-03
1002,ben okafor,NG,"1,080.00",Y,2026-09-02,2026-09-01
1003,Chen Wei,CN,n/a,no,2026-09-02,2026-09-05
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1005,Dara Singh,IN,64.00,0,03/09/2026,2026-09-06
1006,Ben Okafor,NG,310.00,1,2026-09-04,2026-09-07
1007,Chen Wei,cn,89.90,yes,2026-09-05,2026-09-05
1008,Dara Singh,IN,455.00,N,2026-09-06,2026-09-09
1009,ana lima,BR,72.25,y,2026-09-07,2026-09-08
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
print(len(df), "rows")   # 10 rows

Which cleaning steps does Block 1 name, and what do they look like?

Objective 1.2.4 lists them in one sentence: string manipulation, format standardization, boolean normalization, case normalization and string-to-number conversion. Each one is a single line in pandas.

BOOL = {"yes": True, "y": True, "true": True, "1": True,
        "no": False, "n": False, "false": False, "0": False}

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df["customer"] = df["customer"].str.strip().str.title()
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["paid"] = df["paid"].str.strip().str.lower().map(BOOL)
for col in ("order_date", "ship_date"):
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df["order_id"] = df["order_id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes)

order_id               int64
customer                 str
country                  str
amount               float64
paid                    bool
order_date    datetime64[us]
ship_date     datetime64[us]
dtype: object

The key argument is errors="coerce". As the pandas.to_numeric reference explains, it turns a value that cannot be parsed into NaN instead of raising an exception. That is what you want during cleaning: the bad value becomes a marker you can count and report, not a crash halfway through a file.

The same idea applies to dates. Passing an explicit format means 03/09/2026 becomes NaT rather than being guessed as March 9 or September 3. Whether that date was day-first or month-first is a question for the data owner, not for the parser.

What do type, range and cross-field checks look like in pandas?

Objective 1.3.1 names three kinds of validation: type, range and cross-field. Build each check as a boolean column, then keep the rows where no check fired. A table of named checks is easier to report to a stakeholder than a chain of filters.

checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount_not_numeric": df["amount"].isna(),            # type
    "order_date_unparsed": df["order_date"].isna(),       # type
    "amount_not_positive": df["amount"] <= 0,             # range
    "shipped_before_order": df["ship_date"] < df["order_date"],  # cross-field
})
bad = checks.any(axis=1)
print(checks[bad].set_axis(df.loc[bad, "order_id"]))
clean = df[~bad]
print(len(clean), "rows pass")

          amount_not_numeric  order_date_unparsed  amount_not_positive  shipped_before_order
order_id
1002                   False                False                False                  True
1003                    True                False                False                 False
1004                   False                False                 True                 False
1005                   False                 True                False                 False
5 rows pass

Two details are worth knowing for the exam. First, a comparison with NaN or NaT is always False, so a missing amount does not trip the range check; that is why the type check exists separately. Second, the duplicate of order 1004 was already gone, because drop_duplicates() ran before validation. Removing or imputing a row is a decision with consequences, and objective 1.2.4 asks you to discuss imputation against exclusion. Here exclusion is the honest choice: there is no sensible value to invent for a missing order amount.

How do Python types map to SQLite columns?

Objective 2.4.5 is about converting data types between SQL and Python. The sqlite3 module documentation lists exactly five Python types that go into SQLite without help: None, int, float, str and bytes.

Python value SQLite storage What to do
None NULL Nothing
int INTEGER Nothing
float REAL Nothing
str TEXT Nothing
bool INTEGER (0 or 1) Store as int(value)
datetime or pandas Timestamp No date type Store as ISO 8601 text

SQLite has no boolean and no date storage class. The SQLite page on datatypes and type affinity says booleans are stored as the integers 0 and 1, and dates as ISO 8601 text, a real number or an integer. Here is what happens if you skip the conversion:

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT    NOT NULL,
    country    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    amount     REAL    CHECK (amount > 0),
    paid       INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_date TEXT    NOT NULL
)""")
first = clean.iloc[0]
try:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (first["order_id"], first["customer"], first["country"],
                 first["amount"], first["paid"], first["order_date"]))
except sqlite3.ProgrammingError as e:
    print("ProgrammingError:", e)

ProgrammingError: Error binding parameter 6: type 'Timestamp' is not supported

So convert each row explicitly and insert the batch with executemany. The with con: block commits on success and rolls back on an exception, and the CHECK constraint in the table is a second line of defence for the range rule:

rows = [
    (int(r.order_id), r.customer, r.country, float(r.amount),
     int(r.paid), r.order_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    for r in clean.itertuples(index=False)
]
with con:
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone())   # (5,)

try:
    with con:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    (1010, "Eve Park", "KR", -5.0, 1, "2026-09-08"))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("IntegrityError:", e)   # CHECK constraint failed: amount > 0

Why does the exam keep asking about parameterized queries?

Two Block 2 objectives, 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, come back to the same point: never build SQL by pasting values into a string. The demonstration takes four lines.

name = "x' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = '{name}'"
print(con.execute(unsafe).fetchone())        # (5,)  every row matched
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = ?", (name,)).fetchone())   # (0,)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = :who",
                  {"who": "Ana Lima"}).fetchone())   # (2,)

The f-string version closes the quote early and turns the filter into a condition that is always true. With a ? placeholder the driver sends the value separately from the SQL text, so the quote characters are just part of a name that matches nobody. The third line shows the named style, :who with a dictionary, which reads better once a query has several parameters.

How do you get query results back into pandas?

Objective 2.4.1 lists the clauses the exam expects you to combine: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT. The query below uses all of them, with a LEFT JOIN so that an order from a country missing in the lookup table is kept and labelled rather than dropped.

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE countries (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO countries VALUES ('BR', 'Americas'), ('NG', 'Africa'), ('IN', 'Asia');
""")
QUERY = """
SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unmapped') AS region,
       COUNT(*)                       AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2)        AS revenue,
       MIN(o.order_date)              AS first_order
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN countries AS c ON c.code = o.country
WHERE o.paid = :paid
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_orders
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5
"""
summary = pd.read_sql_query(QUERY, con, params={"paid": 1, "min_orders": 1})
print(summary)
print(summary.dtypes)

     region  orders  revenue first_order
0    Africa       1   310.00  2026-09-04
1  Americas       2   192.75  2026-09-01
2  Unmapped       1    89.90  2026-09-05
region             str
orders           int64
revenue        float64
first_order        str
dtype: object

The params argument of pandas.read_sql_query passes values to the driver, so the placeholder rule still holds. Look at the last dtype, though: first_order came back as text, because that is how SQLite stored it. Add parse_dates=["first_order"] to the call and the column comes back as datetime64. The round trip from Timestamp to text and back is exactly the kind of conversion objective 2.4.5 has in mind.

The Chen Wei order lands in "Unmapped" because CN is not in the lookup table. With an INNER JOIN that paid order would vanish from the revenue total without any warning, which is a classic scenario question.

Is there a short video on preparing for PCAD?

This three-minute video from the EduSum channel gives preparation tips for the PCAD exam. It is about study habits rather than code, so it pairs well with the hands-on script above.

What should you practise after this script?

Run the script, then break it on purpose. Add a row whose paid value is maybe and see what map() produces; it gives NaN, and the column is no longer boolean. Then write a validation check for it. That loop of breaking the data and then catching the break is a fast way to learn Blocks 1 and 2.

To track the rest of the syllabus objective by objective, this PCAD-31-02 syllabus breakdown with exam details lists every block and topic on one page.

For Blocks 3 to 5, write small scripts of the same kind: a bootstrap of the mean with NumPy, a linear and a logistic regression with a train and test split, and one Matplotlib chart with labelled axes, a title and a legend.

When you want to see how the scenario items are phrased, work through these PCAD sample questions with answers and note which block each one belongs to.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the PCAD-31-02 exam, and what score do I need to pass?

The exam has 48 single-select and multiple-select items, and you have 60 minutes plus the NDA screen. You pass with a cumulative score of at least 75%.

2. How much does the PCAD exam cost?

The Python Institute lists the exam from $195, the exam with a retake from $225, the exam with a practice test from $215 and all three from $245. The practice test alone is $49.

3. Is PCAD-31-01 still available?

No. PCAD-31-01 was retired on July 14, 2025, and PCAD-31-02 has been the active version since July 15, 2025. Use the PCAD-31-02 syllabus when you study.

4. Do I need PCAP or PCED before taking PCAD?

There are no formal prerequisites. The Python Institute recommends PCAP and PCED, or equivalent knowledge, plus field-specific skills.

5. How long is the PCAD certification valid, and when can I retake a failed exam?

The certification is valid for 6 years. After a failed attempt you must wait 15 days before you can take the exam again.

title: Tenant Cohort Monitoring: 3 Node.js Docker Kubernetes Readiness Liveness Startup Signals
description:
A restart tells you that a container failed. It does not tell you whether the failure hit the control cohort, the experiment cohort, or both. TL;DR: expose separate startup, readiness, and liveness endpoints; let Kubernetes own the restart decision; and emit matching state transitions as logs plus metrics. For a small property-management SaaS, this is the leanest setup that can reconstruct a tenant-cohort incident without turning monitoring into a second product.

Choice Best fit Reconstruction strength Main boundary
App probes + metrics + logs Small service, weekly releases Strong with cohort and request IDs in logs You operate queries and notifications
Datadog or Grafana Cloud Several services or an on-call team Broader telemetry workflows More platform surface to manage
Better Uptime Public endpoint checks Strong outside-in timeline A healthy homepage can miss a stuck job
Healthchecks.io Cron and worker silence Excellent missed-heartbeat evidence It does not replace request-path probes

My recommendation is the first row for a one-person SaaS with one or two deployable services, plus an outside-in monitor for the failure it cannot see. Keep the contract yours: three HTTP responses, structured events, and a small metric vocabulary. A backend vendor can change later without changing application semantics. Ship the useful boundary now.

Three signals. One timeline.

How should Node.js on Docker use Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes?

Startup, readiness, and liveness answer different questions. Mixing them creates bad evidence and worse automation.

A startup probe asks whether initialization has completed. Until it succeeds, Kubernetes does not run readiness or liveness probes. That protects a deliberately slow boot from a premature restart. Readiness asks whether this pod should receive traffic now. A temporary database dependency failure can make a pod unready without proving that its process is dead. Liveness asks whether the process is stuck beyond recovery; repeated failure lets the platform restart the container.

Keep liveness narrow. If it fails whenever a downstream API is slow, Kubernetes can restart every healthy process during somebody else's outage. That destroys local state and muddies the timeline. Readiness is the better place for a dependency that makes serving requests unsafe.

For the property-management experiment, log the tenant cohort at the request boundary, not inside the probe. Probes have no tenant context. During reconstruction, join the deployment version and time window from health events to request logs carrying cohort, trace_id, and span_id. This distinguishes a rollout-wide failure from an experiment path affecting only lease_reminder_v2.

The trade-off is explicit: this design favors evidence that can survive a backend swap over a rich vendor-specific data model. I would make that choice while one person still owns deployment and feature delivery. Once cross-service debugging becomes routine, the time saved by a full suite can outweigh the portability.

Implement the evidence contract

The app should calculate health once, then expose that state to Kubernetes and telemetry. This TypeScript service is runnable after installing express, prom-client, and the relevant TypeScript types. It models three endpoints, exports Prometheus metrics, and adds cohort evidence to application logs.

import express, { Request, Response } from "express";
import { Counter, Gauge, Registry } from "prom-client";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!apiKey || !baseUrl) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL");
}

async function readLogContract(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/discovery/logs.ingest", baseUrl), {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });
  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readLogContract(attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

const app = express();
const registry = new Registry();
const failures = new Counter({
  name: "app_probe_failures_total",
  help: "Failed application health probes",
  labelNames: ["probe"] as const,
  registers: [registry],
});
const ready = new Gauge({
  name: "app_ready",
  help: "Whether this process can receive traffic",
  registers: [registry],
});

let startupComplete = false;
let databaseReachable = false;

function respond(
  probe: "startup" | "readiness" | "liveness",
  healthy: boolean,
  res: Response,
): void {
  if (!healthy) failures.inc({ probe });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "health_state",
    probe,
    healthy,
    deployment: process.env.DEPLOYMENT_VERSION ?? "unknown",
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(healthy ? 200 : 503).json({ healthy });
}

app.get("/health/startup", (_req, res) => {
  respond("startup", startupComplete, res);
});
app.get("/health/ready", (_req, res) => {
  ready.set(databaseReachable ? 1 : 0);
  respond("readiness", databaseReachable, res);
});
app.get("/health/live", (_req, res) => {
  respond("liveness", true, res);
});
app.get("/metrics", async (_req, res) => {
  res.type(registry.contentType).send(await registry.metrics());
});
app.get("/leases/:id", (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const cohort = req.header("x-experiment-cohort") ?? "control";
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "lease_viewed",
    lease_id: req.params.id,
    cohort,
    trace_id: req.header("x-trace-id") ?? null,
    span_id: req.header("x-span-id") ?? null,
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(200).json({ id: req.params.id, cohort });
});

async function initialize(): Promise<void> {
  databaseReachable = true;
  startupComplete = true;
  ready.set(1);
}

app.listen(3000, () => {
  void Promise.all([initialize(), readLogContract()]);
});

The Kubernetes configuration can also live in typed deployment code. These values are examples, not universal thresholds: measure normal initialization and recovery before tightening them. The relationship matters. Startup gets its own budget, readiness removes traffic, and liveness restarts only a process that cannot recover.

type Probe = {
  httpGet: { path: string; port: number };
  periodSeconds: number;
  timeoutSeconds: number;
  failureThreshold: number;
};

const containerHealth: Record<string, Probe> = {
  startupProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/startup", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 2,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 30,
  },
  readinessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/ready", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 5,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 2,
  },
  livenessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/live", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 10,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 3,
  },
};

console.log(JSON.stringify(containerHealth, null, 2));

There is a deliberate asymmetry. A failed readiness check changes routing quickly, while liveness waits longer before replacing the process. Fast restarts feel decisive, but false positives erase evidence and amplify dependency trouble.

Read the 14:03 tenant timeline

A useful dashboard needs only two health measures at first: the rate of app_probe_failures_total split by probe, and the current app_ready gauge split by deployment. Do not add the cohort label to either metric. Tenant or cohort labels can grow without bound and create noisy time series; cohort belongs in request logs.

Suppose lease_reminder_v2 requests begin failing at 14:03, readiness drops at 14:04, and Kubernetes replaces a container at 14:05. Start with the counter and gauge to bound the window. Inspect health_state logs for the deployment version. Then search request logs in that interval and compare control with lease_reminder_v2, following trace_id and span_id where they exist. Those IDs support log correlation, but they do not create a distributed trace or span tree.

This answers the business question: did the experiment path fail, or did the whole deployment lose its dependency? It is not enough to map a failure across five services. Be honest about that boundary.

Keep the log schema and metric names stable so the storage vendor can move behind the contract. Infrai is one reasonable backend when a solo operator values one plain REST API that needs no installed SDK; its public, self-describing discovery surface lets the app read the real request schema before binding an adapter. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules with one API key and one bill, so adding another backend capability does not create another credential rotation or invoice-reconciliation job for the same operator. Its observability surface can ingest logs and report metrics.

The limitations are substantial. It has no threshold notification route, distributed trace query, synthetic heartbeat, source-map decoding, or session replay. Query polling must provide notifications, and discovery does not declare filters for log search or metric query, so verify requests from the public discovery response rather than inventing parameters. It is not suitable when native alerting or span-tree investigation is a requirement; choose Datadog or Grafana Cloud instead. A stable contract saves replacement work, but polling creates operational work. That is the trade-off.

No span tree.

Draw the product boundaries

Choose Datadog when cross-service investigation, mature alert workflows, and a broad integrated telemetry product justify the added platform surface. It fits once several services and people share on-call work. Grafana Cloud suits teams already committed to Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana dashboards, especially when they want logs and traces in the same ecosystem while retaining familiar open telemetry formats.

Better Uptime is the stronger runner-up for outside-in availability and incident response. It can observe that a public endpoint is unreachable even when internal probes look healthy. Healthchecks.io solves a different blind spot: a nightly rent-ledger job that never starts emits no application failure. A dead-man's-switch heartbeat detects that silence. Pair it with probes rather than asking either tool to cover both jobs.

No choice wins every axis. A small SaaS can start with app-owned probes, logs, and metrics, then outsource the undifferentiated edge: public checks to an uptime service and missed-job detection to a heartbeat service. Add a full observability suite when cross-service reconstruction consumes feature-shipping hours. That revenue-per-hour threshold is more useful than a feature-count contest.

One more boundary matters for property data. If logs contain tenant identifiers, deletion and retention controls are part of the design. A backend without per-user log deletion cannot by itself satisfy an erasure workflow. Minimize identifiers before ingestion, define retention deliberately, and choose controls that match the legal obligation.

Govern the evidence, then stop

Keep automation and evidence separate. Kubernetes acts on three low-cardinality health decisions. Logs preserve cohort and request context. Metrics show frequency and present state. An external checker covers failures the cluster cannot observe.

Start with the smallest version that answers one reconstruction question. After each incident, record the unanswered question. Buy or build the next layer only when the same missing evidence recurs; otherwise, ship the tenant feature.

title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
description:
arXiv:2610.19191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.

title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.

title: Reducing the Gap Between Spatial and Space-Filling Curve Neighbors in 3D Point Cloud Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.19530v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As a lightweight and highly accurate method for nearest-neighbor search in 3D point clouds, approaches based on space-filling curves (SFC) have been proposed. However, due to the inherent properties of SFC, a gap arises between proximity relationships along the SFC and those in the original Euclidean space. In this study, we propose a loss function that reduces the influence of this gap. Specifically, we compute the distances between adjacent points along the SFC and train the model to optimize feature similarity between pairs of points that are distant from each other in the original 3D space. We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.

title: Updates to Legal Terms
description:
The proliferation of agentic workflows means developers now regularly grant AI tools direct access to their infrastructure, use services that act autonomously, and build on platforms that themselves use AI to operate. We’ve updated our Terms of Service and Marketplace terms to clarify shared responsibility when actions on your account may be taken by AI, whether Vercel's own or a third-party tool you've connected, as well as other important updates detailed below.

What is changing?

AI Functionality and Third-Party Tools

Vercel's platform increasingly includes AI-powered services, including v0, Vercel Agent, WAF natural language rules, and AI Gateway. These services may take actions on your behalf. We've introduced two new concepts to make the responsibilities around this explicit:

AI Functionality refers to Vercel services that are AI-powered, that help you build AI products (like AI SDK), or that connect to AI providers (like AI Gateway).

Third-Party Tools refers to any non-Vercel tool, script, service, or automation (AI-powered or not) that you grant access to your Vercel account. This includes CI/CD pipelines, third-party agents, and integration scripts.

The key responsibilities:

  • You control how AI Functionality behaves through your settings. Those settings define the scope of what AI Functionality can do on your behalf.

  • You are responsible for reviewing and authorizing the actions AI Functionality takes, and for evaluating its outputs against your own requirements.

  • If you grant a Third-Party Tool access to your Vercel account (e.g., giving it your API key), you are responsible for what it does, including any costs it incurs.

  • You are responsible for actions taken by AI Functionality or Third-Party Tools on your behalf.

Billing flexibility

We are updating our billing terms to reflect the expansion of our product surface area beyond subscription plans.

  • Fees are no longer exclusively tied to a subscription plan. Services like AI Gateway credits can be purchased and charged independently.

  • For non-subscription services, charges may occur at the time of purchase or top-up.

  • If your account shows unusually high or suspicious usage, Vercel may charge accrued fees ahead of your regular billing cycle. Learn more about Partial Invoices.

We have also added a direct link to vercel.com/pricing in the terms.

Enterprise Managed Accounts

Enterprise customers who have verified ownership of an email domain can now claim email addresses on that domain that are associated with existing Vercel accounts. If your account email falls within a claimed domain, Vercel will notify you and you'll have the option to update your email address. If the account was used for work with that organization, it may instead be added to their Team. In either case, the Enterprise customer does not gain access to your account or your content without your consent.

Representations

Two new customer representations have been added:

  • You confirm you have the rights to provide any third-party credentials or API keys to Vercel (for example, through Vercel Connect or other integrations).

  • You confirm you are not subject to applicable OFAC sanctions.

Marketplace

The Marketplace terms now introduce the concept of Authorized Users, which includes Third-Party Tools. Actions taken by Authorized Users are bound to you as the customer, and you are responsible for reporting any unauthorized Authorized User activity.

Privacy Policy

We have updated the Data Privacy Framework section. Previously, unresolved EU/UK/Swiss privacy complaints were directed to data protection authorities. We've now designated VeraSafe as our private complaint handler. Complaints can be submitted directly to VeraSafe before escalation to a regulator.

Frequently asked questions

The full updated Terms of Service are at vercel.com/legal/terms. The Marketplace terms and Privacy Policy are linked from the same page.

title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.

title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2610.14382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.

title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

title: ARC Region switch adds four new capabilities
description:
Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch helps you orchestrate the failover of multi-Region applications to achieve a bounded recovery time during a Regional impairment. Today, Region switch adds four new capabilities: AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block, payloads for custom action Lambda execution block, service quota parity checks, and wait for target group health feature for compute scaling actions.

AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block. During failover, you often need to run commands on managed instances and VMs. This execution block lets you invoke Run Command actions on managed instances during failover, with plan evaluation verifying that command documents target valid instances and that IAM permissions are correctly configured.

Payloads for custom action Lambda execution block. ARC Region switch now lets you pass payloads to your custom action Lambda execution block, allowing reusability of your Lambda functions across recovery plans.

Service quota checks. Service quota limits are a common failure mode during recovery. Region switch now verifies quota parity between your primary and standby Region, and automatically submits quota limit increases, reducing the risk of insufficient service quotas during recovery.

Wait for target group health. Amazon ECS service scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution blocks help you provision compute capacity during recovery, but provisioned capacity may not be ready to serve traffic. The optional wait for target group health feature verifies that your provisioned capacity is ready to serve traffic.

To get started, see the documentation for AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block , custom action Lambda execution block , Service quota checks  and the Wait for target group health for Amazon ECS service scaling execution block  and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution block .

title: What To Do When a Free LLM API Says 429 (A Field Playbook)
description:
What To Do When a Free LLM API Says 429 (A Field Playbook)

Every free LLM API says yes right up until the moment it says no. The no arrives as an HTTP 429, usually forty requests into a demo or halfway through a batch job, and most tutorials end the story at "add a retry loop." Here is what actually works when you are building on free tiers, provider by provider and layer by layer.

First, find out which limit you hit

A 429 is not one problem, it is four. Free tiers meter you on several axes at once, and the fix depends on which one fired:

  • Requests per minute (RPM): you are asking too often. Smoothing helps, capacity does not.
  • Tokens per minute (TPM): a few long prompts ate the whole minute. Shorten contexts, cap max_tokens.
  • Requests per day (RPD): you are done until the reset. No code fix exists, only spreading work across days or providers.
  • Concurrency: two in-flight requests when the tier allows one. Queue, do not parallelize.

Read the response body and headers before you touch your code. Groq sends x-ratelimit-remaining-requests (daily) and x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens (per minute) plus retry-after, so the 429 tells you which window is empty and when to come back. The Gemini API returns 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and names the violated window in details[].quotaId, with retryDelay set for per-minute limits; its daily quotas reset at midnight Pacific. OpenRouter free-model caps jump from a small daily allowance to a larger one once the account has purchased credits, and its error text and x-ratelimit-reset-requests header say which window closed. Some providers, sadly, send nothing: if a 429 comes back bare, treat every window as closed and back off to the hour.

Then, retry like it means something

Three rules that cover most cases:

  1. Honor retry-after when present. It is the provider telling you the truth; guessing is worse.
  2. Exponential backoff with jitter when it is not: 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s, plus random offset, capped at a few minutes. Retrying a daily cap in a loop accomplishes nothing, so stop after 3 to 5 attempts and surface the error.
  3. Count tokens, not requests. A retry loop tuned for RPM will still fail when TPM is the real wall, because the retry itself burns more tokens per minute.

Then, stop depending on one well

One provider's free tier is one quota pool. The structural fix is to treat free tiers as a pool of pools:

  • Keep several OpenAI-compatible keys (Gemini, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, OpenRouter, Cloudflare Workers AI, Cerebras and others each publish their own caps) and fail a request over to the next provider when one window closes. Because all of them speak the OpenAI chat format, your client code does not change, only the base URL and key.
  • Route by limit shape, not just availability. A nightly summarization job wants RPD headroom (Groq's daily allowances, or Gemini's daily caps). An interactive prototype wants RPM smoothness. A one-shot extraction can burn a per-token-limited tier without hurting anything.
  • Watch the terms. Several free tiers (Cohere's trial key, Mistral's La Plateforme free tier) are explicitly for evaluation, not production. OpenRouter's terms prohibit reselling API access. Read them before you build a product on top.

Hand-rolling this means a provider abstraction, a per-provider window tracker, a queue, and health checks for every one of them, which is most of a side project by itself. If you would rather not own that layer, there are routers that do it: I build FreeLLMAPI, an open-source, self-hosted router that keeps your provider keys, handles 429s and retries with backoff, falls back to other providers and models, and exposes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint at the end. The same job can be done by hand with the playbook above; the router just means you write it once and self-host it.

And log the shape of your traffic

Whatever you choose, log per-request: provider, model, latency, status, and the rate-limit headers. A week of logs tells you which window you actually bump, and that single fact decides whether you need smoothing, shorter prompts, a second provider, or honestly, the $5 paid tier. Most "we need more quota" problems turn out to be "one long prompt repeated in a loop" problems. The 429 is information. Read it before you reroll the key.

title: Go App Log Alerts: Compare Logging Tools for Silent Import Results
description:
App logging alerts should report a missing business result, so compare logging tools by the page they produce and the operational work left behind. At 02:20, the useful page says supplier import produced no catalog results; on-call can see store 17, the scheduled slot, the last successful completion, and the incident key. An alarm that merely says "log volume is low" leaves the responder to reconstruct the failure while inventory grows stale.

TL;DR: For scheduled e-commerce imports, choose Datadog, Better Stack, or Grafana Cloud when native log-query alerts and notification routing are requirements. Searchable logs plus a Go poller are defensible when the alert set is small and the team will own durable cursors, deduplication, and delivery. Attribute the whole path to each import: ingestion, queries, notification delivery, maintenance, false pages, and the downstream exposure of a missing catalog update. A low storage line item does not make an unreliable page inexpensive.

Infrai fits the narrower searchable-logs boundary. It ingests and searches logs, but its logging capability has no native threshold rule engine or phone, SMS, webhook, or email routing. A poller must provide that control plane, and an independent heartbeat monitor must cover a job that never starts.

How should I compare app logging tools with log alerts?

Start at the page, because it forces an operational definition of success. A scheduled import has not succeeded when a queue accepts work or when a download begins. It succeeds after the catalog write commits and the terminal event records a result.

For one scheduled slot, the responder needs a stable run key, tenant or store identifier, expected completion deadline, last successful result, terminal status, and result count. The incident key should be derived from the store and scheduled slot. Retries can then refer to one incident rather than opening several.

One page. One owner.

Nothing vague.

Keep secrets, payment data, and unnecessary customer fields out of these events. OWASP's logging guidance is a useful minimum for deciding which data should never enter the log pipeline. Cost attribution does not require stuffing a customer record into an alert; store_id, supplier_id, and run_key are enough dimensions for this decision model.

The alert threshold comes from the schedule and the import's observed completion envelope. A five-minute window has no meaning by itself. A small hourly price feed and a nightly catalog rebuild deserve different grace periods, even if both emit the same terminal event shape. Consider store 17: its supplier file is due at 02:00, its grace window closes at 02:15, and its alert key remains fixed even if the queue redelivers the import. A page at 02:20 should say which proof is missing. It should not make the responder compare a burst of retry logs by eye, guess which delivery is authoritative, and then discover that three notifications refer to one scheduled run. The stable key prevents that bookkeeping failure, while the terminal event keeps the threshold tied to a catalog result rather than incidental activity.

Trace backward from the page

At 02:20 the worker evaluates a closed grace window. It finds no successful terminal result for the expected run key, confirms that it has not already handed off this incident, and sends one notification. Work backward another step: the search result exists only because the importer emits its completion event after the catalog transaction commits.

There is an important split here. A started event proves that some scheduling path ran. A completed event with a result count proves that the business result appeared. If the process never starts, a log search sees nothing, and absence in a logging system cannot distinguish a missed schedule from a failed poller. Use a dead-man's-switch service such as Healthchecks for that heartbeat. Infrai has no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so it cannot supply this proof by itself.

Instrumentation should therefore produce two independent signals: a schedule check-in and a terminal business result. Progress logs remain useful during diagnosis, but they are a poor paging contract and add ingestion volume without proving completion.

Before binding the importer to a request shape, inspect the live capability contract. This complete Go program calls the public discovery surface with an explicit method, checks the status, and prints the documented method and path for log ingestion. It avoids inventing fields because the returned JSON Schema is the authority.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest",
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s", resp.Status))
    }

    var c capability
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s %s available=%t schema_bytes=%d\n",
        c.Method, c.Path, c.Available, len(c.Params))
}

Generate the production request from the returned path and schema. Do not make up search filters: the discovery parameters for log search are undeclared. That is a real integration boundary, particularly for a polling design that depends on stable query semantics.

Put every cost on the run key

A useful cost model follows the same key as the incident. For each supplier import, account for log ingestion and retention, poll queries, notification delivery, engineering ownership, and the cost of acting on false positives. Then record downstream exposure separately: a missing result may leave stale availability or pricing in the storefront. Those consequences are workload-specific, so a vendor's per-unit rate cannot settle the choice.

The allocation rule can stay plain. Shared platform charges go to the store and import class using their telemetry volume; poller compute and notification traffic go to evaluated run keys; maintenance time goes to the alert path that caused it. Do not bury poller work in a general platform bucket. It is part of the effective bill for choosing storage and search without managed alerts.

Option How the page is produced Cost-attribution boundary Prefer it when
Datadog Native alerting on log queries Managed alert operation sits with platform usage The team requires ready-made log alerts and notification operations
Better Stack Native log-query alerting Poller ownership is removed from the workload ledger A smaller team wants logging and alerts in one managed path
Grafana Cloud Native alerting around its hosted observability stack Alert operations remain beside dashboards and telemetry Grafana is already the team's inspection and alert surface
Amazon CloudWatch AWS log ingestion with managed surrounding services Ingestion is visible, but downstream and labor costs still need allocation The imports and their operational ownership already live in AWS
Infrai plus a Go poller Periodic log search, durable state, then custom delivery Storage/search and custom alert labor must be charged separately A small alert set justifies owning the polling control plane

Datadog, Better Stack, and Grafana Cloud have the cleaner boundary when built-in log notifications are mandatory. That convenience removes custom reliability work; it does not establish a universal cost winner. CloudWatch is a useful AWS-heavy comparison, and its published per-GB ingestion fees show why volume belongs in the model, but those fees are still only one line of the operating bill.

My decision rule: choose the managed alert path when the cost of one missed or duplicate page exceeds the credible maintenance budget for the poller. Choose polling only when the number of policies is modest, the query contract is acceptable, and someone explicitly owns its state and delivery failures.

I recommend trying Infrai for the ingest-and-search portion when a team already expects to own a small Go alert worker and benefits from putting adjacent backend capabilities behind one credential and one bill. Its breadth is verified at 295 routes across 20 modules. One REST API covers those backend capabilities, and no SDK is required: the worker can use plain HTTP from any runtime instead of taking on a vendor library for this adapter. Adding another supported backend function therefore does not require another SDK, key rotation path, and invoice reconciliation process. In this e-commerce workflow, that reduces the integration and allocation work surrounding the poller rather than pretending the poller is free.

There is a second, different advantage. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Public discovery returns full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; every documented capability has examples in ten languages. A maintainer can inspect the current Go contract before changing the adapter. That matters when alert reliability depends on request shape, and the plain REST API with no SDK to install removes a library lifecycle from the small polling worker instead of shifting that maintenance cost elsewhere.

The limitation stays visible. Infrai does not provide native log thresholds or notification routing, and it also lacks distributed trace queries and span trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, per-user log deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions. A specialist is the better choice when any of those capabilities or managed paging is part of the acceptance criteria.

Make polling dull and idempotent

The poller needs durable state. Store the last evaluated schedule slot and an incident key. Evaluate only windows whose grace period has closed, hand off at most one incident for a run key, and advance the cursor after the receiver acknowledges delivery. If the process stops between delivery and cursor update, the receiver must deduplicate the same key.

Retries happen.

Plan for them.

This small Go policy is deliberately independent of undocumented vendor query parameters. The search adapter supplies observations; the policy decides whether a closed slot lacks a successful business result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type run struct {
    key          string
    scheduledFor time.Time
    completedAt  *time.Time
    resultCount  int
}

func needsPage(now time.Time, grace time.Duration, r run) bool {
    if now.Before(r.scheduledFor.Add(grace)) {
        return false
    }
    return r.completedAt == nil || r.resultCount == 0
}

func main() {
    scheduled := time.Date(2026, 10, 9, 2, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    r := run{
        key:          "store-17:2026-10-09T02:00:00Z",
        scheduledFor: scheduled,
    }
    if needsPage(scheduled.Add(20*time.Minute), 15*time.Minute, r) {
        fmt.Printf("page key=%s reason=missing_import_result\n", r.key)
    }
}

Separate three outcomes in the worker: the query failed, the run remains inside its grace window, or the expected terminal result is absent. Only the third supports the catalog page. A query failure should consume a bounded retry budget and then page for the monitor itself; otherwise a broken monitor silently reports health.

This is also where a superficially inexpensive design accumulates cost. Durable cursors need storage and migration. Delivery needs backoff and deduplication. The worker needs its own health signal. Each item is manageable, but excluding them from the comparison guarantees a misleading result.

False positives are part of the bill

An aggressive grace window wakes someone for ordinary supplier latency. A loose window leaves stale catalog data visible longer. Neither cost appears cleanly in an ingestion quote.

Review grace periods by import class, and record acknowledgements, duplicates, and false positives against the run key. Change a threshold through the same review path as the schedule. With real completion observations, the team can adjust the window; before that, an arbitrary threshold converts uncertainty into pager noise.

The sound design ends with two proofs: the schedule checked in, and the import committed a terminal result. Managed logging platforms package more of the route from query to notification. Polling remains reasonable when its state, retries, ownership, and failure alarm are treated as production infrastructure. If that boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
  • Datadog log monitors
  • Better Stack log-based alerts
  • Grafana alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing

title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
description:
arXiv:2610.19399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.

title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
description:
arXiv:2610.19038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward.
  We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal.
  Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.18880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.
