title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
description:
arXiv:2610.19142v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied. We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.

title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
description:
arXiv:2610.14487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.

title: What I told the CFO when he asked why design matters
description:
How to sell design and show the impact of design outcomes to business and finance leaders.

Many years ago a business unit CFO told me: “I don’t need another presentation explaining why design is important. I need to know whether investing another million dollars in design will outperform investing it in engineering or marketing.”

That conversation changed how I talk about design. Showing the value of design with quantitative data is one of the greatest challenges for a design leader. Our field has been a C-suite priority for years, but it’s still treated as a secondary contributor to business performance.

And part of that is on us. Many of us think of ourselves as artists of digital businesses, creative outsiders in conversations where everyone else talks numbers.

That may be true, but it sounds too convenient. We design products, so we have to lead with business outcomes: know our numbers, sell our ideas, and quantify the real-world impact of what we do.

If your CFO asked why design matters and what the value of your work is, what would you say?

Here are the five answers I gave mine.

#1. “Hold design to the same standard as any other investment: payback period and rate of return”

Every request that crosses a CFO’s desk gets the same two questions: how fast does the money come back, and how much value will it create beyond that? Finance calls them the payback period and the rate of return, and it applies them to every investment (machinery, software, headcount…).

My answer to that CFO was to judge design with those same two questions. Before giving him that answer, I had done my research and looked at real-world cases. In 2025, Forrester studied six global companies for the research platform UserTesting and tallied how much they spent on user research versus what they got in return.

The design work is right there in the findings: validating designs with users before launching shortened iteration cycles by 25% and avoided $2.5 million in developer rework. The overall ROI was 415% over three years, and the spending paid for itself in less than six months. Most investments a CFO approves take years to do that.

That study confirmed something I now repeat to every design leader I meet: finance already has the tools to evaluate design fairly, because it evaluates everything as an investment. We just have to hand over our numbers in that format.

When designers can clearly show the value of their work, it’s hard to question the budget, and that’s when you get the opportunity to try more ambitious work. Measured wins buy credibility.

#2. “Conversion is revenue we’ve already paid to acquire”

Companies know to the cent what they pay to bring a visitor in: marketing audits every campaign, every channel and every cost-per-click (CPC, CPA, cost per lead…). All of that money is spent by the time someone loads a shopping cart.

What happens after the click is, in most cases, considered the designer’s job and treated as a cosmetic layer. It’s hard to connect it to money. However, there’s data that proves it’s more tied to revenue than it seems.

The numbers I sometimes use to make this case come from Baymard Institute, which has calculated that seven out of ten shopping carts die at checkout (an average of 70.22%).

In many cases, this issue can be solved through design changes. According to their research, large e-commerce sites can lift conversion by 35.26% if they fix known checkout design issues. They estimate $260 billion in lost orders is recoverable in the US and EU through those fixes alone!

Every time I’ve presented these numbers to a non-design audience, the reaction has been the same: nobody had ever counted checkout friction as lost revenue. The money was always there, but it had no owner.

That’s why conversion is where I tell design leaders to start if they’ve never connected design to revenue. The attribution is clean, the results show fast, and finance tracks the metric for you.

#3. “User research is capital protection”

Every product idea can be tested before it’s built by making a prototype. You put it in front of a certain number of users, and within a few weeks you know whether the idea works. Total cost: one designer’s time.

Or you can skip the test, spend months building the product with several teams, and find out at launch that the idea didn’t work.

That’s what validation is for. When a test kills a bad idea early, the company saves everything it would have spent building it. Those savings never appear in reports, because nobody documents the disasters that didn’t happen. That’s why research always looks like the easiest thing to cut when budgets get tight, which is precisely why cutting research often proves expensive later.

If you need external proof, I recommend you read McKinsey’s Business Value of Design study. In this report, McKinsey tracked 300 companies over five years. The top performers grew revenue 32 percentage points faster and returned 56 percentage points more to shareholders (share price gains plus dividends) than their industry peers. One of the practices those companies shared was continually testing and iterating with users during development.

Validating pays twice: less money wasted on bad ideas, better products when the idea is good. These days I pitch it as ‘capital protection’ instead of research. Same work, faster approval.

#4. “A design system compounds like capital: build once, deploy everywhere”

Every quarter, I have a sense of the hours my teams saved by reusing components and UX patterns, translated into cost savings. It’s the design number finance verifies fastest, because it’s included in the timesheets and payroll data they trust.

That habit exists thanks to our design system: the library of components (buttons, forms, menus…), patterns and reusable experiences, that teams design and code once and then reuse everywhere. Those pieces are one of design’s few compounding assets. You pay for them once, and they keep paying back every time someone reuses them.

If you don’t have your own numbers yet, Sparkbox has public ones. In a small, controlled experiment, eight developers built the same page twice: first from scratch, then using an open-source design system. The scratch version took a median of 4.2 hours; with the design system, they built it in 2 hours.

Scale those hours across everything a product team ships in a year and the savings add up to weeks of work. With consistent components, there’s less quality assurance. and fewer support tickets. New designers can ship sooner because the pieces they use are there from day one.

Any team running a design system can pull the same numbers from its own tools.

#5. “When features become commodities, design is the pricing power”

Today, any feature we ship can be copied by a competitor within weeks. AI accelerated this for everyone. The AI in Design Report 2026 (a survey of 906 designers in 60+ countries) found that 91% of designers now use AI at least weekly, up from 54% the year before.

When every team builds with the same tools, products end up with similar features. And when two products do the same thing, people choose the one that’s easier and nicer to use. Customers are often willing to pay more for that experience and remain loyal longer. Finance has a name for being able to charge more without losing customers: pricing power.

Experience has become the differentiator and one of the main reasons a customer would choose your product over competitors’. It’s what protects the price. The responsibility of building an outstanding user experience is, of course, on designers.

There’s measurable financial impact behind our craft

None of the five answers I’ve shared in this article required inventing new math. Payback, conversion, validation, reuse and pricing power are terms your CFO uses daily.

If you lead a design team, your job is to translate what you do into terms and numbers your finance team can understand and validate.

Two habits have helped me. The first is to talk to finance before you need something from them. Ask what they report every month and which numbers they argue over, because that’s the fastest crash course in how your company measures itself. The second is to report design metrics on a schedule. You’ll build more trust with your C Suite if you present your team’s performance, in business terms, periodically. It shows you understand that design, like every other function, answers for its results.

One thing I always clarify in these conversations is that money is only half of the design’s value. Besides the monetary value (productivity, fewer user errors, lower training and support costs), there is also human value (user satisfaction, inclusion, customer loyalty, adoption).

I’ve never had a CFO reject the human half when it came with the monetary one.

As for being ‘the artists of digital businesses’: We can keep the craft and speak numbers at the same time. In my experience, that combination is what gets design taken seriously.

Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. The above article is personal and does not necessarily represent SAP’s positions, strategies or opinions.

What I told the CFO when he asked why design matters was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Prepare Email-Safe Images: A 4-Step Convert, Compress, and Host Pipeline
description:
TL;DR: Convert generated promotional images to a conservative format, compress them aggressively, store them privately, and put a time-limited hosted link in the email instead of attaching the bytes. Treat moderation as a separate release gate before delivery. For a team also generating short promo videos from prompts, that boundary matters more than an attractive dashboard: the page should fire when unsafe media can escape or recipients cannot load an asset, not merely because a conversion job took a little longer than usual.

This is a four-step delivery pipeline, but the operational question is narrower: what will the person carrying the pager actually see? A useful alert says that an email campaign contains an unmoderated asset, that signed links are failing, or that output size has crossed the team's tested ceiling. A weak alert says only that a media dashboard turned red. At 3 a.m., the first kind leads to an action; the second leads to tab hunting.

Infrai is an early candidate when the same team needs conversion, compression, private storage, and email behind one REST contract. That can remove three SDK and credential boundaries from the incident path, but it does not choose a format, set a size budget, or define moderation policy for you.

What should the first page say?

Start at the failure visible to a recipient: an image is absent, rejected, or mishandled by the mail client. Work backward. The stored object may be healthy while its signed URL has expired; the URL may be valid while the converted file is too large; and the conversion may have succeeded while a generated promotional asset never passed the required moderation policy. Those are different incidents with different owners, so collapsing them into one “image pipeline failed” counter discards the information needed to respond.

The signal that should fire earlier is a per-campaign release invariant. Before a message can be sent, every referenced image should have a successful conversion, a compression result, a private object key, a usable signed URL, and the moderation decision required by the publisher's policy. This is also the right place to stop an unsafe still derived from a prompt-generated video. It keeps moderation coverage explicit instead of assuming that a successful generation request implies approval.

Instrument the transitions, not the dashboard. Record a correlation ID, campaign ID, source media ID, output format, output bytes, moderation state, object key, link expiry, and send state. Do not log the signed URL itself. Then alert on broken invariants near the send boundary and include the failed transition in the page. “Campaign 8f2 has 17 messages ready and one asset without a moderation decision” is actionable; “media errors > 0” is not.

No single byte threshold is universally correct. Establish it from the clients and templates you actually test, then keep it as configuration rather than folklore embedded in code. A threshold set too high allows slow or rejected mail through. Set it too low and harmless variation in generated imagery pages the on-call, encouraging people to mute the alert that later matters.

How should Node.js prepare and convert email-safe images?

Even when an application is written in Node.js or Express, the safest first integration step is to inspect the live contract rather than copy a stale request body. The following Go utility calls Infrai's public discovery surface for image.convert, prints the full JSON Schema and runnable examples, handles HTTP errors, and backs off on rate limits. It uses the required environment-based bearer credential convention even though public discovery itself does not require a key. This is intentionally a contract-discovery example: the supplied API facts do not establish conversion payload fields, and guessing them would make a copyable sample actively harmful.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := discover(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if err != nil { fatal(err) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    if apiKey == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.convert"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay): continue
            case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited")
}

func fatal(err error) { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }

Run this during integration, use the returned schema and runnable example to implement the conversion request, reject a result that violates your tested size policy, and retain the source media ID beside the object metadata so an incident responder can trace the artifact without searching a campaign by filename. The distinction is deliberate: discovery can be generic and safe to automate, while conversion parameters should remain schema-driven.

For remote processing, I would not fabricate payload fields in a sample: the public discovery response supplies the full request and response JSON Schema plus runnable examples, so production code should generate or validate requests against the discovered contract. This is where a broad service surface is useful. Image processing, private storage, and email sit behind one REST contract rather than three unrelated SDKs and credential sets; the supporting advantage is that each documented capability has runnable examples in ten languages, which shortens the path from discovery to a first valid request.

Teams that want one contract for conversion, compression, private storage, and email delivery should try Infrai for this pipeline, because reducing credential and SDK sprawl leaves fewer integration boundaries to diagnose during a send incident. The public discovery surface reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules. That breadth does not remove the need to test recipient clients or define a moderation policy.

Choosing the processing boundary

There are at least four defensible choices. They are not interchangeable.

Option Setup and credentials Best fit Boundary to watch
Sharp An application dependency and no hosted-service credential Teams that want conversion in their own Node.js worker The team owns capacity, patching, storage, signed delivery, and moderation integration
Cloudinary A specialist media account, delivery model, and SDK or API integration Rich managed image and video transformation workflows Email and the rest of the backend remain separate integrations
Imgix A specialist image-delivery integration connected to an origin URL-driven transformation and image delivery It is narrower than a combined processing, storage, and messaging surface
ImageKit A specialist account with media delivery and transformation APIs Teams centered on managed image and video optimization Messaging and broader backend operations use separate contracts
Infrai One REST contract and credential across multiple backend modules A small team minimizing SDK and credential sprawl Use discovery schemas rather than assuming fields; specialist media workflows may deserve specialist tooling

Sharp is the cleanest starting point when the worker already runs Node.js, the input set is controlled, and the team is prepared to operate the surrounding queue and storage path. Cloudinary is a reasonable specialist choice when sophisticated media lifecycle and transformation features dominate the architecture. Imgix fits particularly well when there is already an origin and delivery-time image transformation is the center of the problem. ImageKit belongs on the shortlist when managed image and video optimization is the dominant concern. A specialist is the better answer when its media-specific controls, delivery network, or workflow depth matter more than consolidating backend contracts.

The platform's advantage is integration shape, not an assertion that one abstraction wins every comparison. Its API is self-describing; GET /v1/discovery/{capability} returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That is concrete friction removed: an engineer can inspect the exact contract before installing anything or distributing credentials. It also reports readiness per capability, including vendors that are ready or pending, which is relevant to media teams that must prove coverage rather than infer it from a product landing page.

Store privately, then link

An email should reference a hosted result rather than carry the image as an attachment. Byte size matters acutely in email, and clients can reject or mishandle modern formats, so conservative encoding is a reliability decision rather than nostalgia. Hosting also makes open observation possible, provided it is disclosed and implemented consistently with the sender's privacy obligations.

Keep the object private or signed-only and issue a presigned URL. Never put an Infrai bearer token into that URL request: a presigned URL is already the scoped authorization mechanism, while the API key belongs only on calls to the API host. Avoid public-read buckets and static-hosting patterns for generated campaign assets. The object key should be stable enough for traceability but should not contain recipient data.

There is a real trade-off here. Short link lifetimes reduce exposure but can break an old message when a recipient opens it later; very long lifetimes preserve rendering but expand the authorization window. Pick the duration from the promised lifetime of the campaign, document it, and page on signing failures before sending. Do not page merely because an individual recipient opens after the documented expiry.

Moderation is a release gate, not a generation feature

For prompt-generated promotional video, moderation coverage needs to be stated as a matrix: original prompt, generated video, extracted poster frame, resized email image, and any user-supplied overlay. A product name in the architecture does not prove that each artifact was reviewed. The release record should show which policy and which artifact version produced the decision.

This matters during retries. If conversion changes the actual pixels, decide whether policy requires the derived asset to be checked again; do not silently reuse an approval for a different byte sequence. Likewise, a send retry must refer to the same approved object rather than regenerating content. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, but idempotency is still not a substitute for recording the moderation decision attached to the released artifact.

Keep the stop condition boring: no decision, no send.

Stop there.

The false-positive cost deserves equal attention. If a moderation alert fires on every reviewable item rather than on an unresolved item approaching release, responders learn that the page has no immediate consequence. Alert when the invariant is broken at the action boundary; send routine review volume to a work queue or report. The same discipline applies to image size and link expiry. Pages are for a response, not for displaying anxiety.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • Imgix rendering API
  • ImageKit documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema for each capability before writing the integration.

title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19166v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

  • A conversation that includes a live agent during business hours. A bot-only flow does not pass.
  • Customer-initiated entry points. The channel is not for unsolicited outbound iMessages.
  • A built journey Apple can review: support, booking, commerce, or concierge, using the interactive features the MSP actually ships.

The approval write-up, including what Apple looks at in the review, is here: How to get approved for Apple Messages for Business.

The steps before that review, starting with Apple Business Register and MSP selection, are here: How to apply.

After the review

Once the account is commercial, customers can start from the website, Maps, and the other entry points the brand turns on. Patterns from brands that are already live are in best practices.

title: Nobody wants your AI app
description:
The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.

We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.

Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.

The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.

A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.

The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.

This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.

You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.

Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.

On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.

They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.

This is bigger than a retention problem.

The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.

The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.

While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.

Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.

Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.

We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.

The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.

The app everyone downloaded and nobody kept

Surprise, it’s not Quibi!

Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.

The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.

They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.

People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.

This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.

Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.

Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.

Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.

Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).

Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.

MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.

A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.

Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.

Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.

We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.

That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.

The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.

What the people buying AI actually want

Larger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.

Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.

The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.

That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.

This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.

The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.

The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.

Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”

Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.

Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.

That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.

The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.

The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.

That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.

Nobody has figured out invisible, but watched

The answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.

Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.

They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.

In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.

The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.

A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.

Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.

Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.

Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.

The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.

Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.

The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.

It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.

Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.

OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.

There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.

The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.

A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.

This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.

Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.

Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.

Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.

Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in It

If you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.

The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.

Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.

The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.

Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.

The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.

The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.

The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.

Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.

Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.

Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.

The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.

The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.

This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.

The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.

The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.

The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.

The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.

References and further reading

Why the app model is collapsing

Malika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. Stickiness depends on the underlying model, not your interface; fewer than 10% of users switch despite zero cost.

RevenueCat, 2026 State of Subscription Apps Report. AI apps churn 30 to 36 percent faster than non-AI apps; only about 1 in 5 subscribers remains after a year.

Bessemer Venture Partners, Seven Product Strategies to Prevent Churn for B2B AI App Leaders. Even B2B AI tools face the churn cliff unless embedded in a daily workflow.

Brian Balfour (Reforge), on product-market fit collapse. In AI, customer expectations reset almost instantly and switching is trivial.

Google+ (Wikipedia). The destination that signed up hundreds of millions and became a ghost town, with 90 percent of sessions under five seconds.

MoviePass (Wikipedia). Spectacular sign-ups, no durable business underneath, fast collapse.

What the buyers actually want

Snyk, State of Agentic AI Adoption. Across 3,000-plus enterprise environments, organizations are embedding AI into their existing stack rather than buying standalone tools; the real AI footprint is roughly 3x the model list.

The Enterprise MCP Guide. The Model Context Protocol’s near-vertical adoption, roughly 97 million monthly downloads and production use in about 40 percent of technical organizations.

Gartner, via OutSystems research. 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents by the end of the year.

Patrick Neeman, Headless AI Will Make Every Product a Platform. The design work has moved to the contract underneath the product.

Mark Weiser (Wikipedia). The father of ubiquitous computing: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.”

Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol (via FifthRow). The Linux Foundation standard that lets one AI hand a task to another, adopted across 150-plus organizations.

Invisible, but watched

Writer, 2026 Enterprise AI Adoption Report. A third of employees say they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent.

The MCP and AI Governance Gap (Techstrong). Enterprises need to answer basic questions about every AI action, and most can’t.

Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. Employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a year to 45 percent of the workforce, two-thirds via personal accounts.

Cyberhaven, shadow AI analysis. The average employee feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report. A growing majority of breached companies had no governance to manage or detect AI use.

Kong, enterprise AI governance research. Fewer than 1 percent of organizations have AI-specific governance controls; almost 98 percent of AI requests go to third-party services.

OutSystems, State of AI Development. 94 percent worry about AI sprawl; only about 12 percent have centralized management.

Where the work goes

Nielsen Norman Group, on AI-native UX. AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives; the interface is becoming a commodity.

Patrick Neeman, Designing for AI Means Designing Like It’s 1999. Conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product.

UXmatters, The Era of the Invisible User Interface. Invisible AI works only if people trust it, which requires transparency and real control.

James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross, Answering the Call of Automation (Quarterly Journal of Economics). When switchboards automated, the job vanished and the incumbents mostly did not move up with the work.

Nobody wants your AI app was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Testing a Retro Text Generator as Two Different Products
description:
A text-image generator can look like a single form: enter a phrase, choose some visual settings, generate, and download. From a product-engineering perspective, however, a logo route and a poster route do not have the same success criteria.

This article shows how to turn those two creative intentions into observable UI contracts. It is a black-box test plan based on public-facing workflow language, not an analysis of private source code, model architecture, API design, or performance.

Start with intent, not the Generate button

A successful server response tells us very little about whether the result is useful. A logo-oriented user needs a compact identity asset that survives repeated use. A poster-oriented user needs a headline that works inside a one-off information hierarchy.

That suggests two top-level contracts:

Surface Primary user question Failure that matters most
Logo route Is the name still recognizable across contexts? The word shape collapses at small size or depends on one background
Poster route Can the viewer find the message in the intended layout? The headline overwhelms the date, place, or call to action

The public Fontify retro workflow describes short text entry, font color and background choices, image-size selection, preview or generation, and image download. Those are useful observable stages. They should not be confused with guarantees about trademark distinctiveness, production-ready vectors, accessibility, or an installable font file.

Model only states a user can observe

Keep the test model deliberately modest:

type CreativeIntent = 'logo' | 'poster';

type ObservableState =
  | { kind: 'editing'; text: string }
  | { kind: 'generating'; requestId?: string }
  | { kind: 'preview-ready'; intent: CreativeIntent }
  | { kind: 'download-ready'; formatLabel: string }
  | { kind: 'recoverable-error'; messageVisible: boolean };

This is a proposed test vocabulary, not a claim about the product’s implementation. Its value is that bug reports become reproducible. “The tool failed” turns into “after editing a completed preview, a second Generate action left the old image visible without a progress or error state.”

Also test what happens when intent changes. If a person moves from a square logo exploration to a wide poster composition, are the prior text and settings intentionally preserved, intentionally reset, or silently mixed? Any of those behaviors can be valid, but the interface should make the outcome understandable.

Define a logo-specific matrix

Use the Retro Font Logo Generator as the logo-focused entry point and prepare inputs that reveal recognition problems:

  • a short name with repeated letters;
  • a name containing a narrow and a wide character;
  • mixed case, if the current interface accepts it;
  • a name near the apparent input boundary;
  • light, dark, and transparent-background attempts when those options are available.

For each case, review the preview at three scales: the editor size, a compact card, and a favicon-like thumbnail. The automated check can confirm that a preview exists and that an enabled download action follows. Human review still has to answer whether letters merge, internal counters close, or an important terminal is cropped.

Do not encode guessed DOM selectors into the article as if they were stable product contracts. A real automation suite should inspect the live accessible roles and labels first. An illustrative Playwright skeleton might look like this:

test('logo journey exposes a reviewable result', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto(LOGO_ROUTE);
  await page.getByRole('textbox').fill('MOONROOM');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /generate/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('img')).toBeVisible();
  // Project selectors, completion signals, and download assertions
  // must be verified against the current live UI before use.
});

Define a poster-specific matrix

The Retro Poster Font Generator needs scenarios that expose hierarchy and canvas problems rather than only glyph problems:

  1. A two-word event name in a wide composition.
  2. A long headline that may wrap.
  3. A date containing numbers and punctuation.
  4. A high-detail uploaded background, if the live page currently permits one.
  5. A mobile viewport where controls and preview compete for space.

The critical visual assertions are not merely “image exists.” Check safe margins, wrapping, cropping, foreground-background contrast, and whether a changed ratio is reflected in the newest preview and downloaded asset. When pixel-diff testing is used, keep tolerance and baseline updates under review; generative output may not be deterministic enough for strict full-image comparison.

A more durable split is to automate workflow invariants and reserve aesthetic judgment for a review checklist. Workflow invariants include input persistence, visible loading or error feedback, prevention of accidental duplicate actions, and consistency between selected settings and the export metadata visible to the user.

Test failure and recovery paths

Creative tools are often tested only on the happy path because the preview is the exciting part. Recovery deserves its own matrix:

  • empty or whitespace-only input;
  • unsupported or unrendered characters;
  • network interruption during generation;
  • a second click while work is in progress;
  • changing text after a preview is ready;
  • navigating back from a download-ready state;
  • retrying without losing the creative brief.

For each failure, record whether the message identifies the problem, preserves recoverable input, and presents a clear next action. Avoid inventing a character-support promise: verify behavior with the current interface and document the result.

Keep the product boundary visible

QA can verify that a route accepts input, exposes settings, produces a reviewable result, and offers a download path. It cannot certify that a generated logo is legally unique or that a poster is effective for every audience. Commercial projects also require a current license check, and teams should distinguish a rendered text image from an editable font family.

The main engineering lesson is simple: do not let a shared component erase distinct user intent. The same generator shell can support multiple creative surfaces, but each surface needs its own fixtures, visual-review questions, and release criteria. Test the job, not just the button.

title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.19026v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

title: Measuring the Inference Energy Efficiency of Open-Weight LLMs across Benchmarks, Reasoning Modes, and Hardware
description:
arXiv:2610.14389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.

title: See every Google ad a competitor runs, from just their domain (cURL, Python, n8n)
description:
Google's Ads Transparency Center lists the ads that advertisers run on Google Search, YouTube, Shopping, Play and Maps, with the dates each ad was first and last shown. For media buyers, agencies and B2B sales teams, that is a goldmine: what are my competitors running right now, since when, and in which format?

Getting it into a pipeline is the annoying part. Some tools ask you to open the Transparency Center, find the advertiser by hand and paste its URL. That is fine for one brand. It is not fine for 50 competitors or a list of 1,000 prospects.

So I built a small tool that takes plain domains (nike.com, adidas.com) and returns the ads as JSON.

What it does

The Google Ads Transparency Scraper runs on Apify:

  • Domains in, ads out. No advertiser IDs, no copy-pasting Google URLs.
  • No browser, no proxies. It reads the data through an API backend, so runs take seconds.
  • Two output modes: ads returns one record per ad, for swipe files and monitoring. summary returns one compact record per domain (does it advertise, how many ads, which formats, latest ad), for lead lists, Clay tables and AI agents.
  • "Only new ads" monitoring: schedule it daily or weekly with only_new_ads: true, and each run returns only ads you have not seen before.
  • Every advertiser behind a domain: results include every advertiser whose ads lead to the domain, not only the brand itself. When I looked up adidas.com, the advertisers included "Adidas America, Inc", the media agency "MediaCom L.L.C" and an individual advertiser name I did not recognize. That is useful for brand protection too.

1. Quick start with cURL 

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/hirepulse~google-ads-transparency-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "domains": ["nike.com"], "country": "US", "max_ads_per_domain": 5 }'

2. Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("hirepulse/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["gusto.com", "rippling.com"],
    "country": "US",
    "platform": "google_search",   # all, google_search, youtube, google_shopping, google_play, google_maps
    "format": "all",               # all, text, image, video
    "max_ads_per_domain": 40,      # up to 120
    "mode": "ads",
})

for ad in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if ad.get("ad_id"):
        print(ad["domain"], ad["advertiser_name"], ad["format"], ad["days_running"], "days", ad["transparency_url"])

3. n8n: weekly "new competitor ads" alert

  1. Schedule Trigger: every Monday at 09:00.
  2. HTTP Request (POST) to the run-sync-get-dataset-items URL above, with: 
   { "domains": ["competitor1.com", "competitor2.com"], "only_new_ads": true, "max_ads_per_domain": 40 }
  1. IF ad_id is not empty (records without ad_id are notes, such as "No new ads since the last run").
  2. Slack or email: post the advertiser, format and transparency_url of each new ad.

Honest limitations

  1. No spend or impression numbers. Google does not publish them for commercial ads, so no tool can give you real numbers.
  2. No separate ad text field. Google renders text ads as images. You get the image (preview_image_url), which shows the full ad copy.

title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

title: UsersTable — the dumb component I copy into every admin panel
description:
Every admin panel I've ever built has a users table. Or a products table. Or an orders table. They're all the same shape: rows of records, a couple of status pills, edit and delete actions on the right. And every time, there's a temptation to build the clever version — sorting, filtering, pagination, inline editing — before the panel even works.

In my starter kit, the users table is deliberately dumb. Here's the entire contract:

export default function UsersTable({ users, onEdit, onDelete }) {

Three props. Data in, callbacks out. The component fetches nothing, authenticates nothing, routes nowhere. It renders a table with name, email, a role pill (indigo for admin, gray for everyone else), a formatted creation date, and Edit/Delete buttons that call the callbacks with the user object.

That's it. And that restraint is the feature.

Because the component knows nothing about where the data comes from, the parent page owns all the interesting decisions: how users are fetched, what the edit modal looks like, what happens after a delete (refetch? optimistic removal? confirmation dialog?). I can reuse this exact component in a demo build that runs against an in-memory mock API — the kit has a demoMock seam for exactly that — and in production against the real Laravel API, without changing a line of it. Props in, actions out. The component doesn't care.

This is also how I keep admin features cheap to add later. When a client asks for a products table next month, I don't build a new abstraction; I copy this file, change the columns, and wire new callbacks. Ninety percent of the code is identical. People call this boring. Boring is what lets me ship an admin panel in an afternoon.

A few small details I do keep in the "dumb" version: overflow-x-auto on the wrapper so the table scrolls horizontally on mobile instead of breaking the layout; whitespace-nowrap on cells so dates don't wrap weirdly; hover:bg-gray-50 on rows because affordance matters even in internal tools. And the role pill — a tiny inline conditional — because the person staring at this table is an admin, and the fastest thing their eyes need is "who here is an admin."

The lesson I keep re-learning: the smartest component in your admin panel is the one that knows the least. Push the knowledge up to the page, keep the table stupid, and you'll thank yourself on every project after this one.

The full admin loop — this table, the Users page that drives it, the API behind it, and the tests proving it — ships in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. The admin panel is done; go build the product.

title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

title: ELARSpeech: A 30K-Hour Dataset Across 675 Underrepresented Languages for Long-Tail Multilingual Speech Technologies
description:
arXiv:2610.19388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Massively multilingual speech modeling has made remarkable progress in recent years, yet existing training resources and benchmarks still underrepresent much of the linguistic long tail. To address this gap, we introduce ELARSpeech, a large-scale multilingual speech resource comprising 30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive. Combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings, the corpus spans diverse recording conditions, domains, and language families. Beyond corpus construction, our experiments show how ELARSpeech supports extending ASR and TTS capabilities to diverse underrepresented languages, with further benefits from pseudo-labeling unlabeled data. At the same time, our speech representation analysis reveals remaining limitations in transferring existing multilingual models to the linguistic long tail. Together, ELARSpeech provides both a resource and a testbed for extending multilingual speech technology further into the linguistic long tail. We publicly release the dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the complete data construction pipeline to facilitate research on long-tail multilingual speech technologies.
