title: Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, a platform that gives your entire company the ability to ship with AI safely, behind your access and security boundaries.

Over the past year, employees across Vercel shipped hundreds of agents and internal apps. Getting to production was the easy part, because we built them with eve on top of the Agent Stack and deployed them on Vercel.

The difficult questions came after those agents were being used by our employees across the company:

  • Who is allowed to use each agent?

  • How do we keep internal agents internal?

  • Which data and systems are agents allowed to touch?

  • Which models are agents using, and how much are they costing us?

Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to answer these questions for ourselves. It makes ownership, access, and security the defaults your builders inherit instead of the projects your platform team queues.

Platform components

Security implementation

Vercel Passport

Puts every internal app and agent behind your identity provider by default

Vercel Connect

Gives agents short-lived, scoped credentials for the systems they use, like Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear

Enterprise Managed Users

Full lifecycle control over every Vercel and v0 user through your existing directory

Bring your own cloud on AWS

Runs apps and agents inside your own AWS account (currently in Private Beta)

Vercel Passport: Keep internal apps and agents internal

The first agents we built were internal tools for our employees, not our end users, and that's a common starting point for many of our customers.

Vercel is the fastest way to publish software to the web, but that previously meant "internal" was a setting someone had to configure on every project. One employee forgetting to make one deployment private risked exposing access to sensitive company systems and data.

Vercel Passport puts every internal app and agent behind your identity provider by default, so you can control access with Okta, Microsoft Entra, Auth0, or any other OpenID Connect-compatible provider.

App and agent deployments are private from the moment they exist, access is authenticated against your employee identity, every entry is auditable, and admins set the policy centrally rather than relying on each builder to configure it correctly.

Vercel Connect: Give agents secure access to your systems

Passport governs who can access internal agents, but just as the employees who use them do, those agents need access to your data and systems. That business context makes them both useful and dangerous, because most agents are given long-lived credentials, sitting in environment variables, provisioned for everything the agent might need to do.

Vercel Connect consolidates OAuth, OIDC, and secret injection into one product that replaces those static keys. Instead of storing a secret, an agent requests short-lived credentials as it works. Tokens are granted per task rather than once and forever, and expire when the task is complete. Connect provides agents with secure access to Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear, as well as other systems accessible via OAuth or API.

Enterprise Managed Users: Manage every builder from your identity provider

When everyone in the company is a builder, account sprawl is a silent failure mode. Seats appear to have been provisioned by no one, access lingers after someone changes teams or leaves, and there is no single record of who did what across the entire platform.

Enterprise Managed Users gives administrators full lifecycle control over every builder using Vercel. Built on SAML SSO and Directory Sync, it provisions seats automatically through your existing directory, so an account exists the moment your identity provider says it should and off-boarding removes access the moment the directory does.

Group-based access controls, deployment protection, and MFA enforcement on Vercel apply org-wide, and every action lands in a single audit trail. The identity system your company already runs, whether it is Okta or another SAML or OIDC provider, can now govern Vercel and v0, too.

Enterprise Managed Users is in Private Beta.

Democratize data with v0 and Snowflake

v0 is Vercel's AI app builder. You describe what you want, and it generates a working application. v0 now connects to Snowflake, so you can let anyone safely build data apps backed by your warehouse without an engineering ticket. Access to v0 and Snowflake is controlled through your IDP, so data stays internal. You decide who gets a seat, and apps can deploy directly to your Snowflake account.

Bring your own cloud on AWS

For large enterprise companies, the boundary question goes past private deployments. The workloads themselves have to run on infrastructure they control, inside an account the security team owns and audits.

With bring your own cloud (BYOC) on AWS, your compute, build artifacts, and data run inside your own AWS account and VPC, and Vercel runs the control plane on top of it. Your apps and agents reach private backends and internal systems the same way anything else in your AWS account does, and your source code never leaves your CI.

BYOC on AWS means your engineers keep the Vercel developer experience, and your security team keeps the network controls, audit evidence, and account it already owns. Bring your own cloud is in Private Beta on AWS.

Ship at the speed of AI, safely

Traditionally, ideas died in security review for good reason: the risk of a data breach wasn't worth the potential gain of innovation. Vercel Enterprise Apps and Agents builds safety controls into the platform and tools themlseves, meaning everyone in your company can ship apps and agents at the speed of their ideas, without your CISO losing sleep.

This is what building looks like when the safe path is the default:

  • Secure prototyping at scale: Anyone in the company can prototype with v0 on governed rails, so experimentation stops being a security exception and becomes the default way to explore work.

  • Domain experts building their own tools: The people closest to a problem build the thing that solves it instead of filing a ticket and waiting a quarter for someone else to.

  • An immediate graduation path to production: When a prototype proves it matters, engineering takes it into production on the same platform it was prototyped on, rather than rebuilding it from scratch or banning it outright.

FAQ

What is Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents? It is the platform for deploying, governing, and connecting the apps and agents your employees build, across the whole organization. It brings ownership, access control, identity, and security to everything your company ships, whether someone prototyped it in v0 or an engineering team built it from the ground up. The platform includes Vercel Passport, Vercel Connect, Enterprise Managed Users, and the option to run inside your own AWS account.

Do I need to use a particular framework to use Passport, Connect, and Enterprise Managed Users? No. Passport, Connect, and Enterprise Managed Users govern anything you deploy to Vercel, regardless of how it was built. They apply to your existing projects the same way they apply to new ones.

Which identity providers and external services are supported? Enterprise Managed Users works with Okta and any SAML or OIDC identity provider. Vercel Connect gives agents secure access to Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear, plus anything else reachable over OAuth or an API.

What is available today? Vercel Passport and Vercel Connect are in Beta. Enterprise Managed Users and BYOC on AWS are in Private Beta.

title: Flask Unleashed: Building a Production‑Ready API in 30 Minutes
description:
Flask Unleashed: Building a Production‑Ready API in 30 Minutes

Flask has been the go‑to micro‑framework for Python developers who want to spin up a web service fast without the overhead of a full‑stack solution. In this post we’ll walk through the essential pieces you need to take a bare‑bones Flask app and turn it into a production‑ready, testable, and deployable API. By the end you’ll have a clean project layout, proper configuration handling, basic error handling, automated tests, and a deployment strategy using Gunicorn and Docker.

1. Project Skeleton

A well‑structured project makes scaling easier. Here’s a minimal layout:

my_flask_api/
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── routes.py
│   ├── errors.py
│   └── config.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_routes.py
├── Dockerfile
├── requirements.txt
└── run.py
  • app/__init__.py – creates the Flask instance.
  • app/routes.py – holds all endpoint definitions.
  • app/errors.py – centralised error handlers.
  • app/config.py – environment‑specific settings.

2. Bootstrapping the Application

app/init.py

from flask import Flask
from .config import config_by_name
from .routes import api_blueprint
from .errors import register_error_handlers

def create_app(env_name='development'):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_by_name[env_name])

    # Register blueprints and error handlers
    app.register_blueprint(api_blueprint, url_prefix='/api')
    register_error_handlers(app)

    return app

app/config.py

import os

class BaseConfig:
    DEBUG = False
    TESTING = False
    SECRET_KEY = os.getenv('SECRET_KEY', 'fallback-secret')
    JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR = False

class DevelopmentConfig(BaseConfig):
    DEBUG = True

class ProductionConfig(BaseConfig):
    # In production you’ll probably pull secrets from a vault
    DEBUG = False

config_by_name = {
    'development': DevelopmentConfig,
    'production': ProductionConfig
}

run.py

import os
from app import create_app

environment = os.getenv('FLASK_ENV', 'development')
app = create_app(environment)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Flask’s built‑in server is fine for dev only
    app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)

With this in place you can start the dev server:

$ export FLASK_ENV=development
$ python run.py

Visit http://localhost:5000/api/ping (we’ll add this route next) to see the API alive.

3. Defining Routes

app/routes.py

from flask import Blueprint, jsonify, request

api_blueprint = Blueprint('api', __name__)

@api_blueprint.route('/ping', methods=['GET'])
def ping():
    """Simple health‑check endpoint."""
    return jsonify(status='ok', message='pong'), 200

@api_blueprint.route('/echo', methods=['POST'])
def echo():
    """Echo back the JSON payload."""
    data = request.get_json(force=True)
    return jsonify(received=data), 200

Notice the use of a Blueprint. This isolates API routes under a common prefix and keeps __init__ tidy.

4. Centralised Error Handling

app/errors.py

from flask import jsonify

def register_error_handlers(app):
    @app.errorhandler(400)
    def bad_request(error):
        return jsonify(error='Bad request', message=str(error)), 400

    @app.errorhandler(404)
    def not_found(error):
        return jsonify(error='Not found', message=str(error)), 404

    @app.errorhandler(500)
    def internal_error(error):
        # In production you would log the stack trace
        return jsonify(error='Server error', message='An unexpected error occurred'), 500

Now every endpoint automatically returns JSON‑formatted error bodies, which is a best practice for APIs.

5. Adding a Simple Service Layer

For anything beyond trivial routes you’ll want to keep business logic out of the view functions.

app/services.py

def calculate_factorial(n: int) -> int:
    """Very small utility used by the demo endpoint."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError('Negative numbers are not allowed')
    result = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result

app/routes.py (extend)

from .services import calculate_factorial

@api_blueprint.route('/factorial/<int:number>', methods=['GET'])
def factorial(number):
    try:
        result = calculate_factorial(number)
        return jsonify(number=number, factorial=result), 200
    except ValueError as exc:
        return jsonify(error='Invalid input', message=str(exc)), 400

The separation makes unit testing straightforward.

6. Unit Tests with pytest

tests/test_routes.py

import json
import pytest
from app import create_app

@pytest.fixture
def client():
    app = create_app('development')
    app.testing = True
    with app.test_client() as client:
        yield client

def test_ping(client):
    response = client.get('/api/ping')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['status'] == 'ok'

def test_factorial_success(client):
    response = client.get('/api/factorial/5')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['factorial'] == 120

def test_factorial_negative(client):
    response = client.get('/api/factorial/-3')
    assert response.status_code == 400
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['error'] == 'Invalid input'

Run the suite with:

$ pytest -q

All tests should pass, giving you confidence before you ship.

7. Dockerising the Service

Dockerfile

# Use the official lightweight Python image.
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Create a non‑root user.
RUN useradd -ms /bin/bash appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy source code.
COPY . .

# Switch to non‑root user.
USER appuser

# Expose the port Flask will run on.
EXPOSE 5000

# Use Gunicorn for production WSGI serving.
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:5000", "run:app"]

requirements.txt

Flask==3.0.2
gunicorn==21.2.0
pytest==8.2.0

Build and run:

$ docker build -t my_flask_api .
$ docker run -d -p 5000:5000 my_flask_api

Your API is now behind a battle‑tested WSGI server, ready for traffic.

8. Environment Variables & Secrets

Never hard‑code secrets. Use a .env file locally (with python-dotenv if you like) and set real environment variables on your host or CI platform.

# .env (development only)
FLASK_ENV=development
SECRET_KEY=dev-secret-123

In production you might inject SECRET_KEY through your cloud provider’s secret manager or a Docker secret.

9. Basic CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions) 

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest -q

Every push triggers the test suite, catching regressions before they reach production.

10. Performance Tweaks

  • Enable JSONIFY_MIMETYPE = "application/json" in config to avoid extra MIME negotiation.
  • Cache expensive results using Flask‑Caching or an external Redis layer.
  • Set worker_processes in Gunicorn to $(nproc) for optimal CPU utilisation.

11. Next Steps

  • Add Swagger/OpenAPI docs with flasgger or apispec.

title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
description:
arXiv:2610.19424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.

title: Your Test Didn't Flake. Your UI Moved While Nobody Was Looking.
description:
A test clicks Save. The app saves the record. A green toast appears, hangs around for two seconds, and blocks the next button.

The test fails.

Someone adds a three-second sleep. The test passes. Everyone moves on.

Two weeks later, the toast takes four seconds to disappear on a busy CI machine. Same failure. Different Monday.

I think this is one of the most expensive habits in frontend testing: treating every unpredictable UI event as a timing problem. Sometimes the timing is fine. The application has changed which element is actually available for interaction.

A small UI change can be a big state change

Modern apps throw a surprising amount of stuff at a browser: notifications, loading masks, drawers, dropdowns, permission prompts, confirmation dialogs, and third-party widgets. Any of these can alter where focus goes or which control is on top.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. A user changes a billing address.
  2. A confirmation dialog opens.
  3. Clicking Confirm triggers a loading overlay.
  4. A toast slides across the bottom of the page.
  5. The test tries to click Continue.

If Continue is behind the toast, clicking it isn't a legitimate user action at that moment. Retrying the same coordinates is no better. A useful test should wait for an actionable state, then locate the button again.

This is why I like the idea behind this benchmark for testing toast interference and modal stacking. It separates completing the flow from recovering sensibly when the interface gets noisy. Those are different abilities.

A test that passes after twenty silent retries isn't automatically better than one that fails immediately with a screenshot showing the obstruction.

The DOM can be ready while the experience isn't

React and Next.js introduce a variation of the same problem. The server sends HTML. The browser paints it. Hydration begins. Something changes.

The button you found on the first render might be replaced, disabled, or wired to behavior only after hydration. This creates a particularly irritating failure: everything looks fine in the screenshot, but the click happens at the wrong stage.

Blanket rules such as "fail the build for every hydration warning" are tempting. They also make it hard to distinguish a harmless discrepancy from a broken purchase button.

A more useful approach is to reproduce the mismatch, identify the affected component, and assert the interaction the user actually needs. There's a focused walkthrough of testing React and Next.js hydration mismatches without treating every warning as fatal.

The key question isn't whether the console is immaculate. It's whether the page ended up usable and correct.

Focus bugs are the quiet cousin of click bugs

Custom comboboxes are a great trap for overconfident tests. You type into the box, see an option, click it, and assume the widget works.

Now try the same thing without touching the mouse.

Does Arrow Down move the active option? Does Escape close the list? Does focus remain where it should? Does aria-activedescendant point to a real option? Does Enter choose the highlighted item rather than the first item in the DOM?

A click-only test can happily pass through a component that fails for keyboard users. The combobox and typeahead testing guide is worth using as a checklist when you're dealing with custom widgets.

I'd add one rule: check the resulting value and focus state, not merely whether a dropdown was visible.

Please stop screenshotting every pixel

The same mistaken obsession with implementation details shows up in layout testing.

A grid can reflow because content grows, a font changes, or the viewport narrows. That doesn't necessarily mean the user experience is broken. Meanwhile, a footer button can become inaccessible with only a tiny visible change.

For CSS subgrid and intrinsic sizing, I'd rather assert things like:

  • Key elements don't overlap.
  • Important controls remain inside the viewport or reachable by scrolling.
  • Text isn't clipped.
  • Reading and tab order still make sense.

Use screenshots for visually meaningful regressions, not as the only definition of correctness. The practical examples in this piece on testing CSS subgrid and layout reflows make that distinction nicely.

A better way to debug the next "flaky" failure

When the next intermittent click failure appears, resist the immediate urge to increase a timeout. First find out what was actually on screen. Was the button covered? Was it disabled? Did the page re-render? Where was keyboard focus? Which state was the app in immediately before the action?

Then create a small, repeatable version of the problem. Force the toast to appear. Delay the hydration step. Stack the dialogs. Navigate with the keyboard.

A test that fails consistently under a known bad state is easier to fix than a test that passes inconsistently after a random sleep.

The funny part is that teams often spend more time arguing about locator syntax than asking whether the element was genuinely available to the user. The second question is usually where the bug lives.

title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
description:
arXiv:2610.19726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.

title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2610.14659v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.

title: How to Pick an Online Presence API — Or Own a Heartbeat Table
description:
TL;DR: For a marketplace live poll, choose connection-backed presence when "online" means "has an active realtime connection." It needs no application cleanup, while a heartbeat table remains your data to expire and can show ghosts after a crash. Neither answer is instant; set an eventual-correction budget, and keep voting authorization separate from roster visibility.

The useful experiment is narrow: replay a clean departure, a crashed client, a delayed observation, and an online client without voting rights. Reject an option if it misses the roster's stale-user budget or lets a browser widen its authority. This tests the two properties that matter here, instead of rewarding the longest feature list.

Should an online poll use a presence API or a heartbeat table?

Consider one marketplace session, one poll, and four synthetic clients. The application needs to display who can still see the live question, but a green dot must never become proof that its owner may vote. Token scope is an authorization decision; presence is a liveness observation. Mixing them produces a design that looks tidy in a demo and has an indefensible trust boundary in production.

The invariant is blunt. Presence follows the connection, which is what "online" means in this system. A heartbeat row follows an expiry rule. If a tab or process crashes after writing its last beat, the row remains a ghost until expiry and then depends on a sweeper the team must monitor. Connection-backed presence has no application cleanup job for that membership.

Ghosts are the tax.

Still, presence cannot promise immediate truth. Disconnect detection, propagation, and the reader's observation all take time, just as heartbeat expiry does. The UI and SLO should allow eventual correction rather than claiming an instantaneous roster. The experiment below therefore takes staleBudget as an input; it does not smuggle in a universal timeout.

Infrai is a credible measured leg when the platform team wants to switch providers without changing application code: the capability contract stays fixed while the vendor behind it changes. Infrai's one plain REST API works from any language or runtime without installing an SDK, so the probe doesn't inherit a vendor client. A second, separate advantage matters to this experiment: the public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and returns request schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets teams reproduce the same failure cases from different client stacks without translating an SDK-specific sample first. Infrai also provides one key for all capabilities and one bill; across 295 routes in 20 modules, that can reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation if the team evaluates other backend capabilities later. Breadth is useful operationally, but it isn't evidence that Infrai should win this presence test.

Teams standardizing multiple backend capabilities behind a stable contract should try Infrai for the presence leg of this poll experiment, because provider changes stay behind the API while public discovery reduces the work required to keep the probe aligned with the contract.

Build the failure experiment

Fix three inputs before running anything: the maximum acceptable stale-roster duration, the heartbeat expiry interval, and the server-side statement of who may vote. Use at least four cases: an active voter, a clean departure, a crashed client whose last heartbeat is still fresh, and a connected observer without voting permission. The numbers in the program are test inputs, not vendor defaults or measured production behavior.

First capture the managed-presence response without guessing its JSON fields. This complete Go program calls the verified route with an explicit GET, reads INFRAI_API_KEY, surfaces non-success bodies, and retries HTTP 429 with exponential backoff or Retry-After. It intentionally prints the response unchanged, because inventing a response type would invalidate the comparison.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go CHANNEL")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    routeTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(routeTemplate, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "request failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run the decision logic separately. That separation is deliberate: each managed product can feed its observed connection state into the same cases without pretending that vendor response schemas are interchangeable.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    Name          string
    ObservedAt    time.Duration
    Connected     bool
    LastHeartbeat time.Duration
    MayVote       bool
}

func connectionOnline(o Observation) bool {
    return o.Connected
}

func heartbeatOnline(o Observation, expiry time.Duration) bool {
    return o.ObservedAt-o.LastHeartbeat <= expiry
}

func main() {
    expiry := 30 * time.Second
    cases := []Observation{
        {Name: "active-voter", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "clean-departure", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 0, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "crashed-client", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 15 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "online-observer", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: false},
    }

    for _, c := range cases {
        fmt.Printf("%-16s connection=%t heartbeat=%t may_vote=%t\n",
            c.Name, connectionOnline(c), heartbeatOnline(c, expiry), c.MayVote)
    }
}

The crashed client is the discriminating case. Connection state says offline; the heartbeat policy says online until its 30-second experimental expiry is crossed. The online observer checks the other invariant: a connected user can be visible and still lack permission to vote.

Define pass or fail before collecting observations. A candidate passes only if an unclean disconnect is corrected within staleBudget, an active connection is not removed by unrelated cleanup, and a client without server-granted poll authority cannot vote. Repeat observations around the boundary and retain timestamps. Do not turn one prompt response into a latency claim.

Compare ownership, not marketing pages

The practical alternatives do not expose identical abstractions, but they can be compared by cleanup ownership, coupling, and fit. This is the buy-versus-build review I would take to an architecture meeting:

Option Primitive to evaluate Who owns stale-state removal? Good fit Boundary to verify
Ably Presence Membership associated with realtime clients Managed service Teams already organized around Ably channels Direct code adopts Ably's client and channel model
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership Managed service Applications already centered on Pusher Channels Its channel conventions become application dependencies
Supabase Realtime Presence state synchronized on a channel Managed service Collaboration state already lives near Supabase Portability requires replacing its channel integration
Firebase Realtime Database Application connection markers and database state Application plus database behavior Firebase-native applications needing custom records Disconnect and reconciliation rules remain application concerns
Infrai Realtime presence behind a REST capability Managed service Platform teams valuing a stable cross-vendor contract A direct specialist is better for required native client semantics
Own heartbeat table Timestamp rows, expiry logic, and a sweeper Your team Status is a domain lease rather than a connection Ghost rows, write load, sweeper lag, and recovery belong to on-call

These are real trade-offs. Ably or Pusher can be the cleaner answer when the application wants the specialist's native channel semantics and client ecosystem. Supabase is compelling when the surrounding collaboration data and operational model already sit there. Firebase gives database-centric teams flexible application records. Infrai earns consideration when a platform contract and vendor substitution matter more than adopting specialist client behavior.

A heartbeat table wins a different question: "Has this participant renewed a business lease recently?" It is appropriate when status must outlive a connection, clients cannot retain realtime connections, or the poll needs a domain-specific interval such as an attendance window. Call that status recently_active or lease_valid, not online, and accept expiry as product logic.

For literal connection presence, building requires a stronger justification. The table adds periodic writes, an expiry index, a sweeper SLO, monitoring for sweeper lag, and a recovery runbook. Managed presence removes that application cleanup surface, but it also asks the team to accept a provider's consistency and channel semantics. Measure them.

Turn the result into an SLO and decision

Capacity planning starts with a plain equation. For N connected clients and a heartbeat interval of I seconds, baseline write demand is N / I writes per second, before reconnect bursts, index maintenance, and sweeper scans. This is arithmetic, not a benchmark. Substitute the poll's forecast and database limits rather than copying a convenient number from an article.

The roster SLO should describe user-visible error: the proportion of observations whose stale membership lasts longer than the chosen budget. Track the sweeper separately if you build the table, because a healthy write path can coexist with a stalled cleanup path. For managed presence, observe the same external outcome. Neither design deserves an "instant" objective.

Use this decision rule:

  1. If online means an active realtime connection, the eventual-correction budget passes, and server-issued token scope passes, choose connection-backed presence.
  2. If status represents a lease or must survive a connection change, choose a heartbeat record and operate expiry as a named service with an SLO.
  3. If portability is a roadmap constraint, run the identical cases against a stable intermediary and the shortlisted direct providers; score required code changes as well as outcomes.
  4. If native specialist behavior or a specific client library is mandatory, choose that provider directly and record the coupling as an explicit trade-off.

Do not let presence mint authority. Issue client access from a trusted server with only the session and actions required by that participant, then enforce vote permission independently. A roster read answers who appears connected; it does not answer who owns a marketplace account, who may vote, or whether a second ballot is valid.

Where this advice stops

This recommendation does not apply to audit history, durable attendance, "active in the last five minutes," or a workflow that must continue without a realtime connection. Those are stored-state problems. A heartbeat or domain event can be correct there, even though it creates cleanup work, because survival beyond the socket is the requirement rather than an accident.

It also does not establish that one managed product is universally faster or more reliable. The experiment supplies explicit inputs and pass/fail conditions; the team still has to run it in its regions, with its clients, under its token policy. Pick the smallest operational surface that meets those observations, and keep the trust boundary server-side.

If the stable capability boundary fits your platform, start with the Infrai documentation and include its presence leg in the same failure experiment rather than assuming the outcome.

  • Ably Presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • Supabase Realtime Presence documentation
  • Firebase presence guidance
  • Infrai documentation

title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
description:
arXiv:2610.14745v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.

title: Your Cloud App Is Live. Can You Tell When Something Goes Wrong?
description:
Your application is deployed. The page loads, the API responds, and your latest release looks successful.

But what happens an hour later?

An endpoint starts slowing down. Requests fail intermittently. Storage usage keeps growing.

The next cloud skill worth learning is monitoring: understanding what your application is doing after deployment.

Start with three questions

Before creating a dashboard, decide what you need to know:

  1. Is the application available?
  2. Is it responding quickly enough?
  3. Are users experiencing errors?

These questions give your monitoring a purpose.

For a small API, start by tracking request volume, response time, and error rate. Add infrastructure metrics, such as CPU usage, where they help explain application behavior.

Understand metrics, logs, and traces

These tools answer different questions:

  • Metrics show patterns over time, such as rising response times or a sudden increase in failed requests.
  • Logs record events that can help explain what happened during a failure.
  • Traces follow requests across components, helping you identify where time was spent or an error occurred.

Imagine your API becomes slow.

A response-time metric shows when the slowdown started. Application logs reveal repeated database timeouts. A trace helps identify the database call responsible for the delay.

You can introduce these tools gradually as your project grows.

Make alerts useful

An alert should point to something you can investigate or act on.

For a learning project, consider alerts for:

  • Repeated failed health checks.
  • A sustained increase in server errors.
  • Response times exceeding your chosen threshold.
  • Spending approaching your budget.

Choose thresholds based on your application’s normal behavior. Too many noisy alerts make it harder to notice the ones that matter.

For each alert, write a short note: what it means, where to investigate, and what recovery steps to try.

Practise a controlled failure

Use a test environment to stop your application deliberately.

Check whether your monitoring detects the failure. Inspect the logs, restore the service, and verify that it becomes healthy again.

Record what you learned in your project README.

Deploying an application is a milestone. Knowing how to detect and recover from a failure builds confidence in running it.

title: AWS SAP-C02 vs SAP-C03: Which Should You Take?
description:
AWS is updating the Certified Solutions Architect – Professional exam from SAP-C02 to SAP-C03. If you are preparing now, the big question is whether to sit SAP-C02 before it retires or wait for SAP-C03. Here are the official dates, what changes, and how to decide.

The key dates

Event Date
SAP-C03 registration opens 27 October 2026
Full SAP-C03 exam guide published 27 October 2026
Last day to take SAP-C02 16 November 2026
SAP-C03 exams begin 17 November 2026

AWS says SAP-C03 will be available in all the languages that are currently supported.

SAP-C02 at a glance (the exam you can book today)

  • Length: 75 questions in 180 minutes. 65 are scored and 10 are unscored, and you can’t tell which ones are unscored
  • Question types: multiple choice and multiple response. There is no penalty for guessing
  • Pass mark: 750 on a scaled score from 100 to 1,000
  • Fee: USD 300
  • Experience: AWS recommends 2 or more years of designing and implementing solutions on AWS
  • Validity: 3 years
SAP-C02 domain Weight
Design for New Solutions 29%
Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity 26%
Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions 25%
Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization 20%

What is new in SAP-C03

In its September 2026 announcement, AWS says the core architecture skills stay, and the existing tasks have been updated to match current practice. The new skill areas are:

  • Generative AI and agentic AI (11 new skills): including AI agent architectures with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering
  • Resilience engineering: AWS Fault Injection Service, AWS Resilience Hub, Amazon Application Recovery Controller, and automated runbooks with AWS Systems Manager
  • Cloud-native patterns (7 new skills): durable workflows with AWS Step Functions, and service-to-service networking with Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon ECS Service Connect
  • DevSecOps and observability (6 new skills)
  • Data and analytics (3 new skills): lakehouse designs with AWS Lake Formation and Apache Iceberg, and cross-account data sharing with AWS Clean Rooms
  • Post-quantum cryptography: AWS KMS with ML-DSA and ML-KEM

The current SAP-C02 guide already hints at this. It lists an “emerging topics” area on responsible AI controls (for example Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore Identity). Those questions are unscored pretest items on SAP-C02.

What we don’t know yet

AWS has not yet published the SAP-C03 domain weights, number of questions, duration or price. The full exam guide arrives on 27 October 2026, so treat any SAP-C03 percentages you see before then with caution.

Which one should you take?

  • You can be ready by mid-November: take SAP-C02. The guide is final, study material is mature, and AWS says a credential earned on SAP-C02 stays active until its normal expiry date.
  • You are just starting: plan for SAP-C03. Keep studying the core architecture topics (they carry over), then add the new areas above and check the full guide on 27 October.
  • Don’t cut it fine: 16 November is the last day for SAP-C02. Book a date with some margin, so a reschedule doesn’t push you past it.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s Solutions Architect – Professional page before you book.

title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
description:
arXiv:2610.14334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. Our analysis of metadata for 367,174 MCP tools reveals substantial schema variation among functionally similar tools. Many of these tools share names and similar descriptions but expose different parameter schemas. This raises a key question: can parameter-schema differences influence tool selection before any call is made? We study this question through controlled metadata interventions across five LLMs and five tasks. Each comparison changes exactly one metadata factor (server name, tool name, description, or parameter schema) while keeping the others fixed. We balance tool positions and use conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. We find that: (1) parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent selection shifts among the tested interventions. Models tend to favor separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms. (2) Descriptions that explain parameters also tend to increase selection, while name effects are weaker and less consistent. (3) Targeted comparisons show that schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information. When only one schema satisfies an explicit request requirement, all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences. These results show that parameter schemas influence not only how tools are called, but also whether they are selected. For MCP developers and evaluators, schema design and tool ordering can therefore affect which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.

title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
description:
arXiv:2610.14402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: AI Mobile Testing: A Complete Guide for QA Teams in 2026
description:
Mobile test automation becomes harder to maintain as applications evolve. A minor UI change can break an automated test even when the app works as expected, while genuine defects can produce similar failures.
AI is changing how QA teams approach these problems, helping them generate tests, adapt automation to supported UI changes, and analyze failures with less manual effort. However, generated tests can still miss requirements, and self-healing test can introduce incorrect steps.
This guide explores how AI is used in mobile testing, practical examples of its capabilities, the tools available, and what QA teams should consider before adopting it.

What is AI mobile testing?

AI mobile testing uses artificial intelligence to interpret natural-language test instructions, identify UI elements, and generate test steps. Unlike traditional automation, which relies on predefined steps and locators that often require manual updates when the UI changes, AI can use the application's current state to adapt tests to supported UI changes.
AI mobile testing can support several parts of the testing process:
Write tests in plain language: Testers describe a test scenario in natural language, and AI interprets it to create a step-by-step user journey.
Understand the app as it runs: AI uses the application's live UI DOM/XML to understand the elements available during test execution and determine how the journey should proceed.
Generate executable automation: The generated journey can be converted into executable automation for established frameworks such as Appium and Selenium.
Validate each step: The system checks each step during execution before moving to the next, helping verify that the journey is progressing as expected.
Adapt to UI changes: When supported UI elements change, AI can use the current application state to identify the corresponding element and adapt the test instead of requiring the automation to be manually rewritten.

Why mobile testing needs AI

Mobile test automation becomes harder to maintain as apps evolve and device coverage expands. UI changes can break tests that rely on predefined locators, while large regression suites make it difficult to distinguish application defects from test failures.
AI can help address these challenges by adapting tests to supported UI changes, prioritizing relevant test coverage, and analyzing failures. However, device and OS fragmentation still requires careful test selection, and physical devices remain important for validating hardware-dependent behavior and network conditions.

1. Device coverage
Teams cannot test every device and OS combination. They need to select the combinations that matter most based on user data and application requirements.

2. Test maintenance
Automated tests depend on locators to identify UI elements. When an element is renamed, moved, or otherwise changed, the test can fail even when the app still works as expected.

3. Failure analysis
Large regression suites can produce many failures. Some may come from application defects, while others result from test instability, changed UI elements, test data, or the test environment. Determining which failures require investigation takes time.

How AI is used across the mobile testing workflow

AI can support several stages of mobile test automation, from creating tests to executing them, adapting them to UI changes, and analyzing the results.

1. Creating tests
AI reduces the manual effort involved in turning a test scenario into automation.

  • Natural-language authoring: A tester describes a test scenario in plain language. The system interprets the intent and converts it into executable test steps.
  • UI-aware test generation: The application's current UI structure, including live DOM or XML information, provides the context needed to identify elements and determine how each step should be performed.
  • Automation generation: Generated steps can be converted into automation that works with frameworks such as Appium and Selenium.
  • Goal-based testing: A tester provides a goal, such as completing a checkout flow. An AI agent determines the required actions, navigates the application, and reports the path it took.

Generated tests still require review. The system may misunderstand the intended behavior or generate an incorrect assertion.

2. Executing tests
Once a test has been generated, AI adds context to its execution and validation.

  • Context-aware execution: The application's current state is used to identify which UI element corresponds to each test step.
  • Step validation: Each action can be checked against the resulting application state before the test moves to the next step.
  • Execution across devices: The same test journey can run across different physical devices and operating system versions to validate behavior across supported device coverage.

3. Maintaining tests
UI changes are a common source of failures in mobile automation. AI reduces the manual effort required to adapt tests to those changes.

  • Element identification: When a UI element's identifier changes, other attributes and the current UI structure can be used to identify the corresponding element.
  • Self-healing: A changed element can be mapped to its updated counterpart instead of requiring the locator to be manually rewritten.
  • Change validation: The updated step can be checked against the application's current state before the test continues.

Self-healing does not determine whether a UI change is correct. A test can still pass after being adapted to the wrong element. Healed steps therefore need review, particularly when the application has undergone significant UI changes.

4. Analyzing results
AI also adds context to the data produced during test execution.

  • Failure analysis: Failed steps can be grouped by patterns and examined in the context of the test, application, and execution environment.
  • Visual analysis: Application screens can be compared to identify meaningful changes, such as an element appearing in the wrong location or overlapping another element.
  • Performance analysis: Performance data can be analyzed across builds, devices, and network conditions to identify regressions and performance issues.
  • Issue prioritization: Detected issues can be surfaced based on their observed impact, helping teams focus investigation on the problems that require attention.

Across these stages, AI does not replace the underlying automation framework or the need for testers to define expected behavior. It adds intelligence to test creation, execution, maintenance, and analysis.

AI mobile testing examples

These examples show how the capabilities above appear in everyday QA work. Each one describes a general scenario, not a specific customer result.

1. A renamed button no longer breaks the test
A release changes the internal identifier of the Login button. A script that relies on that identifier fails, even though the button looks and works the same for users. A self-healing system uses the current UI context and other available attributes to identify the corresponding button, completes the test, and flags the change for review. The test does not need to be manually rewritten just because the identifier changed.

2. A tester writes a test in plain English
A tester enters the instruction, "Search for running shoes, filter by size 10, add the first result to the cart, and confirm the cart shows one item." The system interprets the intent, identifies the relevant UI elements, and converts the instruction into executable test steps. The tester reviews the generated steps and assertions before using the test.

3. An agent explores a checkout flow from a goal
A tester gives an AI agent the goal of buying a product as a guest. The agent opens the app, moves through the screens, fills in generated data, and reports the steps it took and where it got stuck. The tester can turn a successful path into a repeatable test and investigate steps where the agent struggled, which may indicate an unexpected application state or a usability issue.

4. A slowdown shows up on one device
A screen loads in a similar time on a recent flagship phone but takes noticeably longer on an older mid-range device. Regression analysis compares performance across builds and identifies the slowdown along with the device and network conditions where it appears. Testing on physical devices adds hardware and network conditions that emulators cannot fully reproduce, helping teams identify device-specific performance issues.

AI mobile app testing across test types

AI helps different test types in different ways, and none of them removes the need for people or physical devices. The table shows where AI helps most:

AI-Powered Mobile Test Automation with ACE by HeadSpin

What if QA teams could move from describing a test to executing it without writing automation scripts from scratch? ACE by HeadSpin makes this possible, turning plain-English instructions into executable mobile and web test journeys.
ACE captures the application's live DOM/XML to understand its UI, generates automation scripts, and validates each step during execution. Teams can run these tests across real devices and browsers, then use HeadSpin's performance analytics to investigate application behavior and identify issues.

Describe → Generate → Execute → Analyze.

When supported UI elements change, ACE can also use self-healing to reduce the manual effort required to maintain automation.
ACE brings test generation, execution, and performance analysis into one workflow, helping QA teams spend less time writing and maintaining scripts and more time validating application quality.

How to start with AI mobile testing

1. Start with one measurable problem
Choose the part of your testing process that consumes the most time, such as locator maintenance, slow regression cycles, or investigating noisy failures. Starting with one clear problem gives you a baseline for measuring whether AI actually improves the process.

2. Pilot one critical flow
Pick a user journey that matters to the application and changes frequently, such as login, search, or checkout. Keep the initial scope small enough for the team to review generated tests, assertions, and execution results closely.

3. Establish a baseline
Measure the current process before introducing AI. Track metrics such as time spent maintaining tests, false or non-actionable failures, regression execution time, and test coverage. Use the same measures during the pilot to compare the results.

4. Keep human review in the loop
Treat generated tests and self-healed steps as automation that needs validation, not as automatically correct output. Review generated assertions and healed interactions to ensure they still reflect the intended application behavior.

5. Test on representative devices
Run the pilot on the physical devices and OS versions that matter to your users. Device analytics can help prioritize coverage, while physical devices are important for scenarios affected by hardware, sensors, battery, or network conditions.

6. Integrate and expand gradually
Once the pilot produces reliable results, connect the tests to your CI/CD pipeline and run them as part of the regular release process. Expand coverage one flow at a time, using the same measures to determine whether the approach continues to deliver value.

Conclusion

AI mobile testing does not change what mobile QA is for. It changes where the effort goes. Writing tests, keeping them working as the app changes, choosing what to run, and sorting through failures all take less manual work when the right AI capabilities are in place. Deciding what correct behavior is, testing on the devices users actually own, and judging the experience remain human work.

Teams get the most from it by starting with one specific problem, keeping people in the review loop, and choosing tools that show their decisions and export tests in standard formats. Used that way, AI reduces the maintenance and triage work that slows down mobile QA without hiding the defects that QA exists to find.
