title: Postgres SMS Alert Service Alternative — Startup App Receipts for Property Viewings
description:
Keep property-viewing message templates in the application, put suppression and send intent in Postgres, and treat the SMS provider as a replaceable delivery adapter. TL;DR: for a healthtech startup coordinating property viewings, the simplest defensible design is an app-owned template rendered into an immutable message snapshot, an idempotent send command, and a polling worker that records delivery evidence. Choose a polling-oriented API when uncomplicated wiring matters more than live event streams or multi-channel journeys.

This decision keeps the business contract stable while the vendor behind delivery changes. It also draws a hard line around what a delivery receipt proves: transport state, not that a patient, caregiver, or agent read the message.

Which SMS alert service alternative should a startup app choose?

The first invariant is suppression before dispatch. A recipient who has opted out, or whose number has been classified as invalid, must not receive another viewing confirmation merely because a job was retried. Maintain the provider suppression state, but mirror the decision in an application ledger so that the send path has a local, auditable gate.

The second invariant is that one business event creates one send intent. Use a stable key such as viewing-confirmation:{viewing_id}:{recipient_id}:{template_version}; store it under a unique constraint before making the network call, and carry an idempotency key through any provider adapter that supports one. Exactly-once delivery over a network is not a credible promise. Exactly-once intent plus deduplicated side effects is the useful target.

The third invariant is evidence preservation. Store the rendered body, template version, consent basis, destination in the minimum form your retention policy permits, provider message identifier, state transitions, and timestamps. Do not overwrite sent with delivered; append a transition. Compliance limits still apply: delivery logs can contain personal data, so retention, access, redaction, and regional handling need explicit policy rather than an indefinite debug table.

Failure boundaries follow from those invariants. The database owns eligibility and intent; the adapter owns submission; the receipt worker owns observations. A timeout after submission is ambiguous, so a blind second send is unsafe. A missing receipt is unknown, not failed. Keep it that way.

No guesswork.

Template ownership decides the architecture

The central choice is not the smallest advertised per-message rate. It is who owns the template contract and therefore controls versioning, review, localization, evidence, and migration.

Option Template ownership Receipt model Best fit Boundary to accept
Twilio Messaging Application or provider-managed content, depending on the product selected Status callbacks are documented Teams wanting a mature messaging-specific surface and push-style status handling The application still needs its own consent, suppression, and audit model
AWS End User Messaging SMS Application-centered message construction with AWS-managed origination resources Delivery event destinations are documented AWS-centered systems that already operate IAM, CloudWatch, or event destinations More cloud resource configuration enters the delivery path
Vonage SMS API Application-owned message content Delivery receipts are documented Teams wanting a focused SMS API with asynchronous receipt handling Vendor-specific receipt semantics belong behind an adapter
Infobip SMS Application content plus platform messaging features Delivery reports are documented Programs likely to grow into broader communications workflows The larger platform surface may exceed a small alert service's needs
Infrai Application-owned template snapshot behind one REST API Polling, with no webhook event push A startup prioritizing one credential, explicit sender setup, suppression APIs, and a stable contract when the underlying vendor changes It is a poor fit when webhook receipts, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or provider-hosted journeys are required; receipt latency is polling-bound and cost attribution stays local

Sender setup is part of the system, not an onboarding footnote. Registration rules differ by destination and use case, so model a sender as a deployable dependency with states such as requested, active, and retired; never let production choose an arbitrary sender string. Geographic anti-abuse limits and country-level spend circuit breakers also belong in the application layer. That is particularly important when US and EU traffic share one product workflow but do not share one regulatory regime.

The comparison favors different answers under different constraints. Twilio or Vonage is a natural fit when callback-driven receipts are a firm requirement. AWS is coherent when operational ownership is already concentrated there. Infobip earns consideration when SMS is likely to become a wider engagement program. SendGrid, Postmark, Resend, Mailgun, and Amazon SES solve email delivery, so they are not substitutes for an SMS alert service; they belong in a separately owned fallback path if email is required. A polling-first unified API is reasonable when a small team values a stable backend contract and accepts delayed state convergence, but its limitations rule it out when immediate event push is a product requirement.

The critical path in Go

The first runnable program below makes the actual SMS request without inventing a vendor request schema. Set INFRAI_SMS_JSON to a JSON object produced against the current public discovery schema; the program verifies that it is an object, submits it with Bearer authentication and an idempotency key, checks every response, and backs off on HTTP 429. INFRAI_BASE_URL is explicit because this independent article does not link to the service. The response is retained as raw evidence rather than decoded into fields that were not specified here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || len(body) == 0 {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and INFRAI_SMS_JSON are required")
    }
    var object map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &object); err != nil || object == nil {
        panic("INFRAI_SMS_JSON must be a JSON object matching the current discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "viewing-confirmation-viewing-482-recipient-19-v3")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    panic("send remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The next program demonstrates the application contract boundary. The in-memory maps stand in for Postgres unique constraints and append-only tables, making the ordering visible without hiding it in framework code. Swap MockAdapter for the HTTP adapter above; the domain service remains unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type State string

const (
    Accepted  State = "accepted"
    Delivered State = "delivered"
    Bounced   State = "bounced"
)

type SendCommand struct {
    IntentKey       string
    Recipient       string
    RenderedBody    string
    TemplateVersion string
}

type Receipt struct {
    ProviderID string
    State      State
    ObservedAt time.Time
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(context.Context, SendCommand) (string, error)
    Receipt(context.Context, string) (Receipt, error)
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu          sync.Mutex
    suppressed  map[string]bool
    providerIDs map[string]string
    transitions map[string][]Receipt
}

func (l *Ledger) reserve(cmd SendCommand) (string, bool, error) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.suppressed[cmd.Recipient] {
        return "", false, errors.New("recipient suppressed")
    }
    if id, exists := l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey]; exists {
        return id, false, nil
    }
    l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey] = "pending"
    return "", true, nil
}

func (l *Ledger) recordID(intentKey, providerID string) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.providerIDs[intentKey] = providerID
}

func (l *Ledger) appendReceipt(r Receipt) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.transitions[r.ProviderID] = append(l.transitions[r.ProviderID], r)
}

type MockAdapter struct{}

func (MockAdapter) Send(_ context.Context, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    return "msg-" + cmd.IntentKey, nil
}

func (MockAdapter) Receipt(_ context.Context, id string) (Receipt, error) {
    return Receipt{ProviderID: id, State: Delivered, ObservedAt: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

func dispatch(ctx context.Context, ledger *Ledger, sms SMSAdapter, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    id, reserved, err := ledger.reserve(cmd)
    if err != nil || !reserved {
        return id, err
    }
    id, err = sms.Send(ctx, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    ledger.recordID(cmd.IntentKey, id)
    return id, nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := &Ledger{
        suppressed:  map[string]bool{},
        providerIDs: map[string]string{},
        transitions: map[string][]Receipt{},
    }
    cmd := SendCommand{
        IntentKey:       "viewing-confirmation:viewing-482:recipient-19:v3",
        Recipient:       "+15555550199",
        RenderedBody:    "Your property viewing is confirmed for 10:30 AM.",
        TemplateVersion: "v3",
    }
    id, err := dispatch(context.Background(), ledger, MockAdapter{}, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    receipt, err := (MockAdapter{}).Receipt(context.Background(), id)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    ledger.appendReceipt(receipt)
    fmt.Printf("%s %s\n", receipt.ProviderID, receipt.State)
}

Production Postgres changes two details. Reserve the intent with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and use an outbox worker so a committed intent cannot be stranded between the transaction and the network call. Encrypt or tokenize recipient identifiers according to the threat model; a hash alone may still be personal data when the input space is enumerable.

That ordering is the design.

Polling needs restraint. Schedule the next check with backoff and jitter, stop at a documented terminal state, and cap the observation window. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present; otherwise back off exponentially. The worker must persist each raw observation before advancing its cursor, because audit trails assembled after the fact are usually incomplete.

Bounces, invalid numbers, and cost attribution

“Bounce” is email vocabulary, but the operational response maps cleanly to SMS: normalize a terminal invalid-recipient result into a suppression reason, record its source, and block future sends before dispatch. Keep provider-specific status strings in the evidence record while exposing a small internal state machine to product code. That preserves detail for reconciliation without coupling every caller to a vendor taxonomy.

Do not suppress on every non-delivery. Temporary carrier conditions and an invalid destination have different consequences, and the adapter must translate only documented terminal outcomes. Likewise, an opt-out suppression should not be silently removed by a later profile edit. Require a new, auditable consent event.

Cost attribution needs its own ledger because the unified option does not expose tag-level aggregated cost reporting. Record tenant, campaign, intent key, and the returned per-call cost metadata in the same reconciliation stream; aggregate locally. Finance can then reconcile totals against the provider bill without making mutable message tags the accounting system of record.

Why reject provider-owned templates here?

Provider-owned templates can be valid. They reduce application rendering code, and they are attractive when non-engineering teams must edit copy inside an established communications platform, especially for multi-step journeys with provider-side approval workflows.

I would reject them for this confirmation path because a property-viewing event already originates in the application, while the audit record must preserve the exact content and consent decision associated with that event. Splitting template history between the database and a provider console complicates replay analysis and vendor migration. It also makes the adapter contract larger than Send(rendered message).

There is a limit to this decision. If a jurisdiction or message class requires provider-hosted, pre-approved content, compliance wins; store the provider template identifier and immutable version evidence beside the intent. Application ownership is an architectural preference, not permission to bypass sender registration or local messaging rules.

The final rule is compact: own eligibility, content snapshots, idempotency, and audit history; rent transport. Select the transport whose receipt model and sender-registration workflow match the operational team. For this startup-shaped alert path, polling is an acceptable trade when it buys a smaller integration surface and the product does not promise real-time delivery state.

References

  • Twilio, “Outbound Message Status in Status Callbacks”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/guides/outbound-message-status-in-status-callbacks
  • Twilio, “What is the SMS character limit?”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit
  • AWS, “Amazon SNS SMS delivery status”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats.html
  • AWS, “AWS End User Messaging SMS User Guide”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sms-voice/latest/userguide/what-is-service.html
  • Vonage, “SMS delivery receipts”: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Infobip, “SMS delivery reports”: https://www.infobip.com/docs/sms/delivery-reports
  • PostgreSQL, “INSERT”: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html
  • IETF, “Retry-After” in HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-retry-after

title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

title: Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition: Separating Selection from Redistribution in Training-Data Filtering
description:
arXiv:2610.19343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how training mass is distributed across those regions, so a gate-versus-random comparison does not isolate these mechanisms. We introduce Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition (CGSD), a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution and decomposes the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction. The practical constraint is finite-pool realizability: we characterize mass and token-assembly conditions under which the required arms can be constructed, together with a support-extinction case in which the ordinary design is undefined. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, the mean within-support selection component is the only one that exceeds its calibrated null band (+29.7 and +5.6 holdout items; 30/30 positive replicates), decisively in Korean-English and marginally in Korean-Japanese; redistribution and interaction remain unresolved at the available power. The same pattern holds for a second, unrelated gate family -- a model-confidence threshold rather than a deterministic verifier -- judged against its own null (+27.3 items, 9/9 positive), so the result is not a property of one gate's mechanism. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget, while the extended design is constructible only inside narrow budget bands that an exhaustive scan locates and that the natural operating point misses -- the assembly condition separating a property of the pool from a limitation of the packer. CGSD therefore returns a decomposition, a constructible-but-underpowered design, or an explicit non-constructibility result, and says which; it prevents support redistribution from being silently interpreted as sample-level gate quality.

title: Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters
description:
title: "Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-24T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [systemdesign, backend, redis, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of system design architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Comparing Rate Limiting Algorithms: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Implementing Atomic Sliding Window With Redis Sorted Sets (Zadd: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Zremrangebyscore): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Memory Footprints: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: System design Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Comparing rate limiting algorithms, implementing atomic sliding window with Redis Sorted Sets (ZADD, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), and memory footprints."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: I Turned 44 Blog Posts Into a Frontend Roadmap You Have to Pass
description:
It's Sunday night, the interview is on Thursday, and the frontend roadmap in your other tab has more topics than you have evenings. You're sure about half of them and fairly sure about the rest.

The roadmap can't tell you which "fairly sure" is real. It only knows what you ticked.

So test the topics before you read them. Here's what that looks like for HTML: ten questions drawn at random, seven right to pass, and the whole stage counts as cleared.

No account and no reading, just ten questions. Here's why that beats a checkbox, and how it works.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself overstates what you know, using a 2006 study of re-reading versus testing
  • Compare seven well-known frontend roadmaps and courses on price, sign-up, checks, skipping and certificates
  • Use checkpoints to skip the stages you already know and find the gaps you don't
  • Compute learning progress from quiz attempts instead of storing it
  • Tell when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead

Who this is for

You've shipped frontend code for a year or more, in Vue or React, and you want to find out quickly what you actually know: for an interview, a promotion or your own peace of mind. If you build learning tools, read "Under the hood". If you're starting from zero, read "When not to use it" first.

Table of contents

  • Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working
  • What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses
  • Where today's options break
  • The mental model
  • Enter the Frontend Developer path
  • How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps
  • Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts
  • When not to use it
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working

Strip a self-marked roadmap down to its data, and this is all of it:

type Status = "done" | "learning" | "skipped" | "pending";

const progress: Record<string, Status> = {
  "semantic-html": "done",  // ticked two years ago
  "event-loop": "done",     // read the article, felt fine
  promises: "skipped",      // "I use them every day"
  specificity: "pending",
};

Every value in that object is an opinion, typed in by the person it describes. Nothing can make it wrong, and that is the bug.

It fails in three ways:

  1. "done" records reading, not knowing. Reaching the end of an article and answering a question about it are different events. The tick records the first one.
  2. "skipped" is a guess, in both directions. You skip HTML because you've written it for years. Whether you know what inert does, or what showModal() gives you that show() doesn't, the tick can't say. Some of what you skip, you don't know; some of what you re-read, you did.
  3. Nobody else can read it. A lead, a mentor or an interviewer can't tell your "done" from anyone else's.

The fix isn't a better checkbox. It's taking the checkbox away from the person being measured.

What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses

Here's how the best-known options handle it, checked on their own pages on 14 October 2026:

Free? Account How your learning is checked Skip what you know Certificate
roadmap.sh frontend roadmap Yes; AI quizzes: 2 on the free plan, unlimited on Pro ($10/month) To save progress You mark topics done; AI quizzes and self-graded flashcards sit alongside Mark a topic "skipped" yourself None found
freeCodeCamp v9 certifications Yes To save progress Questions after every lesson, 20-question module quizzes, 5 projects, then a 50-question closed-book exam No placement test found Yes, free
The Odin Project Yes Optional, to check off lessons Projects, compared with other students' solutions Cherry-pick lessons and projects "We don't provide a certificate"
MDN Curriculum Yes No Not graded: a syllabus with recommended resources, plus "Test your skills" self-checks in MDN's Learn modules A self-paced reading list None
Codecademy Front-End Engineer No: Pro, from $15.99/month billed annually Yes 103 quizzes, 77 projects, certification exams "Skip ahead to the exam" Professional certification (Pro)
Scrimba Frontend Developer path No: subscription Yes Coding challenges inside the screencasts, solo projects, some quizzes None found Certificate of completion
Frontend Mentor learning paths Mostly To submit (GitHub login) Feedback on what you build: the community, plus AI review (1 a month free, every solution on Pro) Pick any challenge None found

Three of these deserve more than a row.

roadmap.sh is the best map of what to learn. Its roadmaps are free, the project has 369K GitHub stars, and the site counts more than 3.2 million registered users. If you want to know what exists, look there first; nothing here argues against it.

freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications are the most rigorous free credential in that table, and more rigorous than the quizzes in this article. The new Responsive Web Design certification ends each lesson with three comprehension questions and each module with a 20-question quiz (18 right to pass). Then it asks for five certification projects before a 50-question, closed-book exam: one attempt a week, reviewed by staff before the result is released.

The Odin Project is right about proof. It gives no certificate because, in its FAQ's words, "Employers will be much more impressed with your amazing personal portfolio of projects." Projects are the strongest evidence anywhere in that table.

Where today's options break

None of these is broken. The gap only shows when you want four things at once: free, no sign-up to start, a check on every step, and a skip you have to earn.

On roadmap.sh you mark a topic done. Its AI-generated quizzes sit beside the roadmap rather than gating it: two on the free plan ("These don't reset"), unlimited on Pro at $10 a month. freeCodeCamp checks properly, but it is built to take you from the start: its own figure is 300 hours per certification, and the exam waits for five projects. Right for learning, heavy for finding out what you already know.

Codecademy built exactly the skip I wanted ("Don't waste time learning what you already know") and put it behind Pro, from $15.99 a month billed annually. The Odin Project and MDN Curriculum have nothing to pass, Scrimba is paid, and Frontend Mentor checks what you build rather than what you know.

No single piece of what I built is new; quizzes, skipping, forks and certificates all exist in that table. What I couldn't find among those seven was all four together.

The mental model

The mental model: reading is input, answering is evidence, and progress should be computed from the evidence, never typed in by the person being measured.

The evidence isn't only for other people. Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, Test-Enhanced Learning (Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255), compared re-reading with testing. On a test five minutes later, re-reading came out ahead. Two days later, and again a week later, testing did, even though re-reading had left students more confident. No feedback was given in that study: nobody told the tested students what they had missed.

Three things follow:

  • Skipping is evidence arriving early. If you can pass the check without reading, the reading would have been re-reading, the strategy that lost at two days and at a week.
  • A check can be open-book and still be a check. Its job is to make you answer, and to show you exactly where you couldn't.
  • Failing is the useful part. A wrong answer that arrives with an explanation is a reading list. A tick never told you anything.

Enter the Frontend Developer path

I'd already written the articles. Between July and October, 44 of my posts each taught one piece of frontend, from the native <dialog> to the back/forward cache, and every one has a quiz. What they lacked was an order, and a reason to take the quiz.

So I put them on a map: a free frontend developer roadmap on bestpractic.org, where every step is an article and a quiz you have to pass. Read it. Pass it. Unlock the next stage.

Honestly, in one sentence: 44 existing articles and their 336 quiz questions, in 7 stages that each close with a checkpoint, free, with no account needed to start, about 16 hours by the site's own estimate, and 7 more levels still being written.

  • 🗺️ The map: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer
  • ⏭️ The HTML checkpoint: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer/checkpoint/html
  • 1️⃣ Level 1, the native <dialog>: https://bestpractic.org/blog/dialog-element-native-modal?path=frontend-developer
  • 📚 All learning paths: https://bestpractic.org/paths

How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps

Step 1: the map

The route has seven stages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Vue or React, Nuxt or Next.js, TypeScript, and Ship it, the production stage. The two forks make nine stage cards, each pair sharing one tier of the map: Nuxt follows Vue, Next.js follows React, and TypeScript opens from either side.

The longest route is 34 levels, through Vue and Nuxt; through React and Next.js it is 33. JavaScript includes the event loop, Next.js starts with Cache Components, and TypeScript with generics. Seven more levels show as "Being written": from-zero openers for HTML, JavaScript, Vue and React, then the box model and cascade, Flexbox, and inferred type predicates.

Key concept: the percentage measures your route, not the whole map. Each tier counts once, so finishing one branch is 100%.

Step 2: a level is an article plus its quiz

Each level is one of the 44 articles plus its quiz: 6 to 9 questions, four options each. The article's badge says where it sits ("Level 1 of 4 in HTML"). Pass the quiz at 70% to clear the level. Your best score counts, retakes are unlimited, and each cleared level leaves a crystal on the map, gold at 100%.

Answers stay hidden until you submit. Then every question is explained: why the right option is right and, if you picked another, why yours was wrong. Two-thirds also link to a source, mostly MDN and the frameworks' own docs.

Levels open one at a time. A locked one is still readable: its drawer offers "Read it anyway", because every article is free.

Key concept: the lock orders the route; it never hides the article. A quiz you passed before its level opened, from the blog, say, still counts.

Step 3: the checkpoint, and how to skip a stage

Every stage ends in a checkpoint: 10 questions drawn at random from that stage's level quizzes, a fresh draw on each attempt, 70% to pass. The last one, Ship it, draws 15. Beat it, and the stage is clear and the next one opens.

A checkpoint is open from the moment its stage is. That's the skip from the top of this article: "Know HTML? Skip it" goes straight there, and a pass clears HTML without a single level. The levels stay open, so you can go back for the crystals; skipping earns none.

Fail it, and the review explains every question; the next attempt is a new draw. One honest caveat: a checkpoint has no questions of its own, so if you have just cleared every level in a stage, you have already met every question it can ask.

Key concept: a checkpoint is a placement check built from the stage's own quizzes. It asks the same of someone who read everything and someone who read nothing.

Step 4: your run, and the finish line

No account is needed to start: a guest's run is saved on that device for a year, in a cookie set when you first start a quiz. Sign up, and your guest attempts move to your account, run and all.

The "Your run" card does the arithmetic. Clear level 1 and you're at 3%: one of five units in HTML (four levels plus the checkpoint), averaged over seven tiers. Beat the HTML checkpoint and you're at 14%.

You finish by beating one checkpoint per tier: seven passes, at least 75 questions. The certificate needs a free account and lives at a public link (/certificates/BP-…) that anyone can open to check it. It states what it certifies: earned by every checkpoint.

Key concept: finishing is defined by checkpoints alone, which is why a skipper and a completionist end up at the same finish line.

Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts

If you build learning tools, this is the part worth taking.

Progress is computed, not kept. The map never reads your progress from a table; every load works it out again from the map and your best attempt at each quiz. The real path-progress.ts is covered by 13 Vitest cases. This simplified sketch follows the same rules:

// A simplified sketch of path-progress.ts. The real one also places the "You"
// marker, follows the branch you started at a fork, and marks perfect scores.
type Stage = {
  slug: string;
  tier: number;              // forks share a tier: Vue and React are both 4
  unlockedBy: string[];      // [] for HTML, ["nuxt", "nextjs"] for TypeScript
  checkpoint: string;        // the checkpoint's quiz id
  levels: (string | null)[]; // level quiz ids in order; null = "Being written"
};
type Attempt = { quiz: string; score: number; maxScore: number };

export function pathProgress(stages: Stage[], attempts: Attempt[]) {
  // 1. Only your best attempt at each quiz counts, wherever you took it.
  const best = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const { quiz, score, maxScore } of attempts) {
    best.set(quiz, Math.max(best.get(quiz) ?? 0, (score / maxScore) * 100));
  }
  const passed = (quiz: string) => (best.get(quiz) ?? 0) >= 70;

  const ordered = [...stages].sort((a, b) => a.tier - b.tier);
  const cleared = new Set<string>();
  const levels = new Map<string, "open" | "locked" | "cleared">();

  for (const stage of ordered) {
    // 2. A stage opens when ANY stage in its unlockedBy is cleared.
    const open = stage.unlockedBy.length === 0 || stage.unlockedBy.some((s) => cleared.has(s));
    // 3. Its checkpoint, and nothing else, clears it.
    if (open && passed(stage.checkpoint)) cleared.add(stage.slug);

    // 4. Levels open one at a time. A "Being written" level is skipped: it blocks nobody.
    let previousPassed = true;
    for (const quiz of stage.levels) {
      if (quiz === null) continue;
      const ok = passed(quiz);
      levels.set(quiz, ok ? "cleared" : open && (previousPassed || cleared.has(stage.slug)) ? "open" : "locked");
      previousPassed = ok;
    }
  }

  // 5. Percent along your route: each tier counts once, scored by its best
  //    stage, and a checkpoint is worth one level.
  const tiers = [...new Set(ordered.map((s) => s.tier))];
  const tierScore = (tier: number) =>
    Math.max(...ordered.filter((s) => s.tier === tier).map((s) => {
      if (cleared.has(s.slug)) return 1;
      const written = s.levels.filter((q): q is string => q !== null);
      return written.filter(passed).length / (written.length + 1);
    }));
  const pct = Math.round((tiers.reduce((sum, t) => sum + tierScore(t), 0) / tiers.length) * 100);

  return { cleared, levels, pct };
}

That one decision pays for four features:

  • Guests get a working map with no account, because their quiz attempts were already rows, keyed to a cookie.
  • A quiz passed on the blog before the path existed counts the day the path does.
  • Adding a level needs no backfill.
  • Signing up keeps the run, because the run was only ever the attempts.

A signed-in run also writes its latest percentage to an enrollment record, after the fact; the map never reads it back. The rest follows the same instinct:

  • The map is the same for everyone; you are fetched. The server renders the map without anyone's progress in it, so every visitor gets the same one. Your place on it arrives after hydration, and the default is a newcomer's view, so a first visit never shows padlocks flicking open.
  • Looking costs nothing. The progress endpoint never sets a cookie. The anonymous ID is only set when there is something to save, like a quiz attempt, so a crawler that only looks never gets one.
  • Forks are data. Each stage lists the stages that open it (unlockedBy), and the map draws one road per entry: the line, the fork and the join, from one rule.
  • Checkpoints are assembled, not written. Each release builds a stage's checkpoint from its level quizzes. They issue no certificate of their own; the path certificate is the proof.
  • The catalogue is code. A level whose article isn't written yet shows as "Being written" and blocks nobody. Publishing that article and its quiz under the planned slug is all the map needs; the next release picks it up.

When not to use it

Here's when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead.

  • You're starting from zero today. The from-zero openers aren't written yet, and the first live level, the native <dialog>, assumes you've built a modal before. Start with the MDN Curriculum, free and beginner-level, or freeCodeCamp for questions after every lesson, and come back for the checkpoints.
  • You learn by building. A quiz checks understanding, not whether you can ship a page. The Odin Project is free and project-based, and Frontend Mentor gives you real designs to build, with feedback on the result.
  • You need a closed-book credential. These quizzes are open-book and unsupervised. freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications end in a closed-book exam and cost nothing.
  • You learn from video. Every level here is text. Scrimba's Frontend Developer path is about 81 hours of interactive screencasts, on a paid plan.
  • You want the whole map of the field. This is one path through 44 articles; roadmap.sh shows everything around it.
  • You work in Angular or Svelte. The forks are Vue and React only.
  • You'll switch devices before signing up. A guest run lives in one browser, and clearing its cookies loses it. Create the free account first.

FAQ

Is this frontend roadmap really free?

Yes. Every article, quiz and checkpoint on the path is free, and so is the account the certificate needs.

Do I need an account to start the frontend roadmap?

No. A guest run is saved on that device for a year. A free account carries it to every device, keeps what you did as a guest, and is required for the certificate.

How long does the frontend developer roadmap take?

The site estimates about 16 hours for one route; the read-time labels alone add up to 324 minutes on the Vue route and 302 on the React one. Skip everything you can, and the floor is seven checkpoints: 75 questions.

Should I learn Vue or React first?

The path doesn't rank them. Both open when you clear JavaScript, and TypeScript opens after either Nuxt or Next.js, so neither branch is a dead end. Pick the one your job, or the job you want, uses; your percentage only counts one branch.

Can I skip HTML and CSS?

Yes, if you can pass their checkpoints, 7 of 10 on each. Beat HTML's and CSS opens; beat CSS's and JavaScript opens. A stage only counts once it is open, so you skip in order.

What happens if I fail a checkpoint?

Nothing is lost. The review explains every question you missed, and you can retake it straight away: each attempt is a new random draw, with no cooldown and no attempt limit, and your best result counts.

Is the frontend developer certificate worth anything?

It records one thing: that the named account passed one checkpoint per stage at 70% or better, open-book, at least 75 questions in all. Anyone can open its public link to check it. It is not a closed-book credential; freeCodeCamp's is the free one built for that. Treat it as a receipt, not a diploma.

Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

The numbers below come from the live map as of 14 October 2026; "live levels" counts written levels only.

Stage Live levels Checkpoint Two example levels
1 · HTML 4 10 questions, 7 to pass Native <dialog>, The inert attribute
2 · CSS 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Specificity with :where(), Viewport units: dvh, svh, lvh
3 · JavaScript 6 10 questions, 7 to pass Closures, The event loop
4 · Vue (or React) 6 10 questions, 7 to pass ref vs reactive, Composables & shared state
4 · React (or Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Re-render vs remount, React Compiler
5 · Nuxt (after Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass useAsyncData keys, Hydration mismatches
5 · Next.js (after React) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Cache Components, proxy.ts
6 · TypeScript 3 10 questions, 7 to pass Generics, satisfies
7 · Ship it 5 15 questions, 11 to pass Core Web Vitals, Web Workers

That's 44 written levels across both forks, 34 on the Vue route and 33 on the React route, plus 7 being written.

The rules in five lines:

level       article + quiz (6–9 questions). Pass at 70%; your best attempt counts.
order       Levels open one at a time. A locked article is still free to read.
checkpoint  10 random questions from the stage (15 for Ship it). 70% clears it.
skip        A checkpoint is open as soon as its stage is. Beat it early to skip.
finish      One checkpoint per tier. Certificate: free account, public link.

Key takeaways

  • A tick you give yourself records what you read, not what you can answer. Compute progress from answers.
  • In Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, re-reading won at five minutes; testing won at two days and at a week, with no feedback.
  • Skipping is evidence arriving early: pass the check, and the reading was optional.
  • Building a learning tool? Store the attempts and derive everything else.

Back to Sunday night, and the roadmap that only knows what you ticked. Spend the first evening on checkpoints instead of chapters. The stages you pass are done, and the ones you fail hand you every missed question, explained: a better reading list than a column of ticks ever was.

Which checkpoint do you think you could pass without reading anything, and which one would surprise you?

Written with AI assistance; every fact checked against the live site and primary sources.

🚀 Want more like this? Every guide, playground, and quiz lives on bestpractic.org — open it and sign up free so the next one finds you.

Thanks for reading! Let's stay connected:

  • ⭐ GitHub — follow me and star the projects: github.com/parsajiravand
  • 📸 Instagram — frontend best practices, daily: @bestpractice___

title: Textbook Conventions vs. Creative Niche Layouts: A Front-End Engineer’s UX Dilemma
description:
We’ve all been there. You get a new freelance client—maybe a boutique local bakery, a high-end tattoo parlor, or a trendy fitness studio. You open up your code editor, full of creative energy, ready to build a bespoke, visually breathtaking masterpiece with asymmetric grids, smooth custom animations, and a completely unique navigation experience.
Then, reality hits.
You remember the cardinal rule of user experience: “Users spend most of their time on other sites.” (Shout out to Jakob’s Law). If your website layout forces them to relearn how to browse, they don’t marvel at your creativity—they just bounce.
As front-end developers, we constantly walk this tightrope. Do we build the predictable "Textbook Layout" that converts like crazy but feels generic? Or do we build a highly customized "Niche Layout" that looks amazing but risks confusing the average user?
Let’s break down this UX dilemma and look at how we can balance engineering creativity with real-world business conversions.

📘 The Case for the "Textbook" Layout (The Safe Bet)

The textbook layout is the UI blueprint we can all code in our sleep. Logo in the top left, nav links spread across the right, a massive hero section with a crisp H1 and a primary Call-To-Action (CTA) button, followed by a predictable 3-column feature grid.
From an academic and conversion standpoint, this layout is undefeated for a reason: Cognitive Load is zero.
When a user lands on a standard layout, their brain doesn't waste energy figuring out how to use the site. They instantly scan in an F-shape pattern, consume the value proposition, and know exactly where to click.

The Problem? It’s Boring.

If every local accountant, plumber, and consultant uses the exact same template, the web becomes a homogenous sea of sameness. As developers, building these sites feels like assembly-line work. It starves our creative problem-solving.

🎨 The Case for the "Niche" Layout (The Creative Risk)

On the other side of the coin, we have industry-specific, niche layouts. These designs completely throw out the generic blueprint to prioritize the absolute most critical action for that specific business type.
• For Restaurants: Bypassing traditional informational blocks to place a responsive, interactive menu and a sticky "Order Online" widget directly in view.
• For Photographers/Agencies: Swapping standard text containers for immersive, full-screen masonry grids where the imagery dictates the UI flow.
• For Salons/Clinics: Building the entire homepage experience around a persistent booking calendar API.
text
[ Textbook Layout ] [ Niche Layout (e.g., Restaurant) ]
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Logo Nav Links │ │ Logo [ORDER NOW] │
├─────────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────────┤
│ Hero Image │ │ [ TODAY'S SPECIALS ] │
│ [Learn More CTA] │ │ - Dish 1... $12 │
├─────────────────────────┤ │ - Dish 2... $15 │
│ Feature1 Feature2 Feat3 │ ├─────────────────────────┤
└─────────────────────────┘ │ 📅 [Book a Table Widget]│
└─────────────────────────┘
Use code with caution.
When done right, a niche layout feels incredibly premium. It creates an instant vibe that aligns with the business identity, drastically improving brand retention.

The Catch? Over-Engineering & Friction

If you make a layout too clever—like hiding the main menu behind an experimental, floating interactive particle bubble—you break the user's mental model. If a hungry customer can't find a restaurant's phone number or address within five seconds because it's buried in a parallax scrolling animation, they will leave and order from a competitor.

🤝 Resolving the Dilemma: The "Hybrid" Approach

So, how do we build something that looks fresh without killing our client’s conversion rates? We use a hybrid approach: Standard Architecture, Niche Execution.
Keep the structural skeleton predictable so the user never feels lost, but use your front-end skills to inject personality into the visual components, micro-interactions, and asset layouts.

A Quick Example: A Clean Tailwind Service Grid

Instead of a boring, static 3-column card section, you can keep the standard grid layout but make it feel incredibly intentional and polished using modern CSS and subtle transitions:
html

<h3>Our Niche Service</h3>
<p>Familiar layout structure, but the micro-interactions feel distinctly modern and premium.</p>
<a href="#book">
  Book Now <span>→</span>
</a>

Use code with caution.

🛠️ The Developer's Rule of Thumb

Before you start writing code for your next client project, ask yourself these two questions to choose your layout path:

  1. Is the user's intent informational or transactional? If they just need to find a phone number or a list of services (like a law firm), stick to a Textbook layout. If they are there to execute a highly specific task (like buying a shirt or booking a haircut), pivot to a specialized Niche layout designed around that action.
  2. Will this layout decision scale? Niche layouts often rely on third-party APIs and complex database states. If the small business owner doesn't have a developer on retainer, keeping the layout simple and standardized ensures they can maintain it long after you hand over the repository. What about you? Do you lean toward strict UI conventions for maximum conversions, or do you like to push the boundaries of layout design for your clients? Let’s talk in the comments! 👇 #ux #frontend #webdev #css

title: No Bootstrap, No Principal: The Day My Audit Log Became Fiction
description:
My v0.1.0 series couldn't talk about authorization, because there wasn't any. v0.2.0 shipped RBAC-lite, scoped API keys, and an encrypted secret vault on HivePlane — and the first thing the field test taught me is that attribution has a cold-start problem.

I shipped a control plane with roles, permissions, and an audit trail — and for an hour, none of it was reachable, because there was no way to mint the first API key.

This is the article about the prerequisite for every governance claim I made in the earlier series: a principal. Without one, your audit log is fiction.

The cold start

The finding was D-10. RBAC was wired. /auth/login existed. Scoped keys were implemented. And the entire model was unreachable end-to-end, because there was no HTTP bootstrap to mint the first admin key. The roles existed; nobody could assume one.

The fix was a dev-grade env admin key — boot the first principal from the environment, then issue scoped keys from there:

# the first principal has to come from outside the API
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ENABLED=true
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ADMIN_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
# now you can POST /keys to issue scoped, tenant-bound keys

The lesson is that authn is the admission gate for the operators. Until there's a principal, every "who did this" question is unanswerable, and every other governance feature is theater.

The audit log that named the wrong person

Then I found the worse one. Pause, resume, stop, kill-switch, quarantine — every privileged operator action — was attributed to a client-supplied actor field. The caller put --operator alice in the request. The audit log recorded alice. Any caller could sign an action as anyone.

tip: A who column populated by the request body is a confession that you don't know. The actor must come from the authenticated principal, not the payload. A client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction.

Findings #560, #561, and #541 were all the same shape: the action was real, the attribution was a string the caller chose. The fix is that the principal resolves the actor; the field is read-only. You can attribute an action to yourself. You cannot attribute it to someone else.

The endpoints that had no permission at all

Then the field test found the gaps RBAC was supposed to cover and didn't:

  • #537 — registry mutation endpoints had no permission checks. A viewer could DELETE /workloads.
  • #526 — destructive immune-system endpoints (quarantine, kill-switch) were ungated.
  • #563 — pause/resume/stop had no permission gate; a viewer could stop any run.
  • #566 — the UI session secret shipped a hardcoded public default.

A role system that doesn't gate the destructive verbs is a role system in name only. The fix is server-side authorization on every privileged action: approve, promote, kill-switch. A viewer cannot approve. A viewer cannot stop. A viewer cannot delete a workload. The 401/403 is the product.

HMAC-first, not bearer-first

The one I didn't see coming was #515. With auth enabled, GitHub and Alertmanager webhooks got 401 before the HMAC signature was verified. The bearer-first model broke event ingest from ≥3 sources — which is a release gate. Triggers are the autonomy layer; if they can't authenticate, the fleet doesn't run itself.

The fix is that webhook ingest is HMAC-first, not bearer-first. The signature is verified before any bearer token is required; the trigger source is trusted by its HMAC, not by a login. Autonomy and authorization have to coexist, or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

What I learned

Bootstrap the first principal, or none of it exists — the env admin key is the admission gate for operators. Attribution comes from the principal, never the payload: a client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction. Gate the destructive verbs — a viewer who can delete a workload doesn't have a role, they have root. And webhooks are HMAC-first: bearer-first auth breaks event ingest, and autonomy and authorization have to coexist or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

The v0.2.0 field test asserts per-tenant budget/policy/key isolation with a viewer who cannot approve, and a secret that never appears in logs/traces/agent context (verified by test). Full evidence in the field-test report; the auth bootstrap and key-rotation runbook is at docs/runbooks/auth-bootstrap-and-key-rotation.md.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Auth bootstrap & key rotation runbook
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit design
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit (User Guide)

title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.

title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
description:
arXiv:2610.19164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
description:
arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.
