title: Your browser agent pays to look at pictures: opencli vs claude-in-chrome token use
description:
We run a lot of clickops through Claude Code: reading dashboards, checking settings, pulling a number out of a web app. There are two ways we do it. claude-in-chrome drives Chrome and can return screenshots. opencli drives the same logged-in Chrome but returns the page as text.

We wanted to know what each one costs in tokens, so we measured it.

What we measured

We went through our own Claude Code session logs: 7,500+ browser tool calls. For each call, we took the token counts the API reported before and after it. The difference is how many tokens that call's result added to the context.

These are real API counts, not character-based estimates.

Screenshots are the bill

claude-in-chrome call type Share of calls Median tokens per call
Returned a screenshot 23% 1,855
Returned text only 77% 373

A screenshot call cost about 5x a text call. The 23% of calls that returned screenshots made up 49% of all claude-in-chrome tokens.

An opencli call had a median of 397 tokens. That is about the same as a claude-in-chrome text call. The difference between the two tools comes from screenshots, not from the text.

Same sites, both tools

Nine websites had at least 10 calls with each tool. Here is the change in median tokens per call when we used opencli instead of claude-in-chrome:

Site claude-in-chrome opencli Change
telegram.org 1,879 275 −85%
github.com 580 336 −42%
cloudflare.com 578 378 −35%
google.com 605 437 −28%
linkedin.com 736 594 −19%
youtube.com 542 470 −13%
lokerdollar.com 432 386 −11%
nvidia.com 363 384 +6%
bing.com 270 353 +31%

opencli won on 7 of the 9 sites, about 27% fewer tokens per call when weighted by call count. The big wins were logged-in web apps like Telegram Web, GitHub and the Cloudflare dashboard. On simple public pages the two tools were even, and on Bing opencli used more. The nvidia.com and bing.com rows have under 30 calls each, so take them loosely.

Our clickops rule now

  1. Use the API or curl when one exists.
  2. Read the page as text with opencli.
  3. Take a screenshot only to check something visual.

Limits of this measurement

The site comparison matches calls by website, not by identical task. We did not run the same task twice with each tool, so this is a field measurement, not a lab A/B. Screenshot results also stay in context and get re-read on later turns. We left that out because session length differed between the tools, so the real cost of screenshots is likely higher than shown here.

title: Credential Stuffing Starts With One Reused Login: A Password Setup That Survives a Breach
description:
A small business almost never loses an account because one person picked a lazy password. It loses the account because nobody ever decided how passwords would work. A spreadsheet shared between three people, one password reused across the accounting tool and the inbox, a sticky note under the keyboard — that is the entire attack surface an outsider needs.

This is the practical version of that fix: what makes a setup genuinely safe, where a browser vault is enough, how to audit what you already have, how to hand access to staff without handing them your identity, and how to move everything to a new tool without spilling it on the way.

None of it requires enterprise software or a security budget. It fits in one working session on Windows, macOS, or a phone.

The chain reaction: one leaked login becomes five

The reason password reuse is so damaging is not the first breach. It is the automated retry that follows it.

When a site is compromised, the attacker walks away with a list of email addresses and matching passwords. Those pairs are then replayed against mail providers, banks, marketplaces, and admin panels by software that never gets tired. Security people call this credential stuffing. It works for one reason only: the same string opens more than one door.

Here is how the common habits compare once a leak has already happened.

Habit What a leak exposes Exposure
One password everywhere Inbox, banking, and client files at the same moment Critical
Written beside the machine Anyone standing in the room High
Stored in a shared file Everyone with the file, plus everyone who ever had it High
Unique passwords in one browser The single site that leaked Low
Unique passwords plus a second factor Not enough to sign in Lowest

So the target is not a clever password. The target is that no login shares a secret with another login, and that nobody has to hold those secrets in their head.

Stop treating a password as something you remember

Memorability and strength pull in opposite directions, and for years people were asked to satisfy both. Managers break that trade-off: the machine invents the string, the machine types it back, and the human only has to remember one thing — the key that unlocks the vault.

That single key deserves more attention than any individual site password. If it falls, everything inside falls with it.

What a browser vault really protects

Chrome, Edge, and Firefox all encrypt saved credentials into a local store tied to your operating system account. On Windows that store sits behind the OS credential encryption; on macOS it is tied to Keychain. A different person logging into the same machine with their own account cannot open it.

That protection depends on two conditions, and both are easy to break by accident.

  • The computer account itself has a password. A machine that boots straight to the desktop with no prompt has effectively published every saved login to whoever opens the lid.
  • That account is not shared. A single staff login with saved passwords is the same as leaving a printed list on the counter.

The browser also cannot defend a machine that is already infected. Malware running inside your own user session can read the vault, which is why patch level and working antivirus protection still matter next to any password plan.

The real gap is collaboration. A browser profile is built for one person on one device. It cannot grant a colleague access to one credential, revoke that access when they leave, or tell you who opened what. For a solo operator that is fine. Once two or three people need the same supplier portal or ad account, it stops being fine.

The quarterly check you can finish in one sitting

Chrome and Edge ship a free check that compares your saved logins against known breach data. It is the fastest way to see where the damage already is.

Run it and sort the findings into three buckets:

  • Compromised — that password appeared in a public leak. Replace it today, starting with mail and anything that moves money.
  • Reused — one string guarding several accounts. Split them, at minimum everywhere business-critical.
  • Weak — short or guessable. Replace these wherever customer data or payments are involved.

Then work in order of blast radius, not order of appearance.

  1. Primary email — it can reset almost every other account you own.
  2. Banking, payment processors, marketplaces — direct financial exposure.
  3. Ad accounts, social profiles, the domain registrar — a hijack here damages customers and brand trust.
  4. Supplier portals and rarely used subscriptions — lower stakes, still worth cleaning.

When you replace a password, take the generated suggestion instead of inventing one. Long random strings beat human-chosen ones outright, and since the vault remembers it, you never need to type it from memory. Repeat the exercise every quarter: breach dumps keep arriving, so a clean report this month proves nothing about next month.

Handing access to staff without creating a liability

Sharing is where most small teams quietly fall apart. The usual methods — a spreadsheet, a chat message, a verbal handover — fail in the same way. You cannot say who holds the credential, and you cannot take it back.

If sharing has to happen today, four rules limit the damage:

  • Never send a credential through chat or email. Both keep history forever, and both get compromised regularly.
  • Send a one-time link from a tool built for secrets instead of pasting the password itself.
  • Change the password the moment a role ends. No exceptions, no "we will do it later".
  • Prefer separate accounts over a shared one. Most platforms now support multiple users, which gives you per-person revocation and an actual trail.

For a team where more than a couple of people need the same access, this is where a dedicated manager starts paying for itself. Judge candidates on these capabilities rather than on the price of the cheapest tier:

Capability Why it decides the purchase
End-to-end encryption The provider cannot read your vault either
Shared folders Access is granted per team, not per password
Per-user permissions View or edit rights that can be withdrawn
Access log Who opened which credential, and when
Data export You can leave without losing the vault

Migration follows a fixed order: export from the browser, import into the new tool, confirm a few critical logins actually work, delete the export, then clear those entries from the browser so you are not maintaining two sources of truth.

The export file is the most dangerous thing in your backup folder

A vault can disappear with a failed disk, a Windows reinstall, or a corrupted profile. Back it up — but understand what the backup is. A CSV export holds every password as plain readable text. It is the single most valuable file on the machine to anyone who wants in.

Four rules apply every time you export:

  • Move the file out of Downloads immediately. It is the first place a stranger looks and the first place malware scans.
  • Never send it by mail or chat. Nothing encrypts it on the way.
  • Encrypt it before it sits anywhere long-term — inside a password-protected archive, on an encrypted drive, or in encrypted cloud storage.
  • Delete it after the import, including from the recycle bin.

For routine safety, syncing beats exporting. With sync on, credentials are encrypted before they leave the device and come back automatically when you sign in somewhere new. Keep the CSV route for genuine moves between tools.

Two habits make the whole arrangement sturdier. Turn on a second factor for the account that holds your synced vault, because that account now unlocks everything inside it. And keep recovery codes somewhere offline — a printed sheet in a locked drawer — rather than inside the mailbox those codes are meant to rescue.

A one-page policy for a team under twenty

A policy nobody follows is worse than no policy, because it buys the feeling of security without any of the substance. Keep it short enough to enforce and specific enough to check.

A baseline that holds up:

  • Every business service gets its own password. "Internal only" tools are not exempt.
  • Everyone uses a manager. Browser-based is acceptable at the start; move to a shared tool once more than a couple of people need the same login.
  • A second factor is mandatory on email, banking, ad accounts, and the domain registrar. Those four control everything else.
  • Access is granted to a person, never to a team. When someone leaves, disable their account instead of rotating one shared password.
  • Run the health check every quarter and fix the worst findings within a week.

Two smaller habits close most of what remains. Review active sessions monthly in your mail and cloud accounts — an unfamiliar device or city is the earliest sign of a takeover. And treat a sudden password prompt as a warning: if your browser stops autofilling on a site you visit daily, read the address bar before typing anything, because a lookalike login page is the standard way credentials get harvested.

Write the whole thing on one page and keep it where staff can find it. The point is not paperwork. It is making the safe option also the easy one, so following the rules costs less effort than ignoring them.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to let the browser save passwords?

For one person, or a very small team, yes — as long as the computer account has a password and is not shared. Those entries are encrypted and tied to your OS login, which beats reusing one string everywhere. The limit is collaboration: a browser cannot share one credential, revoke it, or produce a log, so move to a dedicated manager once several people need the same login.

A password of mine just leaked. What comes first?

Change that password, then change it everywhere you reused it. Start with the primary email, because it can reset everything else, then banking and payment services. Add a second factor so the leaked string alone is useless, and check active sessions so you can sign out anything you do not recognise.

Are CSV password exports dangerous?

Only if they are handled carelessly — but a CSV holds every password in plain text with no encryption at all. If you must export, get it out of Downloads, encrypt it before storing it, keep it away from mail and chat, and delete it after the import. For ordinary backup, syncing is safer because the data never leaves encrypted.

Should I invent my own passwords or accept the generated ones?

Accept the generated ones. They are long and unpredictable, while anything a person invents follows dates, names, or familiar words that attackers try first. The vault stores and autofills it, so memorising is no longer a requirement. Just protect the account holding your synced vault with a second factor.

How often should a small business review passwords and access?

Run the health check once a quarter and clear the highest-impact findings within a week. Review active sessions in mail and cloud accounts monthly, since an unrecognised device shows up before anything else. Review access every time a role changes or a person leaves. A quarterly rhythm catches new exposure without turning into a task people skip.

title: I turned my book recommender into an AI app in a day. Here are the two bugs that taught me the most.
description:
I read a lot of fantasy, especially romantasy, and I’ve always wanted to ask an AI for something specific, like “enemies to lovers in a fae court,” and get back real books, not made-up titles.

So I built BookDNA: it reads a book’s “DNA” (its tropes, setting, and tone), recommends books that match, and checks every single suggestion against Open Library, so it never recommends a book that doesn’t exist.

This week I turned it into an MCP server using mcp-use and deployed it on Manufact Cloud. Now any AI chat that supports MCP can use it.

What I built

Four tools an AI can call: search_book, get_book_dna, recommend, and recommend_by_tropes. The recommend tools return a small app that appears right inside the chat: a parchment shelf of book covers, each with a one-line reason it was picked.

My favorite moment: I tested it in Manufact’s Inspector chat using a GPT model, not Claude, and it worked perfectly. One server, any AI. That’s the promise of MCP, and seeing it happen was really satisfying.

Bug 1: only one cover showed up

My first shelf showed one cover and four broken images. Every book had a valid cover link, so the data wasn’t the problem.

It turned out that older Open Library covers redirect to a different server on archive.org. MCP App widgets run with a strict security policy that lists which sites they’re allowed to load images from, and I’d only allowed Open Library. The redirected images were silently blocked. The one cover that loaded was newer and didn’t redirect.

The fix was to allow archive.org too. I also added a fallback: if a cover ever fails, the card shows a parchment “title page” with the title and author instead of a broken image.

Lesson: if your widget loads images, allow every site in the redirect chain, not just the first one.

Bug 2: everyone shared one rate limit

The server is public, so I added rate limits to protect my AI budget, including a per-user limit. Testing it against the live deployment showed something I didn’t expect: the platform’s proxy rewrites the header that identifies the user, and the address I was reading belonged to the proxy, not the user. So every user was sharing one limit.

One small change fixed it, but I only found it because I tested against the real deployment instead of trusting my local setup.

Lesson: test anything that depends on request headers against your real deployment.

How I built it

I built this with Claude Code. I made the decisions, reviewed every change, and tested it myself, and I kept a “friction log” of everything that confused me along the way. A few items are already in this post.

Try it

GitHub: github.com/ksaivarsha/bookdna
MCP server: https://calm-wave-h30fs.run.mcp-use.com/mcp

If you build MCP Apps, I’d love to hear what tripped you up.

title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.

title: Copy-Paste Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
description:
arXiv:2610.19095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
description:
arXiv:2610.19494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time monocular human pose estimation is an important sensing component for human-centered intelligent systems. While recent camera-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy, fundamental challenges persist, particularly when visual observations are incomplete, such as during lower-body occlusion or short out-of-frame intervals. In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations. To systematically investigate this, we first collect a synchronized multimodal dataset and then propose a part-decoupled temporal fusion framework. The proposed model fuses foot-sensing features into the lower-body branch to compensate for incomplete visual evidence, while a lightweight coordinator exchanges information between the upper- and lower-body temporal representations to maintain whole-body consistency. The framework is evaluated with three representative real-time visual backbones based on 2D keypoints, 3D landmarks, and SMPL-based human mesh recovery. We evaluate our framework on three representative real-time visual backbones. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that incorporating simple foot sensors consistently improves pose accuracy, motion smoothness, and gait-related measurements over vision-only baselines, with the most significant gains observed under occlusion and short visual-dropout conditions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unobtrusive foot sensing provides vital and complementary physical observability when camera observations are temporarily unavailable.

title: Apple Messages for Business is not an iMessage API
description:
Most “iMessage API” products are a different system from Apple Messages for Business.

An unofficial sender uses Apple IDs or Macs to push blue-bubble messages. Apple Messages for Business is the channel inside the Messages app that a brand reaches through an approved Messaging Service Provider. It is how a customer starts a chat from a website, Apple Maps, Safari, or a Message Suggest result. It is not a public API key a brand calls on its own.

What a brand actually integrates

Apple does not give brands a standalone REST API. The MSP implements Apple’s server-to-server Messages for Business API. The brand connects to the MSP. Automation has to go through that MSP, with a live agent available during business hours, and the experience has to pass Apple’s Experience Review before it can go public.

The requirement list and the message flow are here: Apple Messages for Business API requirements.

Why the distinction matters

A blue-bubble sender will not put a business in Maps, will not add an Apple Pay button inside Messages, and will not survive Experience Review. If the job is customer-initiated support, booking, or commerce on iPhone, the path is an approved MSP.

A directory of those providers, compared by capability, is at amb.directory/msps.

Disclosure: I publish amb.directory, a directory of brands using Apple Messages for Business and the MSPs that implement the channel.

title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
description:
arXiv:2610.14523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.

title: Go Logistics Queue 2026: Publish Per Waiter Under Burst Recovery
description:
Short answer: send a small recipient-specific delta when a customer may see only their own queue position; send a whole-queue snapshot only to an authorized display that genuinely needs the entire ordered set. For a small SaaS, the least complex defensible design is usually a versioned delta plus a periodic or on-demand snapshot for repair. Every update carries a monotonically increasing queue version, clients reject older versions, and a detected gap triggers resynchronization.

The page says customer queue display stale, and the on-call sees an apparently healthy publisher beside a growing count of clients whose acknowledged version trails the current queue version. That is the useful symptom. A page based only on publish errors arrives too late, because a successful publish says nothing about whether the customer view converged.

The publisher was green.

This distinction drives the message-size comparison. A snapshot can repair state in one delivery but repeats data that most recipients neither need nor should receive; per-recipient deltas keep the hot path small but require explicit gap detection. Do the byte arithmetic with encoded messages, then choose the smallest disclosure boundary that still meets the recovery SLO.

Should a queue publish one message per waiter?

A logistics dispatch session is a state machine. A shipment request joins a queue, changes position, becomes ready, or leaves. The customer-facing display needs to converge on an authorized projection of that state. If one subscriber misses version 418, version 419 may still arrive, and a green publish counter can coexist with a wrong screen.

The signal that should fire earlier is version lag, measured at the receiving edge: current_queue_version - last_applied_version, grouped by session and bounded by the service-level objective. Transport acknowledgements help diagnose the path, but they do not prove that the UI applied the state. Define the SLO in terms of visible convergence, such as the proportion of active displays that apply the current authorized version within the chosen time window. The target and window must come from the product's tolerance for stale queue positions; there is no honest universal number.

Start with three counters: produced versions, applied versions, and resynchronizations. Add a histogram for convergence time and a gauge for connected displays by session. Do not put customer IDs into metric labels. High-cardinality identity belongs in sampled traces or structured logs with suitable access controls and retention.

One trap is paging on a single late client. A browser in the background, a device losing radio coverage, or a closed tab can all stop acknowledging progress without indicating a service-wide failure. Page on an SLO-burning cohort; retain per-connection lag for diagnosis. Otherwise the alarm measures client churn and trains the on-call to ignore it. The limitation of this cohort view is equally plain: aggregation can hide one customer who has been stale for a long time, so the dashboard still needs a longest-lag view even when that view does not page anyone.

Message size is multiplication, not a payload contest

Compare encoded bytes over the same observation window. Let S be encoded snapshot bytes, D encoded recipient-delta bytes, N connected recipients, C queue changes, and R snapshot repairs. Ignoring shared framing for a moment, whole-queue fan-out costs roughly C * N * S; recipient deltas cost roughly C * N * D + R * S. Add transport framing, authentication metadata, retries, and compression as measured terms rather than intuition.

For a capacity-planning example, suppose a test fixture has 80 waiting customers. Its encoded authorized snapshot is 6,400 bytes and its encoded per-recipient position update is 120 bytes. With 80 connected customers and 10 queue changes, the payload arithmetic is 5,120,000 bytes for repeated snapshots versus 96,000 bytes for deltas, before repairs and framing. These are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks. Serialize your actual schema because field names, identifiers, timestamps, and encoding choices change the result.

The ratio is informative; the absolute result decides capacity.

Eighty recipients matter.

Decision concern Recipient delta Authorized snapshot
Normal-path bytes Scales with the changed projection Scales with the full authorized projection
Recovery Needs gap detection and a snapshot fetch or push Replaces prior state when accepted
Ordering Version check is mandatory Version check is still mandatory
Privacy boundary Can disclose one customer's projection Must be filtered for the display's authorization
Server work More projections or routing keys Larger serialization and filtering work
Client work Apply a transition Replace and render state

Compression does not settle the architecture. It may reduce repeated fields in snapshots, but the sender still constructs the authorized payload and the receiver still handles it. Measure compressed and uncompressed sizes with representative data, then preserve hard limits for both. The trade-off is workload-dependent: a slowly changing, publicly visible depot board can make snapshots the simpler choice, while a private customer view with frequent position changes makes whole-queue publication inappropriate. Recipient deltas are not suitable when clients cannot preserve a version or request repair; snapshots are not suitable when their contents exceed the recipient's authorization boundary.

Instrument the version contract

The useful instrumentation sits beside the state transition. A message needs a session identifier, a queue version, a type, and the smallest authorized payload required for that recipient. This Go sketch shows application semantics, not a transport guarantee:

package queue

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Update struct {
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Version   uint64 `json:"version"`
    Kind      string `json:"kind"`
    Position  int    `json:"position,omitempty"`
}

type View struct {
    SessionID string
    Version   uint64
    Position  int
}

var ErrVersionGap = errors.New("queue version gap")

func Apply(view View, update Update) (View, error) {
    if update.SessionID != view.SessionID {
        return view, errors.New("session mismatch")
    }
    if update.Version <= view.Version {
        return view, nil // Duplicate or reordered old delivery.
    }
    if update.Version != view.Version+1 {
        return view, fmt.Errorf("%w: have %d, received %d", ErrVersionGap, view.Version, update.Version)
    }
    if update.Kind != "position_changed" {
        return view, errors.New("unsupported update kind")
    }

    view.Version = update.Version
    view.Position = update.Position
    return view, nil
}

Old duplicates become harmless, while a forward gap becomes observable and recoverable. The resync path returns an authorized snapshot with a version; the client replaces local state only when that version is newer. A reconnect begins the same way. The end-to-end claim should remain modest: the display converges under the retry and repair policy you test.

No version, no guarantee.

Persisting the state transition and publishing its notification in unrelated operations creates an ambiguity: either the state commits without an event, or an event escapes before the state does. A durable change record processed asynchronously can close that gap, provided its retry behavior and retention meet the recovery objective. Test the crash points around commit, publication, acknowledgement, and client application.

Test disorder deliberately. Duplicate version 418, deliver 419 before 418, disconnect after receipt but before acknowledgement, expire retained events, and reconnect from an older snapshot. Also test authorization changes during a session. A whole-queue payload cached under yesterday's access decision is a data exposure, not a harmless stale view.

Delivery guarantees belong in the buy-versus-build review

A managed transport can remove socket operations from the on-call queue; a self-hosted path can offer tighter control over retention, placement, and protocol behavior. Neither choice removes the application version contract. Ask where acknowledgement occurs, how long replay remains possible, what ordering scope exists, what happens under subscriber backpressure, and which side owns reconnect storms.

Operating question Managed path Self-hosted path Decision evidence
Who pages for saturation? Service boundary may absorb part of it Platform team owns the full path Documented responsibility and drill results
Can retention meet repair time? Constrained by the offered contract Configurable within team capacity Tested maximum disconnect window
How is lock-in contained? Adapter and export paths matter Protocol and storage choices still create coupling Recovery exercise using the abstraction
What is the real cost? Usage plus integration and incident work Compute, storage, upgrades, and on-call load Same traffic model and staffing assumptions

WebRTC data channels are one standards-based option for peer-to-peer data exchange, and the W3C specification defines their behavior and API surface. That does not make a peer mesh the default for a customer queue: topology, authorization, discovery, and recovery remain system responsibilities. Apply the same encoded-byte and convergence tests to any transport.

The deployment gate should include a shadow calculation of both message shapes against production-like fixtures, a load test with synchronized reconnects, and a rollback rule tied to convergence rather than publisher throughput alone. Capacity must include headroom for repair traffic. If every client requests a snapshot after a brief network interruption, the recovery path can become the largest burst in the system.

Set the alert where action changes

Use recipient deltas for routine customer updates when authorization is narrow and changes are frequent. Use a versioned snapshot for initial load, verified gaps, and displays authorized to render the whole queue. If a client cannot implement version checks and repair, repeated snapshots may be simpler, but account for disclosure and fan-out before accepting that simplicity.

Then tune the page. An alert threshold below the normal tail of client behavior creates noise, interrupts sleep, and consumes the same engineering capacity needed to improve recovery. A threshold that waits until many displays are stale protects the pager while abandoning the SLO. Start from the error-budget burn that requires human action, validate it during disconnect and reconnect drills, and keep lower-severity signals on a dashboard for trend work.

False positives have a concrete cost: an engineer investigates transport health while the underlying event is a backgrounded browser or a session that has already ended. Filter inactive sessions, distinguish disconnected from connected-but-behind, and require enough affected traffic to justify a page. The final architecture is credible only when its alert points to an action the on-call can take.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
description:
arXiv:2610.19291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.19419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.

title: MonoMIP: Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping for Monocular 3D Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.19071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monocular 3D object detection methods increasingly rely on depth-guided transformers, but they operate entirely in the perspective image plane where spatial relationships are distorted by foreshortening. We propose MonoMIP, a dual-decoder framework that adds complementary 3D geometric reasoning through Bird's-Eye View (BEV) features constructed via Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping. We perform IPM at K elevation planes spanning ground to rooftop, producing an ordered stack of height-conditioned metric BEV features that reduces above-ground misprojection and exposes depth-dependent appearance variation across planes. A BEV decoder with multi-scale deformable attention aggregates this multi-height evidence per query, while a depth-guided 3D decoder provides complementary perspective-space predictions. Without extra training data, MonoMIP attains 25.84% Moderate AP3D|R40 on KITTI val and 21.66% on the official test set for Car, outperforming recent published monocular methods on both the KITTI and Waymo benchmarks.

title: Building the MyZubster Metaverse: What We've Shipped and What's Next
description:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: What We've Shipped and What's Next

From account-linked experiences to distributed abuse protection — an open-source development update.

Over the past development cycle, we've made meaningful progress on the MyZubster Metaverse.

Our goal is not simply to build another virtual environment. We're exploring how a metaverse can connect people, independent projects, digital identities, knowledge, and real-world communities through an open-source ecosystem.

Here's what we've completed, what we've tested, and what still needs work.

✅ What we've completed

1. Account-linked Metaverse experience

The public Metaverse route is available at:

https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse

We have implemented and tested the account-linked flow, connecting the Metaverse experience with MyZubster's broader authentication and user ecosystem.

This provides a foundation for future interactions between digital identity, community participation, and independent projects.

2. Distributed rate limiting

One of our latest milestones is the implementation of MongoDB-backed abuse protection.

The system introduces rate limits for four Metaverse operations:

  • join — entering a session
  • sync — synchronizing session state
  • chat — sending messages
  • emote — submitting interactions

Using a shared MongoDB-backed limiter helps coordinate abuse controls across application instances instead of relying exclusively on individual server memory.

3. Privacy-conscious throttling

We've introduced HMAC-derived identifiers for throttling, rather than storing raw identifiers directly as rate-limit keys.

The implementation also includes:

  • Automatic TTL-based expiration
  • HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses
  • Retry-After information
  • Protection against spoofed proxy headers
  • Documented privacy and retention boundaries

These measures are intended to reduce abuse while limiting unnecessary retention of identifying information.

4. Fail-closed production behavior

During review, we identified an important issue: if MongoDB became unavailable, the limiter could fall back to local in-memory behavior.

We corrected this behavior so that the production configuration fails closed when the shared rate-limiting dependency is unavailable.

This is an important security trade-off: availability may be reduced during an infrastructure failure, but abuse protection is not silently weakened.

5. Automated testing and GitHub integration

The final development work included:

  • 21 backend test suites passing
  • 125 backend tests passing in the final local verification
  • Clean Git diff checks
  • GitHub pull request review and merge

The distributed abuse protection was merged through:

PR #30 — feat(metaverse): add distributed abuse rate limits

https://github.com/danieldirimini-myzubster/myzubster/pull/30

Merge commit: d911cadd824a1ca00b50cfead7929eb8f80934d0

This represents completed implementation work, not a claim that every production-readiness requirement has been satisfied.

⚠️ What still needs to be completed

1. Dependency security remediation

Our security pipeline continues to flag an existing dependency backlog.

The latest reported audit included:

  • 61 vulnerabilities in total
  • 43 high-severity vulnerabilities
  • 1 critical vulnerability

Some remediation paths involve potentially breaking dependency upgrades, including a major Hardhat migration.

We don't want to hide these findings or blindly apply incompatible updates.

Next step: review production versus development dependencies, assess actual exposure, submit targeted fixes, and rerun the security pipeline.

2. Final production verification

The pull request has been merged, but the final production verification was interrupted before completion.

We still need to verify the deployed commit, production health, and real behavior of the new rate limits.

3. Multi-user and load testing

Passing unit and integration tests is not the same as demonstrating scalability.

We want to validate:

  • Concurrent user sessions
  • Distributed synchronization
  • Chat and interaction throttling
  • MongoDB availability and recovery behavior
  • Performance under realistic traffic

4. Contributor-led testing

We're inviting open-source contributors to test the Metaverse independently, report reproducible bugs, review security assumptions, and improve documentation.

A useful contribution doesn't have to be a large feature.

A clear bug report, a failing test, or a small targeted pull request can move the project forward.

5. Independent infrastructure and decentralization

MyZubster is also exploring interoperability with contributor-owned infrastructure.

Our N4K48 pilot is an early step toward connecting independently managed projects and nodes.

However, an independently hosted VPS is not automatically a decentralized network.

We still need documented interfaces, tested recovery procedures, access controls, and independently reproducible interoperability tests.

This work remains in progress.

🌍 The bigger vision

We want MyZubster to become a place where people can connect their real-world activities, creative work, services, and technical contributions to a shared digital ecosystem.

The Metaverse is one component of that vision, alongside Zorgax, the Marketplace, and the Contributor Passport.

But our immediate priority is simpler:

Make the existing features reliable, secure, understandable, and useful before expanding their scope.

🤝 Join the development

We're looking for contributors interested in:

  • Security and dependency remediation
  • Backend and MongoDB testing
  • Metaverse frontend testing
  • Accessibility and user experience
  • Docker and infrastructure automation
  • Documentation and reproducible test cases

GitHub repository:

https://github.com/MyZubster-Ecosystem/myzubster

Contributor coordination:

https://github.com/MyZubster-Ecosystem/myzubster/issues/1609

Metaverse:

https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse

If you're interested, explore the repository, choose a focused task, and join the discussion.

We're building MyZubster in the open — one verified contribution at a time.

Daniel Ioni (h4x0r)

title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.19046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19387v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.
