title: Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II
description:
By Yogesh Nagarur

Introduction

In Part 1 of this series, we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII.

If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it.

Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime.

Let’s dive in.

A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata Registry

When an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two.

In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry, a Key-Value store:

  • When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry.
  • It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small.
  • Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event.

This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth.

But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear.

Why we needed to evolve

The forcing function was Live. Netflix’s live slate has grown rapidly, from NFL games to blockbuster fight nights to the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027, and viewership keeps growing. That traffic looks nothing like Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD): a single event can surge toward tens of millions of concurrent viewers within minutes, then drain just as fast when it ends. Building the ad pipeline for Live meant building for that trajectory.

To see why the old design could not get there, let’s put some numbers on it. When Netflix streamed the Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson fight to more than 100 million viewers, a single ad break at that scale would generate an enormous volume of ad events. Serving those ads in the old design would have meant writing metadata for each of them to the Metadata Registry and waiting for acknowledgment before the ads could serve: millions of must-succeed database writes per second on the ad-serving critical path. That pattern created three core problems at Live scale:

  1. It was a scaling bottleneck. Every ad and every ad break is a write. Multiply that by tens of millions of concurrent viewers, keep it non-lossy (a dropped write is a dropped ad, and lost revenue), add Live’s spiky on/off pattern, and the write load becomes enormous. But you cannot safely scale the registry up once the event starts. Adding nodes reshuffles data across the cluster to rebalance it, and doing that in the middle of a live event could slow or even fail the very writes you are adding capacity for. That leaves one safe option: pre-scaling for the peak in advance and hoping the forecast is accurate.
  2. Fewer dependencies on the critical path. Serving an ad meant a synchronous, must-succeed write to the registry, followed by a wait for its acknowledgment. Every system on the critical path is one more thing that can stop an ad from serving, and the metadata registry had no fallback, so an unhealthy registry meant serving stopped. Taking hard dependencies off that path was the goal, and the registry was the biggest one we could remove.
  3. It put event freshness at risk. If writing slowed down under load, or lookups timed out, events spilled into retries and dead-letter queues, and enriched ad events were delivered late. Some systems might be fine, but others, such as frequency capping, cannot. It needs events under a strict SLA to decide whether the next selected ad can run without breaking policies.

So we asked a simple question: the ad server already knows and logs everything about the ad it served. Does it really need to write that to a database on the hot path? Can we match that against the downstream Kafka stream of client events, which is always there, after the fact?

The write leaves the critical path entirely; no shared datastore outage can stop serving, and enrichment becomes something we scale elastically with Live rather than a cluster we babysit.

Matching two streams after the fact is a streaming join, and that is where Flink comes in.

Why Flink

We chose Apache Flink because near-real-time, stateful stream processing is exactly what it is built for, and because it has deep, production-tested platform support at Netflix. Just as important, we already knew how to run it. As Part 1 noted, our Ads Sessionizer is a large stateful Flink job, so operating one at scale, tuning state, checkpoints, and recovery under production load, was familiar ground for the team. Enrichment on Flink was built on that experience rather than starting from scratch.

The new architecture

At its core, the new Ads Event Publisher is built as an Apache Flink streaming job. Each event moves through a handful of stages:

  1. Normalize. Client events arrive from several sources, including SVOD, live, playback, and embedded ad breaks, each with a slightly different shape. We first normalize them into a common form.
  2. Re-route. Client events and response events may appear in different regions; we inspect and reroute them to the correct job-processing region for a successful join.
  3. Join. The heart of the job: we match each client event to the ad-serving response for the same impression, enriching it with the full serving context using a KeyedCoProcessFunction
  4. Deduplicate. Revenue-bearing events are de-duplicated, so nothing is counted twice.
  5. Publish. We extract measurement beacons for our partners and route the enriched ad event to its downstream consumers.

The join is the interesting part. Client events and ad serving responses arrive on separate streams at different times, so the job holds recent responses in memory and matches events against them over a 60-minute window. Three things can happen:

  • The response is already there when an event arrives → we enrich it on the spot.
  • The event arrives first → we hold it for a configuration duration (currently set to 60 minutes) until the matching response shows up, then enrich it.
  • No response arrives within the window → we mark the event as unmatched for later recovery.

We built the join as a custom Flink operator (a KeyedCoProcessFunction) rather than a built-in windowed join. We do not need a windowed join ordering and time-window semantics, since downstream consumers handle ordering; we simply match each client event to its response by key. Owning the operator at its lowest API form lets us control the matching state directly, including how long we hold it and what we do with an event that never matches. This allows us to tune retention per stream or persist unmatched events to a durable store later without rewriting the join. Our goal is always to build a strong base to reap the benefits later as we scale.

To make that concrete, picture a member watching a live game. When the ad server decides which ad to show, it logs its response, and a few seconds later, the member’s device fires a “first quartile” event carrying the opaque token. Both arrive at the job keyed to the same impression, and because the response is already waiting, the event is enriched on the spot with its campaign, creative, price, and tracking URLs, then published downstream in near real-time.

Why 60 minutes? Almost all events, roughly 99.999% of them, reach the job well before that, so extending the window further would only grow the state store and lengthen checkpoints for a vanishingly small gain. The remaining 0.001% still matters for precise billing and reporting, and we recover those events via a separate path described later on.

Cross-region: matching events where their data lives

The Metadata Registry handled cross-region enrichment for us because it was built on a globally replicated key-value store: a client event could land in any region and still find its ad’s metadata. Global replication was a feature the platform provided (see Netflix’s Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer), so serving an ad in one region and enriching its events in another was simply not something we had to think about.

A streaming join does not come with that convenience, and here the two sides of the join live in different places. The ad serving response stays in the region where the ad was served. The client event, though, is fired by the device, and the device can be anywhere: a member might start an ad on home wifi and switch to mobile data partway through, and that network change can route the event to a different region than the one that served the ad. So a client event is routed to a region that does not have the matching serving response.

The tempting fix is to stream every region’s serving responses into every other region so that each region can match any client event locally. We rejected it: that would mean every region storing every serving response worldwide, the vast majority of which will never be used in the join, which is wasteful in both cost and compute.

Instead, we treat this as a routing problem and route the client event rather than replicating the response. We encode the serving region into the ad token, so when a client event arrives in the wrong region, we forward it to the region that owns its response. For example, an ad is served in us-east-2, the member’s device switches from wifi to mobile data mid-ad, and the resulting event arrives in us-east-1. That region reads the token, sees the ad belongs to eu-west-1, and forwards the event back there, where its serving response is waiting. Only the small trickle of genuinely cross-region events pays for the extra hop.

Catching the long tail of late-arriving events

Sixty minutes covers the vast majority of events, but not all of them. A device may have been offline, an ad paused, or an engagement event delayed by hours. Rather than drop these stragglers, we set them aside and recover them through a companion path: an hourly Spark batch job, orchestrated by Maestro, Netflix’s workflow orchestrator, re-pairs each straggler with its serving response from our data warehouse (which has a far longer retention than our in-stream window) and publishes it through the same downstream sinks. This keeps the streaming job’s memory bounded while still catching the long tail.

This also lets us support event types that arrive well after the 60-minute window, including certain tracking-related events, while keeping the door open to extending the system to additional event types down the line and improving our match rate as needed. We also designed this offline job with reuse in mind: it can replay dead-letter queues and backfill historical data, giving us a single mechanism for both long-tail recovery and operational recovery.

What was hard

Beyond the architecture itself, three things took real work, and together they are what made the pipeline stable, correct, and safe to switch on.

Keeping the core lean.

Operating a stateful streaming join at live-event scale took real tuning, and most of our hard-won lessons come back to one idea: the job’s only job is matching events. Anything else we were tempted to bolt on, such as external lookups or incidental side-processing, was better moved off the hot path, or it eventually showed up as instability under load. Getting this right was the difference between a job that comfortably kept pace with live traffic and one that fell behind. It is unglamorous work, and it is most of the work.

De-duplicating Events

Duplicates are a fact of life here in an event processing pipeline. A client may retry an event, and our upstream delivery is at-least-once so that the same event can arrive more than once. For revenue-bearing events, the ones that feed billing, nothing should be counted twice.

The solution here is a simple and idempotent key. For each event, we compute a stable ID by hashing a few fields that uniquely identify it, such as the ad ID, the event type, and, for repeatable events, an offset or timestamp. The same underlying event always hashes to the same ID, so if we have seen an ID before, we drop the repeat.

What changed with Flink is where we remember those IDs. The previous design kept them in an external key-value store and did a check-and-write over the network for every event; Flink lets us keep that state local to the job instead. We key the stream by event ID, which routes every copy of a given event to the same place, and a local state store with a short time-to-live remembers the IDs we have recently seen. Keying by ID also removes the race the external store had to guard against, since a given ID is handled in only one place at a time, with no network hop on the hot path. Multiple improvements here alone.

We are deliberate about the guarantee: at-least-once delivery with best-effort de-duplication, not exactly-once. In-stream dedup removes the vast majority of duplicates within its window. However, a few can still slip past, for instance, through a cross-region reroute, a late-arriving recovery, or a restart that replays recent events. So we also carry the event ID through to the enriched ad event itself, which lets consumers who need exact counts, such as billing, run their own idempotent de-duplication over their own, longer windows.

Production Rollout

This was the most challenging part of the project. For a system that feeds billing and frequency capping, “trust me, the new one is correct” is not good enough, so we ran the Flink pipeline alongside the legacy one and made it earn its traffic.

Both pipelines continuously processed the full event stream, allowing us to compare them in real time: we published their outputs side by side. We ran automated audits that alerted us when the two drifted apart. Those audits earned their keep, surfacing subtle discrepancies we would never have caught from dashboards alone.

How do we know the enrichment logic between the two systems was equal for the audits to make sense? Early in development, we extracted that logic into a shared module that both the legacy service and the Flink job depend on, so any change to how an event is enriched is applied to both at the same time. A failure in the audits, therefore, pointed to a real difference in the pipeline mechanics.

Cutover was a separate question from comparison, and this is the part that warrants precision. We could not simply send a random percentage of events to each pipeline, because the same event landing in both would be double-counted downstream. Instead, the split was deterministic: a stable key on each event decided which pipeline was responsible for publishing it, so every event was published exactly once, even though both pipelines saw all of them. Raising the threshold moved events from the legacy pipeline to Flink a slice at a time, and we could dial it back instantly if anything looked off.

By the time we fully cut over, the two pipelines agreed on well over 99.99% of events, and we rolled it out region by region rather than all at once. Then came the satisfying part: we turned off the ad server’s writes to the Metadata Registry, and decommissioned the legacy service and the registry itself. The single point of failure on the ad-serving critical path is simply gone. One of the oldest ad serving components at Netflix was deleted.

Operating the Flink platform

Operating a large stateful streaming job in production is its own job, and we did not build that muscle alone. We leaned heavily on Netflix’s Flink platform team. Early on, the job’s checkpoints were slow and heavy. The first checkpoint in particular took a long time, and we were holding more state in memory than we needed. Working with the platform team, we trimmed the state, reduced checkpoint durations, and validated the gains in load tests. That is what keeps the job from stalling during Live bursts.

The same team also gave us operational scaffolding we did not have to invest in, including continuous delivery and canary deployments, so we could ship and roll out the Flink job with the same guardrails and confidence as the rest of our production systems. Netflix operates more than 25,000 Flink jobs (see Building a Scalable Flink Platform at Netflix), and that maturity is what we have to build on. We layered on custom canary metrics that catch issues before a release, CI/CD that lets us stagger rollouts, and a deploy flow that keeps the old job running until the new one has detected healthy checkpoints, so we never destroy a working job before the new job gives us the green light.

The results

  • Enrichment is off the critical path for ad serving. The ad server no longer performs a synchronous, must-succeed database write to serve an ad. It logs and moves on, and an entire class of “the lookup store is down, so ad serving is down” failures no longer exists.
  • Fewer systems, fewer schemas, fewer hops. We retired both the legacy service and the Metadata Registry.
  • Built for Live, and continuously tested for it. An ad break is what this service is designed to handle, so during our journey, we also ran large-scale load tests to simulate real-life traffic. In our latest load test, a single AWS region handled one ad break for a large concurrent audience, processing hundreds of thousands of events per second, joining the large majority of them against their serving responses in real time, and outputting enriched ad events at a comparable rate, all with negligible timeouts and errors. We test this throughout development and keep doing so as live audiences grow, and we are not at the ceiling yet.
  • We delivered the Part 1 roadmap. Live-stream ad events, in-stream de-duplication, and richer real-time enrichment all shipped on this foundation.

Key takeaways

  • Take the database off the hot path when you can. Our biggest win wasn’t raw performance — it was blast radius. Trading a synchronous write-and-wait for a fire-and-forget log plus a downstream join removed an entire failure mode from ad serving.
  • Match events where their data lives. Real-time joins beat global replication by routing events to their data rather than copying the data everywhere.
  • Earn the cutover. Running both systems in parallel and diffing their output on live traffic was slower than a flag-day switch — and it’s the only reason we trust the result.

What’s next

We have an exciting list of projects on the horizon: scaling the live path for the next tier of concurrent audiences, bringing the remaining delayed engagement events fully into the streaming world, reducing the Flink state size we need to manage, working on bringing even more resilience to the eventing processing pipeline, and continuing to add new event types and richer signals for our downstream consumers.

Re-architecting the engine of a running, revenue-critical pipeline in place was a real multi-team effort. If building real-time systems at this kind of scale sounds like your thing, Ads Engineering is hiring.

Acknowledgements

This was a multi-team effort across Netflix. Thank you to everyone who designed, built, validated, and operated the new pipeline:

Ads Engineering: Yogesh Nagarur, Kinesh Satiya, Jeet Mehta, Nitin Saini, Persis Shah, Guangyu Chen, Jimmy Liu, Riley Berton, Simon Spencer, Aadesh Patel

Ads Data Engineering: Eugene Yusim, Brandon Nicklas, Indu Narayan

Ads SRE: Max Michaels, Kevin Chung, Carlos Avalos, Brian Christie

Data Movement: Mark Cho, Herbert Wang, Shraddha Ladda, Nikhil Sulegaon, James Lubin, Daniel Trager

Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
description:
arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

title: Mastering Go: From Zero to Scalable Services in 2024
description:
Mastering Go: From Zero to Scalable Services in 2024

Go (often called Golang) has been quietly taking over the backend landscape for the past few years. Its clean syntax, built‑in concurrency primitives, and zero‑dependency binaries make it a perfect fit for everything from tiny CLI tools to massive, distributed systems. In this post we’ll walk through the language fundamentals, show you how to spin up a production‑ready HTTP service, and sprinkle in some best‑practice patterns you can adopt right away.

TL;DR – By the end of this article you’ll have a working Go HTTP server, a test suite, and a Dockerfile ready for deployment on any cloud provider.

Why Go Still Matters in 2024

Feature What It Means for You
Compiled, statically typed Fast startup, predictable performance, and early‑catchable bugs.
First‑class concurrency Goroutines + channels let you write concurrent code without the mental overhead of locks.
Standard library Batteries‑included HTTP, JSON, crypto, and more – no external dependencies needed.
Built‑in tooling go fmt, go vet, go test, and go mod are ready out of the box.
Cross‑compilation One binary runs anywhere – perfect for Docker and serverless.

If you’re still on the fence, remember that companies like Google, Uber, Dropbox, and Cloudflare ship critical services written in Go. The ecosystem is mature, and the language’s roadmap is steady – a safe bet for long‑term projects.

Getting Started: Your First Go Program

Create a directory for the project and initialize a module:

mkdir hello-go && cd hello-go
go mod init github.com/yourname/hello-go

Now add a simple “Hello, World!” server:

// main.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

func helloHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "👋 Hello, Go!")
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/", helloHandler)
    log.Println("🚀 Server listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Run it with go run . and visit http://localhost:8080. You should see the greeting.

Key takeaways:

  • package main tells the compiler this is an executable program.
  • func main() is the entry point, just like int main() in C.
  • The standard library’s net/http makes a web server a few lines of code.

Structuring a Real‑World Service

In production you’ll want a clearer separation of concerns. Let’s refactor the above into a small, testable service.

/cmd
  /server
    main.go
/internal
  /handler
    hello.go
    hello_test.go

/cmd/server/main.go

package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/yourname/hello-go/internal/handler"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/", handler.Hello)

    log.Println("🚀 Starting on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux))
}

/internal/handler/hello.go

package handler

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
)

// Hello is a plain‑old‑function handler – easy to test.
func Hello(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "👋 Hello from a structured Go app!")
}

/internal/handler/hello_test.go

package handler

import (
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"
)

func TestHello(t *testing.T) {
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    w := httptest.NewRecorder()

    Hello(w, req)

    resp := w.Result()
    body := w.Body.String()

    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        t.Fatalf("expected %d, got %d", http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
    }
    if !strings.Contains(body, "Hello") {
        t.Fatalf("unexpected body: %s", body)
    }
}

Run the test suite with go test ./.... The output should be PASS.

Embracing Concurrency with Goroutines

A common Go idiom is to launch background work as a goroutine. Let’s add a simple health‑check that runs every 10 seconds and logs the current time.

package main

import (
    "log"
    "time"
)

func healthTicker() {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(10 * time.Second)
    for t := range ticker.C {
        log.Printf("🩺 Health check at %s", t.Format(time.RFC3339))
    }
}

func main() {
    go healthTicker() // fire‑and‑forget
    // ... start HTTP server here
}

Because goroutines are cheap (they start in a few kilobytes of stack), you can spawn thousands without exhausting resources. Just remember to coordinate shutdowns with context.Context to avoid orphaned goroutines.

Dependency Management with Go Modules

Go modules have become the de‑facto standard for dependency handling. Adding a third‑party library is as easy as:

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@v1.8.0

Your go.mod now records the exact version, and go.sum stores cryptographic checksums to ensure reproducible builds.

// Using gorilla/mux for richer routing
package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/gorilla/mux"
)

func main() {
    r := mux.NewRouter()
    r.HandleFunc("/users/{id}", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        vars := mux.Vars(r)
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "User ID: %s", vars["id"])
    }).Methods(http.MethodGet)

    log.Println("🚀 Listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", r))
}

Modules also make it trivial to vendor dependencies for environments where external network access is restricted – just run go mod vendor.

Containerizing the Service

Docker is the lingua franca of modern deployments. Here’s a minimal Dockerfile that builds a static binary and runs it on Alpine:

# Build stage
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server ./cmd/server

# Runtime stage
FROM alpine:3.20
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/server .
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["./server"]

Build and run:

docker build -t hello-go .
docker run -p 8080:8080 hello-go

Your service now runs in a ~15 MB container – perfect for cost‑effective cloud VMs.

Observability: Logging and Metrics

Production services need visibility. The standard log package works, but structured logging makes downstream analysis easier. A popular choice is zap:

go get go.uber.org/zap@v1.26.0

package main

import (
    "go.uber.org/zap"
)

func main() {
    logger, _ := zap.NewProduction()
    defer logger.Sync()
    logger.Info("🚀 Server starting", zap.Int("port", 8080))
}

For metrics, expose a Prometheus endpoint:

import (
    "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp"
)

func main() {
    http.Handle("/metrics", promhttp.Handler())
    // other routes…
}

Now you can scrape /metrics with any Prometheus server and set alerts based on request latency, error rates, etc.

Deploying to the Cloud

With a static binary and Docker image, you have a lot of options: managed Kubernetes, serverless platforms, or simple VPS instances. Below are two reliable providers that make Go deployments painless.

Recommended Tools

  • Kinsta – Kinsta offers managed cloud hosting with automatic Docker support, daily backups, and a global CDN. Their Go‑ready environments let you spin up a container in seconds, and the built‑in monitoring tools pair nicely with the observability setup we discussed.

  • DigitalOcean – If you prefer a more hands‑on approach, DigitalOcean’s Droplets and App Platform give you full control over the VM or Kubernetes cluster. Their straightforward pricing and extensive tutorials make it a go‑to for startups looking to scale without breaking the bank.

Both services provide generous free tiers or credits for new accounts, so you can experiment without upfront costs.

Wrapping Up

Go’s simplicity is deceptive – underneath the clean syntax lies a powerful runtime that can handle high‑throughput workloads with minimal effort. By mastering modules, testing, concurrency, and containerization, you’ll be ready to ship production‑grade services that scale effortlessly.

Give the code snippets a spin, tweak the health‑check logic, and push your Docker image to your favorite cloud. In the Go ecosystem, the next step is always just a go get away.

Happy coding!

Feel free to leave comments or share your own Go stories below. Let’s build a faster, safer web together.

title: React History in Plain Words: What Each Era Took Off Your Plate, and What It Billed You
description:
Here is a component every app has. A user profile: load the user by userId, show their name, and show a green dot while they're online.

I'm going to write it again for most eras of React, from 2013 to today.

Most histories of React go version by version: 0.13, 16.8, 18, 19. You finish reading and you know the dates, but not why any of it happened. I wanted to try a different angle. Every era of React made a deal with you. It took something off your plate, and it sent you a new bill. I'll keep score as I go: what you stopped doing, and what you started paying.

One warning about order. This article follows problems, not dates. Next.js (2016) shows up after hooks (2019), because that's where its problem hurts most.

1. Before React: you are the sync engine

The jQuery version:

$.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}`, (user) => {
  $('#name').text(user.name);
});

presence.on('change', (id, online) => {
  if (id === userId) $('#status').toggleClass('online', online);
});

It works. Now add a second place that shows the same user, say a header avatar. Then a list of friends with their own dots. Every piece of data lives in two places: in your variables and in the DOM (the browser's live tree of page elements). Every change has to be copied by hand, to every place that shows it. Miss one, and the header says "online" while the profile says "offline".

Backbone, Knockout and AngularJS were already attacking this with data binding. React's answer, open-sourced in 2013, was different. Pete Hunt's Why React post from June 2013 makes the case: stop updating the DOM yourself. Describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and let the library work out what to change.

In plain words: before React you were a waiter who memorizes every table's order and runs to the kitchen with each correction. React gave you an order pad. You write down what the table wants now, and the kitchen works out the difference.

One detail almost nobody mentions: that same 2013 post already lists server rendering as a selling point. Keep it in mind. It comes back later with a different name.

Took off your plate: keeping the DOM in sync by hand.
Billed you: HTML inside JavaScript, and a build step to compile it. JSX looked like heresy in 2013, and a lot of the first year was spent arguing about it.

2. createClass and mixins: sharing logic, badly

Early React components were objects passed to React.createClass. A mixin was a plain object of methods that got copied into every component that listed it. That's how you shared logic:

var Profile = React.createClass({
  mixins: [FetchUserMixin, PresenceMixin], // each one adds state and lifecycle methods
  render: function () {
    if (!this.state.user) return null;
    return <div>{this.state.user.name} {this.state.online && 'online'}</div>;
  },
});

React called every mixin's componentDidMount, so that part worked. The trouble was everything you couldn't see. Which mixin set online? What happens when two mixins both define handleChange? You found out when the page loaded and threw.

React added ES6 classes in 0.13, in March 2015, and classes had no mixins at all. In 2016 Dan Abramov wrote the post that explained why that was a feature, Mixins Considered Harmful. One line from it: "There is no guarantee that two particular mixins can be used together."

So mixins saved you from copy-pasting logic, and charged you in coupling you couldn't see. Rename a method, and the page load told you which mixin had depended on it.

3. Classes: one feature, three methods

Here's the profile as a class (written with class properties, the Babel syntax most teams used):

class Profile extends React.Component {
  state = { user: null, online: false };

  componentDidMount() {
    fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
    this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
  }

  componentDidUpdate(prev) {
    if (prev.userId !== this.props.userId) {
      fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
      this.unsubscribe();
      this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
    }
  }

  componentWillUnmount() {
    this.unsubscribe();
  }
}

(presence.subscribe returns a function that unsubscribes. Both versions in this article rely on that.)

Look at where the presence logic lives. Subscribe in one method, re-subscribe in a second, unsubscribe in a third. One feature, split by when it runs instead of what it does. The fetch is copied twice. Forget the componentDidUpdate branch and the dot keeps showing the previous user.

And there's a race here that's easy to miss: whichever response arrives last wins. Click from user 1 to user 2 quickly. Two requests are in flight. If user 1's response arrives last, setState writes it, and the profile of user 2 shows user 1's name. Nothing in the class shape protects you from that.

Sharing logic got its own problem too. Mixins were out, so the community moved to patterns that wrap one component in another. A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a wrapped one. A render prop is a function you pass as a prop so another component can decide what to render. Both work, but every shared behavior adds a layer. Open the component tree of a 2018 app and you'd scroll through withRouter(connect(withTheme(...))) before reaching your own code.

The React team listed all of this when they introduced hooks. The motivation section reads like a bug report for this exact component: "It's hard to reuse stateful logic between components", complex components where related logic is split across lifecycle methods, and "Classes confuse both people and machines".

Took off your plate: hidden mixin coupling, mostly by not supporting mixins at all.
Billed you: this, logic split across lifecycle methods, and deeply nested wrappers.

4. Hooks: logic grouped by what it does

Hooks were announced at React Conf in October 2018 and shipped in React 16.8, in February 2019. The profile:

function usePresence(userId) {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => presence.subscribe(userId, setOnline), [userId]);
  return online;
}

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const online = usePresence(userId);

  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
    return () => { ignore = true; };
  }, [userId]);

  if (!user) return null;
  return <div>{user.name} {online && 'online'}</div>;
}

The whole presence feature is now one small hook, in one place. Subscribe and unsubscribe sit together (the effect returns its own cleanup), and [userId] re-runs it when the user changes. usePresence is just a function. Any component can call it, and there's no wrapper in the tree.

The race from the class version is fixed with the ignore flag: when userId changes, the old effect's cleanup marks its request as stale. But notice who fixed it: you did. React gave you the place to put the fix and left the fix itself to you.

The new bill is the dependency array. Leave a value out of it, and the effect keeps using the value from the render where it was created. That's a stale closure, and it's the most common hooks bug there is. Lint rules catch most of these bugs, though keeping the linter quiet often means restructuring the code.

Hooks also made "fetch in an effect" the default way to load data. Classes had the same problem, but now it was everywhere. Say the profile shows the user's posts, in a child component that fetches them. The child can't start its request until the parent has fetched the user and rendered it. Then the posts component fetches comments. Each level waits for the one above. That's a waterfall. Libraries like TanStack Query, SWR and Relay helped a lot, but the requests still started in the browser, after the JavaScript arrived.

Took off your plate: this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers.
Billed you: dependency arrays, stale closures, and cleanup you write yourself.

5. Next.js: render it on the server

Everything in sections 3 and 4 happens in the browser, after the JavaScript bundle (the files the browser downloads) arrives. Until then the user stares at an empty page. Then a spinner. Then another spinner, one per level of the waterfall.

Next.js launched in October 2016, from ZEIT (now Vercel). Its announcement describes where the industry had gone: the pendulum of "'fully server-rendered' swung abruptly to the extreme of 'single page app'". Next.js swung it back with server-side rendering: the page is rendered to HTML on the server with its data, and the browser gets real content right away.

This file-per-page setup is what's now called the Pages Router, to tell it apart from the newer App Router in section 7. At launch the data function was getInitialProps. Since Next.js 9.3 in March 2020, the usual way is getServerSideProps, which runs only on the server:

export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const user = await fetchUser(params.id);
  return { props: { user } };
}

export default function ProfilePage({ user }) {
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

The fetch runs on the server, close to the data. No empty page, no first spinner.

Remember the detail from 2013? Server rendering was already on React's list of selling points. Next.js didn't invent it. It made it the default, so you stopped wiring up the server yourself.

The price is hydration. The server sends finished HTML, and it looks right, but it's dead: buttons do nothing yet. Then the browser downloads the same components as JavaScript and runs them again to wire up the clicks. That wiring step is hydration. You pay for the page twice. If the server and the browser render anything differently (Date.now(), a window check, a locale-formatted date), React throws a hydration mismatch. And data loading lives in one function at the top of the page, so a component deep in the tree still can't fetch its own data on the server.

Took off your plate: the blank page, and setting up server rendering by hand.
Billed you: hydration, hydration mismatches, and page-level data loading.

6. React 18: the era everyone skips

Timelines often jump from hooks straight to Server Components, and React 18 gets less attention than it deserves.

React 18, March 2022, brought three things. I'll take them one at a time.

Concurrent rendering. React can start an update, pause it to handle a click, and come back to it. You opt in through APIs like useTransition.

Suspense. You wrap a slow part of the page, say the user's posts, and React shows a fallback there, like a spinner, until it's ready.

Streaming. On the server, the parts of the page that are ready go out first. The slow part arrives later and fills in its spinner.

In plain words: before 18, the server was a restaurant that brought your whole order at once, so everyone waited for the slowest dish. After 18, starters come out when they're ready, and the steak follows.

There's no new profile code here, and that's the point. This era changed what React can do under the hood, and the next one is built on it.

The bill came from somewhere else. Strict Mode, React's opt-in wrapper for extra checks in development, started mounting every component twice to catch missing cleanup. If your profile fetched twice in dev after upgrading, this is why. Usually the fix was the cleanup function you'd skipped. So 18 took "the whole page waits for the slowest request" off your plate, once a framework wired up streaming for you, and billed you in effects that suddenly ran twice.

7. Server Components: components that never reach the browser

The idea was presented in December 2020, before React 18. It reached most developers through the App Router, Next.js's newer routing system: in beta in Next.js 13 in October 2022, stable in Next.js 13.4, in May 2023. React 19 is when the Server Components APIs were declared stable for frameworks to build on. The 13.4 announcement says the App Router is "built on the foundation of React Server Components and Suspense", the Suspense and streaming that React 18 shipped.

Server Components are not the same as server rendering. With SSR, a component renders on the server and then its code ships to the browser anyway, for hydration. A Server Component renders on the server and its code never ships at all.

The profile, today:

// app/users/[id]/page.tsx: a Server Component
import { PresenceDot } from './PresenceDot';

export default async function ProfilePage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params; // Next 15+. In 13 and 14, params was a plain object.
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  return (
    <>
      <h1>{user.name}</h1>
      <PresenceDot userId={user.id} />
    </>
  );
}

// app/users/[id]/PresenceDot.tsx: ships to the browser, because state and a live subscription only exist there
'use client';
import { usePresence } from '@/hooks/usePresence';

export function PresenceDot({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const online = usePresence(userId);
  return online ? <span className="dot" /> : null;
}

The component is async. It fetches its own data with a plain await, on the server, and no useEffect is involved. Any component in the tree can do this, not only the page. The heading and the rest of the page never ship to the browser as JavaScript. Only PresenceDot does, because it's the only part that needs a live subscription.

In plain words: with the Pages Router, the server sent a printed photo of the page, and then the camera too: all the code that built it, so the browser could retake the shot and make it interactive. Server Components send the photo and only the code for the parts that actually move.

The bill is bigger than one line per file. Three costs show up first:

  • 'use client' marks where the browser part starts, and everything that file imports ships with it. Put it on the page instead of on PresenceDot, and you're back in section 4: 
  'use client'; // on page.tsx: the whole profile ships as JavaScript again,
  // the component can't be async anymore, and fetchUser moves back into a useEffect
  • Server files can't use useState, useEffect or context, because there's no browser there to hold state. That's why context providers move down into small client files, and why many third-party UI libraries need a 'use client' wrapper before they work.
  • Props that cross the boundary must be serializable: plain data that can be sent as text. No functions, no class instances.

Then the quieter ones. Waterfalls can come back on the server, as sequential awaits in nested components, so you reach for Promise.all and Suspense boundaries. Next.js caches fetches, routes and navigations in separate layers whose defaults have changed between versions, so "why is this data stale" became a new kind of question. And Server Components need support from the bundler (the tool that packages your code), which in practice means a framework such as Next.js. Your app is tied closer to it than before.

Took off your plate: fetching in effects, the client waterfall, shipping JavaScript for parts that never change.
Billed you: the server/client boundary, caching, and framework lock-in.

8. Today: React 19 and the Compiler

React 19 went stable in December 2024. ref is now a regular prop, so the forwardRef wrapper is on its way out. Actions give you primitives (useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, <form action>) for the pending states, errors and optimistic updates of a form, the parts you used to build with three useState calls. (An optimistic update shows the expected result right away, before the server confirms it.)

Then in October 2025, React Compiler 1.0. Memoization means caching a result so it isn't recomputed on every render. For years, a fast React app meant doing it by hand:

const onSelect = useCallback((id) => router.push(`/users/${id}`), [router]);
const sorted = useMemo(() => friends.toSorted(byName), [friends]);
return <FriendList friends={sorted} onSelect={onSelect} />; // FriendList wrapped in memo()

The compiler is an opt-in build step that adds that memoization for you. You write the plain version, and it works out what to cache. It can even memoize code after an early return, which manual useMemo can't, because hooks can't be called after a return.

One honest caveat. The docs keep useMemo and useCallback as escape hatches, options for the rare cases where the default isn't enough. The routine was handed off, not deleted.

The compiler also assumes you follow the Rules of React: render is a pure calculation, so props and state aren't mutated and nothing outside changes during render. When it detects a violation, it safely skips that component. A violation it can't detect can make a compiled component misbehave at runtime. Say the profile reads the current theme from a global variable during render: the compiler only sees props and state, so it caches the output, and the profile keeps the old theme after the global changes.

Took off your plate: manual memoization, forwardRef, the boilerplate of form state.
Billed you: the Rules of React, now enforced.

The ledger

Same order as the article. The dates are in each section.

Era Took off your plate Billed you Where you'll see the bill
React itself Keeping the DOM in sync by hand JSX, and a build step Your first webpack/Babel config
createClass + mixins Copy-pasting logic Hidden coupling between mixins A name clash error on page load
Classes Hidden mixin coupling this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers A wrapper-deep component tree in DevTools
Hooks this, lifecycle splits, wrappers Dependency arrays, stale closures, your own cleanup react-hooks/exhaustive-deps warnings
Next.js The blank page, manual SSR Hydration, mismatches, page-level data loading A hydration error in the console
React 18 Waiting for the slowest request Double-run effects in Strict Mode Effects firing twice in dev
Server Components Effects for data, shipping static UI The client boundary, caching, lock-in A "needs 'use client'" error at build
React 19 + Compiler Memoization, forwardRef, form state The Rules of React, enforced Compiler lint errors, skipped components

Not every era took a chore. React 18 and Server Components mostly added things you couldn't do before. And the bills didn't get smaller. They moved: from your DOM code, to your effects, to the line between server and browser.

Closing

In 2013 the bill was a whole job: you were the sync engine. In 2026 it's knowing which side of one line your code runs on. That's real progress. It just isn't free, and every React release since has moved the cost rather than cancelled it.

Which bill are you paying right now: stale closures, hydration mismatches, or the 'use client' boundary?

title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
description:
arXiv:2610.19708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an
  explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a
  sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our
  representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For
  reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory.
  For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and
  then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera
  controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
description:
arXiv:2610.19298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.

title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
description:
arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: Local Invoice & Receipt Sorter for Freelancers — Open-Source AI Side Hustle
description:
What I Built
I built LocalFolio, an offline-first invoice and receipt organizer specifically designed for freelancers, independent contractors, and sole proprietors.

Handling client receipts and expense invoices is tedious, manual, and privacy-sensitive. Freelancers often hesitate to upload sensitive financial documents containing client names, tax IDs, and bank details to cloud-based proprietary APIs. LocalFolio solves this by running entirely on the user's local machine. It ingests messy folders of PDFs, screenshots, and scans, uses a local vision-language model to extract structured metadata (vendor, date, total amount, category, and tax status), and automatically sorts them into clean, structured folder hierarchies with a fully searchable SQLite ledger.

Demo

(Link to video demo showing drag-and-drop receipt ingestion, local extraction, and auto-sorting in action)

Code
You can check out the complete project repository on GitHub:
LocalFolio GitHub Repository

Python

Core local inference pipeline snippet using Ollama and Llama 3 Vision

import json
from pathlib import Path
from ollama import chat

def process_receipt(image_path: Path) -> dict:
prompt = """
Extract the following invoice details in strict JSON format:
- vendor_name
- date (YYYY-MM-DD)
- total_amount
- currency
- category
"""
response = chat(
model='llama3.2-vision',
messages=[{
'role': 'user',
'content': prompt,
'images': [str(image_path)]
}],
format='json'
)
return json.loads(response['message']['content'])
How I Built It
LocalFolio is built around modern open-source AI tools and frameworks:

Open-Weight Models: Powered by Llama 3.2 (3B Vision) running locally via Ollama, allowing high-accuracy multi-modal OCR and structured information extraction without relying on external cloud endpoints.

Agent Harness & Framework: Built using Python, LangChain for structuring extraction prompts, and Pydantic for rigorous data validation.

Local Storage & UI: A lightweight desktop GUI built with Streamlit backed by a local SQLite database and local file system operations to organize documents directly in the user's chosen directory.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
Open innovation was non-negotiable for LocalFolio due to three core pillars:

Absolute Data Privacy: Financial invoices contain sensitive PII, proprietary client names, and banking details. Running open-weight models locally ensures that confidential client data never leaves the freelancer's laptop, satisfying strict client confidentiality agreements.

Zero Recurring Infrastructure Costs: Cloud-based OCR and proprietary vision APIs charge per request, which would quickly eat into thin freelancer margins or require a burdensome subscription model. Local inference costs $0.00 per scan, making the side hustle sustainably profitable.

Customizability & Fine-Tuning: Generic invoice parsers often fail on regional tax formats (like GST/VAT structures or niche local currencies). Open models allowed custom prompt engineering and local few-shot tuning specifically tailored to freelance expense categories.

My Agent Session
During the development of LocalFolio, I used DevRelay to record and track my agentic debugging and coding sessions:
View my DevRelay Agent Session

My First User
I tested LocalFolio with my friend Sarah, a freelance graphic designer who spends hours every month sorting through messy PDF invoices and mobile snapshots of tax receipts.

Her Feedback: She loved that she didn't have to create an account, configure API keys, or worry about uploading confidential client retainer agreements to a third-party server.

What she asked for next: She requested an automated export feature to generate a CSV summary sheet formatted specifically for her annual tax filing software.

Would she pay? She stated she would gladly pay a one-time fee of $29 for a polished desktop installer so she never has to manually categorize receipts again.

title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity, identity-preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try-on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training-based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training-free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian-the first generalizable and model-agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training-based and training-free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post-processing, adaptive attacks, and cross-dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent-L/IDGuardian.git.

An educational account is generally provided to an eligible member of an institution. Its features and duration depend on the organization's policies, the user's status, and the services connected to the account.

This guide explores the common uses of educational email, the advantages of authorized access, potential third-party account risks, and practical ways to protect digital information. It also discusses legitimate alternatives for people who need academic tools or online learning resources.

Understanding the Meaning of Old EDU Accounts
An EDU account usually refers to an email address or digital account connected to an educational institution. Some institutions use .edu domains, while others use different academic domain extensions.

An account described as “old” has generally existed for an extended period. Its history may include academic messages, course notifications, saved contacts, and access to institutional services.

Account History
An established account may contain years of authorized communication and saved information. That history can be useful to its legitimate owner, but it does not automatically prove that the current user has permission to access it.

Institutional Association
Educational accounts are often connected to a particular school, university, or organization. The institution determines who is eligible to use its services.

Service Availability

title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering
description:
arXiv:2610.19551v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image models increasingly generate readable Chinese text that still contains local rendering defects, such as a character with an extra or missing stroke or a malformed component. Such errors are invisible to OCR and vision-language models, which are trained for recognition and are therefore invariant to the very structural deviations that define a rendering error. We formalize text rendering verification as a target-conditioned problem: given a target character and an image crop, decide whether the crop is a correct rendering of that character. Our verifier TEXTVERIFIER feeds the text tower a character's Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) rather than a single-character symbol, and is trained on 12.7M crop-IDS pairs plus label-free "same-character, different-quality" hard pairs sampled from the training trajectory of a text-region inpainting model. To evaluate this ability we build TEXTRENDERBENCH-ZH, the first per-character benchmark for generated Chinese text, annotating position, identity, and correctness for 7,358 characters. TEXTVERIFIER reaches an F1 of 0.844, far above OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Used as a per-character reward for Flow-GRPO post-training, it further reduces rendering errors, showing that its score can both detect and correct errors.

title: Stop Hand-Numbering Staggered Animations. CSS sibling-index() Is Here
description:
TL;DR: sibling-index() returns an element's position among its siblings, and sibling-count() returns how many siblings there are, both as integers you can use in calc(). They have been Baseline Newly available since August 2026, so stagger delays and even splits no longer need JavaScript or a pile of selectors.

The ladder nobody wants to extend

You want a list to fade in one item after another. So you write this:

li:nth-child(1) { animation-delay: 60ms; }
li:nth-child(2) { animation-delay: 120ms; }
li:nth-child(3) { animation-delay: 180ms; }
li:nth-child(4) { animation-delay: 240ms; }
/* ...and you stop at 10 and hope */

Or you give up on CSS and number the items in your template:

<li style="--i: 1">...</li>
<li style="--i: 2">...</li>
<li style="--i: 3">...</li>

Both work. Both break the moment the list grows, gets filtered, or gets a new item at the top. The browser always knew which child was which. It just would not tell you as a number.

Meet the two functions 

sibling-index()  /* 1, 2, 3, ... */
sibling-count()  /* how many children the parent has */

Neither takes an argument. Both return an <integer>, so they work anywhere a number does, including inside calc(), min(), and color functions.

A few details, straight from the spec and MDN:

  • sibling-index() starts at 1, like :nth-child(), not at 0 like your arrays.
  • Only element children count. Text and comment nodes between them are ignored.
  • sibling-count() includes the element itself.

A minimal example

The stagger ladder becomes one rule:

li {
  animation: fade-in 400ms backwards;
  animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 80ms);
}

@keyframes fade-in {
  from { opacity: 0; }
}

backwards keeps each item at the from keyframe while it waits, so nothing flashes in early.

And an even split without counting by hand:

ul {
  display: flex;
  width: 600px;
}

li {
  width: calc(100% / sibling-count());
}

In Chrome 155, with five items, the computed delays came out as 0.08s, 0.16s, 0.24s, 0.32s, 0.4s, and each item was 120px wide. Add a sixth item with JavaScript and the next frame reads 0.08s through 0.48s, at 100px each. No observer, no re-render.

A realistic example: a notification stack

Real lists can get long, and a 30th item waiting 1.8 seconds to appear is not a feature. Cap the stagger with min(), give every item its own hue, and reverse the order on the way out:

.toast-list li {
  animation: slide-in 300ms ease-out backwards;
  animation-delay: calc(min(sibling-index(), 8) * 60ms);
  background: hsl(calc(360deg / sibling-count() * sibling-index()) 70% 45%);
}

.toast-list li.leaving {
  animation-delay: calc((sibling-count() - sibling-index()) * 60ms);
}

@keyframes slide-in {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 12px;
  }
}

With 12 items, the entry delays climbed from 0.06s to 0.48s and then stayed at 0.48s for items 9 to 12. The hues spread evenly around the color wheel, from rgb(195, 115, 34) on the first item to rgb(195, 34, 34) on the last. With .leaving, the delays ran backwards, from 0.66s on the first item down to 0s on the last, so the bottom of the stack leaves first.

The same trick works for z-index: sibling-index() on overlapping cards, or order: calc(sibling-count() - sibling-index()) to flip a flex row without touching the markup. Both computed as expected in the test page.

Can I use it?

Yes, in every current major engine:

Browser Version Released
Chrome 138 June 2025
Safari 26.2 December 2025
Firefox 154 August 2026

Firefox 154 completed the set, which made both functions Baseline Newly available in August 2026. Older browsers drop the whole declaration, so put a plain value first if the effect matters:

li {
  animation-delay: 100ms;
  animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 80ms);
}

Every value in this post comes from running the CSS in Chrome 155.

Gotchas

1. Hidden siblings still count. The count comes from the DOM, not from what is rendered. With one of five items set to display: none, the four visible items were still 120px each, leaving a 120px gap in a 600px row. If you filter a list, remove the items from the DOM, or the math is off by however many you hid.

2. A custom property does not store the number. This looks like it saves the parent's index for its children:

li { --i: sibling-index(); }
li b { width: calc(var(--i) * 10px); }

It does not. An unregistered custom property keeps the text sibling-index(), and var() pastes that text into the child, where it runs against the child's own position. A <b> that was the 4th child of the 3rd <li> came out 40px, not 30px. Register the property and it computes on the <li> first, then inherits the number:

@property --i {
  syntax: "<integer>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: 0;
}

With that in place, the same <b> measured 30px. Sneaky, and the kind of bug that only shows up on the third item.

3. Pseudo-elements borrow their parent's position. ::before and ::after resolve against the element they belong to. On the 3rd <li>, width: calc(sibling-index() * 7px) in ::before gave 21px. Usually that is what you want.

4. It counts from 1. calc(sibling-index() * 80ms) means the first item waits 80ms too. Use calc((sibling-index() - 1) * 80ms) if the first one should start right away.

Wrap-up

sibling-index() and sibling-count() are the numbers your --i attributes and :nth-child ladders were faking. Go find that stagger loop in your template and delete it.

Sources

  • MDN: sibling-index()
  • MDN: sibling-count()
  • CSS Values and Units Level 5: Tree counting functions
  • web.dev: August 2026 Baseline monthly digest
  • Chrome 138 release notes
  • WebKit: Features in Safari 26.2
  • Firefox 154 for developers

title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.14721v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.

title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.14489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.
