title: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher's Advantage Live?
description:
arXiv:2610.19145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher's advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher-student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher's 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15-18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.

title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.19628v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.

title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.14574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.

title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
description:
arXiv:2610.19536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

title: Two new x402 APIs for AI agents: x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain verifier + OWASP API Top 10 (2023) one-call audit (2026-10-15, cycle 151)
description:
We just shipped 2 new paid x402 endpoints on our URL metadata API — both $0.0005/call, USDC on Base, x402 settlement via pay.openfacilitator.io.

Endpoints:

  1. GET /api/x402-receipt-parse?receipt_b64=<BASE64> OR ?tx_hash=0x... OR POST JSON — x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain tx verifier
  2. GET /api/owasp-api-top10-audit?url=<TARGET> — OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) one-call composite audit

Why these matter for AI agents

1. /api/x402-receipt-parse is the post-settlement companion to /api/x402-payment-trace (c142, pre-send decoder). When an x402 server returns an X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE base64, the AI agent needs to verify on-chain that the payment actually went to the right address, for the right amount, with enough confirmations. The endpoint accepts either the base64 receipt OR a raw tx hash (0x + 64 hex) and fetches it via the Base public RPC (base.gateway.tenderly.co with 1rpc.io/base + base.drpc.org fallbacks), then decodes the USDC Transfer event from the receipt logs (USDC on Base = 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913).

The function-selector decode distinguishes transfer vs transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) vs approve — so the agent knows whether the payment was a settled transfer (good) or just an approval (not a payment). It also computes confirmations = latest_block - block_number and warns if <12.

Returns receipt_summary (tx_hash + block_number + from + to + value_atomic + value_usdc + asset + status_is_success + confirmations + function_selector + function_name) + verification (to_matches_our_wallet [0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c] + value_matches_amount + transfers_to_our_wallet_count + total_received_usdc) + findings + x402_receipt_score 0-100 A-F.

2. /api/owasp-api-top10-audit is the one-call composite that answers the single most-asked question by an AI agent deciding whether to use a paid API: "is this API safe to call?". Fetches the target + probes 24 conventional API paths in parallel via ThreadPoolExecutor, then runs all 10 OWASP 2023 category checks:

  • API1 BOLA: compare /api/users/1 vs /api/users/2 response equality (identical = no per-object authz)
  • API2 Broken Auth: no-auth + no-bearer on /api/me + /api/users/1
  • API3 BOPLA: PII keywords in unauth response (password/ssn/credit_card/secret/token/api_key) + over-exposure >=15 top-level fields
  • API4 Unrestricted Consumption: no RateLimit-* headers + huge response >5MB
  • API5 BFLA: /admin returns 200 + dangerous methods PUT/DELETE/PATCH open on /api/users/1
  • API6 Sensitive Business Flow: /api/checkout /api/payment/api/cart open without CAPTCHA
  • API7 SSRF: live test /api/fetch/api/proxy/api/avatar with internal URL http://127.0.0.1/ + http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata) + http://localhost:8080/
  • API8 Security Misconfiguration: X-Debug + X-Powered-By + X-AspNet-Version disclosure + ACAO=* wildcard + stack trace in 404 body
  • API9 Improper Inventory: multiple /api/v1+/v2`+ /openapi.json publicly exposed + staging subdomain returns 200
  • API10 Unsafe Consumption: 3p scripts from risky TLDs .tk/.ml/.ga + http:// subresources on https:// page

Returns per_category[10] {id, name, status pass/warn/fail, score, findings[]} + summary {fail_count, warn_count, pass_count} + composite api_top10_score 0-100 A-F + verdict (production_hardened / standard / weak / vulnerable).

The full catalog is now at 217 paid x402 routes

The service runs at https://mins-alternatively-meanwhile-lauderdale.trycloudflare.com and accepts USDC on Base via the standard x402 flow (payTo: 0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c, asset: 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913, network: eip155:8453). Discovery at /.well-known/x402 (217 endpoints), GET /openapi.json (213 paths), GET /llms.txt (116KB), GET / (landing HTML 119KB).

The first 2 endpoints are free (just GET /api?url=... returns JSON metadata). Everything else is $0.0005–$0.005 per call.

Test self-settle still works: a buying agent signs a real EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization envelope, the Flask server POSTs to pay.openfacilitator.io/verify + /settle, and the wallet 0xCa0a6c... receives real USDC on Base.

Categories: 24 API path probes, 10 OWASP checks, 2 base JSON-RPC endpoints (tenderly + 1rpc + drpc fallback chain).

title: I’ve Been Building a Student Hub, and I’d Love Some Feedback
description:
Hey everyone!

This is my first post on DEV.to, so I thought I'd start by sharing something I've been working on.

I'm currently a Psychology student from the Philippines. Before switching programs, I spent three years studying Computer Engineering. I still enjoy programming, though, so I've been continuing to learn on my own and working on different projects whenever I have the chance.

One of those projects is Unified Student Hub.

It's a web app I've been building to help students keep track of their schoolwork, organize their study materials, and figure out when to study.

It's far from finished, but I wanted to share it here and see what other people think.

Why I started working on it

Being a student means dealing with a lot of different things at once.

Sometimes assignments are posted in group chats. Other times they're on a school platform. Lecture slides end up in random folders, and important PDFs get buried somewhere in your downloads.

Then there's the problem of actually finding time to study, especially when multiple deadlines are coming up.

I know there are already plenty of productivity apps out there, but I wanted to try building something myself that combines the things I personally find useful.

At first, it was mostly about keeping deadlines organized. Then I started adding other features, and the project slowly grew into something bigger.

What I've built so far

Right now, the app lets you add assignments, exams, and other deadlines, then organize them by subject.

There's also a weekly planner. You can set the hours you're available, add your classes or other commitments, and estimate how much time you need to finish your tasks.

The app uses that information to put together a study schedule.

It isn't AI-powered or anything. It's just scheduling logic that I've been working on and improving.

I've also added a few other things along the way:

A place to store PDFs, PowerPoints, documents, and other study materials

A PDF reader with highlighting and drawing tools

A study timer with customizable breaks and cycles

Calendar and syllabus imports

Optional reminders

Some offline features, including access to locally saved materials

I also worked on Canvas and Moodle imports, although those depend on what each school allows.

Not everything is as polished as I'd like, but the main features are there.

Here's a screenshot

The design is still changing. I've been trying to make the interface less cluttered and easier to understand, especially for someone opening the app for the first time.

What I'm using

For anyone curious about the stack:

React and Vite for the frontend

FastAPI for the backend

PostgreSQL for the hosted database

SQLite for local development

I've learned quite a bit while working on this, especially about connecting the frontend and backend, handling user accounts, and getting everything deployed.

I still have a lot to learn.

Since I'm studying Psychology now, most of my programming practice happens during my free time. Building projects has been one of the ways I keep learning.

Sometimes I spend more time figuring out why something isn't working than actually writing the feature, but I guess that's part of it.

The parts I'm still working on

One problem I've run into is that I keep thinking of new things to add.

At some point, I realized the app was starting to become confusing even to me.

There were too many sections, settings, and buttons competing for attention.

So I'm trying to focus less on adding features for now and more on making the existing ones easier to use.

I want someone to be able to open the app, add their schoolwork, set their available hours, and understand their study plan without needing a tutorial for every little thing.

There are also bugs I haven't found yet, and some features still need more testing.

I'm not going to pretend it's ready for everyone to rely on. It's an early version, and I'm still figuring things out.

I'm looking for people to try it

I figured I should probably start getting feedback instead of just deciding everything myself.

If you're a student, I'd love to know whether something like this would actually be useful to you.

And if you're a developer, feel free to look through the code. Suggestions and criticism are welcome.

Here are the links:

Try the app:
https://unified-student-hub-vg2s.vercel.app/

GitHub:
https://github.com/cabauatanhans47-cyber/unified-student-hub

I'd recommend trying it with sample assignments first since it's still in beta.

I'm especially curious about whether the interface makes sense when you first open it. Is it obvious what to do? Are there features that seem unnecessary? Is anything broken?

Even if you only spend a few minutes exploring it, I'd appreciate hearing what you think.

I'll probably share more updates as I continue working on it.

Anyway, that's what I've been building lately. Thanks for reading!

Claude Fable 5 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway. A Mythos-class model, Fable 5 is a notable step up over prior Claude models on long-running, ambiguous, multi-step tasks, executing end-to-end on work that previously required frequent human check-ins.

The model sustains productive output across multi-day runs and dependably dispatches parallel sub-agents, and lower effort settings often match what prior Claude models produced at their highest effort. Code review, bug-finding, and repository investigation are stronger, and first-shot correctness on complex problems is noticeably higher.

Fable 5 ships with blocking classifiers in place that refuse offensive cybersecurity, biology, and summarized-thinking extraction, because the model's capabilities in those areas introduce real misuse risk. Anthropic also does not support Zero Data Retention because some misuse patterns only become visible across cumulative requests. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude.

To use Fable 5, set model to anthropic/claude-fable-5 in the AI SDK.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, dynamic provider sorting by latency and cost, and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Learn more about AI Gateway, view the AI Gateway model leaderboard or try it in our model playground.

title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
description:
arXiv:2610.19728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

title: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads
description:
By Oleksii Tkachuk, Rajiv Shringi, Chris Lohfink, Abe Ratnofsky, Kartik Sathyanarayanan

Introduction

In an earlier post, we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes.

However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access, is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage:

  • Solution 1: Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3
  • Solution 2: Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3

We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier.

Challenges

As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges:

  • Growing retention demands: Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs.
  • Escalating costs: Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive.
  • Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations.
  • Operational strain: High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability.
  • Latency requirements: Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis.

This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API. Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend.

TimeSeries Abstraction

Before we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices.

This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post.

This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table:

Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables.

With that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering.

Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink

Our first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra.

Getting Data Into S3 Efficiently

To optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads.

Enter the Compaction job.

Compaction Job to Optimize Reads

The compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace.

The job further optimizes the Parquet files in the following ways:

  • Small Row Groups: Creates small (4–8 MB) row groups to minimize lookup cost. We can then use the Parquet Java library to perform range reads of row groups from S3. This is intentionally well below Parquet’s recommended row group floor — smaller groups were better because our reads are dominated by point/range lookups rather than full scans.
  • Event Sorting: Sorts events within a row group by time, eliminating brute-force scans when querying for a time range.
  • Bloom Filters: Caches Bloom filters and file metadata in EVCache, allowing the TimeSeries query planner to efficiently skip unnecessary reads from S3.

Once the compaction job completes, all compacted files per partition are recorded in the TimeSeries control plane, and the hot storage slices can now be truncated!

On some of our largest datasets, this job typically takes about 12 hours, prioritizing lower compute costs over execution speed.

Streaming Cold Tier Read

Once compacted files are optimized in cold storage, they are ready to be read. The TimeSeries data plane fans out a given query across both the hot and cold tiers and merges their result. The users still use the same query interface:

The Cold Tier Data Plane uses compaction metadata for aggressive planning and pruning, which dramatically reduces the S3 query fan-out. As a result, retrieving a full day of data requires at most three sequential S3 reads, even in the uncommon case where an ID spans two row groups. This yields a p50 latency of ~150 ms and a p99 latency of ~500 ms per read.

At the time of writing, the streaming cold tier implementation was processing up to 1,250 reads per second from cold storage globally:

Why not stop here?

The streaming cold tier has delivered real savings, shrinking both Cassandra’s EBS footprint and the Cassandra backup footprint in S3. But the streaming infrastructure itself is expensive and adds moving pieces that widen the team’s on-call scope:

We wanted to improve this further and asked ourselves:

  • Can we avoid streaming data into the object store and the associated data transfer costs?
  • Can we reduce the compute and operational overhead of new components?

That led to a more radical question: Can we read directly from existing Cassandra backups in S3?

Solution 2: Cassandra Cold Storage for Immutable Data

At Netflix, we back up Cassandra data into S3 at regular intervals for disaster recovery. The idea for tiering is simple:

Read directly from these S3 backups instead of paying a separate data transfer cost to S3.

Once TimeSeries marks a hot Time Slice as ready for cold storage, we can customize Cassandra to read directly from its backups, allowing us to delete the on-disk data copy. This would also incur minimal changes to the TimeSeries read path!

To make this viable in production, we had to answer a series of “How…?” questions.

How Can We Read the Backups Efficiently?

We introduced a new compaction strategy in Cassandra, which we call ReadOnlyCompactionStrategy (ROCS). Here is how it works:

Once a time slice crosses the user-configured cold-tier boundary, TimeSeries stops accepting writes for that time slice making it immutable. This immutability unlocks significant optimization opportunities:

  • SSTable overlap: Standard strategies (LCS, TWCS) often produce SSTables that overlap in the token space, and so a single partition key may exist across multiple files.
  • Read fan‑out: Because a read must touch every SSTable covering the key’s token range, this overlap turns a single point-read into multiple lookups, increasing latency across all tiers.

ROCS re-compacts all SSTables once, aligning them precisely with token ranges:

ROCS applies more broadly to all TimeSeries use cases, driving tail latency down on all storage tiers by reducing the SSTable fan-out during read operations:

Once the immutable Time Slices have been optimized, it is time to trigger backups.

How Would We Leverage Backups?

Cassandra backs up every node in the cluster, organizing each backup on S3 as a declarative manifest, along with the SSTables backing the keyspace’s tables:

 {bucket}/
  └── {prefix}/                             ← cluster identity (env_backup/hash_app)
      └── {token}/                          ← node identity (ring token)
          ├── META_V2/                      ← manifests, one per snapshot
          │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json
          │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json
          │   └── ...
          └── SST_V2/                       ← actual SSTable files
              └── {backupTimestamp}/        ← snapshot timestamp
                  └── {keyspace}/
                      └── {table-with-uuid}/ 
                          └── {compression}/
                              └── {encryption}/
                                  ├── {component-file}
                                  └── ...

The backup manifest orchestrates the backup, listing the paths to all its SSTables:

manifest.json
  ├── info
  │   ├── appName              "cass-cluster"
  │   ├── region               "us-east-1"
  │   ├── snapshotInstantMs    1748908800000
  │   ├── backupPathPrefix     "prod_backup/1234_cass/token"
  └── data[]
      └── [0]
          ├── keyspaceName     "ks"
          ├── columnfamily     "tbl-a1b2..."
          └── sstables[]
              └── [0]
                  └── components[]
                      ├── na-1-big-Data.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Index.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Filter.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Statistics.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Summary.db
                      ├── na-1-big-CompressionInfo.db

Alongside the large Data.db file, backups include a compact set of index, metadata, and integrity files. This structure allows us to quickly locate, validate, and restore specific partitions or data ranges without scanning the entire dataset. Furthermore, since the manifest catalogs every S3 path, we can download most of these components directly to the Cassandra node (excluding the Data.db file) where they occupy negligible space. These local components enable efficient query planning before any data is read from S3.

How Would Cassandra Read From Backups?

Cassandra reads typically pull data from two sources: the Memtable, which holds recent unflushed writes, and flushed SSTables on durable storage. As of Cassandra 4.1, we can leverage pluggable Memtables to redirect reads from “cold” tables directly to the backup storage in S3.

-- create table for a given Time Slice
CREATE TABLE data_20260616_00_04 (
    ...
    ...,
    PRIMARY KEY ((time_series_id, time_bucket, event_bucket), event_time, event_id, key)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id DESC, key DESC)
    ...
    AND compaction = ...
    AND compression = ...
    AND memtable = 'backupmemtable:timestamp=1781953200000' ← Custom memtable
    ...

The timestamp marks the point at which the backup is guaranteed to cover the full table, and the table is guaranteed to be immutable.

Opening a backup Memtable kicks off a state-machine initialization that pulls the index data from S3 onto the node once:

This process ensures all SSTable components are downloaded reliably through several resilience mechanisms:

  • Retries and backoff: All S3 operations and file-system cache writes use retries with exponential backoff.
  • Resource isolation: Initialization runs on a dedicated thread pool, isolated from normal Cassandra operations.
  • Partial download protection: If a downloaded component’s size doesn’t match the manifest, it is deleted and re-downloaded.
  • DDL change protection: A .timestamp file marks completed initialization and ties it to the backup timestamp. If the table’s backup timestamp changes, this file is removed and initialization restarts for the new timestamp.
  • Read protection: Memtable initialization is asynchronous; reads to an initializing memtable block for at most half the read RPC timeout.

Once initialization has pulled every SSTable component (except Data.db) from S3 onto the local disk, the Memtable is ready to serve reads. Here is what the read process looks like:

To minimize latency, the system parallelizes S3 reads across requests, SSTables, and individual chunks. A shared cache deduplicates fetches and prefetches data, so chunks are ready before they are needed.

We further optimize cluster and table settings to reduce the number of S3 calls:

  • Larger compression chunks: Reduce S3 calls per partition by reading fewer, larger chunks (accepting some over-fetch on small reads).
  • Read repair disabled: Avoid expensive, unnecessary repair traffic against immutable, pre‑repaired backup data.
  • Speculative retries disabled: Prevent S3’s higher latency from triggering redundant, overlapping reads.

How Would We Know When It Is Safe To Read From Backups?

However, before the Memtable can point to a backup, we must confirm two things across the whole ring, and we use Cassandra Virtual Tables to do that.

First, that ROCS re-compaction succeeded:

cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.cluster_view                                                                                                                                                          
       WHERE keyspace_name = 'system_views' AND table_name = 'sstable_tasks';

keyspace_name | table_name    | host     | value                                                                                                                                                        
--------------+---------------+----------+------------------------------------------------
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.1 | [{"table_name":"<.>","kind":"compaction", ...}]
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.2 | [] <---- no active compactions
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.3 | []

And second, that backups were fully captured (denoted by uploaded=True):

cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.complete_backups                                                                                                                                                      
       WHERE keyspace_name = 'my_ks' AND table_name = 'my_table';

keyspace_name | table_name | timestamp     | num_tokens | num_uploaded | uploaded                                                                                                                       
--------------+------------+---------------+------------+--------------+----------
my_ks         | my_table   | 1765211400000 |          3 |            3 |     True
my_ks         | my_table   | 1765213200000 |          3 |            2 |    False

How Would We Automate This Entire Flow?

The TimeSeries control plane automates the entire transition as slices cross the immutable boundary:

Each slice can be in any lifecycle stage at any time without impacting system availability, and the system remains resilient to delayed backups or lagging compactions.

How Would Cassandra Handle The Additional Load?

Serving data from S3 is much more CPU-intensive than reading from local storage. A sudden spike in read requests can overwhelm the Cassandra cluster and affect the hot path, turning a cost-saving feature into a reliability risk.

To avoid this, cold reads can optionally run on a separate Cassandra cluster that points its backup Memtables at the hot cluster’s backups:

The cold Cassandra cluster must match the original cluster in topology but need not match it in hardware! We can run the cold cluster on much smaller, cheaper, storage-light instances.

Real World Performance

Cassandra Cold Tier was rolled out to the most storage‑intensive TimeSeries Abstraction clusters. It currently stores over 15 PB of compressed data in Cassandra cold storage and has allowed us to cut attached storage significantly on all affected clusters:

At the same time, it serves thousands of reads per second from cold tier storage in any given region:

Cassandra Cold Tier improves p90 latency by ~30% over the previous cold storage implementation, thanks to more efficient S3 access patterns and smaller read sizes, while keeping p99 latency under ~500 ms. Cassandra already handles bursts of cold reads gracefully via its chunk cache, so this design preserves that same resilience for the S3-backed cold tier:

Acknowledgements: Special thanks to our stunning colleagues who contributed to the TimeSeries Abstraction’s success and collaborated with us on the cold storage solutions: Kaidan Fullerton, Matt Lehman, Sumanth Pasupuleti, Carlos Matias Herrero, Nick Pavlakis, Bryan Keller, Francesco Di Chiara

TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?
description:
arXiv:2610.19314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable.
  Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
description:
arXiv:2610.14542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models' true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods.

title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
description:
arXiv:2610.14576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
description:
arXiv:2610.14209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.

title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.19361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.

title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
description:
arXiv:2610.18877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19549v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.19362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

title: Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React
description:
Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React

EyeZen v1.0.0 is now available. It's an open-source desktop workspace-personalization application built with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript.

The guiding idea is simple: the preferences you want while coding may not be the ones you want while reading, editing a video, or working late.

I wanted to build a desktop app that treats those different contexts as configurable workspaces while keeping core configuration local.

What ships in v1.0.0?

The first release includes ten interface themes:

  • Light
  • Dark
  • System
  • Warm Dark
  • Warm Light
  • Sepia Reading
  • Midnight
  • AMOLED-Inspired
  • High Contrast
  • Grayscale

Users can change accent colors, text scale and motion preferences.

EyeZen includes nine starting workspace profiles covering activities such as coding, reading, office work, productivity, gaming, editing and accessibility.

Profiles can be created, edited, applied, imported and exported as JSON.

A scheduling system supports weekday and overnight time windows, priorities for overlapping rules, and a visible manual override.

The optional Break Assistant provides configurable reminder intervals and quiet hours. Notifications depend on OS permissions and environment support.

Settings are stored locally with validation, export/import, and recovery behavior for corrupted files.

The first-run setup introduces the key choices, while an explicit capability report explains which platform integrations are implemented.

Why use Rust, Tauri 2 and React?

Rust provides a foundation for the desktop command layer, validation, persistence and scheduling utilities.

Tauri 2 bridges the application and its native platform features.

React and TypeScript provide the customizable interface, feature views and tests.

The codebase separates the UI, scheduling logic, imports and platform-support boundaries.

Automated frontend and Rust checks run through GitHub Actions across desktop build targets.

Passing CI is useful, but it isn't a replacement for installing and testing the app on real hardware.

Local-first by design

EyeZen's core functionality doesn't require an account, location permission, telemetry service or cloud backend.

Profiles and settings remain on the device, with manual backup/export options.

That is useful both for privacy and for keeping basic workspace personalization independent of an internet connection.

Honest limits in v1.0.0

An important distinction: EyeZen v1.0.0 does not adjust physical monitor brightness or operating-system color temperature.

Warmth and intensity controls save preferences but do not control Night Light, Night Shift, HDR or an external monitor. There is no color overlay or monitor enumeration in this version.

Scheduling and reminders currently run while the application webview is active, so their operation after closing or suspending the app is not guaranteed.

Release installers are CI-built and unsigned, and OS-specific manual acceptance tests are still needed.

EyeZen is a customization tool, not a medical device, and I don't want to make unsupported claims about eye-health outcomes.

Where the project goes next

The roadmap includes more robust background scheduling, broader tray and shortcut controls, improved theme/profile creation, and eventually carefully validated platform-specific display integrations.

Those are future goals, not features in today's release.

Try EyeZen and contribute

I would love feedback on the onboarding experience, theme choices, scheduling logic, keyboard navigation, package installation, and how EyeZen behaves on different desktops.

  • Source code
  • EyeZen v1.0.0 release and downloads
  • Platform support and known limitations

Your screen. Your comfort. Your environment.

title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
description:
arXiv:2610.19025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.

title: Quicken iPhone App: A Companion, Not a Source of Truth
description:
AI Mode Answer
The Quicken iPhone app has improved, with a 4.6 average rating on the App Store and regular updates, but sync issues are still reported, including a known problem where the mobile budget doesn't update after new transactions. It works best as a companion to the desktop app: build the budget on the desktop, then use the phone to check balances and capture spending. When sync keeps failing, an independent Quicken consultant can review the setup.

Quick Answer

  • The app can show your budget and transactions and accept new entries on the go.
  • Sync complaints continue, so treat the desktop as the source of truth.
  • Verify important numbers on the desktop before acting on them.

A recent question on Reddit's Quicken community asked whether the iPhone app has finally been fixed. The poster wanted Quicken on the go, mainly to get a grip on their budget.

It's a good question to look at the way an engineer would, because most of the frustration with a companion app is really about sync, not about the app itself.

This reflects information available in mid-October 2026. Check the current App Store listing and Quicken's support pages before relying on it.

What the app is designed to do

According to the App Store listing, the app lets you see spending trends and check your budget, view balances, accounts and transactions, enter transactions even when offline, and sync automatically with the desktop. Quicken's mobile help page describes the same pattern: create the budget on the desktop and check it on the phone. (That page was last updated in 2020, so treat its details with caution.)

What the evidence says

Signs of improvement

  • A 4.6 out of 5 average from about 15,000 ratings on the App Store
  • Regular "improvements and bug fixes" releases, with dark mode added in 8.4.0

Signs of remaining problems

  • Sample reviews on the same listing mention edits not carrying over between desktop and mobile
  • A Quicken community thread on the iOS companion app budget not updating describes budget totals that don't change after new transactions are entered, even after refreshing. A reported workaround is logging out and back in. Quicken said it escalated the issue, and as of mid-May 2026 it was still marked ongoing with no estimated fix date.

So "fixed" overstates it. A more accurate summary is: usable, actively maintained, with a known sync issue on budgets.

A mental model that helps

This is my own framing, not a description of Quicken's internal design: think of the setup as a primary store with a sync client.

Desktop file  <--sync-->  Cloud  <--sync-->  Phone app
(primary)                                    (companion)

When two copies of data can be edited in more than one place, you get the usual distributed-data headaches: stale reads, delayed updates, and the occasional conflict. A few habits keep those under control.

Habits that make it reliable

  1. Build and edit the budget on the desktop. Treat the phone as a viewer and a quick-entry tool.
  2. Let the desktop finish syncing first. Then open the phone app. Letting both run at once is an easy way to create mismatches.
  3. If the budget looks stale, try the known workaround. Log out of the mobile app and back in. It's a workaround, not a fix.
  4. Cross-check important numbers on the desktop. If the two disagree, trust the desktop and look for the cause.
  5. Keep both apps current. Version mismatches can cause odd behavior.
  6. Back up the desktop data file before changing sync settings or troubleshooting.
  7. Watch for duplicates. A transaction entered by hand on the phone can also arrive from the bank. Review the downloaded transactions list and accept or match items carefully.

Debugging checklist when it still doesn't match

  • [ ] Desktop fully synced?
  • [ ] Phone app updated?
  • [ ] Logged out and back in?
  • [ ] Budget category matches on both sides?
  • [ ] Duplicate or unaccepted transactions on the desktop?
  • [ ] Recent Quicken or iOS update that could explain the change?

If all of that checks out and the mismatch continues, the issue may lie in your specific setup, such as the version, the account connections, or how the data file syncs.

Getting a second pair of eyes

Quick Advisors Hub is an independent advisory service for Quicken users. You send a description of the problem, the scope and fee are confirmed in writing before you pay, and you receive written, prioritized steps. It doesn't use remote access or ask for passwords. For billing, subscription or Quicken ID matters, go to Quicken directly through its official website.

Takeaway

The iPhone app is worth another look if you treat it as a companion to the desktop. Keep one place as the source of truth, sync in a consistent order, and verify the numbers that matter.

This post is independent and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Quicken® or Intuit® Inc. Quick Advisors Hub provides independent advisory guidance only, not official Quicken support.

title: Self‑distilled spatial reasoning improves accuracy without large latency penalty
description:
Distilling privileged depth cues into an RGB‑only vision‑language model closes the long‑standing gap between accuracy and inference speed. SpatialOPSD shows that a single forward pass can inherit most of the reasoning power of a tool‑driven teacher without the heavy latency penalty.

Before this work, spatial coding agents boosted multimodal models by calling external tools to generate verified execution traces, but each trace required multiple API calls and slowed down deployment. Fine‑tuning (SFT) or reinforcement‑learning approaches such as GRPO could not internalize geometry because they never saw the privileged depth information during training.

SpatialOPSD improves the Qwen3.5‑9B baseline from 45.9 to 51.9, with specific efficacy in allocentric transformations (e.g., Among +11.7) [1]. The gain comes from feeding summarized agent traces as privileged inputs during on‑policy self‑distillation, which teaches the model a spatial chain‑of‑thought that it can later reproduce without any external depth sensor.

In a single tool‑free forward pass, SpatialOPSD retains 91% of the performance of its iterative, tool‑dependent teacher, SpatialClaw (51.9 vs. 57.3) [1]. This means the distilled model eliminates virtually all runtime overhead from external calls while sacrificing only a modest fraction of accuracy.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self‑distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization [1]. The advantage holds across varied tasks, confirming that the distilled spatial reasoning is not a narrow trick but a broadly useful capability.

The authors acknowledge that privileged‑information leakage remains a concern, mitigated only by Repetition‑Aware Distillation’s masking and unlikelihood regularization; the 9% residual gap to the teacher suggests further work is needed on scaling or tighter leakage control. One inference is that larger models may close this gap, but empirical evidence is still missing.

If these numbers hold in practice, developers should replace iterative tool‑dependent spatial pipelines with a distilled RGB model and re‑run latency budgets on VSI‑Bench; the expectation is a >90% reduction in execution time while keeping success rates within a few points of the original teacher.

References

  1. SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces
