title: Designing an Audit Trail for Attendance Edits Without Overwriting Source Events
description:
An attendance correction looks like a simple update:

UPDATE attendance_records
SET clock_out_at = '2026-10-15T18:04:00+09:00'
WHERE id = 8412;

That query fixes the current row, but it also destroys the answer to several questions: What was recorded first? Who requested the correction? What evidence supported it? Who approved it? Which value was used for payroll before the change?

For systems that affect pay, deleting that context is a design problem. A safer model treats the original clock event as immutable and records corrections as a separate, reviewable trail.

Start with two different kinds of truth

Attendance software usually contains at least two truths:

  1. Observed truth: the raw event produced by a device, browser, QR scan, or administrator import.
  2. Operational truth: the approved interpretation used for schedules, overtime, and payroll.

Those values can disagree without either being useless. A raw 18:47 clock-out may be genuine, while an approved 18:00 work end may reflect an employee who forgot to clock out after changing clothes. The system should preserve both facts instead of rewriting one into the other.

In Korean workplaces, teams often search for these tools as 출퇴근기록기 (clock-in recorder) or 근태관리기 (attendance management tool). Whatever label the product uses, the important architectural question is the same: does a correction replace evidence, or does it add a decision to the evidence?

Model source events as append-only data

A source event should identify where it came from and when the server received it. Device time alone is not enough because a phone clock can be wrong or an offline client may synchronize later.

CREATE TABLE attendance_events (
  id                BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  event_type        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (event_type IN ('clock_in', 'clock_out')),
  occurred_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  received_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source_type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  source_reference  TEXT,
  payload_hash      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The application role that inserts these rows should not have permission to update or delete them. Retention and privacy rules may eventually require controlled deletion, but that should be a separate administrative process rather than an ordinary edit endpoint.

Put corrections in their own workflow

A correction request is not another clock event. It is a proposal to interpret one or more source events differently.

CREATE TABLE attendance_corrections (
  id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  work_date           DATE NOT NULL,
  requested_clock_in  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  requested_clock_out TIMESTAMPTZ,
  reason_code         TEXT NOT NULL,
  reason_detail       TEXT,
  requested_by        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  requested_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status              TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'cancelled')),
  decided_by          BIGINT,
  decided_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  decision_note       TEXT
);

The correction should reference the affected source events through a join table. This matters when one workday has duplicate scans, a missing clock-out, or a shift that crosses midnight.

Build the effective record instead of mutating it

Read models can combine raw events with the latest approved correction. The calculation can live in a database view, a materialized projection, or an application service.

effective attendance
  = original source events
  + latest approved correction
  + policy version used for interpretation

Keeping the policy version is important. A record calculated under a 30-minute break rule should not silently change when the company later adopts a 45-minute rule.

For a practical example of the employee-facing recording flow, this attendance record management guide is useful context. The implementation detail to preserve is the boundary between captured events and later administrative decisions.

Make state transitions explicit

Do not let clients set any status they want. Define legal transitions in one domain function:

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected" | "cancelled";

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  pending: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: [],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
};

export function canTransition(from: Status, to: Status): boolean {
  return allowed[from].includes(to);
}

If an approved correction is wrong, create a new correction that supersedes it. Reopening and editing the old decision makes the audit trail ambiguous.

Protect the workflow from concurrency bugs

Two managers can open the same pending request and approve different values. Use optimistic locking or a conditional update:

UPDATE attendance_corrections
SET status = 'approved',
    decided_by = $1,
    decided_at = now()
WHERE id = $2
  AND status = 'pending';

The update must affect exactly one row. A zero-row result means the request was already handled and the client should refresh instead of pretending the approval succeeded.

For payroll export, store a snapshot identifier or cutoff time. Otherwise, an approval that arrives during export can create a file that cannot be reproduced later.

Log business meaning, not just HTTP requests

An infrastructure log saying PATCH /attendance/8412 200 is not enough. Emit a domain event with the decision context:

{
  "event": "attendance_correction_approved",
  "correction_id": 392,
  "employee_id": 117,
  "work_date": "2026-10-15",
  "previous_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:47:12+09:00",
  "new_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:00:00+09:00",
  "reason_code": "forgot_to_clock_out",
  "decided_by": 42,
  "policy_version": "attendance-policy-2026-09"
}

Avoid copying free-form notes, precise location data, or device identifiers into every analytics system. The audit store can retain necessary evidence with stricter access controls, while downstream events carry only the fields needed for operations.

Test invariants, not only endpoints

The most valuable tests assert properties that must remain true across refactors:

  • A source event cannot be updated through the normal application role.
  • A pending correction can be decided only once.
  • A rejected correction never changes the effective attendance record.
  • An approved correction does not erase the referenced source events.
  • Payroll export can be reproduced from a recorded cutoff and policy version.
  • A manager cannot approve a correction outside the manager's authorized team.

Property-based tests are particularly useful around overnight shifts, duplicate events, daylight-saving transitions, and late offline synchronization.

A small implementation checklist

Before shipping an attendance correction feature, verify that the system can answer these questions without reading application logs by hand:

  1. What did the employee or device originally submit?
  2. When did the server receive it?
  3. What replacement value was requested, and why?
  4. Who approved or rejected the request?
  5. Which policy version produced the payable result?
  6. Which version was included in a specific payroll export?

If any answer disappears after an edit, the design is still overwriting history.

The goal is not to implement event sourcing everywhere. It is to preserve the few boundaries that matter: observations remain observations, decisions remain decisions, and payroll results remain reproducible. That separation makes corrections easier to explain, safer to authorize, and much less painful to debug.

title: How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year
description:
How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year

Two years ago, I was paying for three cloud storage services at once. Today, I pay $10/year for one domain, and everything else runs on hardware I own. This is the step-by-step story of how I got here, what went wrong, and what I'd recommend.

The 2024 peak: $240/year on cloud storage

I had:

  • Dropbox Plus ($120/year, 2 TB) — for daily work files
  • iCloud+ ($36/year, 200 GB) — for iPhone photos
  • Backblaze Personal ($99/year, unlimited) — for backups

Total: $255/year. And the worst part? I was running out of space — Dropbox wanted me to upgrade to 3 TB for another $20/year, iCloud was constantly nagging me about being full, and Backblaze was uploading at 4 MB/s over my home connection.

Step 1: cancel iCloud, switch to phone-direct Nextcloud

iCloud's 200 GB was always too small because of Live Photos (each Live Photo is ~3 MB, so 1000 photos = 3 GB, and I take a lot of photos). Switching to Nextcloud with the official iOS app was straightforward:

  • Open the iOS Nextcloud app
  • Settings → Auto Upload → enable for Camera Roll
  • Choose "keep on device" for favorites only

After 3 months I had 47 GB of photos on my Nextcloud, all viewable in the iOS Photos app via the native share sheet. Saved $36/year.

Step 2: cancel Dropbox, move work files to WebDAV mount

This was the harder one. I had 10 years of work files in Dropbox and was deeply integrated with the Dropbox desktop client. The migration:

  1. Set up Nextcloud on my server (Ubuntu 24.04, Nextcloud Hub 9 in Docker)
  2. Set up ScsDriver to mount it as a Windows drive letter (Z:)
  3. rsync the entire Dropbox folder from ~/Dropbox to the Z: drive over 2 nights (~400 GB)
  4. Disable the Dropbox desktop client
  5. Use Z:\work\... paths in all my scripts

The ScsDriver WebDAV mount is the missing piece. Without it, the Nextcloud desktop client syncs one folder at a time, can't be remapped to existing paths, and is slow. With ScsDriver, the entire Nextcloud is just a drive letter.

Saved $120/year.

Step 3: cancel Backblaze, do real 3-2-1 backups

Backblaze was uploading my entire machine continuously, which meant my home internet was constantly saturated. The replacement: proper 3-2-1 backups.

  • Primary copy: on my home server (RAID 1, 16 TB)
  • Secondary copy: rsync nightly to a friend's house (8 TB external drive he keeps plugged in)
  • Tertiary copy: encrypted Backblaze B2 of just the truly critical stuff (financial documents, photos) — about 50 GB, costs $0.50/month

The 3-2-1 setup took one weekend and has been running for 18 months without drama.

Saved $93/year.

What I run now (annual cost)

Item Cost / year
Domain (scsoi.com equivalent, any TLD) $10
Backblaze B2 (50 GB critical stuff) $6
Home server electricity (25W × 24h × 365) $25
Total $41/year

That's a saving of $214/year vs the 2024 setup. And I have 16 TB of usable storage, which is 8x what I had with Dropbox Plus.

What I'd recommend for someone starting from zero

  1. If you have < 200 GB of data and a Mac, just keep iCloud+ ($36/year). Don't self-host.
  2. If you have 200 GB - 2 TB and you're a power user, self-host Nextcloud on a $200 mini PC. Use ScsDriver to mount on Windows.
  3. If you have > 2 TB, definitely self-host. $200 hardware + $10/year domain is unbeatable.
  4. If you have > 10 TB, you're probably already doing this — but the ScsDriver mount trick is the productivity multiplier that most setups miss.

The ScsDriver piece in detail

I keep mentioning ScsDriver because it's the part that most self-hosted cloud guides skip. Without a proper mount, the workflow is:

  • Open Nextcloud web UI → click file → edit → save → re-upload

With ScsDriver:

  • Click file in Windows Explorer → edit in any app → save → automatic

That second workflow is the same as Dropbox. It is what makes self-hosted cloud actually usable on Windows.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

What I would NOT recommend

  • Syncthing only (without a mount). Syncthing is great, but you still have to set up a NAS at the other end.
  • Renting a dedicated server ($50+/month). At that price you're paying for someone else's hardware, and you might as well use Dropbox.
  • Using only the Nextcloud desktop client (without ScsDriver). The Nextcloud client is reliable but slow and clunky on Windows.

FAQ

Q: Is $10/year really all you pay for storage?
A: Yes. $10 for the domain, $6 for Backblaze B2 of 50 GB, $25 for electricity. The hardware ($200) was a one-time cost.

Q: What happens when the server dies?
A: RAID 1 means one disk can fail and I keep going. If the motherboard dies, I move the disks to a new box and import the ZFS pool (or mergerfs in my case).

Q: Is your data safer than on Dropbox?
A: Different tradeoff. On Dropbox, my data is on someone else's redundant infrastructure. On my setup, my data is in my house, but I have 3 copies. Both approaches are reasonable.

Q: Can I do this on a laptop?
A: Not really — you need something that's on 24/7. A mini PC or used desktop is the right form factor.

Disclaimer: I run all this on my own hardware. The ScsDriver link above is the public pricing page.

title: DeepSeek enters the fight for token volume, Anthropic continues to dominate spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — June 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs, giving us visibility into what AI usage actually looks like, separate from leaderboards and benchmarks. We publish the data monthly in the AI Gateway production index.

June 2026 summary

The July index reports on AI Gateway data collected in May 2026.

  • Total AI Gateway tokens grew +20% MoM; total spend grew +43% MoM. Customers paid almost 20% more per token on average than in April.

  • DeepSeek’s share of tokens jumped from under 1% to 17% in a single month, while its share of spend stayed near 1%.

  • Anthropic’s share of spend grew from 61% to 65% in May, holding 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case (AI app generation, back office agents, and coding agents).

  • Cost-consciousness meant smarter routing between low-cost and frontier models. Customers got more deliberate about which model did which work, while overall usage kept climbing.

Last month, headlines about blown token budgets dominated tech news: Uber burned through its annual Claude Code budget shortly after Q1 and Amazon shut down KiroRank to curb unproductive tokenmaxxing. While runaway cost is a real problem, this month’s report shows that spend on production use cases still increased.

Two insights emerged from AI Gateway data in May:

  • Low-cost models entered production: New models shipped at price points that made the established labs look even more expensive, and they are capable enough to enter the mix in production.

  • Spend is increasing, but with smarter model mixes: Teams are still increasing token budgets, but they are implementing smarter routing strategies to get more value out of every dollar.

Low-cost models saw significant production volume for the first time

From February to April, volume distribution across labs on AI Gateway changed slowly, but in May, DeepSeek V4's launch completely shifted token share. The low-cost end of the market that barely existed in April became AI Gateway’s third-largest provider by volume in May, without a significant impact on overall spend.

In April, DeepSeek accounted for less than 1% of AI Gateway tokens and less than 0.2% of spend. In May, its volume share jumped to 17% of tokens, putting it in third place, ahead of OpenAI. Almost all of the volume comes from two models: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, both released in May.

The spend picture tells the other half of the story. Even though DeepSeek’s token share grew to 17% in a single month, its cost share stayed near 1%.

DeepSeek V4 Flash launched at $0.14 input / $0.28 output per million tokens, roughly 20–50× lower than comparable Anthropic models and 8–12× lower than other value-tier flagships like Qwen 3.6 Plus and Kimi K2.6. With a savings gap that big, teams adopted V4 Flash quickly.

Price alone wouldn’t have shifted DeepSeek’s volume that much in a month, meaning teams testing DeepSeek V4 against their existing evals found the output good enough to ship, not just low-cost enough to try.

Value-tier models have always been available on AI Gateway, but have never captured token share at this scale, meaning DeepSeek V4 was the first model at its price point to clear the quality bar for production work.

Frontier labs continued to capture a majority of new spend

Even as the low-cost end of the market grew fastest in volume, the expensive end grew faster in dollars.

Anthropic’s token share grew from 26% to 32%, and its spend share from 61% to 65%. OpenAI’s token share held near 13%, but its spend share ticked up from 12% to 13% on a much larger total, so customers were paying more per OpenAI token in May.

The average token got more expensive in May, even with DeepSeek pulling the average down. That increase happened because the work that demands frontier models grew faster than the work that doesn’t. The AI coding agent use case shows the low-cost/frontier split most clearly:

  • DeepSeek drove 49% of the segment’s token volume, but only 4% of the cost.

  • Anthropic drove 28% of tokens and 70% of the cost.

Lower-cost models are now a meaningful part of production workflows, but frontier model use is still growing, driving the increase in overall spend.

The frontier is getting more expensive per token, and customers are still paying. Anthropic continues to lead on spend, taking 65% of all gateway spend in May, and 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case.

Cost discipline became a routing strategy

Increased overall spend showed that demand for AI continued to grow in May, but teams applied more precision to their budgets through routing. They sent the cheap, high-volume work to lower-priced models and used frontier models where quality mattered most. Slow adoption of Google's latest Flash model is a clear example.

Gemini 3.5 Flash launched in May at a higher price point than Gemini 3.0 Flash, but migration didn’t happen at scale. By month-end, 3.5 held only 7% of the Flash family’s tokens while 3.0 held 90%.

Compared to the rapid adoption of Gemini 3.1 Pro across February and March, slower migration to 3.5 Flash shows that teams happy with 3.0 Flash aren't willing to pay the higher cost yet.

Conclusion: Cost-effective, capable options mean smarter model mixes

This month's report signals increased pricing sensitivity in the market, even as overall spend and token volume grow. That means developers are looking for ways to get more out of every dollar.

Data revealed two optimization strategies:

  1. Using DeepSeek's cheap, but capable V4 family for lower-risk, high-volume tasks

  2. Choosing to delay model family upgrades until the ROI makes sense

Routing gives teams the ability to adjust their model mix, and budget, in real time as the labs compete for different layers of production AI workloads.

Appendix

Token vs cost share by B2B classification

B2B applications run fewer, more expensive calls, while B2C applications run many cheap ones. On a per-token basis, B2B cost roughly 60% more than B2C in May.

Agent tool use across tokens and requests

Just under a quarter of requests end in a tool call, but those requests carry well over half of all tokens. Both metrics are roughly flat month-over-month.

Model diversity distribution by request volume

The more requests an app serves, the more models it runs in production. Single-model setups dominate the lowest-volume tier, while at 1M+ requests the majority of apps route across 11 or more models.

Cost vs volume share by use case

Use case cost share indicates how expensive a wrong answer is, not how many tokens it burns. Personal assistants and coding agents run cheap per token, while back-office and recruiting work costs far more.

Previous reports

Read the May 2026 AI Gateway production index.

About this data

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through May 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend uses market-rate pricing (published list price) to provide a normalized view across teams that bring their own API keys.

  • Volume counts tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • B2C, B2B, and use-case classifications are aggregate. No individual team or workload is identified.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as data completes.

title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
description:
By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis Garcia

Introduction

Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.

This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.

We believe:

A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.

It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.

A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example,

A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.”

Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build.

Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them.

What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks.

The Lifecycle at a Glance

Figure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them.

We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset.

Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters.

In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated.

Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases.

System components

Four automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them.

  • Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision.
  • Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement).
  • Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations.
  • Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale.
  • Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out.

Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground Truth

Everything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later.

Why we built our own benchmark

Off-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources:

  • Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces.
  • Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own.
  • Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs.

Two details that mattered

  • The benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale.
  • Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning.

Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to Humans

The failure mode: right answer, wrong reason

There is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance.

We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output:

  • a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), and
  • a short natural-language rationale for that label.

Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast.

The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below.

Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning

We tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop.

Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale.

At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows.

  1. Score the training data with the current rubric.
  2. Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop.
  3. Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric.

The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes:

  • Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s.
  • Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match.

So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning.

Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses.

RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it.

Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them.

Alignment metrics

We run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics.

  • Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard.
  • Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low.
  • Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason.

Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve.

Ablation: does the reasoning signal help?

To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales.

Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t.

Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to Work

Once deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests.

Two roles for one judge

Once we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation:

  • Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails.
  • Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again.

The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision.

Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serve

We cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served.

That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget.

Do judge-approved explanations help members?

Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period.

Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful.

Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge Aligned

A judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop.

The weekly human review

For each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark.

Setting the bar with human disagreement

The panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread.

Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We require

so the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt.

Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback.

What human review catches that metrics can’t

Beyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things?

In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much.

When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references.

Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both.

  • Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric.
  • Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members.

What We Learned

Five lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge:

  1. Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s.
  2. Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable.
  3. One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once.
  4. Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten.
  5. Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped.

Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making.

Acknowledgements

This post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations.

Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage.

The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
description:
arXiv:2610.19344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
description:
arXiv:2610.19367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.14381v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
description:
arXiv:2610.19210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}

title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
description:
by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian Shang

Intro

Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets.

Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values.

Initial Problem

Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required:

  • extensive business knowledge
  • familiarity with experimentation conventions
  • and complex engineering practices

This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform.

Enter DataJunction

To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case.

DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform.

Architecture Decisions

A critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention.

API First, UI and Other Interfaces Later

A metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request.

Consistent Graph First, Other Features Later

A complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them:

  • semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoring
  • metric and dimension query / definition generation
  • metric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine)
  • data visualization and data tracking
  • performance optimization (aka caching or materialization)
  • integration layer with other tools and
  • any / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more.

Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core.

Cube as The Perfect Consumption Protocol

Analytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects.

In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below.

We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters.

One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset.

Experimentation at Netflix

Metrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions.

At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation.

This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models.

Conclusions

With experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both:

  • find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ)
  • easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stack

That will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix.

Related resources:

  • 2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck)
  • 2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video)
  • 2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog)

DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: How to Practice Coding Interviews Without a Partner (5 Options, Prices Checked)
description:
A practice partner gives you three things: a problem you haven't seen, follow-up questions (what's the complexity, what about an empty input, can you do better), and someone watching. Alone, the first is easy. The other two need someone, or something, on the other side.

Your options

Option Asks follow-ups Spoken Feedback Price as billed
Self-mock routine No You talk to yourself You grade yourself Free
DevInterview.ai (mine) Yes Live voice interviewer Scored report with a hire verdict First interview free; $19.99/mo, $49.99/qtr, $99.99/yr
interviewing.io's AI Interviewer Not stated Not stated Feedback at the end Free
ChatGPT voice mode Not stated Yes Not stated Free with daily limits; Plus $20/mo
Peer mocks on Aced (formerly Exponent) Yes, from another candidate Live Notes from your partner Free, 5 a month

1. The self-mock routine (free)

  1. Pick a problem you haven't seen, at your level, like an untouched one from the NeetCode 150.
  2. Set a timer for 30 to 45 minutes and don't pause it.
  3. Talk the whole time: restate the problem, walk an example, state the brute force and its complexity, improve it, code it, test it by hand.
  4. Record yourself. Listen back once and count the silences.
  5. Grade four things: did you clarify the problem, state the complexity, test your code, and keep talking.

Its limit: nobody pushes back, so you never practice the follow-up question, which is where a lot of interviews are decided.

2. An AI interviewer that talks: DevInterview.ai

This is the one I built. It runs a 30-minute coding round in an editor that runs your code, in any of 7 languages, set to your target company and level. The interviewer talks, asks follow-ups, and is told never to say whether you're right and never to hand you the solution. Each interview ends with a scored report and a hire verdict. The same plan covers a 45-minute system design round on a canvas and a 30-minute behavioral round. First interview free, then $19.99 a month.

Where it falls short: it's an AI, not a person who runs real hiring loops, and it won't give you the nerves of a stranger watching.

3. interviewing.io's free AI Interviewer

Per its site, it runs coding and system design interviews in the style of a FAANG mock, with feedback at the end, for free. The site doesn't say whether it speaks or runs your code, so try a session and see.

4. ChatGPT voice mode

Tell it to act as an interviewer, give it a problem, and ask it to push back. Free with daily limits, Plus is $20 a month. OpenAI doesn't describe an interview mode or scoring, so the structure is whatever you prompt for.

5. Peer mocks, if a stranger counts

Aced (formerly Exponent) matches you with another candidate and you interview each other. Free accounts get 5 a month, and afterwards you trade notes using realistic rubrics, in Aced's words. Every session needs scheduling.

System design without a partner

Harder alone, because the interviewer's questions steer the design. DevInterview.ai's 45-minute system design round runs on a canvas and asks those questions. Hello Interview's Guided Practice walks you through the steps of an interview with personalized feedback; it comes with Premium, at list price $59 for 1 month, $119 for 1 year or $399 lifetime, with a sale running when I checked.

Where this fits

Practicing alone is step 3 of the plan I'd give a friend: learn the patterns on NeetCode, study system design on Hello Interview, practice out loud on DevInterview.ai, and, super optional, one human session on interviewing.io. The full 8-week version is here.

Checked on each vendor's own site between October 8 and October 14, 2026. The full article, with sources, is on devinterview.ai.

title: AWS Transfer Family now supports AWS Secrets Manager storage for SFTP server host keys
description:
AWS Transfer Family now lets you store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in your own AWS account. This gives you greater control over your server identity and helps simplify server migrations and failover.

Previously, Transfer Family stored host keys within the service, so you could not retrieve the associated private key material. With this launch, you can choose Secrets Manager as the storage type when creating a server or importing a host key. You can then retrieve the private key material and reuse the same host key across servers and AWS Regions. For example, you can use it on a standby server for failover or on a replacement server during migration, without requiring clients to trust a new host key. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies let you control who can retrieve the stored keys. You can also migrate existing host keys to Secrets Manager, which may require additional steps; see the AWS Transfer Family User Guide for details.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transfer Family is available. To learn more, see Store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide. To get started, go to the AWS Transfer Family console.

title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
description:
arXiv:2610.19041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.

title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
description:
arXiv:2610.19218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

title: MicroSDF: Microfacet-Driven Hybrid Neural SDFs for Mixed-Reflectance Surface Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.

title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.
