title: PII Redaction for Web Scraping: A Practical Python Pipeline
description:
TL;DR:

  • Remove unnecessary personal fields before storing scraped records.
  • Detection and redaction are separate operations with different failure modes.
  • A redaction middleware reduces data exposure; it does not establish GDPR compliance by itself.

A scraping pipeline can collect contact details even when its business task only needs organization names or product descriptions. Those details may enter logs, storage, embeddings, and model prompts before anyone notices them. The useful place to reduce exposure is immediately after extraction and before those downstream systems receive the record.

This tutorial implements a small middleware with Presidio. It uses synthetic contact information, a narrow pattern-based detector, and an explicit storage allowlist. The example is intentionally limited so you can see which entities it recognizes and which responsibilities remain outside the code.

Pipeline at a Glance

The pipeline runs acquisition, extraction, detection, redaction, validation, and storage in that order. Acquisition returns page content. Extraction selects business fields. The privacy stage then examines the selected text and removes recognized contact details before the storage stage receives anything.

Keep this boundary close to extraction. If raw HTML is logged upstream, a later redaction function cannot remove the copy already written to your logs. Treat raw captures as restricted diagnostic material when they may contain personal data, and give them a separate retention policy.

The Scrapeless Web Unlocker guide describes a URL acquisition path. Your middleware remains responsible for the field-level decisions after acquisition.

Identify Fields You Need to Keep

Define the allowed business fields before selecting a detector. If your task needs an organization name, category, and public description, do not persist contact emails merely because the page includes them. An allowlist makes that decision visible in code.

Also distinguish redaction from pseudonymization and anonymization. Removing a matched substring is a text transformation. Replacing a value with a stable token may still let records be linked. An anonymous result requires a broader assessment of whether a person can be identified from the remaining data and available context.

The pseudonymization discussion in the EDPB consultation guidelines explains why replacing an identifier alone does not settle whether a record can be attributed to a person. Whether a particular workflow has an appropriate legal basis, notice, retention policy, or transfer arrangement depends on its circumstances. The middleware below does not answer those questions.

Detect PII with Presidio

Presidio separates recognition from text transformation. Its regular-expression tutorial shows how PatternRecognizer accepts patterns with entity types and scores.

Install the analyzer and anonymizer:

python -m pip install presidio-analyzer presidio-anonymizer

This starter uses pattern recognizers directly. It does not load a language model or claim to identify names, addresses, or all phone formats. Add suitable recognizers and evaluate them against your actual language and data distribution before expanding the scope.

Redact, Tokenize, or Quarantine Records

The following program processes synthetic data, redacts two supported patterns, and writes only approved fields. The example.com email address and phone format are demonstration inputs, not scraped personal information.

import json
from pathlib import Path

from presidio_analyzer import Pattern, PatternRecognizer
from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine
from presidio_anonymizer.entities import OperatorConfig

recognizers = [
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="EMAIL_ADDRESS",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="email",
            regex=r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}",
            score=0.8,
        )],
    ),
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="PHONE_NUMBER",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="demo_us_phone",
            regex=r"\b\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}\b",
            score=0.7,
        )],
    ),
]
engine = AnonymizerEngine()
allowed_fields = {"organization", "description", "source_url"}


def detect(text):
    found = []
    for recognizer in recognizers:
        found.extend(recognizer.analyze(
            text=text, entities=recognizer.supported_entities
        ))
    return found


def clean_record(record):
    cleaned = {}
    for key, value in record.items():
        if key not in allowed_fields:
            continue
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("This schema permits string fields only")
        cleaned[key] = engine.anonymize(
            text=value,
            analyzer_results=detect(value),
            operators={"DEFAULT": OperatorConfig("replace", {
                "new_value": "<REDACTED>"
            })},
        ).text
    if any(detect(value) for value in cleaned.values()):
        raise ValueError("Recognized contact data remains")
    return cleaned


synthetic = {
    "organization": "Example Research Lab",
    "description": "Contact sample.person@example.com or 202-555-0143.",
    "source_url": "https://example.com/",
    "raw_contact": "sample.person@example.com",
}
result = clean_record(synthetic)
assert "raw_contact" not in result
assert "sample.person@example.com" not in result["description"]
assert "202-555-0143" not in result["description"]
Path("clean-record.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(result, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
)
print(result["description"])

The synthetic demonstration prints:

Contact <REDACTED> or <REDACTED>.

The Presidio anonymizer supports different transformations. Choose them deliberately. A reversible transformation needs key management and access rules; a stable replacement can preserve relationships that you may not want to retain.

If a required business field becomes unusable after redaction, quarantine the record for review instead of restoring the removed personal value automatically. Store a reason code without copying the sensitive substring into that reason.

Apply the Middleware to Scrapeless Output

Run the middleware after your parser maps the acquisition response into the declared record schema. Pass only the extracted fields to clean_record, rather than treating every HTML attribute as an approved business field.

For a page fetched through Scrapeless Web Unlocker, the sequence is: check the API envelope, verify page identity, parse the selected content, clean each record, and then export accepted records. A browser session follows the same storage boundary after its extraction step.

Some personal information lives outside body text. Query parameters, document names, images, and free-form metadata need their own treatment. If a URL can identify a person, do not assume it is safe merely because your current contact regex does not match it.

Validate Missed Entities and Retention Rules

A detector needs both positive and negative test cases. Positive cases check that supported personal values are removed. Negative cases check that normal product identifiers, dates, and technical strings are preserved. Include nonstandard formatting and the languages present in your real data.

The final detector call in the code confirms that its own recognized patterns are absent. It cannot detect an entity type the recognizer never supported. Document that scope so the check is not presented as a complete privacy assessment.

Keep raw captures out of routine logs. Record counts, entity types, reason codes, and schema outcomes instead of raw snippets. Define who can review quarantined records and when diagnostic captures are deleted. Apply the same controls to embeddings and model inputs, because those are additional downstream copies.

Conclusion

A practical privacy boundary starts with collecting and storing fewer fields. Add detection and redaction for the fields you still need, test the recognizers on realistic examples, and keep raw diagnostics separate. The software can enforce those decisions consistently once the decisions have been made.

FAQ

Does replacing matched emails make a dataset anonymous?

No. Other fields and contextual information may still identify a person. Anonymity depends on the complete dataset and use context.

Does this code recognize names and addresses?

No. It recognizes its configured email pattern and one demonstration phone format. Additional entity types need their own recognizers and evaluation.

Why use an allowlist as well as a detector?

An allowlist prevents unnecessary fields from reaching storage. Detection handles supported personal values inside fields that remain allowed.

Is a privacy middleware enough for GDPR compliance?

No. The workflow also needs decisions about its purpose, legal basis, transparency, retention, security, and other applicable obligations.

Only collect data you are authorized to access, and review applicable terms and privacy requirements. This article provides technical information, not legal advice.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
description:
arXiv:2610.19003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

title: Building a reading ruler that floats over every Android app: touch pass-through, Android 12's opacity cap, and masks
description:
I make ReadFocus+, a small Android app that floats a translucent strip (a "reading ruler") over the screen, mainly for people with dyslexia or ADHD who lose their place in long text. It has to work on top of any app: ebooks, PDFs, browsers, news apps. So it is built on a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay. These are the parts that took the most time.

Layout: one strip, two masks, one control panel

  • The strip: one window, MATCH_PARENT wide with adjustable height. TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (TYPE_PHONE below API 26), PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT.
  • Line highlight mode: a View inside the strip painted with a GradientDrawable in the theme colour; the View's alpha sets the strength. No custom onDraw.
  • Reading mask mode: two separate windows, a solid View pinned to Gravity.TOP and one to Gravity.BOTTOM, with the gap between them as the reading window. When you drag the strip, both masks follow.
  • Control panel: another window holding the mode switch and the lock button.

Letting touches through to the app underneath

(The code below is simplified for the article.)

A reading ruler is only useful if you can keep scrolling the app under it.

int flags = WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN;
if (locked) flags |= WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE; // locked = touches pass through
  • The default is locked (touch pass-through). To move the strip you unlock it from the panel, then drag the strip itself with ACTION_DOWN/MOVE/UP and updateViewLayout on params.y.
  • When toggling FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, I remove the window and add it again rather than only updating the flags.
  • y is clamped between the status bar and the navigation bar, using WindowInsets (statusBars, navigationBars, systemGestures, displayCutout).

Android 12: the opacity cap on pass-through windows

From Android 12 (API 31), an overlay that lets touches pass through to another app has a maximum opacity. Go above it and the system blocks the touches instead (the "untrusted touches" protection).

float maxAlpha = 1f;
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) {
    InputManager im = getSystemService(InputManager.class);
    maxAlpha = (im != null) ? im.getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch() : 0.8f;
}
params.alpha = maxAlpha;

So the window alpha is pinned to that ceiling, and the visible strength comes from the inner View's alpha and the theme colour. This is also why the mask can never be fully black.

Display cutouts

On phones with a notch, the top mask must not leave a gap above it:

  • API 30+: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS
  • API 28–29: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_SHORT_EDGES

On rotation, onConfigurationChanged re-clamps the strip and redraws the masks. Every window also has FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON, so the screen doesn't go dark mid-page.

Staying alive and coming back after process death

  • A foreground service with foregroundServiceType="specialUse" (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE) and a low-importance, ongoing notification.
  • Besides START_STICKY, the overlay is restored on app launch, on process restart, and by a WorkManager watchdog every 15 minutes.
  • Users can revoke the overlay permission at any time, and adding a window after that throws BadTokenException, so Settings.canDrawOverlays() is checked before every addView.

The permission flow

ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION with a package: URI → retry without it → fall back to ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS. The guide screen checks canDrawOverlays() in onResume and returns as soon as it's true.

Wrapping up

Most of the work was in small details that let the overlay sit on top without getting in the way. If you're building an overlay of your own, I hope this saves you some time. The app is here (there's a Windows version too):

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.codedac.readfocus
  • Website: https://codedac.com/apps/readfocus.html

title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.

title: Building Retrieval Architecture for Developer Changelog Tracker — 5 Python Ranking Signals
description:
When a changelog bot cites the wrong release, the root cause is usually a trust-boundary mistake, not a weak language model. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context, then choose ranking signals you can evaluate. Keep region, retention, and deletion policy beside the index design; an AI runtime cannot grant contractual residency for a specialist data store.

The retrieval contract comes before ranking

For a B2B SaaS developer changelog tracker, write the user-visible answer first: “What changed in package X, and when?” Turn that sentence into a contract with required fields: canonical URL, release timestamp, package, version, source region, and a citation span. A result that matches the words but lacks a timestamp is not a valid answer.

I model each chunk with immutable source_id, published_at, updated_at, and deleted_at metadata. The collection is private to the application tenant. Deletions are events, not a cleanup task: remove the record from the collection when the upstream page disappears, and re-index changed content deliberately so an old chunk cannot outrank the current release.

The first stage gathers candidates from lexical web search or a vector collection. The second stage scores them with signals that mirror the contract:

  • lexical overlap for package and version tokens;
  • semantic similarity for paraphrased release notes;
  • recency, with a bounded decay rather than an unreviewed “newer is always better” rule;
  • source authority, such as the maintainer’s canonical feed;
  • metadata completeness and citation-span availability.

That is the trap.

For the orchestration layer, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants a self-describing REST surface: its public discovery endpoint exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, so a Python service can inspect a new retrieval capability without installing another SDK. Keep the tenant's durable records in the system that owns your residency and deletion agreement; the routing layer does not replace that boundary.

How should a Python changelog tracker rank retrieval signals?

Start with a small labeled set: 50–100 real questions, two acceptable citations per question, and a reviewer decision for “stale but relevant.” Measure recall@k for candidate generation and citation precision for the final answer. I would not ship a new weighting because it feels right; I would ship it when the eval harness shows fewer unsupported citations without pushing latency past the product budget. Your mileage may vary because release cadence and tenant vocabulary change the labels.

A simple, inspectable score is often enough for the first iteration:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from math import exp


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    text: str
    lexical: float
    semantic: float
    authority: float
    published_at: datetime
    has_citation_span: bool


def rank(candidates: list[Candidate], now: datetime | None = None) -> list[Candidate]:
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    def score(item: Candidate) -> float:
        age_days = max((now - item.published_at).total_seconds() / 86400, 0)
        recency = exp(-age_days / 180)
        citation = 1.0 if item.has_citation_span else 0.0
        return (
            0.30 * item.lexical
            + 0.30 * item.semantic
            + 0.20 * recency
            + 0.15 * item.authority
            + 0.05 * citation
        )

    return sorted(candidates, key=score, reverse=True)

The exact weights are provisional. Log every component, the selected source_id, and the final citation so a failed answer can be replayed. A 429 from a provider is a control-flow event: back off, honor Retry-After, and keep the user request bounded by a deadline.

A bounded two-stage request in Python

The following example keeps discovery and retrieval separate. It searches the public web for candidate release notes, then queries a named vector collection for internal copies. It uses one timeout budget and exponential backoff; no provider key is embedded in the source.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def post_json(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any], deadline: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    delay = 0.5
    while True:
        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise TimeoutError("retrieval deadline exceeded")
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=min(remaining, 8.0),
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait = float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay
            time.sleep(min(wait, max(remaining, 0)))
            delay = min(delay * 2, 8.0)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()


def retrieve(question: str) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 10.0
    web = post_json("/web/search", {"query": question}, deadline)
    vector = post_json(
        "/vector/query",
        {"collection": "tenant-changelog", "query": question, "limit": 20},
        deadline,
    )
    return web, vector


if __name__ == "__main__":
    web_results, vector_results = retrieve("Python 3.13 deprecation in package acme-sdk")
    print({"web": web_results, "vector": vector_results})

The payload fields should be checked against the current discovery schema before production rollout. The important architectural property is the boundary: web results are candidates, while the tenant collection supplies durable metadata and citation context. Keep raw documents in a storage system whose region, retention, deletion API, and processor terms meet your contract; route only the minimum text needed for ranking.

Infrai is a practical fit when a team wants this wiring behind one plain REST API and a self-describing discovery surface: GET /v1/discovery exposes capabilities, schemas, and runnable examples, so adding a retrieval stage does not require installing another SDK. The same key and consistent interface across backend capabilities also reduce integration bookkeeping. That is an operational benefit, not proof that the service is your data processor of record.

Where the alternatives fit

No single backend wins every trust review. Here is the decision I would put in an architecture record:

Option Strength for changelog retrieval Boundary or trade-off
Elasticsearch Mature lexical ranking, filters, and self-managed deployment choices You own cluster operations, patching, and residency configuration
OpenSearch Open-source distribution with familiar inverted-index and vector features Compatibility and managed-service terms vary by provider
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused operational surface Confirm region, retention, and deletion guarantees for your tenant contract
Weaviate Hybrid search and schema-oriented objects More platform concepts to govern when the bot needs only a narrow index
Infrai Self-describing REST discovery plus a single integration surface for web and vector stages A specialist search or storage provider may be better for contractual residency controls

The catch is important: stick with a regional Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate deployment when legal or procurement requires a processor agreement and deletion evidence that your chosen runtime does not provide. Infrai should be the option to try for the retrieval orchestration layer when transparent discovery and a consistent HTTP integration matter; it should not be used as a substitute for a specialist provider's residency contract.

Ship the eval gate with the index

Before rollout, replay the labeled questions after every re-index. Check that deleted release notes no longer appear, that an updated page has one canonical chunk, and that each answer can point to a source span. Set hard limits for candidate count, query time, and retries; a slow upstream source must not block the user flow.

The eval set should include awkward cases: a package with two releases on the same day, a changelog edited after publication, a superseded security notice, and a question whose answer is “no matching release.” Record the query, candidate IDs, score components, selected span, and policy version. That trace lets a reviewer distinguish a ranking error from a missing document, and it gives you a concrete regression test when the ingestion job changes.

I have found the most useful dashboard is small: recall@20, citation precision, stale-result rate, deletion lag, and p95 retrieval time. Do not collapse those into one vanity score. A bot can improve recall while quietly returning older citations, which is a trust regression even if the language model sounds fluent.

I'm not sure a single global recency half-life will survive every ecosystem. Keep it configurable, record the version of the ranking policy, and inspect misses by package and release age. I've seen enough retrieval reviews to know that a tidy score can hide a messy contract. The useful artifact is a trace, not a confidence adjective; don't ship on confidence wording alone.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector discovery and retrieval guidance and verify the live schema before wiring it into production.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/vector/answers/my-rag-chatbot-s-vector-search-keeps-letting-irrelevant/
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html
  • https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/vector-search/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/search/hybrid

title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.

title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
description:
arXiv:2610.19407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

title: MedScribe AI — An Agentic Radiologist's Assistant
description:
---
title: "MedScribe AI — An Agentic Radiologist's Assistant Built with Open-Source AI"
published: true

tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, ai, healthcare

The Problem

Radiology reporting is slow, expensive, and inaccessible — especially in
low-resource settings like Pakistan where radiologists are scarce. Most
diagnostic AI tools stop at a raw prediction, leaving clinicians unable
to act efficiently.

MedScribe AI changes that.

What We Built

MedScribe AI is an agentic assistant that supports radiologists by
combining computer vision with generative AI to produce full clinical
reports from chest X-ray images — in seconds.

🔗 Live Demo:


How It Works

The system runs in three stages:

1. Computer Vision Model

  • ResNet18 trained on pediatric chest X-rays (Kaggle dataset)
  • 90.5% accuracy, 98.4% precision, 93.2% F1-score
  • Grad-CAM explainability — highlights exactly which regions influenced the prediction

2. AI Agent Pipeline (LangGraph + Groq)

Four agents run in sequence:

Agent What it does
Vision Runs CV model, returns findings + confidence
Reasoning LLM decides which tools to call (ReAct loop)
Reporting Generates structured clinical report
Escalation Flags critical cases for immediate attention

3. Application Interface (Streamlit)

  • Upload chest X-ray → get full clinical report in seconds
  • Doctor-facing report + patient-facing plain language summary
  • Bilingual output: English + Urdu 🇵🇰
  • Downloadable PDF with original X-ray + Grad-CAM heatmap

Why Open Source AI?

  • openai/gpt-oss-120b via Groq — fast, free inference with no data sent to proprietary servers
  • TorchXRayVision — open-source medical imaging foundation model
  • LangGraph — open-source agent framework, fully customizable
  • PyTorch + torchvision — open weights, reproducible training

Running on open models means patient X-rays never leave the
user's control — critical for healthcare privacy.

Who Would Pay For This?

  • Private clinics in Pakistan and South Asia with no on-site radiologist
  • Telehealth platforms needing automated preliminary reports
  • Hospital chains processing high volumes of routine chest X-rays

A clinic paying $50/month for preliminary AI triage is far cheaper
than hiring a part-time radiologist.

Tech Stack

CV Model: PyTorch · ResNet18 · TorchXRayVision · Grad-CAM
AI Agents: LangGraph · Groq (gpt-oss-120b) · ReAct
App: Streamlit · Python

Team

Built in 48 hours at Pak Angels Generative & Agentic AI Hackathon
(Cohort 11) by a team of 6 from Pakistan 🇵🇰

Open source AI isn't just a technical choice — for healthcare in
underserved regions, it's the only choice that makes the economics work.

title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy
description:
arXiv:2610.19492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.

title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
description:
arXiv:2610.19043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19623v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

title: Healthtech Metering in Go: Provision a Scoped API Key with a Setup Script
description:
TL;DR: A setup job should mint a credential restricted to one customer-usage writer, place it in a secret store without printing it, authenticate with the stored value, and fail unless the returned subject, tenant, and scopes exactly match the request. For a healthtech meter, that identity check matters more than a green “secret written” response: the invoice pipeline must be able to show which workload was allowed to append usage for which customer account, while the credential itself stays out of logs and build artifacts.

Treat bootstrap as a small security transaction with an explicit commit point. Provisioning is not complete when a key exists. It is complete only after the key has crossed into the secret store, the setup process has discarded its plaintext copy, and an authenticated probe proves that the stored value represents the intended machine identity. This framing also forces failure handling into the design: before the commit point, any partial key is untrusted and must be removed; after it, rotation becomes an ordinary lifecycle operation with a known owner and version.

How should a setup script provision and verify a scoped API key?

Imagine the incident review, without inventing an incident: a healthtech platform receives one usage event for customer clinic-042, the event later contributes to a metered invoice, and the audit trail says only that “CI” wrote it. The dashboard is green. The useful questions are less comfortable: which subject authenticated, which tenant boundary applied, which scopes were effective, and did the same credential have permission to read patient data or alter invoices?

If those answers cannot be recovered without exposing the key, the bootstrap design has already failed its primary decision axis: auditability of access. The invariant is straightforward: a credential used to append billable usage must resolve to one stable workload subject, one expected account boundary, and the smallest effective scope set. An environment name such as production is context, not identity.

No identity, no commit.

I would page on repeated identity-verification failures, unexpected subjects, or broader scopes. I would not page merely because a rotation occurred. A rotation is expected state change; an accepted credential that cannot prove its owner is the event that threatens attribution.

Model the handoff before choosing an API

There is no universal API-key provisioning protocol, so keep vendor routes outside the safety logic. The core needs three adapters: a provisioner that returns a secret once, a store that accepts bytes under a versioned name, and an identity endpoint that reports the authenticated principal. That separation lets a team replace an account API or secret backend without weakening the checks that decide whether bootstrap succeeded.

For the example meter, request only an append permission for a single tenant. Do not grant a generic admin scope because setup is convenient. Do not reuse the deployment credential either; deployment and usage submission produce different audit questions and deserve different subjects.

Boundary Required evidence Reject when
Provisioning requested subject, tenant, and scope set the request is ambiguous or overbroad
Secret write versioned secret reference, not plaintext the destination is mutable without version evidence
Authentication returned subject, tenant, and effective scopes any field differs from the request
Audit request ID and secret version the record contains the key or its hash

Do not log a key fingerprint as a consolation prize. A stable fingerprint becomes another correlator, is unnecessary for the decision above, and can encourage teams to treat possession evidence as identity evidence. Log the non-secret subject, tenant, scope set, secret version, and request ID instead. OWASP's secrets guidance recommends centralized storage, least privilege, rotation, expiration where possible, and care to prevent secrets from reaching logs.

That is enough evidence.

Make the verification path executable

The following program is deliberately adapter-driven. Its in-memory implementations make the example runnable with go run, while production adapters would call an account control plane and a secret manager over authenticated, encrypted connections. The safety function does not know their URLs.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/base64"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type Request struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Identity struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Provisioner interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error)
    Revoke(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) error
}

type SecretStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, name string, value []byte) (version string, err error)
    Get(ctx context.Context, name, version string) ([]byte, error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, name, version string) error
}

type Authenticator interface {
    WhoAmI(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error)
}

func bootstrap(ctx context.Context, request Request, name string,
    p Provisioner, store SecretStore, auth Authenticator) (string, error) {

    credential, err := p.Create(ctx, request)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("provision credential: %w", err)
    }
    committed := false
    defer func() {
        if !committed {
            _ = p.Revoke(ctx, credential)
        }
        clear(credential)
    }()

    version, err := store.Put(ctx, name, credential)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("store credential: %w", err)
    }

    stored, err := store.Get(ctx, name, version)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("read stored version: %w", err)
    }
    defer clear(stored)

    identity, err := auth.WhoAmI(ctx, stored)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("authenticate stored credential: %w", err)
    }
    wantScopes := append([]string(nil), request.Scopes...)
    gotScopes := append([]string(nil), identity.Scopes...)
    slices.Sort(wantScopes)
    slices.Sort(gotScopes)
    if identity.Subject != request.Subject || identity.Tenant != request.Tenant ||
        !slices.Equal(gotScopes, wantScopes) {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", errors.New("verified identity does not match requested boundary")
    }

    committed = true
    return version, nil
}

type memoryBackend struct {
    value    []byte
    request  Request
    version  string
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Create(_ context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error) {
    raw := make([]byte, 32)
    if _, err := rand.Read(raw); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    m.request = request
    return []byte(base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(raw)), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Revoke(_ context.Context, _ []byte) error { return nil }

func (m *memoryBackend) Put(_ context.Context, _ string, value []byte) (string, error) {
    m.value = append([]byte(nil), value...)
    m.version = "1"
    return m.version, nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Get(_ context.Context, _, version string) ([]byte, error) {
    if version != m.version {
        return nil, errors.New("unknown version")
    }
    return append([]byte(nil), m.value...), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Delete(_ context.Context, _, _ string) error {
    clear(m.value)
    m.value = nil
    return nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) WhoAmI(_ context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error) {
    if !slices.Equal(credential, m.value) {
        return Identity{}, errors.New("unauthorized")
    }
    return Identity(m.request), nil
}

func main() {
    backend := &memoryBackend{}
    request := Request{
        Subject: "ci-usage-writer",
        Tenant:  "clinic-042",
        Scopes:  []string{"usage:append"},
    }
    version, err := bootstrap(context.Background(), request,
        "healthtech/clinic-042/usage-writer", backend, backend, backend)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bootstrap verified: subject=%s tenant=%s secret_version=%s\n",
        request.Subject, request.Tenant, version)
}

The compensating path deserves scrutiny. If storage or verification fails, the program deletes the untrusted stored version and attempts revocation. Production code should use a short, separate cleanup context so cancellation of the main setup context does not prevent cleanup; it should also emit a non-secret request ID for reconciliation. The example keeps one context to expose the transaction shape without pretending that generic adapters share retry semantics.

This sample requires Go 1.21 because it uses clear and the slices package.

One subtle limit remains: Go's clear reduces accidental retention in these byte slices, but it cannot promise that no copy exists elsewhere in a runtime, transport, or backend. The stronger controls are architectural: never place the returned value in command arguments, environment dumps, formatted errors, test snapshots, or shell tracing; restrict the setup runner; and make the secret short-lived enough that rotation is routine.

Test the identity mismatch, not only the happy path

A useful test changes the returned identity after the secret write. Make the fake authenticator return clinic-024, add usage:read, or replace ci-usage-writer with a human subject. Each mutation must make bootstrap fail and trigger deletion plus revocation. Also test a store that acknowledges Put but cannot read the exact version back; “latest” is a race-prone reference when two setup jobs overlap.

Test logs too. Feed a recognizable canary credential through every error path, capture process output, and fail the test if the canary appears. This is where a bland success metric stops helping. The check should distinguish these states: provisioning never happened, provisioned but not stored, stored but not authenticated, identity mismatch, cleanup incomplete, and verified.

Retries require idempotency at the adapter boundary. If the provisioning service accepts an idempotency token, derive a new opaque token for one bootstrap attempt and persist its non-secret request ID. If it does not, reconcile by requested subject and tenant before creating another credential, then revoke superseded credentials after a verified replacement exists. Never infer success from an earlier process exit code alone.

Know when a static key is the wrong primitive

This pattern applies when the target service accepts an API key and the CI system must bootstrap it. It does not make a long-lived bearer secret ideal. When both ends support workload federation or another short-lived, audience-bound mechanism, prefer that design: the pipeline exchanges an existing workload identity for temporary access instead of storing a reusable credential. OAuth 2.0 defines bearer-token handling, and RFC 8707 defines resource indicators that can restrict where an access token is intended to be used; neither specification turns an arbitrary API key into a federated identity.

The decision is operational. Static bootstrap is defensible when its scope is narrow, its owner is machine-specific, rotation and revocation are tested, reads from the secret store are auditable, and the authenticated service can report effective identity. The limitation of this pattern is the reusable bearer secret: it is a poor fit when the service cannot expose identity, when all keys inherit account-wide permissions, or when a CI runner cannot keep secret output out of logs. The trade-off is extra setup and rotation work in exchange for compatibility with services that do not accept workload federation; that reason disappears as soon as both sides can exchange a workload identity for short-lived, audience-bound access.

Prefer federation then.

Before enabling the usage writer, run one synthetic event against a non-billable test tenant, verify the authenticated subject in the access record, and confirm that a forbidden operation is actually denied. Then alert on identity drift and cleanup failures, not on dashboard color. The final artifact is evidence of a bounded principal, not evidence that a string was copied successfully.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707

title: Eloquent vs Query Builder in Laravel: When to Use Each
description:
Use Eloquent when you are working with individual records that have behavior: validation rules, casts, relationships, events, soft deletes. Use the query builder when you are working with rows as data: reports, joins, aggregates, bulk writes and large exports. That rule covers most cases, but the details are where bugs come from, because the two do not behave the same on updates, deletes and inserts. I ran both against a 50,000-row MariaDB table using the real framework code (Laravel 13.35.0) to measure the cost and to check every claim below.

They are the same engine

An Eloquent builder is a wrapper around the query builder. The same fluent methods exist on both, and the SQL is nearly identical. The only difference in this example is the soft delete condition the model adds on its own:

DB::table('posts')
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')->limit(5)->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? order by `id` desc limit 5

Post::where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')
    ->limit(5)
    ->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? and `posts`.`deleted_at` is null order by `id` desc limit 5

So the choice is not about SQL features. It is about what happens to the rows before you see them and when you write them back.

What Eloquent adds, and what it costs

The query builder returns plain stdClass objects with the values exactly as the database driver gives them. Eloquent turns every row into a model: it applies casts, attaches the original attributes for dirty tracking, fires a retrieved event and registers the model with its relations. In the test, the same row looked like this from each side:

Column DB::table() Model
meta (JSON) string: '{"tags":["a","b","c"],"score":1}' array (cast)
published_at string: '2026-10-14 13:38:00' Carbon instance (cast)
Row type stdClass Post

That convenience has a price, and it shows when you load many rows. I loaded all 50,000 rows with each approach, in a fresh PHP process each time, three runs per row, taking the median:

Approach (50,000 rows, all columns) Time Extra memory
DB::table('posts')->get() about 160 ms 59 MB
Post::get() about 980 ms 103 MB
Post::get() then reading the casts on every row about 1,900 ms 105 MB
Post::query()->toBase()->get() about 200 ms 60 MB
DB::table() with select('id', 'title') about 65 ms 28 MB
Post::select('id', 'title')->get() about 880 ms 76 MB
DB::table()->chunkById(1000) about 180 ms 2.3 MB
Post::chunkById(1000) about 1,200 ms 4.2 MB
DB::table()->cursor() about 255 ms 8.4 MB
Post::cursor() about 2,900 ms 9.4 MB

Hydrating 50,000 models took about six times longer than reading the same rows as plain objects, and used less than twice the memory. Selecting only the columns you need helps both sides, but does not remove the hydration cost. Nobody renders 50,000 models in one request, so this matters for exports, reports and background jobs, not for a paginated page of 25 rows. The numbers are from one machine with MariaDB on localhost; a network hop would add the same cost to both sides, which would shrink the percentage gap but not the absolute one.

Two practical notes from the table. First, toBase() is the bridge: it keeps your model's query scopes and gives you plain rows. Second, cursor() keeps memory flat but is the slowest option for models. The Laravel documentation also notes that PDO still buffers the raw results, so for very large result sets it recommends lazy(), and chunkById when you update the column you are filtering on.

Three places where they behave differently

This is the part that causes production bugs. I ran each operation inside a transaction and rolled it back, with listeners registered on the model:

Operation Model events Result
$post->update([...]) saving, updating, updated, saved updated_at changed
Post::where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at changed
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at unchanged
$post->delete() (soft deletes on) deleting, deleted Row kept, deleted_at set
Post::where(...)->delete() none Row kept, deleted_at set
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->delete() none Row permanently deleted
Post::insert([...]) none created_at is NULL
Post::create([...]) saving, saved (the create events fire as well) Timestamps filled

Read it as three rules:

  1. A mass update or delete through Eloquent fires no model events. The Laravel documentation says this directly: the models are never retrieved, so events such as updating and deleting are not dispatched. If you have an observer that clears a cache, writes an audit log or syncs a search index, a Post::where(...)->update() silently skips it. Load the models and save them, or accept that the observer will not run.
  2. The query builder ignores soft deletes. DB::table('posts')->delete() removes the row for good, while the same intent through the model only sets deleted_at. Counts differ too: on my data Post::count() returned 49,000 while DB::table('posts')->count() returned 50,000. A report built on DB::table() will include soft-deleted rows unless you filter them yourself.
  3. Bulkinsert()does not set timestamps, even on a model. Post::insert() goes straight to the query builder, so created_at and updated_at stay NULL unless you supply them. Post::upsert() is different: as documented, it sets the timestamps. In my test it updated updated_at, while DB::table('posts')->upsert() left it untouched.

Mass assignment follows the same split. A model only fills attributes you allow ($fillable in my test; the 13.x documentation shows a Fillable attribute for the same job), and extra keys are silently discarded. In my run, Post::create() with id and an unknown key ignored both, whereas DB::table()->insert() with an unknown column failed with a QueryException. The query builder does protect against SQL injection through parameter binding, but the documentation warns that PDO cannot bind column names, so never let user input pick a column or an order by field.

Which one to use

Task Use Why
Show, create or edit one record in a form or API Eloquent Casts, validation flow, mass-assignment protection, events
Anything with relationships (with(), whereHas()) Eloquent Relationships are the main reason to have models
Rules that must always run (observers, soft deletes, global scopes) Eloquent The query builder skips them
Reports, dashboards, joins across several tables, groupBy aggregates Query builder You want rows and numbers, not objects
Exporting or processing tens of thousands of rows Query builder, or toBase() with chunkById or lazy Roughly 6x faster here, with less memory
Inserting thousands of rows insert() or upsert() Next section
Changing one column on many rows (increment, status flips) One mass update query Next section

Mixing them safely

You rarely need to choose one for a whole application. These patterns use each where it fits.

Read big sets as plain rows but keep the model's scopes (soft deletes included):

Post::query()
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->toBase()                       // stdClass rows, no model hydration
    ->orderBy('id')
    ->chunkById(1000, function ($rows) {
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            // $row->title, $row->views ...
        }
    });

Write a report with the query builder and filter soft deletes yourself:

$top = DB::table('posts')
    ->join('users', 'users.id', '=', 'posts.user_id')
    ->whereNull('posts.deleted_at')
    ->groupBy('users.id', 'users.name')
    ->selectRaw('users.id, users.name, count(*) as posts, sum(posts.views) as views')
    ->orderByDesc('views')
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Insert in bulk and fill the timestamps yourself:

$now = now();

foreach (array_chunk($rows, 1000) as $chunk) {
    Post::insert(array_map(fn ($r) => $r + ['created_at' => $now, 'updated_at' => $now], $chunk));
}

The speed difference is large. Inserting 5,000 rows took about 2,700 ms with Post::create() in a loop (5,000 queries), and about 120 ms with Post::insert() in chunks of 1,000. Updating the same 5,000 rows one model at a time took about 3,000 to 3,200 ms; one Post::where(...)->increment('views') query took about 15 ms. On a remote database each saved round trip is worth more, so the gap grows. The trade is the one from the table above: the fast version skips events, so only use it where nothing depends on them.

Frequently asked questions

Is Eloquent slow?

Not for normal page work. In my test, loading models with get() cost about 0.02 ms per row, including the query itself. It becomes a problem when you load tens of thousands of rows, or run thousands of single-row queries in a loop, which is more often an N+1 or batching problem than an Eloquent problem.

Can I mix Eloquent and the query builder in one project?

Yes, and most mature Laravel apps do. Keep models for your domain objects and use DB::table() or toBase() for reporting and bulk work. Just remember the three differences above.

Does the query builder protect against SQL injection?

Values are bound as PDO parameters, so you do not need to escape them. Column names and order by fields cannot be bound, so whitelist them if they come from user input.

References: Laravel: Eloquent ORM and Laravel: Query Builder.

title: At-Least-Once Queue Retries Explained (and 1 Idempotency Key That Stops Duplicate Digests)
description:
If you just want the weekly digest to stop landing twice in the same inbox, don't go shopping for a better broker. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so a duplicate reminder is ordinary traffic rather than an incident — every broker worth running will replay a message when a worker dies mid-job. What stops the second copy is a send ledger: one uniquely-keyed row per user, per reminder, per scheduled run, written by the consumer before the email leaves the building.

That's it. One row.

The rest of this is the stuff that bites afterwards — how to pick the queue, how to write the worker in Node.js, and which three counters tell you the dedupe is doing anything at all.

Where the second copy of a fintech digest comes from

Picture the Friday 06:00 job at a payments company. A cron trigger fans out one message per active customer — call it 40,000 of them — and a pool of Node.js workers drains the queue, renders the week's balance and transaction summary, and hands it to the mail API. Ten messages per batch, roughly sixty seconds of work each. Nothing exotic.

Now kill one worker between "mail accepted" and "ack sent".

The broker has no idea the mail went out. Its visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible again, a second worker claims it, and a customer receives their account summary twice. At a fintech that lands differently than a duplicate newsletter: support has to establish that the customer got two copies of one statement and not one copy of two settlement runs, and that conversation costs more than the send ever did.

Deploys do the same thing, quietly. Roll the worker pool during the run and every message in flight goes back on the queue — correct behaviour, duplicate processing, same outcome.

FIFO queues help less than the marketing suggests. Content-based or explicit deduplication ids are real, but they cover a window of about five minutes, and the retry that hurts is the one that arrives after a crash loop, a redeploy, or a mail provider that took ninety seconds to answer. Past the window, the broker has forgotten. Your consumer has not, if you gave it somewhere to remember.

There's a cost axis hiding in here too. You can shrink the duplicate window by acking earlier, which trades a risk of losing a digest entirely for lower latency, or you can run fatter batches with fewer workers, which trades wall-clock time for a smaller bill. Both dials move duplicates around. Neither removes them.

Which queue setup should I use if the same reminder message gets sent twice to users?

Pick on two questions: does the platform remember completed work for you, and do you already run the infrastructure it needs. Nothing in the table below makes consumer idempotency optional — it changes how much of the ledger you write yourself.

Option Delivery model Dedupe you get for free Where the send ledger goes
BullMQ on Redis at-least-once, in-process workers job ids are unique while the job is retained your Postgres, or a Redis key with a TTL
Inngest at-least-once with step memoisation completed steps are not re-run on retry the platform, for step results
Temporal at-least-once activity execution none — activities must be idempotent by contract your own activity guard
Upstash QStash at-least-once HTTP delivery optional deduplication id per publish your own store
Infrai queues at-least-once, FIFO dedupe over a 5-minute window an Idempotency-Key convention on writes your own store, behind one REST API and one key

BullMQ is the default pick when Redis is already in the stack and you want the worker to be a Node.js process you can attach a debugger to. The catch is that Redis persistence becomes part of your delivery guarantee, which is a conversation with whoever owns the Redis budget.

Inngest earns its keep when the digest is a flow rather than a send — fetch balances, wait for a reconciliation event, then mail — because step memoisation means a retry resumes instead of restarting. Temporal is the heavier version of that answer, and it's the right one when the workflow spans days and you can staff a cluster. Neither is a good fit if all you have is one queue and one worker.

QStash suits serverless deployments with no long-lived process to drain a queue; it pushes to your HTTP endpoint instead.

Infrai fits the narrower, very common shape of this job: a cron trigger, a queue, and an email send that all belong to the same weekly run and would otherwise mean three signups, three keys, and three invoices to reconcile at month end. One REST API covers the lot, which is mostly a procurement and on-call convenience rather than a technical one — but on a two-person platform team, it's the difference between one runbook and three. It doesn't support DAG-style orchestration or fan-in joins, so if the digest needs a real workflow graph, stick with Temporal or Inngest.

A Node.js worker that claims the reminder before it sends

The ordering matters more than the storage engine. Claim, send, ack — and if any step throws, don't ack, because the message coming back is the behaviour you want.

import { Pool } from "pg";
import { sendDigest } from "./mail.ts";

const BASE = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE!;   // API root for your queue provider
const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY!;
const QUEUE = "weekly-digest";

const db = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

type DigestJob = { user_id: string; reminder_id: string; scheduled_at: string };
type QueueMessage = { message_id: string; receipt: string; body: DigestJob };

async function call(path: string, payload: unknown, idempotencyKey?: string): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
        "content-type": "application/json",
        ...(idempotencyKey ? { "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey } : {}),
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
    if (res.status !== 429) return res;
    const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250));
  }
  throw new Error("rate limited five times in a row; leaving the batch for the next tick");
}

function sendKey(job: DigestJob): string {
  return `${job.user_id}:${job.reminder_id}:${job.scheduled_at}`;
}

// One row per (user, reminder, scheduled run). The unique index is the idempotency.
async function claim(job: DigestJob): Promise<boolean> {
  const { rowCount } = await db.query(
    "insert into digest_sends (send_key, claimed_at) values ($1, now()) on conflict (send_key) do nothing",
    [sendKey(job)],
  );
  return rowCount === 1;
}

export async function drainOnce(): Promise<number> {
  const res = await call("/v1/queue/consume", { queue: QUEUE, max_messages: 10, visibility_timeout: 120 });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`consume returned ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);

  const { data } = (await res.json()) as { data: { messages: QueueMessage[] } };
  let suppressed = 0;

  for (const msg of data.messages) {
    const first = await claim(msg.body);
    if (first) await sendDigest(msg.body, sendKey(msg.body));
    else suppressed++;

    const ack = await call("/v1/queue/ack", { queue: QUEUE, receipt: msg.receipt });
    if (!ack.ok) console.error("ack rejected", ack.status, await ack.text());
  }
  return suppressed;
}

Three details carry the whole thing. The claim happens before the send, so a crash after the insert leaves a row that suppresses the retry rather than a customer with two statements. The same sendKey is passed to the mail call as its idempotency key, so the provider gets a second chance to catch what your database missed. And the ack only runs after the send returns, which is the part people invert when they're chasing throughput.

rowCount === 1 is doing a lot of work in that function, so give the table a unique index on send_key and a claimed_at column you can prune on. Thirty-five days of retention is plenty for a weekly job.

If storing raw account identifiers in a send table is awkward for your data classification, hash the tuple with HMAC (RFC 2104) and store the hex output. Uniqueness survives; the identifiers don't leak into a second table.

Three counters that prove the dedupe is doing something

I teach this as a before/after, because the ledger is invisible until you count it.

Count suppressed claims — the else branch above. A healthy weekly run shows a small non-zero number, usually a handful out of tens of thousands. Zero across several runs means either your workers never crash (possible) or the ledger isn't actually on the send path (more likely, and worth a lunchtime investigation). A number climbing past one percent of the run says the visibility timeout is shorter than your real handler latency, and the fix is the timeout, not the ledger.

Second, track age of the oldest unacked message during the run. That's your real duplicate exposure window: everything older than the visibility timeout is a candidate for redelivery. It's also the honest latency metric for a digest — not how fast one send is, but how long the tail takes to clear.

Third, count sends per send_key from the mail provider's own logs, not yours. Your ledger says the worker behaved. The provider's log says the customer's inbox agrees. Those two disagreeing is the only evidence worth paging someone about, and I'd wire that one to an alert rather than a dashboard nobody opens on a Friday.

What this design doesn't cover

The ledger is now a dependency of sending. If the database is unreachable, the correct move is to let the worker throw and the message return on its visibility timeout — sending blind is how you get the duplicates back.

Two platform limits are worth checking before you commit. Ack usually deletes the message, and retention caps out well short of a log-structured broker, so if replaying last month's digest run is a requirement, stick with Kafka or a stream you control rather than a work queue. Delayed delivery is also bounded — seven days on hosted queues is a common ceiling, which is fine for a weekly cadence and useless for an annual renewal reminder.

Long fan-outs need the same care. A scheduled trigger that runs a single HTTP handler will hit a hard execution ceiling — 900 seconds on some platforms — so the trigger should enqueue and return, and the workers should do the sending. Forty thousand renders inside one cron invocation is a timeout waiting to happen, and a timeout mid-run is exactly the retry that duplicates.

I'm not certain the HMAC step is worth it for every team; if your send table already lives inside the same compliance boundary as the customer record, it's ceremony. The claim row, though, is not optional. At-least-once is a promise the broker keeps by sending twice — idempotency is how your consumer keeps it once.

References

  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview (at-least-once delivery semantics): https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queues, deduplication ids and the 5-minute interval: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html
  • Stripe API: idempotent requests and idempotency keys: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Temporal documentation on activity idempotency: https://docs.temporal.io/activities
  • Inngest step memoisation and retries: https://www.inngest.com/docs/learn/inngest-steps
  • Upstash QStash deduplication: https://upstash.com/docs/qstash/features/deduplication
  • RFC 2104, HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2610.19331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
