title: React and TypeScript Best Practices: Build Reliable Applications
description:
React and TypeScript are a powerful combination for building maintainable, scalable frontend applications. React makes it easier to create reusable user interfaces, while TypeScript catches many common mistakes before your code reaches production.

However, simply adding TypeScript to a React project does not automatically make the codebase reliable. The real benefits come from defining precise types, designing reusable components, handling asynchronous states correctly, and avoiding unnecessary complexity.

In this guide, we will explore practical best practices for React and TypeScript, using JavaScript examples to demonstrate the underlying patterns. These concepts help developers write more predictable components, simplify debugging, and build applications that remain manageable as requirements evolve.

1. Practical Best Practices for React and TypeScript

Define Explicit Types for Component Props

Well-defined component props make component contracts easier to understand and maintain. Instead of passing loosely structured objects, describe the required properties, optional values, and callback signatures using TypeScript interfaces or type aliases.

For example, a reusable button component might accept a label, a disabled state, and an event handler. Explicit types help prevent missing properties and incompatible callback arguments during development, while keeping the component's public API clear.

Avoid Using Any and Prefer Unknown for Untrusted Data

The any type disables most useful type checking, allowing mistakes to spread throughout a codebase. Prefer unknown when handling values from APIs, external libraries, or other untrusted sources, and validate those values before using them.

TypeScript types disappear at runtime, so declaring an API response as a particular interface does not verify that the server actually returned the expected structure. Runtime validation is important whenever data crosses an application boundary, especially when dealing with user input or third-party services.

Model UI States Explicitly

React applications frequently handle loading, success, empty, and error states. Representing these states explicitly prevents contradictory combinations, such as showing an error and a successful result simultaneously.

Discriminated unions are particularly useful because TypeScript can narrow the available properties based on a shared literal field. This approach makes state transitions easier to reason about and helps ensure that each UI state contains the information it actually needs.

Keep Components Small and Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility, whether that means displaying a product, handling a form, or presenting an error message. Extracting repeated behavior into custom hooks can reduce duplication without forcing every small piece of logic into a separate abstraction.

Keep business logic separate from presentation when doing so improves clarity or makes behavior easier to test. Avoid excessive abstraction, however, because a simple component does not need multiple layers of indirection to become maintainable.

Use Type-Safe Event Handlers and Immutable State Updates

React event handlers should use appropriate event types when working with inputs, forms, and other interactive elements. Functional state updates are especially useful when the next state depends on the previous state, because React can apply the update against the latest queued value.

Treat arrays and objects in state as immutable values. Create updated copies with methods such as map, filter, and object spread instead of modifying existing state directly, so React can reliably detect changes and render the correct UI.

Understand What TypeScript Cannot Guarantee

TypeScript provides compile-time checks, but it does not replace runtime validation, application testing, or accessibility checks. A correctly typed component can still contain a logic bug, render an inaccessible interface, or mishandle a failed network request.

Combine static typing with focused tests, linting, strict compiler settings, and clear error handling. A strong React and TypeScript codebase uses these tools together rather than relying on a single layer of protection.

const assert = require('node:assert/strict');

// This runnable JavaScript example demonstrates patterns that can be
// modeled with TypeScript in a real React application.
// JavaScript itself does not enforce TypeScript interfaces or unions.

console.log('Step 1: Define the application's data contract');

// In TypeScript, define this with an interface or type alias.
// interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; }
function createUser(id, name, email) {
  return { id, name, email };
}

const initialUser = createUser(1, 'Ansh', 'ansh@example.com');
console.log('User created:', initialUser);
assert.equal(initialUser.id, 1);

console.log('\nStep 2: Validate untrusted API data at runtime');

// TypeScript annotations alone cannot validate a JSON response.
function parseUser(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'object' || value === null) {
    throw new TypeError('User must be an object');
  }

  if (!Number.isInteger(value.id) || value.id <= 0) {
    throw new TypeError('User id must be a positive integer');
  }

  if (typeof value.name !== 'string' || value.name.trim() === '') {
    throw new TypeError('User name must be a non-empty string');
  }

  if (typeof value.email !== 'string' || !value.email.includes('@')) {
    throw new TypeError('User email must be valid');
  }

  return {
    id: value.id,
    name: value.name.trim(),
    email: value.email.trim(),
  };
}

const apiResponse = {
  id: 2,
  name: '  Priya  ',
  email: 'priya@example.com',
};

const validatedUser = parseUser(apiResponse);
console.log('Validated API user:', validatedUser);
assert.equal(validatedUser.name, 'Priya');

console.log('\nStep 3: Model UI states with a discriminated union pattern');

// A TypeScript version can use a union of loading, success, and error types.
// This JavaScript function demonstrates the same runtime branching.
function describeRequestState(state) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'loading':
      return 'Loading users...';
    case 'success':
      return `Loaded ${state.users.length} users.`;
    case 'error':
      return `Request failed: ${state.message}`;
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown status: ${state.status}`);
  }
}

const loadingState = { status: 'loading' };
const successState = {
  status: 'success',
  users: [validatedUser],
};
const errorState = {
  status: 'error',
  message: 'Unable to reach the server',
};

console.log(describeRequestState(loadingState));
console.log(describeRequestState(successState));
console.log(describeRequestState(errorState));
assert.match(describeRequestState(successState), /Loaded 1 users/);

console.log('\nStep 4: Update collections immutably');

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Soap', price: 99, active: true },
  { id: 2, name: 'Shampoo', price: 199, active: true },
  { id: 3, name: 'Oil', price: 149, active: false },
];

// Never modify an existing React state array directly.
// map creates a new array and spread creates a new product object.
const updatedProducts = products.map((product) =>
  product.id === 2
    ? { ...product, price: 179 }
    : product
);

const activeProducts = updatedProducts.filter(
  (product) => product.active
);

console.log('Original shampoo price:', products[1].price);
console.log('Updated shampoo price:', updatedProducts[1].price);
console.log('Active products:', activeProducts);
assert.equal(products[1].price, 199);
assert.equal(updatedProducts[1].price, 179);

console.log('\nStep 5: Use predictable state transitions');

// This reducer can be shared by UI logic and unit tests.
function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: [...state.items, action.product],
      };
    case 'remove':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: state.items.filter(
          (item) => item.id !== action.id
        ),
      };
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unsupported action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

const emptyCart = { items: [] };
const cartWithProduct = cartReducer(emptyCart, {
  type: 'add',
  product: { id: 10, name: 'Neem Soap', price: 99 },
});

console.log('Cart after adding product:', cartWithProduct);
console.log('Original cart remains unchanged:', emptyCart);
assert.equal(cartWithProduct.items.length, 1);
assert.equal(emptyCart.items.length, 0);

const emptyCartAgain = cartReducer(cartWithProduct, {
  type: 'remove',
  id: 10,
});

console.log('Cart after removing product:', emptyCartAgain);
assert.equal(emptyCartAgain.items.length, 0);

console.log('\nStep 6: Handle asynchronous operations safely');

// In React, manage loading and error states explicitly and consider
// AbortController or effect cleanup when a component unmounts.
async function loadUsers(fetchImplementation) {
  try {
    const response = await fetchImplementation();

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const payload = await response.json();

    if (!Array.isArray(payload)) {
      throw new TypeError('Expected an array of users');
    }

    return {
      status: 'success',
      users: payload.map(parseUser),
    };
  } catch (error) {
    return {
      status: 'error',
      message: error instanceof Error
        ? error.message
        : 'Unexpected error',
    };
  }
}

async function main() {
  const result = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: true,
    status: 200,
    json: async () => [
      { id: 4, name: 'Riya', email: 'riya@example.com' },
    ],
  }));

  console.log('API operation result:', result);
  assert.equal(result.status, 'success');
  assert.equal(result.users.length, 1);

  const failedResult = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: false,
    status: 503,
    json: async () => ({}),
  }));

  console.log('Handled API failure:', failedResult);
  assert.equal(failedResult.status, 'error');

  console.log('\nAll examples completed successfully.');
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error('Unexpected example failure:', error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Conclusion

React and TypeScript work best when types communicate clear contracts, components have focused responsibilities, and state transitions remain predictable. Runtime validation is equally important because external data can violate the assumptions expressed by your TypeScript definitions.

Start by enabling strict TypeScript checks, typing component props and event handlers, avoiding unnecessary any types, and modeling asynchronous states explicitly. Add runtime validation where data enters the application, and test business logic independently from component rendering whenever practical.

The goal is not to add types everywhere simply to satisfy the compiler. It is to make incorrect states harder to represent, make component behavior easier to understand, and help your team deliver changes with confidence as the application grows.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.

title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
description:
arXiv:2610.14644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.

title: Evaluating Browser Storage Handoffs: React PUTs, Express Signing, Private Object Reads
description:
Short answer: use a private object storage bucket, have an Express server create a short-lived presigned PUT URL, and let React upload the bytes directly; issue another signed download URL when an authorized user needs the object. This keeps file transfer out of the application server, but it is not a good fit for permanent public links or a deployment that needs self-service bucket CORS rules.

The interesting part is the handoff. Express owns identity and the object key. React owns the byte transfer. Storage owns the bytes. That division is easy to describe and surprisingly easy to blur once a file becomes input to a RAG pipeline or an evaluation run.

My acceptance test is eval-driven: upload a fixture from the browser, verify the object, read it as the owning user, and confirm that a different user cannot obtain a signed download. Measure completion time by file-size bucket and count records that stay pending. Prompt-cost awareness belongs here too; a failed upload should not silently trigger a second document-ingestion run and double the tokens.

Keep the transfer boring.

How should React and Express handle a private object storage upload and signed download?

Create or check the bucket once during deployment. For each upload, the Express side authenticates the user, generates a server-owned key, records user_id and MIME type in the database, and asks storage for a presigned PUT URL. React sends the file to that returned URL with PUT. The platform credential stays on the server; it must never be sent with the browser's follow-up request.

After the upload, confirm the object before marking the database row ready. A successful browser request means the transfer request succeeded; it does not establish that the application has associated the intended key with the intended user. For a private read, the server checks ownership and returns a fresh signed download URL. There is no permanent public URL in this design.

Here is the control-plane part in Python. The HTTP shape is the same one a Node.js or Express handler would use. The body is kept empty because the current discovery response is the authority for the operation's request schema; do not copy an invented S3 field into production. The sample checks status, honors Retry-After, and backs off on 429.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")


def post_with_backoff(path, body):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            BASE_URL + path,
            data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
            method="POST",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                payload = response.read()
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(
                        f"storage request returned {response.status}: {payload!r}"
                    )
                return json.loads(payload)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"storage request returned {error.code}: {detail}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("presign request exhausted its retries")


def create_private_upload(bucket, object_key):
    path_template = os.environ["INFRAI_STORAGE_PRESIGN_PATH"]
    path = path_template.format(
        bucket=quote(bucket, safe=""),
        key=quote(object_key, safe=""),
    )
    return post_with_backoff(path, {})


signed = create_private_upload("app-files", "users/42/eval-input.json")
print(signed)

The verified signing route is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. Its returned value is for the browser's upload step, not another API call with the platform credential. React should use the URL and the method or headers described by that response, then call your own confirmation endpoint. When the UI later needs the file, the server can use the same presign operation for a signed read according to the discovered request shape, or serve the file through an authorization-checked application endpoint. Never attach Authorization: Bearer ... to a returned presigned URL.

Use a fresh random component in a real key rather than letting the browser choose users/42/eval-input.json. There is no object versioning, no object lock, and no If-Match conditional write, so a reused key can make an accidental overwrite impossible to recover through storage history. A database or queue must coordinate strict replacement. The object key is for bytes; the application row is for ownership, MIME type, display name, and workflow state. It doesn't replace that application record.

What should you measure before copying this browser upload pattern?

The simple approach is a multipart Express endpoint: React posts the file to your app, and the app writes it onward. It is a useful prototype because it has one request to reason about. It is a poor default for large files, slow mobile connections, or a service that also runs ingestion and eval workers. The API process becomes the long-lived pipe, and its transfer load gets mixed with the short control-plane requests that authenticate users and start jobs.

Direct upload moves that pipe to object storage. The application still makes the important decisions, but it no longer buffers every byte. That helps a notebook-to-prod path: an AI builder can test the signer with a fixture, test the React transfer separately, and test the attachment state transition without pretending that a green API response proves the document is ready for retrieval.

Measure three things before standardizing it:

  • upload completion rate and duration by file-size range;
  • pending database rows that never reach verified;
  • duplicate ingestion or evaluation jobs after a browser retry.

The third metric is where prompt-cost awareness becomes operational. The storage URL should not be the event that starts a model call. Mark the object verified first, then enqueue one idempotent application job keyed by the attachment record. Your mileage may vary with mobile networks, so use production-like fixtures rather than a tiny local text file.

How do private buckets, CORS, and signed download URLs change the choice?

Private access changes the product contract. Uploaded objects should be read through short-lived signed URLs or an application-controlled download response. They should not be published as permanent links, and this storage shape is not suitable for static website hosting or a public image host.

React also needs the storage service to accept the deployed frontend origin, the PUT method, and the headers involved in the browser request. A server-generated signature cannot make a browser preflight succeed by itself. This matters because the storage capability has no exposed independent route for managing bucket CORS rules. If operators need to add origins without a provider change, choose a service that offers that control instead.

Lifecycle cleanup has a boundary as well: the shortest lifecycle is one day, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Do not use it as an hour-scale abandoned-upload janitor. Store application metadata in the database because server-side object metadata is not a searchable catalog; listing is prefix-based. There is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool either.

That is a lot of boundaries for one small upload feature. They are still easier to test when the browser and application own separate steps.

Which private object storage option fits this workflow?

The direct-upload pattern exists across the major choices. The decision is about the controls around it and how much integration surface the rest of the product needs.

Option Browser upload and private read Good fit Important trade-off
Amazon S3 Presigned PUT and signed download patterns Teams already operating in AWS More AWS-specific policy and service configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned requests Products centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required access and delivery controls in that platform
Google Cloud Storage Signed upload and download URLs Workloads already using Google Cloud identity The surrounding application still follows Google-specific operational conventions
Infrai storage Presigned object upload and signed access through REST A small AI product that wants storage and other backend capabilities behind one key and one bill Private-only access, no self-service CORS route, and no object history

Infrai's practical advantage here is the single control surface: one plain REST API and one credential can cover storage alongside other backend modules, so a Python service and a JavaScript frontend do not need a storage SDK just to agree on this boundary. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim about lowest price.

The catch is clear. Stick with S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage when public delivery, version recovery, object lock, configurable CORS, cross-region replication, or bulk migration is a requirement you cannot move outside the application. Infrai is not suitable for those cases. It is a reasonable option when the files stay private and the team values a consistent backend contract more than provider-specific storage controls.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls

title: Big Tech Is on Track to Spend $800B on AI in 2026. Can the Economics Hold?
description:
One hot inflation report. A sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks. And a question the whole industry can no longer dodge.

For the last few years, the AI conversation has mostly been about capability.

Can a model write code? Can it answer questions? Can it generate images? Can it browse the web? Can it act like an agent?

Those are important questions. But in October 2026, another question has become impossible to ignore:

Can the AI industry turn massive spending into sustainable, measurable value?

This is no longer only a technology question. It is now a business, energy, infrastructure, policy, and investment question. And the answer will shape which companies lead the next decade.

⚡ TL;DR (save this)

  • Markets wobbled. AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
  • The spending is enormous. The largest US hyperscalers are on track for about $800B of capex in 2026 and around $1.1T in 2027.
  • There is a gap. An Axios-reported analysis found a ~$1T gap between AI-related spending since 2024 and AI revenue so far.
  • Power is a hard limit. Data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 versus about 3% for overall demand.
  • The next winners will not simply spend the most. They will deliver trustworthy execution.

📉 The Market Just Sent a Warning

This week, major AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after the United States released hotter-than-expected inflation data.

Why does inflation matter to AI? Because AI at scale is capital-intensive.

Building and running AI systems requires:

  • Advanced GPUs and specialized chips
  • Large data centers
  • High-speed networking
  • Massive storage systems
  • Reliable electricity
  • Cooling infrastructure
  • Skilled engineering teams
  • Continuous model training and inference capacity

Many companies fund this buildout through debt, future revenue expectations, and investor confidence.

When inflation rises, markets begin to expect higher interest rates. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. When borrowing becomes more expensive, every large infrastructure project becomes harder to justify.

That is why AI stocks reacted sharply.

Reuters reported that shares of debt-heavy AI infrastructure companies fell as investors became more concerned about the financing of the industry's massive buildout. CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle, and Dell were among the companies affected.

This does not mean AI is failing. It means the market is asking a fair question:

Is the spending producing enough real value to justify the cost?

💰 The Scale of AI Spending Is Enormous

To understand why this matters, look at the numbers.

Goldman Sachs has estimated that the largest US hyperscalers are on track to spend about $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. Consensus expectations suggest this could rise to around $1.1 trillion in 2027.

Capital expenditure, or capex, means money spent on long-term assets such as:

  • Data centers
  • Servers
  • GPUs
  • Networking equipment
  • Land and buildings
  • Power infrastructure
  • Cooling systems

This is not ordinary software spending. This is industrial-scale investment.

Alphabet, for example, reported $80.6 billion in capital expenditures during the first half of 2026 and guided to $195-205 billion for the full year.

That is an extraordinary amount of money being committed to compute, data centers, and AI infrastructure.

At the same time, an analysis reported by Axios found a gap of nearly $1 trillion between hyperscaler AI-related spending since 2024 and the AI revenue generated so far.

This does not mean AI companies have "lost" $1 trillion. It means there is a difference between:

  • Money invested in AI infrastructure
  • Money earned from AI products and services

That difference matters. Investors can support long-term investment when they believe future revenue will arrive. But if spending keeps rising faster than revenue, confidence can weaken.

🏗️ AI Is Becoming an Infrastructure Industry

AI used to feel like a software industry. Now, it increasingly looks like an infrastructure industry.

Why? Because modern AI depends on physical resources: electricity, land, water, fiber networks, chips, cooling systems, data centers, and power grids.

A powerful model is not just an algorithm. It is an algorithm running on expensive hardware, inside a data center, connected to a power grid, supported by supply chains, and maintained by engineers.

This changes the conversation. The question is no longer only:

"How smart can the model become?"

It is also:

  • "Can we power it?"
  • "Can we cool it?"
  • "Can we afford it?"
  • "Can we deploy it responsibly?"
  • "Can it create value for customers?"

AI is becoming similar to railways, electricity grids, telecom networks, and cloud computing. Infrastructure industries create enormous value, but they also require enormous capital, planning, and discipline.

🔌 Electricity Is Becoming a Core AI Constraint

One of the most important facts in this debate is energy.

According to IEA data cited in recent reporting, data-center electricity demand grew by 17% in 2025, while overall electricity demand grew by around 3%.

That is a major difference.

AI data centers need continuous power. They cannot simply switch off during peak hours. Training large models and serving millions of users requires stable, high-capacity electricity around the clock.

This creates several challenges:

1. Power availability

Many regions already face grid constraints. Adding a large data center is not as simple as buying land and installing servers. It requires access to sufficient electricity capacity.

2. Grid upgrades

New data centers may require new transmission lines, substations, and grid upgrades. These projects can take years to approve and build.

3. Energy costs

If data centers increase demand faster than supply, electricity prices can rise for nearby communities and businesses.

4. Environmental impact

AI infrastructure affects carbon emissions, water usage, land use, and local communities.

5. Public policy

Governments are beginning to ask who should pay for the infrastructure required to support AI growth.

In the United States, the House passed a bipartisan bill designed to encourage state utility regulators to protect consumers from rising energy costs linked to large data centers. The bill still needs further approval to become law, but the direction is clear.

In Europe, regulators are preparing stricter disclosure requirements for data centers, including water use, clean-power adoption, and energy efficiency.

The message is simple:

AI growth must be matched by responsible energy planning.

🎯 The Shift From Demos to Business Outcomes

The first phase of enterprise AI was about experimentation.

Companies asked:

  • Can we build a chatbot?
  • Can we connect an LLM to our documents?
  • Can we create a proof of concept?
  • Can we show leadership an AI demo?

That phase was necessary. But demos do not pay for data centers. Business outcomes do.

The next phase is about production AI:

  • AI that reduces manual work
  • AI that improves decision-making
  • AI that accelerates customer response
  • AI that automates repeatable workflows
  • AI that improves quality and compliance
  • AI that creates measurable ROI

This is where agentic AI becomes important.

An AI agent is not just a chatbot. It is a system that can understand a goal, plan steps, use tools, interact with systems, and complete a task.

For example, instead of asking:

"What is our leave policy?"

An employee may ask:

"Apply for two days of leave and confirm my balance has updated."

An agent may need to:

  1. Understand the request
  2. Find the correct application screen
  3. Fill in the required details
  4. Submit the request
  5. Verify the outcome
  6. Report success or failure with evidence

This is much more valuable than a simple question-and-answer system. But it is also more demanding. An agent that takes action must be accurate, safe, observable, and accountable.

🛡️ Why Agentic AI Needs Governance

As AI agents become more autonomous, governance becomes essential.

A chatbot that gives a wrong answer is frustrating. An AI agent that submits the wrong form, sends the wrong email, updates the wrong record, or triggers the wrong workflow can create real business damage.

That is why enterprises need:

Human approval for high-risk actions

Not every action should be automatic. Deleting records, making payments, changing production configurations, or sending external communications may require human confirmation.

Least-privilege access

An agent should only have the permissions required for its task. It should not automatically receive broad access to every system.

Audit trails

Every important action should be logged: what the agent saw, what it decided, what it did, and what evidence supports the result.

Clear success and failure states

A good AI system should say:

  • "Task completed successfully."
  • "Task failed because of a product defect."
  • "Task could not be completed because a required screen or precondition was unavailable."

It should not pretend everything is fine when it could not verify the outcome.

Monitoring and observability

Teams need to monitor agent behavior in real time, detect unusual actions, and stop an agent if needed.

This is especially important as agents move from answering questions to operating inside business systems.

🏆 The Real Competitive Advantage: Trustworthy Execution

Many people think AI competition is only about who has the biggest model. That is no longer the full picture.

The next competitive advantage will come from trustworthy execution.

A company may have access to a powerful model, but if it cannot connect that model safely to its data, workflows, permissions, and business processes, the value remains limited.

The companies that win will be those that can deliver:

  • Reliable AI systems. The system should work consistently, not only in a demo.
  • Measurable ROI. Every AI initiative should answer: What time, cost, risk, or quality improvement did we create?
  • Safe automation. AI should automate the right tasks, with the right controls, in the right environments.
  • Evidence-based results. Users should be able to see why the AI reached a conclusion or completed an action.
  • Responsible infrastructure. AI growth should consider power, water, emissions, and community impact.
  • Human-centered design. AI should assist people, not confuse them or remove accountability.

🏢 What This Means for Businesses

For business leaders, the message is clear: do not evaluate AI only by model benchmarks. Evaluate it by business impact.

Ask questions like:

  • Which workflow are we improving?
  • How much time or cost are we saving?
  • How are we measuring quality?
  • What happens when the AI is wrong?
  • Who approves high-risk actions?
  • How do we audit decisions?
  • What data does the AI access?
  • How do we protect customer information?
  • What is the total cost of ownership?
  • How does this affect our energy and infrastructure needs?

AI strategy should not be "adopt AI everywhere." AI strategy should be:

Adopt AI where it creates clear, measurable, responsible value.

👩‍💻 What This Means for Engineers

For AI engineers, developers, and architects, the skills that matter are changing.

It is no longer enough to know how to call an LLM API.

The most valuable engineers will understand:

  • System design
  • Retrieval and context management
  • Tool use and function calling
  • Agent orchestration
  • Evaluation and testing
  • Observability
  • Security and permissions
  • Cost optimization
  • Human-in-the-loop workflows
  • Production deployment

The best AI systems will not be built by prompt engineering alone. They will be built by combining models, data, tools, policies, tests, monitoring, user experience, and business understanding.

That is where real engineering value lies.

🚀 What This Means for Startups

For startups, this is actually good news.

When AI becomes expensive, companies cannot afford vague experiments. They need focused solutions that solve specific problems.

The best startup opportunities will be in areas such as:

  • AI quality assurance and testing
  • Agent governance and auditing
  • AI cost optimization
  • Enterprise workflow automation
  • Domain-specific AI assistants
  • Data readiness and governance
  • AI security
  • Model evaluation
  • Human-in-the-loop review tools
  • Industry-specific automation

A startup does not need to build a foundation model to create value. It can build the layer that makes AI usable, safe, measurable, and trustworthy inside real organizations.

🔭 The Bigger Picture

AI is not disappearing. It is maturing.

The first phase was about possibility. The next phase is about responsibility.

The first phase asked: "What can AI do?"

The next phase asks: "What should AI do, at what cost, with what safeguards, and for whose benefit?"

That is a healthier phase. Because real transformation does not come from hype. It comes from systems that work reliably in the real world.

AI will create enormous value, but only when companies treat it as more than a trend. They must treat it as:

  • A product
  • A system
  • An infrastructure investment
  • A business process
  • A governance responsibility
  • A long-term commitment

The companies that understand this will build durable advantage. The companies that only chase demos may find that the cost of AI is much easier to measure than its value.

💡 Final Thought

The AI race is no longer only about who can build the most powerful model. It is about who can build the most useful, efficient, safe, and economically sustainable AI systems.

The next winners will not simply spend the most.

They will convert compute into clarity.

They will convert automation into accountability.

They will convert data into decisions.

And they will convert AI into measurable business value.

The future of AI belongs to those who can make it work in the real world.

💬 Your turn

What will matter more in the next phase of AI: model capability or practical, trustworthy execution?

Tell me in the comments. If this helped you think about AI beyond the hype, a reaction and a share help other engineers and leaders find it. Follow for more on AI systems, agents and the economics behind them.

title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
description:
arXiv:2610.14643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Cross-Scenario Industrial Defect Detection via Domain-Robust Training and Metric-Aligned Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.19540v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated defect detection of industrial boards must remain highly reliable under cross-scenario variations in lighting, surface contaminants, and production line conditions. This makes cross-scenario defect detection a domain generalization problem, wherein models are required to detect, localize, and classify defects across unseen scenarios while minimizing false alarms on clean boards. For the IDA 2026 Track 1 challenge, we propose a cross-scenario defect detection method that includes four complementary modules: cross-scenario robust training, small-defect-aware learning, score calibration and inference threshold selection, and metric-aligned checkpoint selection. These four modules respectively introduce cross-scenario robust normalization and DSU-style statistic perturbation with progressive random convolution, NWD and parameter-free spatial attention, the VFL learning objective, and a custom SWAD variant driven by the Track 1-oriented proxy. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a Track 1 score of 0.564 with a screening score of 0.696 on the test dataset on a single RTX 4090 GPU. The code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/Dikai.

title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
description:
arXiv:2610.14539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.

title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.19528v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.

title: Mycelium’s useful next step: make the liquidity map easier to act on
description:
For developers building Solana dashboards or agent tools, Mycelium Finance offers something concrete to inspect: a map of liquidity connecting its own tokens with partner projects. $MYC is the core token; $ESF is the staking token. The Mycelium Strategy places liquidity across those partner pools. Its free MCP tools expose the allocation, token distribution, pool addresses and selected market data, giving a builder a starting point for checking the project’s claims.

My free tool calls on 15 October 2026 returned a Strategy allocation of $31,984.17 across ten projects. KNOTS accounted for 20.33%, PRCL 14.98%, and KINS 11.78%. Together, those three represented 47.09%, calculated from the reported shares. The remaining allocation included SOL, GABLE, STREAM, GUAC, DREAMS, JUBJUB and USDC. This is a spread across several projects, with a substantial concentration in its largest positions.

There is also a useful distinction inside that allocation. The tool reports both $MYC and $ESF partner pairs, explaining that pools are being migrated from $ESF to $MYC. KNOTS and SOL have both kinds of pair in this snapshot; PRCL is shown through an $ESF pair, while KINS and DREAMS are shown through $MYC pairs. A developer can therefore show the actual pool structure rather than treating every connection as an identical $MYC relationship. The reported pool addresses make that view traceable.

The supply picture adds context. Against one billion minted $MYC, the distribution tool assigns 55.10% to time-locked supply, 23.34% to unlocked LP liquidity, 14.51% to locked LP liquidity, 6.90% to the category called “trading liquidity,” and 0.14% to burned tokens. Percentages are rounded. That “trading” category includes holder wallets and other pools; it is not a measurement of trading volume.

The tool separately defines 447.56 million $MYC as tradable, with 84.58% of that amount in the identified liquidity pools. This is the important denominator: the figure describes token placement within tradable supply, not the share of all minted tokens. It also does not establish executable trade depth, active demand or fee income. Those need different measurements. Locked liquidity positions and time-locked token supply likewise describe different constraints and should stay separate in an interface.

The performers tool provides another check against overinterpreting the allocation. In this snapshot, pinned partner STREAM showed a −0.25% seven-day price change, PRCL −0.87%, and KNOTS −11.84%. These are individual token price changes, not returns earned by the Strategy’s LP positions. The data can support a comparison screen; it cannot, by itself, show that the Strategy outperformed an alternative.

My concrete suggestion is a pool-level connection dashboard: show each partner’s $MYC/$ESF split, its source timestamp, lock status where verifiable, and links to the underlying pools. Add executable quote depth and realized fees when those data are available, with explicit gaps otherwise. That would build on the useful allocation feed while helping partners and agents distinguish liquidity placement from liquidity performance.

title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.19380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

title: Your Pixel-Perfect Tests Have a Trust Problem
description:
Someone updates the product page. The visual test reports 47 differences.

Most of them are timestamps, an animated banner, and a font rendering change. One is a Buy button that moved below the fold on a common laptop size.

Guess which issue gets lost in the noise.

Visual regression testing sounds beautifully simple: take a screenshot, compare it with yesterday's screenshot, flag what changed. But once you use it on a real product, you discover that detecting differences is the easy part.

Deciding which differences deserve attention is the job.

A diff is not a bug report

A screenshot comparison can tell you that pixels changed. It generally cannot, by itself, tell you whether the change was intentional, harmless, or a customer-facing problem.

Think about a page with live prices or stock levels. A strict pixel comparison may generate a new difference on every run even when the interface is behaving correctly.

Now imagine the opposite: the page renders almost identically, but an important button doesn't respond to a click. The visual check may happily pass.

These tests need context. What content was dynamic? Which viewport and browser did you use? What build produced the baseline? Who approved it, and why?

This benchmark plan for visual platforms gets specific about dynamic-content tolerance, review workflow, and keeping evidence. Those are the questions I'd ask before buying another clever image diff tool.

The baseline is a decision, not a file

A baseline isn't automatically correct because it was approved last Tuesday.

I've seen teams design processes where the easiest way to clear a red build is to click "Accept all changes." That's a dangerous habit. It turns the comparison system into a machine for normalizing whatever the latest build happened to render.

A useful review should make it easy to answer:

  • Which component actually changed?
  • Was the change linked to a known product decision?
  • Did the difference affect a critical workflow?
  • Can reviewers inspect the old and new images side by side?
  • Will the decision still make sense to someone investigating it next month?

You can use a hosted review workflow or keep baselines close to your Git history. Both have benefits. The Katalon Visual Testing vs Reg-suit comparison frames that tradeoff as managed review versus Git-first control. It's a more useful debate than asking which product takes the sharpest screenshot.

The workflow that makes good review decisions easiest is the one I'd favor.

Your screenshots have an expiration date

Suppose a release introduces a visual defect. Two weeks later, customer support forwards a complaint. The responsible engineer asks for the original screenshot and browser details.

They're gone. The CI job expired its artifacts after seven days.

Now the team has to reconstruct a browser state that may no longer exist. The app has changed. The data has changed. The third-party content has changed.

Evidence retention sounds like paperwork until you need yesterday's evidence to explain today's bug.

You don't necessarily need to keep every screenshot forever. But important failed runs should retain enough context to support a useful investigation: baseline and actual images, diff, build ID, browser and viewport, test data identifiers where appropriate, and the approval history.

It's worth deciding retention rules deliberately instead of inheriting whatever your CI provider does by default.

Test output should be readable by someone who didn't write the test

Now for the part I think gets ignored most often: handing a finding to another human.

"Visual difference detected" is a notification. It isn't a reproducible bug report.

A stronger report says something like:

On the checkout page, at 1366 × 768 in Chrome, the order summary overlaps the payment button after the shipping estimate loads. Seen on build checkout-1842. Expected: both sections remain visible and independently clickable. Attached: before image, after image, diff, and reproduction steps.

No mystery. No digging through raw logs to discover what page failed. No requirement that the reader know the testing platform's private vocabulary.

This benchmark plan for turning raw findings into reproducible reports measures an outcome many teams forget to track: how quickly evidence becomes something actionable.

That's especially important as AI-assisted testing discovers more issues. Discovering ten times as many potential problems won't help if people spend ten times as long interpreting them.

I'd measure review effort before counting diffs

If I were improving a visual testing process, I wouldn't start with "How many differences did we catch this month?"

I'd start with three smaller questions. How many alerts were dismissed as harmless? How long did a reviewer spend understanding an alert? How often did someone approve a baseline only to find out later that it contained a defect?

Those answers tell you whether the system helps the team notice real problems or merely gives the team another inbox.

The goal is not a perfectly clean diff report. It's confidence that when a meaningful visual regression happens, the team can recognize it, explain it, and fix it without conducting an archaeological dig through last week's CI jobs.

title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
description:
arXiv:2610.14186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
description:
arXiv:2610.19121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: How Okara runs CMO agents for 120,000 companies on Vercel
description:
Okara on Vercel

  • 4 billion tokens processed daily across a multi-provider AI stack on Vercel

  • AI CMOs actively managing growth for 120,000+ businesses

  • Eight sub-agents handling SEO, GEO, social, content, Reddit, and Hacker News

  • New AI models available to users the same day they ship

Okara is an AI CMO that directs a team of specialized sub-agents to drive marketing, so founders don't have to. Give Okara your website URL, and the AI CMO builds a marketing strategy, develops a brand voice, and activates agents across SEO, content, and social media to drive awareness and pipeline without a single marketing hire.

As Fatima Rizwan, Okara's founder, puts it: "You can build something in a weekend and spend months trying to get anyone to notice." Distribution, she argues, is stuck in the pre-AI era: fragmented across subscriptions and agencies that cost over $15,000 a month before a single dollar comes back.

Okara is built by a team of four and processes 4 billion tokens a day. The company operates on the new model for startups: a small team building a platform that handles growth for thousands of other companies. Fatima quickly learned that serving hundreds of thousands of companies with four people meant infrastructure had to be invisible. Any time spent on it was time not spent building.

Using AI Gateway to integrate multiple providers with one API key

The friction of managing individual provider SDKs

Okara's backend originally talked to eight model providers through separate SDKs, each with its own key management, image handling, and edge cases. When they expanded to open-source models, the approach broke down completely. Every new model meant an engineer stopped shipping product and wrote an adapter instead. Retry logic, fallback routing, and provider health monitoring all lived in Okara's codebase, maintained by hand.

Most AI infrastructure would have required Okara to keep living with that friction. That's why they moved to Vercel AI Gateway.

One endpoint, every provider

AI Gateway replaced every custom integration with a single configuration. Retry logic and fallback handling moved out of Okara's codebase and into Vercel's routing layer entirely, including zero-data retention support for Okara's privacy-sensitive secure chat.

The day a new model ships, Okara's team can make it available to users immediately through Gateway. No adapter, no edge case testing, no deploy cycle.

Running agent workflows in Vercel Sandboxes

Okara's SEO agent can scan for problems and write the code that fixes them. When the agent finds a technical issue on a user's site, it spins up a Vercel Sandbox and runs the analysis in an isolated environment. The findings are passed to a coding agent, which opens a pull request with the fix, ready for the developer to review and merge. Detection, analysis, code change: the entire loop runs automatically, with a human making the final call before anything goes live.

Okara adopted Vercel Sandboxes the day they launched. Rizwan saw the announcement on X and the team started building immediately.

What's next

120,000 websites are now using Okara's AI CMO. The team ships to production six or seven times a day, and every improvement lands for customers the same day it ships. A solo founder using Okara gets the same distribution muscle as a team ten times their size, without the headcount or the $15,000 monthly agency bill.

Okara is expanding its agent suite and moving upmarket to serve larger teams. As the product grows, so does the infrastructure demand. More users, more agents, more tokens. When you're four people handling growth for 120,000 companies, you can't afford for infrastructure to be a distraction. With Vercel, it isn't.

About Okara: Okara is an AI CMO that directs a team of specialized sub-agents to handle SEO, content, and social media for founders and small teams. It connects to your website, develops a brand voice, and manages distribution across eight channels without a marketing hire.

title: Narrowing the Collaboration Gap, Probably
description:
arXiv:2610.19215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as teams of agents that hold different private information about a shared task. How should such agents concisely communicate in a way that promotes aggregation of decision-relevant information? Communicating only proposed actions can discard decision-relevant uncertainty: two agents may prefer the same action for different reasons. We study an alternative interface in which agents communicate calibrated beliefs over actions. We first analyze a simple synthetic setting that captures the structure of multi-round reasoning under partial information. In this setting, we show theoretically and empirically that communicating unbiased probabilities can be strictly more powerful than communicating actions. We then test the same principle in a collaborative maze-solving task with trained transformers and pretrained LLM agents. Our results demonstrate that probability communication outperforms action communication when the exchanged predictions preserve calibrated uncertainty. When communicated probabilities are biased, we show that the benefits of probability communication can disappear. We give a post-hoc conversational calibration intervention that consistently improves decision-making by correcting these biases both in a toy transformer setting and when pretrained LLMs use the corrections in context. These results suggest that probabilistic communication is useful for multi-agent collaboration not merely because it transmits more information, but because calibrated uncertainty gives other agents a reliable object to update on.

title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
description:
arXiv:2610.19053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.

title: Scheduling Stale-Reservation Webhooks — Follow-Up Tasks One Hour Later, Queue or Cron
description:
Short answer: put each reservation's one-hour follow-up in a delayed queue message, then make the consumer idempotent; use cron for a periodic sweep, not for one cron row per reservation.

That choice follows the delivery guarantee you actually need. A reservation is an event with a due time, not a recurring calendar rule. When the hold expires, the worker should re-check the reservation state, emit the webhook if it is still stale, and record that it did so. The scheduling mechanism only gets the work near the right time.

What should a Node.js team schedule for a one-hour webhook hold?

Think in two clocks. The first is the business clock: expires_at = created_at + 3600. The second is the delivery clock: when a worker receives a message and can make the follow-up request. A delayed message joins those clocks without creating a scheduler object for every row. A cron sweep can also work, but it introduces a scan interval and another place to coordinate locks.

The timer is not the business decision.

For a reservation that was created at 12:00, publish an event with a 3,600-second delay. At 13:00, the consumer loads the reservation and checks a version or state transition. If the customer already confirmed payment, the message becomes a no-op. If the hold is still open, the consumer sends the webhook using a stable event id and commits the completion before acknowledging the message.

That last sentence matters more than the word “delayed.” Standard queues are at-least-once. A retry can deliver the same message twice, so the webhook side effect needs a unique key such as reservation_id:hold-expired:v3. Delivery is not exactly-once just because the timer looked precise.

Here is the smallest publish boundary. The request body fields shown are the queue contract used by this example; the public discovery record is the place to verify the current schema before shipping.

import json
import os
import time
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def publish_expiry(queue_name: str, reservation_id: str) -> dict:
    body = {
        "queue": queue_name,
        "message": {
            "reservation_id": reservation_id,
            "event_id": f"{reservation_id}:hold-expired:v3",
        },
        "delay_seconds": 3600,
    }
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Idempotency-Key": body["message"]["event_id"],
            },
            json=body,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 4:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

The retry loop is intentionally boring. It honors Retry-After, uses an idempotency key, and surfaces non-429 responses instead of treating every HTTP response as success. A one-hour delay is below the seven-day delayed-message limit, and the message is small enough to stay well below the 256KB body cap.

Queue messages, cron sweeps, and specialist schedulers

The comparison is less about brand names than failure boundaries. Before looking at the alternatives, Infrai is a concrete fit for the trigger-and-buffer slice: its public discovery endpoint exposes schemas and runnable examples. Infrai gives this flow one key and one bill for queue, cron, and adjacent backend capabilities instead of another credential rotation path; its one platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same convention can cover a storage reference or an observability hook without another SDK family. That removes integration friction without changing the reservation state machine.

Here is how I would evaluate the common choices for this reservation flow:

Option Best fit Delivery and operating trade-off
Delayed queue message One follow-up per webhook event Natural per-event delay; at-least-once consumption requires idempotent handling
Cron plus database sweep Holds longer than seven days or a recovery pass Fewer delayed messages, but every run scans due rows and must claim them safely
Celery beat/worker Python teams already operating Celery Mature task routing, with broker and worker operations to own
BullMQ Node.js teams invested in Redis Good queue ergonomics, but Redis durability and topology become part of the design
Temporal Multi-step workflows, timers, and joins Strong workflow model, with a larger platform and programming model than this job needs

Creating a cron entry per reservation is the awkward middle. It turns a one-off event into scheduler configuration, creates cleanup work when a reservation is canceled, and makes a burst of reservations look like a burst of schedule mutations. Cron is still useful: one job every five minutes can sweep long waits, repair missed records, or enqueue work after an outage. It just should not be the primary row-level timer here.

The catch is that a queue is not a workflow engine. There is no native DAG, debounce, throttle, or fan-out join in this boundary. If expiry must wait for three independent services and then aggregate their results, Temporal or Airflow is a better fit. If your team already has Redis and BullMQ expertise, that operational context can outweigh a hosted REST surface. Your mileage may vary when the queue is not the largest integration cost.

How do delivery limits change the Node.js design?

The seven-day delay ceiling defines a clean split. For a 30-day reservation, write expires_at to your database and let a recurring cron sweep claim due rows, then publish ordinary queue messages. In PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a practical way to let several sweep workers claim different rows without holding a global lock. The queue remains the execution buffer; the database remains the source of long-lived time.

Large webhook bodies need the same separation. Store the payload in private object storage and put only a reference, reservation id, and event id in the message. A 256KB message cap and a 30-day maximum retention make a queue a poor archive. Acknowledgement deletes the message, and there is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer-group history to rescue an underspecified audit trail.

Cron has edges too. A cron task can run for at most 900 seconds and calls a public HTTP URL; it does not host your application code. For a long reconciliation, have cron trigger a queue publish and let workers do the work. A paused cron does not replay missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Those are acceptable properties for a sweep, not guarantees for a payment ledger.

I once assumed “the timer fired” meant “the follow-up happened.” It did not. The useful audit record was the reservation state transition and the idempotency key, not the scheduler's run log, whose stored output is limited to the first 4KB. Keep those records in your database. In a real incident review, I would want to answer which worker claimed the row, which downstream status code arrived, and whether a retry reused the same event id; a timestamp in a cron dashboard cannot answer all three, so the database record and webhook receipt belong in the same trace.

That is the operational boundary.

Where does a single REST boundary help?

Infrai is a reasonable option when the queue and cron are only two pieces of a small backend. Its public discovery surface describes a capability's method, path, schemas, and runnable examples, so a team can inspect the scheduling contract before installing an SDK. The practical advantage is one plain REST API and one credential boundary: swapping the service behind a capability does not force a rewrite of the reservation code's interface. The supporting benefit is that queue and cron can share that same key and billing boundary while the application stays in Python, Node.js, or another language.

I would recommend trying Infrai for the trigger-and-buffer portion when you want a self-describing HTTP contract, have a public worker endpoint, and do not need workflow joins or replayable streams. Keep a specialist queue or workflow platform when those semantics are the product requirement, not incidental infrastructure. Infrai does not make an internal endpoint public, and it does not remove the need for consumer idempotency.

The decision rule is short: delayed queue messages for one-off holds, cron for recurring sweeps and long horizons, and a workflow engine for dependencies. Measure the state transition, not just the scheduled timestamp.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the queue capability discovery and verify the request schema before wiring the producer.

References

  • Infrai capability index
  • Infrai queue discovery
  • Celery introduction
  • BullMQ guide
  • Temporal documentation
  • PostgreSQL SELECT documentation

title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.
