title: Qt, GTK, Flutter, Electron? No: a graphics engine from scratch, entirely in Rust
description:
Llimphi draws every pixel of tawasuyu, even inside an operating system that boots with no Linux underneath. Why it exists, how it works and how true that “from scratch” really is.

Every time you open an application, something has to draw every button, every letter and every window on your screen, dozens of times per second. That something is a graphics engine, and almost nobody builds their own: most of the world’s software is painted with Qt, GTK, Flutter or Electron. Tawasuyu, the software suite with Quechua names being written in the Gioser workshop, chose not to borrow one.

Its engine is called Llimphi, which in Quechua means color, shine, pigment. It draws the whole suite: the desktop, the editor, the video player, the control panels and the interface of the project’s own operating system. Today 276 pieces of the suite are painted with Llimphi.

Fifteen and a half seconds of Llimphi. Everything on screen is drawn by the engine, frame by frame: the controls, the cosmos sky, the supay corridor, the infinite voxel world and the hand.
Why not use one that already exists

Until May 2026, tawasuyu was drawn with GPUI, the engine behind the Zed editor. On May 26 it was removed entirely, and not on a whim: the project has its own operating system, wawa, which boots straight on the hardware, with no Linux underneath. No existing engine knows how to draw there.

Qt, GTK and Flutter take a conventional operating system for granted, with its window manager, its installed fonts and its memory management. Llimphi was designed from day one to paint both in a desktop window and in the video memory of a kernel that has just powered on. That requirement forced it to be written from scratch.
What “from scratch” means

It is worth being precise, because it is the question every programmer asks. Llimphi did not reinvent every piece. Just as Flutter relies on Skia and GTK on Cairo, Llimphi uses four free projects from the Rust community for the most specialized jobs. Everything else is its own: the way an application describes its screen, how it reacts to each click, the components and the paths that lead to the pixels.

Talking to the graphics card: wgpu · community
Drawing curves and fills with antialiasing: vello · community
Working out where each box goes (flexbox and grid): taffy · community
Shaping text: Arabic, Chinese, emoji, ligatures: parley · community
The life cycle of each application: Llimphi
Components, themes, animation, accessibility: Llimphi
Painting without a graphics card, inside the kernel: Llimphi
Isolating an application and painting its drawing from outside: Llimphi

The four community pieces are written in Rust too. That is why the headline says “entirely in Rust”, and stands by it.
How a Llimphi application thinks

Llimphi follows the Elm architecture, named after a language known for applications that almost never crash. The idea is simple: the application does not modify the screen, it describes it. Every time something happens, the engine goes through six steps:

input: A click, a key or a gesture arrives.
update: The application computes its new state.
view: It describes how it should look in that state.
layout: The engine works out the position of each box.
raster: It turns that description into pixels.
present: It shows the finished frame.

Since nothing touches the screen directly, no two parts of the program fight over the same button. It is the same reason this style became popular on the web with React, except here it runs natively, with no browser in between.
One brush, four paths to your screen

The most unusual part of Llimphi is that the same drawing can reach the screen by completely different paths, depending on where the application runs. “Looks about the same” was not good enough: each path was put side by side with the others and the pixels were counted.
With a graphics card

The everyday path on the desktop. It is the reference everything else is measured against.
CPU only

The one the wawa kernel uses, since it has no video driver.
Subscribe to the Medium newsletter

Fills and layers identical bit for bit. Accented text may differ, because the kernel only ships three fonts.
By message

An isolated application doesn’t touch the screen: it sends its drawing as a message and the system paints it on its behalf.

0 pixels of difference across the four test scenes.
For phones

A path that works on mobile graphics chips without general-purpose compute, such as the Mali-G57.

No pixel differs by more than 1/255 out of 19,200.

The “by message” path coming out with zero difference has a practical consequence: an application can live locked away, with no permission at all to touch the screen, and still look exactly the same. Security that costs nothing in appearance.
What it already ships

Close to eighty components: buttons, tables, text editors with multiple cursors, node graphs, panel splitters, calendars and more.
Eleven modules that combine components into complete application pieces.
Real text: right-to-left writing, Chinese characters, emoji, ligatures and input methods for Asian languages.
Accessibility: every element can declare what it is and what it is called, and the tests query it the way a screen reader would.
Image-based tests: a screen is compared with its approved version, and any unexpected change makes the test fail.
A 3D voxel engine that mounts inside the same interface, as just another component.

What it doesn’t do yet

An engine that promises too much loses the trust of whoever tries it, so it is worth saying what is missing too:

The phone path has been tested on real hardware, but no published application uses it yet. The current Android builds take another path that doesn’t work on every chip.
Outside its three built-in fonts, text may look different in the kernel and on the desktop. The cause is known: with no operating system underneath, there is nowhere to get more fonts from.
Part of Llimphi is already published on crates.io, Rust’s official registry, but the release is incomplete and some recent pieces haven’t been uploaded yet.

How to try it

For Rust programmers, the way in is a single package:

cargo add llimphi

The package bundles the core, the themes and the 3D engine. For the rest, the best demonstration is tawasuyu itself: every window in the suite is a Llimphi application.

Originally published at https://gioser.net on October 12, 2026.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components
description:
From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components

Web development has evolved from hand‑crafted HTML pages to massive single‑page applications (SPAs) powered by heavy JavaScript frameworks. While frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular dominate the conversation, there’s a quieter revolution happening under the hood: Web Components paired with CSS custom properties (variables). Together they let you write reusable, framework‑agnostic UI pieces that work anywhere—static sites, SPAs, or server‑rendered pages.

In this post we’ll explore why Web Components deserve a spot in your toolbox, walk through a practical example of a custom <user-card> element, and show how CSS variables keep your design system flexible without adding runtime JavaScript bloat. By the end, you’ll have a production‑ready component you can drop into any project, regardless of the stack you’re using.

Why Web Components Matter in 2024

  1. Native Browser Support – All modern browsers ship with the Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, and HTML Templates APIs. No polyfills required for the majority of users.
  2. Framework Agnostic – A component built once can be used in a vanilla HTML page, a React tree, an Angular module, or a Svelte app without adapters.
  3. Encapsulation – Shadow DOM isolates styles and markup, preventing accidental CSS bleed‑through that often plagues large codebases.
  4. Performance – Because the component lives as native DOM, the browser can optimize rendering and layout better than a virtual DOM abstraction.

Despite these benefits, many developers shy away because they think components are “hard to test” or “lack tooling.” The truth is the opposite: modern tooling (Vite, Snowpack, Lit, and even plain ES modules) makes authoring, testing, and bundling a breeze.

Building a Reusable <user-card> Component

Let’s create a small but useful component that displays a user’s avatar, name, and a short bio. We’ll use Lit (a lightweight library that helps work with the Shadow DOM) to keep the code concise, but the final output is just a native custom element.

1. Project scaffolding 

# Create a new directory
mkdir user-card-demo && cd user-card-demo

# Initialize a Vite project (vanilla JS)
npm init vite@latest . --template vanilla

# Install Lit
npm install lit

2. Defining the component (src/UserCard.js) 

// src/UserCard.js
import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit';
import { property, state } from 'lit/decorators.js';

class UserCard extends LitElement {
  // Public attributes
  @property({ type: String }) name = 'Anonymous';
  @property({ type: String }) avatar = '';
  @property({ type: String }) bio = '';

  static styles = css`
    :host {
      display: block;
      max-width: 280px;
      border: 1px solid var(--card-border, #ddd);
      border-radius: var(--card-radius, 8px);
      overflow: hidden;
      font-family: var(--font-family, system-ui, sans-serif);
      background: var(--card-bg, #fff);
      box-shadow: var(--card-shadow, 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1));
    }
    .header {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: var(--header-bg, #f5f5f5);
    }
    .avatar {
      width: 48px;
      height: 48px;
      border-radius: 50%;
      margin-right: 0.75rem;
      background: var(--avatar-bg, #ccc) no-repeat center/cover;
    }
    .name {
      font-size: 1.1rem;
      font-weight: 600;
      color: var(--name-color, #333);
    }
    .bio {
      padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
      font-size: 0.9rem;
      line-height: 1.4;
      color: var(--bio-color, #555);
    }
  `;

  render() {
    return html`
      <div class="header">
        <div class="avatar" style="background-image:url(${this.avatar})"></div>
        <div class="name">${this.name}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="bio"><slot>${this.bio}</slot></div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
export default UserCard;

Key takeaways

  • Shadow DOM – The component’s styles live inside static styles, guaranteeing they won’t clash with page styles.
  • CSS Custom Properties – Notice the var(--card-border, #ddd) pattern. The component provides sensible defaults but lets any page override them, keeping your design system fluid.
  • Slots – By exposing a <slot> we let consumers inject richer markup into the bio area if they wish.

3. Using the component (index.html) 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>User Card Demo</title>
  <script type="module" src="/src/UserCard.js"></script>
  <style>
    /* Global design tokens */
    :root {
      --card-bg: #fafafa;
      --card-border: #e0e0e0;
      --card-radius: 12px;
      --card-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
      --header-bg: #fff;
      --name-color: #222;
      --bio-color: #444;
      --font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Web Component Showcase</h1>

  <user-card
    name="Jane Doe"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=5"
    bio="Frontend engineer who loves CSS art and open‑source."
  ></user-card>

  <!-- Overriding a token for a single card -->
  <user-card
    name="Sam Smith"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=12"
    style="--card-bg:#fffbe6; --card-border:#ffd54f"
  >
    <p>Full‑stack developer, coffee addict, and occasional jazz saxophonist.</p>
  </user-card>
</body>
</html>

When you run npm run dev (Vite’s dev server), you’ll see two cards with different looks—thanks to the CSS variables defined at the page level and even per‑instance overrides. No extra JavaScript is required after the initial component registration.

Styling Without Bloat: Harnessing CSS Variables

CSS variables are more than a convenience for theming; they’re a performance win. Because they’re resolved by the browser’s CSS engine, changing a variable (e.g., switching to a dark theme) doesn’t trigger a JavaScript re‑render. In the <user-card> example we:

  • Declared defaults inside the component (var(--card-bg, #fff)).
  • Exposed a global token map in :root that the whole site can update with a single CSS class toggle. 
/* Dark theme toggle */
body.dark-mode {
  --card-bg: #2b2b2b;
  --card-border: #444;
  --name-color: #eee;
  --bio-color: #ccc;
}

Toggling dark-mode on the <body> instantly darkens every card without touching JavaScript.

Testing the Component

Even though the component is native, you still want a solid test suite. Here’s a quick Jest + @testing-library/web component setup:

npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom

// tests/UserCard.test.js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { fireEvent } from '@testing-library/dom';
import '../src/UserCard.js';

test('renders name and avatar', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('user-card');
  el.name = 'Test User';
  el.avatar = 'https://example.com/avatar.png';
  document.body.append(el);

  const nameEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name');
  const avatarEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.avatar');

  expect(nameEl).toHaveTextContent('Test User');
  expect(avatarEl).toHaveStyle(`background-image: url(${el.avatar})`);
});

Running npx jest confirms the component behaves as expected, and because we’re testing the Shadow DOM directly we avoid flaky CSS selector issues.

Deploying to Production

When you’re ready to ship, Vite’s build command bundles the component into a single, minified ES module:

npm run build

The output dist/assets/user-card.[hash].js can be served via any static host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages). Since the component is an ES module, you can also import it from a CDN like esm.sh or jsDelivr:

<script type="module" src="https://esm.sh/user-card@1.0.0"></script>

This eliminates the need for a build step on the consumer side—a big win for content‑heavy sites that prefer Markdown‑first workflows.

When Not to Use Web Components

  • Heavy state management – If your UI requires a global store (Redux‑style) across many components, a full framework may still be easier.
  • SSR‑first projects – While you can pre‑render custom elements, the ecosystem around SSR for Web Components isn’t as mature as for React or Next.js.

That said, for most UI widgets—cards, modals, tabs, tooltips—Web Components hit the sweet spot of reusability and performance.

Future‑Proofing Your Frontend

The Web Platform continues to mature. Upcoming proposals like CSS Cascade Layers and Declarative Shadow DOM will make component composition even cleaner. By investing in native components now, you’ll be ready to adopt these enhancements without refactoring a massive framework layer.

Recommended Tools

  • SuperCDN – Fast Global CDN with Free Tier – Serve your compiled component assets instantly worldwide. Their free tier is generous enough for hobby projects, and the analytics dashboard helps you track bandwidth usage in real time.

  • CodeSnap – Instant Code Screenshot Generator – Turn any code block into a beautifully styled image for social media or documentation. It supports custom themes, line numbers, and even animated GIFs, making it perfect for showcasing snippets like the ones above.

Happy coding, and may your components stay lightweight and your users stay delighted!

title: Evidence-Anchored Overdose Death Prediction from Death Investigation Reports
description:
arXiv:2610.19556v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Confirmation of overdose deaths in the United States is often delayed due to the complexities of certifying drug-involved deaths. Death investigation reports represent a rich but underutilized data source that could be used to predict whether a death is a suspected overdose (i.e., a death preliminarily identified as an overdose prior to the final cause and manner of death determination). We present an automated framework that classifies suspected overdoses from death investigation reports, while producing supporting explanations guided by expert knowledge. Through an expert-guided design process, we investigate 1) what type of explanations are best for model prediction performance, and 2) which architecture is better suited for this task: pipeline models that rationalize first and then predict, or self-rationalizing models that jointly predict and rationalize? Our experiments show that a pipeline model with explanations grounded in the input death investigation reports outperforms the other settings. Our best model also outperforms a rule-based system currently in deployment by 15%, while allowing expert interventions for final decisions.

title: Your Swap Screen Is Showing the Wrong Number
description:
A month ago I wrote about what a crypto app should do before you press "Send". There's one more thing that happens before that button, and most swap interfaces still get it wrong: the number they put in the biggest font.

Usually it's the exchange rate. 1 XMR = 0.12 ETH. Clean, comparable, easy to sort.

It's also the least useful figure on the screen.

What lands in the user's wallet is an amount. Between the rate and that amount sit several costs the rate doesn't show.

One quote, four costs

Cross-chain swaps make this easy to see, because each leg has its own costs. Take Monero to Ethereum. CoinMarketCal recently published a breakdown of XMR to ETH exchange fees and counted four separate costs behind a single quote:

XMR network fee   → paid by the user, from their own wallet
Provider fees     → trading fees charged by liquidity sources
Spread            → gap between the market price and the offered rate
ETH payout fee    → gas to send ETH to the user's address

Only the first one is under the user's control. The Monero fee depends on network load and transaction size, not on the amount sent, and wallets let you choose from four priority levels. Everything else is decided by the provider.

The Ethereum side has its own formula. According to ethereum.org, a transaction costs gas units multiplied by the base fee plus a priority fee. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. The base fee can move by up to 12.5% per block with demand, so the same payout can cost noticeably more at a busy moment.

None of this shows up in "1 XMR = 0.12 ETH".

Better rate, worse result

Here's a simple case. Two quotes for a 2 XMR swap (the numbers are illustrative):

  • Quote A shows a rate of 0.12000 ETH, charges a 0.1% trading fee, and takes a 0.002 ETH withdrawal fee afterwards.
  • Quote B shows 0.11925 ETH, with every cost after the deposit already included.

Sort by rate and A wins. Now compute what actually arrives:

function rankByReceived(quotes) {
  return quotes
    .map((q) => ({
      name: q.name,
      received: Number(
        (q.amountIn * q.rate * (1 - q.tradingFee) - q.fixedFees).toFixed(6)
      ),
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.received - a.received);
}

rankByReceived([
  { name: "A", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.12, tradingFee: 0.001, fixedFees: 0.002 },
  { name: "B", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.11925, tradingFee: 0, fixedFees: 0 },
]);
// [ { name: "B", received: 0.2385 }, { name: "A", received: 0.23776 } ]

B pays out more. The gap is small here, but a UI that ranks by rate picks the wrong option every time this pattern appears. And it appears a lot, because "no fees" usually means the fees moved into the spread or into a step that comes later.

The rate wasn't lying. It answered a question the user didn't ask.

Small swaps hurt the most

Network fees are roughly fixed per transaction. They don't scale with the amount, so their share grows as the swap gets smaller.

const feeShare = (receivedEth, fixedFeesEth) => fixedFeesEth / receivedEth;

feeShare(0.24, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0083 → 0.8%
feeShare(0.03, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0667 → 6.7%

Same fees, eight times the impact. This is also why providers set minimum amounts: below a certain point, fees eat most of the order. A screen that shows only the rate hides this completely. A screen that shows the received amount makes it visible the moment someone types a small number.

What the quote object should carry

If I were designing the API behind a swap screen, the response would put the received amount first and say what's inside it:

{
  "amountIn": { "value": "2.0", "asset": "XMR" },
  "amountOut": { "value": "0.2385", "asset": "ETH" },
  "rateMode": "floating",
  "includedInQuote": ["spread", "provider fees", "ETH payout fee"],
  "paidSeparately": ["XMR network fee"],
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-15T12:00:00Z"
}

amountOut is the headline. Anyone who wants the rate can derive it.

includedInQuote and paidSeparately matter more than they look. Two quotes are only comparable if they cover the same costs. Without these fields, the frontend has no way to tell whether it's comparing like with like.

rateMode tells the user what kind of promise they're getting. A floating quote follows the market until execution and can land slightly above or below the estimate. A fixed quote locks the amount for a limited window, usually with a small buffer priced in for volatility. Both are fine. Hiding which one it is isn't.

expiresAt is there for fixed quotes. A locked amount with no visible deadline is a support ticket waiting to happen.

Thin liquidity widens the gap

For pairs with deep markets, the difference between the rate and the received amount stays small. For thinner pairs it grows, and Monero is a good example. Kraken stopped XMR trading and deposits for clients in the European Economic Area from October 31, 2024. Fewer venues usually means wider spreads, and the spread is exactly the cost a rate-first screen never shows.

So the less liquid the asset, the more misleading the headline rate gets. That's the opposite of what users need.

A short checklist for swap screens

  • Lead with the amount the user will receive.
  • Say whether that number is an estimate or a guaranteed amount, and for how long.
  • List what's already included and what the user still pays.
  • Flag amounts close to the minimum, where fixed fees dominate.
  • Compare quotes by received amount, never by rate.

None of this needs new infrastructure. The provider already calculates every one of these numbers to build the quote. The only question is whether the interface passes them on.

People spend what arrives in their wallet. The screen should start there.

title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19526v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.

title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

title: Escape Analysis: How Can a Compiler Eliminate a Heap Allocation Without Changing Your Code?
description:
Consider this Java method:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

Two Point objects are created, used in a calculation, and then discarded. The source code calls new, which in Java means heap allocation, object initialization, and eventually garbage collection. But if you look at this from a different angle: both objects are born at the start of the method, used for arithmetic, and are completely useless after the return statement. Nothing outside the method ever sees them. No other thread can observe them. They exist solely to hold two doubles each.

Does the runtime actually need to allocate heap memory for them? That question is what escape analysis is designed to answer.

What It Means for an Object to Escape

Before a compiler can eliminate an allocation, it needs to prove that the allocation can be eliminated. The key concept is whether an object escapes its local scope.

An object escapes when a reference to it can be observed from outside the context in which it was created. There are several ways this happens:

Return. A method that returns a reference to a locally created object immediately causes it to escape. The caller now holds a live reference, so the object must exist somewhere accessible after the method returns. Stack frames are discarded on return, which means the object cannot safely live in one.

Shared state. Storing a reference in a field of an object that outlives the current scope, or in a static field, allows code anywhere in the program to observe the object. The compiler must assume the object could be read at any time.

Opaque callees. When a method passes an object to another function and the compiler cannot fully analyze what that function does with the reference, it must conservatively assume the object might escape. If the callee stores the reference in a field or returns it to its own callers, the assumption would be violated.

Non-escaping objects are those where the compiler can prove that every reference to the object stays within a bounded scope. It is created, used, and the last reference to it disappears, all within a region the compiler can reason about.

The Point objects in the opening example are non-escaping. The references a and b are local variables. They are never returned, never stored in any field, never passed to an opaque method. The compiler can trace every use of them.

How the Compiler Reasons About References

Escape analysis is not a single yes-or-no check. It is a data flow analysis that the compiler runs over the program's intermediate representation, tracking how references to each object propagate through the code.

The classic formulation, and the one underlying HotSpot's C2 compiler, builds a connection graph: a representation of the relationships between object references, the fields through which they flow, and the boundaries across which they might cross. Each object in the graph carries an escape state. HotSpot's C2 uses three states: NoEscape, for objects whose references are entirely contained within the method; ArgEscape, for objects passed as arguments but not observed to escape further; and GlobalEscape, for objects accessible from outside the method or thread.

The analysis is conservative. If the compiler cannot prove that a reference stays local, it assumes it might escape. Conservative analysis is safe: it never eliminates a necessary allocation. But it also means some allocations that a human could see are unnecessary will be retained because the compiler's model of the code is not complete. Inlining is one of the most important enablers of escape analysis. When a callee is inlined into the caller, the compiler gains full visibility into what the callee does with every argument, which allows escape states to be refined. HotSpot's C2 requires inlining to occur before scalar replacement can work. If a method is not inlined because it is too large or was not compiled at the right optimization tier, the analysis may classify its arguments as escaping, even if they do not.

The Optimization: Scalar Replacement

The natural first guess is that escape analysis moves objects from the heap to the stack. For some compilers and runtimes, that is exactly what happens. The Go compiler does this: if it proves that a value will not outlive the current function, it allocates the value in the goroutine's stack frame rather than on the heap. You can observe this directly with go build -gcflags="-m", which annotates each allocation decision.

HotSpot's C2 JIT takes a different path. According to the OpenJDK wiki: "C2 does NOT replace a heap allocation with a stack allocation for non globally escaping objects." Instead, C2 performs scalar replacement.

Scalar replacement decomposes an object into its constituent fields and eliminates the object itself. Rather than allocating a block of memory and storing field values in it, the compiler treats each field as an independent local variable. The object never materializes as a contiguous region of memory. No allocation happens. No garbage collector ever needs to reclaim it.

The transformation for the Point example looks conceptually like this. Before scalar replacement:

// What you wrote
Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
double ax = a.x;
double ay = a.y;

After scalar replacement, the compiler replaces all field accesses with synthetic local values:

// What the compiler works with internally
double a_x = x1;  // scalar substitute for a.x
double a_y = y1;  // scalar substitute for a.y

The Point object never exists. The field reads (a.x, a.y) become references to local values that can be kept in registers. Aleksey Shipilëv's JVM Anatomy Quarks describes this precisely: HotSpot "does not do stack allocations per se, but it does approximate that with Scalar Replacement."

From there, register allocation can place those scalar values in CPU registers for the duration of the computation. The two doubles that would have been heap-allocated objects end up as register values, with no allocation, no initialization overhead, and no GC involvement.

A Concrete Walk-Through

Take the full distance method from the opening:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

For scalar replacement to apply, C2 needs to:

  1. Inline the Point constructor so it can see that no reference to the new object leaks out of the construction.
  2. Determine that a and b have escape state NoEscape: no return of the references, no field stores into external objects, no passing to opaque methods.
  3. Replace new Point(x1, y1) with two scalar variables a_x = x1, a_y = y1.
  4. Rewrite every a.x and a.y access to use those scalars.
  5. Eliminate the allocation instruction entirely. After this transformation, the method compiles to arithmetic on four double values, none of which requires heap memory. The behavior observed by any caller is identical: they receive the same double result. The only change is internal to the representation of the computation.

Lock elimination is a related optimization that escape analysis enables. If an object is non-escaping, no other thread can hold a reference to it, so any synchronized blocks on that object are unnecessary. The compiler can remove them.

Where the Analysis Fails

Escape analysis has hard limits, and understanding them is as important as understanding what it can do.

The most common barrier is an opaque method call. If distanceBetween passed a to any method that C2 has not inlined, the compiler would have to assume the reference might escape. The Point would remain heap-allocated. This is why HotSpot's OpenJDK scalar replacement documentation explicitly lists non-inlined methods as a case where scalar replacement is prevented.

Interface dispatch is a related problem. When a method is called through an interface, the compiler cannot always determine which concrete implementation will run, which makes it impossible to inline the callee. Without inlining, the escape state of the argument is unknown.

Some operations are identity-sensitive. Java's == operator on objects tests reference identity. If the compiler replaces an object with scalars, two allocations that previously produced distinct references might appear identical or might behave incorrectly if the program depends on them being different objects. The compiler must verify that no code in scope depends on the object's identity before it can safely decompose it.

Synchronization presents a harder constraint. If code synchronizes on an object that the compiler is considering for scalar replacement, the semantics of Java's memory model require that the lock be observable. Lock elimination is sound only when the object is genuinely non-escaping, so the compiler must be certain before removing it.

Conservative analysis also means that HotSpot will retain an allocation if any uncertainty exists. The analysis can handle many cases that appear complex in source code, but it cannot analyze beyond what it can observe. Dynamic loading of classes, reflection, and native code are all effectively opaque.

The Performance Picture

Removing allocations reduces pressure on the garbage collector by producing fewer objects that need to be tracked and collected. In throughput-sensitive code that creates many short-lived objects in tight loops, this can meaningfully reduce GC pause frequency and time spent in allocation paths. Keeping data in registers rather than memory also reduces memory traffic.

That said, allocation in modern JVMs is fast. HotSpot's thread-local allocation buffers (TLABs) allow most allocations to complete with a simple pointer bump. The cost of a single allocation is small. The benefit of elimination comes from the aggregate effect over many allocations, particularly in hot loops, and from the downstream reduction in GC work.

Whether scalar replacement improves a specific workload depends on the compiler's ability to apply it, the allocation rate of the relevant code, and the GC configuration. Profiling with allocation-aware tools is the right way to measure this, not inference from source code alone.

The Developer's Relationship With This Optimization

The existence of escape analysis and scalar replacement changes what source-level object creation actually means. Writing new Point(x, y) in Java does not guarantee that a heap allocation will occur at runtime. Whether one does depends on the JIT compiler's escape analysis, whether the relevant methods were inlined, and the escape state the analysis assigned to the object.

This is intentional. The language specification defines what the program must compute and what observable side effects it must produce. It says nothing about whether intermediate objects need physical representation. The JIT compiler is free to choose any implementation that preserves observable behavior.

Several practical points follow from this:

Write code that is clear and correct. Avoiding allocation for its own sake by using awkward data structures or manual field decomposition will not necessarily produce faster code and will make the compiler's job harder if it disrupts inlining.

Measure before concluding. Allocation sampling profilers can show which allocations actually reach the heap at runtime. An allocation that appears in source code may not appear in profiles if scalar replacement has already eliminated it.

Do not assume Java and Go behave identically. Go's escape analysis operates at compile time and makes stack-allocation decisions that are baked into the generated machine code. HotSpot's analysis operates in the JIT compiler and uses scalar replacement rather than stack allocation. The mechanisms, the triggering conditions, and the diagnostics are different.

Check compiler output when it matters. Go's -gcflags="-m" flag reports escape decisions. HotSpot's -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations flag reports scalar replacement. These are the ground truth; source code is not.

The Deeper Insight

Escape analysis reflects a broader principle in compiler design: a language's specification describes the required observable behavior of a program, not its required internal representation. The compiler is free to transform how data is stored, how operations are sequenced, and how objects are physically represented, as long as anything the program is permitted to observe remains consistent with the specification.

A heap allocation is a mechanism for giving data a lifetime that outlives a function call. When the compiler can prove that a particular datum does not need that extended lifetime, the allocation is unnecessary. The datum can be represented as local values, stored in registers, and discarded the moment the function returns. The program computes the same result. The method's caller observes the same returned value. Nothing that any correct program could observe has changed.

What the compiler has changed is what never needed to exist in the first place.

Sources

  • OpenJDK HotSpot Escape Analysis Wiki — authoritative description of C2's escape analysis algorithm and its explicit statement that C2 does not perform stack allocation.
  • Aleksey Shipilëv: JVM Anatomy Quarks #18 — Scalar Replacement — detailed technical explanation of scalar replacement in HotSpot C2.
  • HotSpot Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement Status (OpenJDK) — analysis of escape analysis coverage and limitations in C2.
  • Oracle Java Magazine: Escape Analysis in the HotSpot JIT Compiler — accessible explanation with GC log evidence.
  • Segment Engineering: Allocation Efficiency in High-Performance Go Services — practical explanation of Go's stack-allocation-first approach and escape analysis flags.
  • Go compiler escape analysis flags — go build -gcflags="-m" documentation.

title: 371 translations crash their Android apps: a census of 1.26 million strings on F-Droid
description:
Made with AI agents by MV2 of Munim, Inc. Every number below comes from code and data you can rerun: android-translation-crash-census (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0).

When an Android app calls getString(R.string.files_left, n), the translation for the user's language goes to java.util.Formatter. If a translator typed %1$ where the English says %1$s, or wrote 50% without escaping it, the call throws. English never breaks, so the developer never sees it. Only people using that language do.

How often does that happen in practice? Searches of GitHub, arXiv and the web turned up single-project fixes (Commons, Firefox for Android, ConnectBot, OsmAnd) but no measurement across apps. The census makes one.

What was checked

  • Every source repository behind F-Droid's index: 4,476 repositories for 4,667 apps, latest commit, read in 11 minutes on 4 cores.
  • 3,755 have Android string resources. 1,703 have translations of strings with printf placeholders.
  • That is 1,262,958 translations. Each one, and its English source, was formatted with OpenJDK 21's real java.util.Formatter, using arguments of the types the English string expects.
  • For repositories with a failing translation, the census also reads the Kotlin and Java code to see whether anything formats that string with arguments. A broken string nobody formats can't crash.

What it found

  • 371 translations in 98 repositories throw with the arguments the English string expects.
  • 238 of them, in 66 repositories, are strings the app's own code formats. Those are the crashes users can actually hit. That count is after two corrections made by reading rows by hand (below).
  • About 1 in 3,400 formatted translations crashes. It's concentrated: ownCloud's Uyghur file alone has 47 reachable crashes (% 1 $ s instead of %1$s), and Cashiro and Wikimedia Commons follow. Most affected apps have one to four.
  • The exceptions are UnknownFormatConversionException 251, MissingFormatArgumentException 48, FormatFlagsConversionMismatchException 48, IllegalFormatConversionException 20 and IllegalFormatFlagsException 4.

Two false positives the census found in itself

The first run reported 382 crashes, 250 of them reachable. Reading the rows against each app's code took 12 out of the reachable 250, and 11 out of the 382:

  • %t and Long. Four Cashiro strings use %t where the English has %d. %t rejects the Integer the census passed but accepts the Long the app passes, so they print the wrong text instead of crashing.
  • Markup that is text. Wikipedia writes some English strings in CDATA: <![CDATA[... attributed to %1$s. <a href="%2$s">Learn more</a>.]]>. To Android that link is plain text, so the app formats it with two arguments and passes it to Html.fromHtml. The checker removed every <...> before reading placeholders, so the %2$s in the href disappeared from the English. Translations whose link markup was itself broken kept their %2$s, and looked like they read an argument the app never passes. They show a broken link, but they don't throw. That is six rows in Danish, Indonesian, Portuguese, Romanian and Russian. Five more were in values-qq, translatewiki.net's notes for translators, which no device loads. All 11 are gone from the totals above, and 8 of them were in strings the code formats.

The real JVM agreed with the static check on all of these, because both read the same extracted text. Checking the checker against a JVM doesn't catch a mistake in what you feed them both. Census 0.3.1 fixes the extraction (only real XML elements lose their markup), and a full re-run will list every row that changes.

The mistakes, by kind

A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 242 reachable rows left after the Wikipedia correction (238 after %t):

Kind Example Rows Repos
malformed index % 1 $ s, %$1s 50 5
stray percent (%1$d%), 电量 %1$d % 45 26
conversion missing %1$ musikspelare, Wideo (%1) 43 18
flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14
argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 27 14
conversion letter in another script %1$с, %1$دم, %1$δδ 26 6
wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5
unknown Latin conversion %1$DH, %2$vs 7 4

A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag.

The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es, not an s), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM, Arabic %1$دم (dal for d), Greek %1$δδ. To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter, с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one.

Every route shipped one

The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.)

A static check you can run in CI

The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Of the 371 JVM crashes it called 364 errors and the other 7 warnings, and it called nothing an error that the JVM accepted. Both share the text-extraction mistake above, which the next l10n-guard release fixes.

python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml

It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations.

Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land.

Reporting them

The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators.

So far:

  • Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings (#397). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019.
  • ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings (#5018).
  • Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets), FadCam #360 (Italian and Greek strings in video deletion and export).

Limits

  • Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform.
  • Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash.
  • It can also overcount, as the two corrections above show. Both were found by reading rows by hand, and more may exist.
  • Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level.
  • I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator.

If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read.

This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

title: RDCompGS: Rate-Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
description:
arXiv:2610.19538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bj{\o}ntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
description:
arXiv:2610.19021v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

title: SaTPO: Text-to-Image Safety Alignment via Transition Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety alignment of text-to-image diffusion models aims to suppress harmful content without compromising useful generation capabilities. However, preferences over completed images compress multidimensional generation factors into a coarse signal, potentially driving changes beyond those required for safety. To address this, we propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO), which enforces step-wise alignment during denoising. SaTPO leverages the insight that an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form a tightly coupled preference pair when conditioned on a shared parent state and noise realization. By anchoring optimization on identical parent states, SaTPO eliminates historical trajectory divergence, confining safety adaptation to an incremental alignment while preserving task-relevant semantics. Multi-scale drift constraints and benign replay further limit behavioral deviation and preserve ordinary generation. We additionally construct CoProPV, a refined dataset ensuring visually verified contrasts. Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate improved safety-quality trade-offs. Compared with AlignGuard, PerspectiveVision unsafe-detection rates on Inappropriate Image Prompts decrease from 12.70% to 6.00% and from 15.04% to 9.30%, respectively, while FID improves from 32.28 to 25.95 and from 36.50 to 27.51. Warning: this paper includes potentially offensive content.

title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.14736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. To address this limitation, we propose a Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (TASA) which summarizes and exploits trajectory to improve solution quality. Specifically, TASA plans the strategy for each step based on the optimization trajectory, which decomposes the optimization process into traceable strategy selections. Moreover, we leverage LLM to construct problem-specific tools and introduce a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner, which efficiently utilizes the information of trajectory to update solutions. We establish local convergence under persistent exploration and evaluate the complete framework under a shared candidate-evaluation budget. The results support its solution quality and the traceability of strategy-guided search.

title: Build in public
description:
While building ShopPilot AI, I’ve been working on a function that checks availability for a requested product color and size.

“Out of stock” and “that variant doesn’t exist” need different answers.

I defined three cases to test:
• The variant exists and has stock.
• The variant exists but has zero stock.
• There’s no matching variant.

The interesting part was the third case.

JavaScript’s .find() returns undefined when nothing matches, so I need to handle that before reading the variant’s stock.

This is a small function, but it’s helping me connect JavaScript fundamentals, TypeScript, and testing to a real customer question.

I’m learning how to use TDD for this logic: define the expected behavior with a failing test, implement it, then refactor.

My main lesson so far: a useful test starts with a clear requirement.
Before checking whether the code works, I need to decide what it should do.

title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.14495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

title: A Go Small-App Observability Stack for Health Monitoring Without Sentry or Datadog
description:
A marketplace import page should fire when scheduled imports stop producing results, not merely when the API process dies. TL;DR: use an external heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks or Better Stack to detect the missing completion, then use errors, logs, and metrics to explain it. For a small Go service, that is the least complex stack that covers silent scheduler failures and still lets the on-call roll back safely.

The page should say which import is late, when it last completed, and how far it is beyond its expected interval. It should not begin with a graph titled “host CPU.” If the 02:00 supplier import normally finishes by 02:20, the actionable event is the absent successful completion after a deliberate grace period.

The page at 02:25 UTC

Start at the pager and work backward. A useful alert reads like this: supplier-catalog-import has not completed; last success 01:58 UTC; grace period 25m. The runbook then asks three questions in order: did a run start, did it fail, and did it finish with a plausible result count?

That order protects rollback safety. If a newly deployed parser started producing zero records, the operator can compare the deployment time, error group, and rows_imported metric before reverting. If no run started, rolling back application code may be pointless; the scheduler or queue path deserves attention first. If the run started twice, the response shifts again: stop duplicate delivery from causing duplicate marketplace writes, using an idempotency key derived from the schedule and supplier.

One signal cannot answer all three questions. An uptime probe proves an HTTP target responds. A heartbeat proves the expected job reached a checkpoint. Logs and errors preserve diagnostic context. Metrics show whether “success” produced 18,000 listings or zero.

That last distinction matters.

What should health monitoring prove without a full observability stack?

A job that never starts emits no fresh error, log, or metric. Querying the observability store can reveal that absence, but somebody still has to run the query on schedule, maintain threshold state, and deliver the notification. That is a monitoring system built beside the monitoring system.

External heartbeat products own that negative-space problem. Healthchecks exposes ping URLs and documents start, success, and failure signals. Better Stack combines uptime monitoring with heartbeat monitoring and incident escalation. Either can watch for a missing completion independently of the process and scheduler being watched.

The threshold needs operational slack. Set it from the schedule plus the observed upper end of normal runtime, then add a grace period for queue delay and upstream variance. Do not invent a universal “two missed runs” rule: for a daily catalog import, waiting for a second miss means discovering the failure a day late; for a five-minute enrichment job, paging on one slightly slow execution may create noise.

Page on missing useful work, not missing telemetry. A metrics backend can still alert on rows_imported == 0 after a run reports, but the external heartbeat is what catches a worker that never got far enough to report anything.

Build the Go integration around completion

The heartbeat should surround the real unit of work. This runnable Go program sends a start signal, runs an import, and sends success only after the result is committed. Set HEALTHCHECKS_URL to the private ping URL supplied by the heartbeat service.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func ping(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, url, suffix, body string) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url+suffix, strings.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        message, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("heartbeat returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(message)))
    }
    return nil
}

func queryErrorGroups(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) error {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("error groups returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        log.Printf("error groups response received: bytes=%d", len(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("error groups remained rate limited after retries")
}

func importCatalog(context.Context) (int, error) {
    return 18000, nil
}

func main() {
    pingURL := os.Getenv("HEALTHCHECKS_URL")
    if pingURL == "" {
        log.Fatal("HEALTHCHECKS_URL is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/start", "supplier=catalog-a"); err != nil {
        log.Printf("start heartbeat failed: %v", err)
    }

    rows, err := importCatalog(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if rows == 0 {
        err = fmt.Errorf("import committed zero rows")
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "", fmt.Sprintf("rows_imported=%d", rows)); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := queryErrorGroups(ctx, client); err != nil {
        log.Printf("diagnostic query failed: %v", err)
    }
    log.Printf("import complete: rows_imported=%d", rows)
}

In production, the import itself also needs an idempotent commit boundary. A deterministic key such as supplier-id + scheduled-window lets an at-least-once queue retry without publishing the same listings twice. Send the success heartbeat after that transaction commits, never when the message is merely dequeued.

The sample treats heartbeat delivery failure differently at the start and the end. A failed start ping is logged because the import can still do useful work. A failed final ping fails the process so the queue can retry; that retry is safe only because the import commit is idempotent. This is a conscious trade-off: monitoring delivery becomes part of completion semantics, which is appropriate when the page depends on that completion record.

OpenTelemetry metrics can add duration, attempted rows, committed rows, and queue age using vendor-neutral instruments. Keep a stable supplier_id only if its cardinality is bounded. Do not put order IDs, listing IDs, or raw error messages in metric labels.

Compare failure coverage, not feature counts

The right choice depends less on dashboard polish than on which failure modes must wake somebody up. These products overlap, but they do not substitute for one another.

Option Strong fit here Boundary that changes the decision
Healthchecks Focused cron and heartbeat monitoring with start, success, and failure signaling Pair it with a separate store for searchable logs, errors, and metrics
Better Stack Uptime and heartbeat monitoring with an incident-management path Broader workflow means more surface area than a heartbeat-only tool
Grafana Cloud Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerting around an OpenTelemetry-oriented stack A missed job still needs an explicit heartbeat or absence rule
Datadog Integrated logs, metrics, traces, synthetic monitoring, and alerting Capability breadth and its ingestion/indexing model deserve review before adoption
Sentry Application error diagnosis, source maps, tracing, and session replay It is not the primary proof that a scheduled backend import ran

Infrai can be the errors, logs, and metrics component when a team wants a self-describing plain REST API whose public discovery response supplies schemas and billing metadata, whose documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and whose single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. For this import worker, that means one credential to rotate and one access boundary to review when another backend capability is added. It does not provide synthetic uptime checks, heartbeat monitoring, native alert delivery, distributed trace querying, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or session replay. Its logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a span-tree UI. For this use case it belongs beside a heartbeat monitor, not in place of one.

For the smallest service, I would begin with Healthchecks plus structured application logs and OpenTelemetry metrics. Move toward Better Stack when the same team wants the alert escalation workflow in that layer. Choose Grafana Cloud or Datadog when cross-signal querying, managed dashboards, and wider infrastructure visibility justify the extra operational surface. Add Sentry when frontend stack traces, source maps, or replay are the diagnostic gap.

This is not a permanent architecture decision. Keep the heartbeat call isolated and the application telemetry in OpenTelemetry-compatible instruments; then changing a backend does not require changing the definition of a successful import.

Plan rollback and migration before the alert

A page needs evidence that separates deploy regression from data and scheduler failures. Record the deployed revision in logs, attach it as a bounded metric attribute, and include it in the import result. Then define the rollback trigger before the incident: for example, a new revision fails across multiple suppliers while the previous revision completed the same scheduled window. The exact trigger must come from the service's own baseline; no honest generic article can manufacture it.

The runbook should preserve the failed payload reference, verify the idempotency key, roll back the worker, and replay the same scheduled window. A rollback that loses the input or changes the deduplication key is not safe. It can turn one missed import into duplicated listings.

Also test the monitor. Disable a staging schedule, verify that the missing heartbeat reaches the intended channel, then restore it and confirm recovery. A green dashboard is weak evidence if nobody has exercised the delivery path.

Account for the cost of a noisy threshold

A short grace period detects a stalled supplier feed quickly, but routine upstream slowness will page the on-call. A long grace period preserves sleep while stale inventory remains visible to buyers. The threshold is therefore a product decision expressed as an SRE setting: how long can this marketplace tolerate stale availability before a human must act?

Review that setting using actual completion durations and queue age, especially after schedule or supplier changes. Keep warning and paging thresholds distinct when the business window permits it. And avoid automatic rollback on one late heartbeat: absence tells you the result is late, not that the newest deployment caused it.

The compact architecture is deliberate: external heartbeat for detection, telemetry for diagnosis, idempotent replay for recovery. More tooling is justified only when it closes a named failure mode. Consider the specific 02:00 supplier run: no start ping points toward scheduling, a start followed by failure points toward execution, and a success with zero committed rows points toward validation. Those three states lead to different actions, so collapsing them into a single “job unhealthy” event makes rollback riskier and the page slower to resolve.

Keep those states separate.

Further reading

  • Healthchecks pinging API: https://healthchecks.io/docs/http_api/
  • Better Stack heartbeat monitoring: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/cron-and-heartbeat-monitor/
  • OpenTelemetry metrics concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • Grafana Cloud documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/
  • Datadog synthetic monitoring documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/synthetics/
  • Datadog pricing and log ingestion model: https://www.datadoghq.com/pricing/
  • Sentry product documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/product/
