title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Installation FAQ: 10 Questions Beginners Ask
description:
Installing GBase Database(GBase 8s) for the first time can raise questions about Linux users, environment variables, character sets, network connections, and instance startup. This FAQ answers 10 common installation questions and explains how to troubleshoot typical issues without making risky configuration changes.

Q1: Can I install GBase Database(GBase 8s) as the root user?

Answer: Yes. In a typical GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation workflow, use root to install the database software and perform system-level configuration, then switch to the dedicated gbasedbt account to initialize and run the database instance.

Typical Workflow

Step 1: Install the software as root.

Run the installation program according to the instructions provided with your GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation package.

Step 2: Prepare the database environment.

Verify that the required directories, ownership, permissions, and environment variables are configured correctly for the gbasedbt account.

Step 3: Switch to the database user.

su - gbasedbt

Step 4: Initialize the instance.

Run the documented instance initialization command under the gbasedbt account. For example, oninit -ivy may be used when initializing a new instance, provided this matches the procedure for your version and configuration.

Important: Do not run instance initialization commands against an existing database as a troubleshooting shortcut. Confirm the instance state and follow the appropriate startup or recovery procedure.

Q2: Why can't I connect when sqlhosts contains localhost?

Answer: The cause depends on the connection protocol, server configuration, and how the hostname resolves.

In GBase Database(GBase 8s), the sqlhosts entry specifies the server name, connection protocol, host, and service or port. For TCP connections, an entry may look like this:

gbase01 onsoctcp 192.168.1.100 9088

This is an illustrative example, not a universal configuration. Replace the server name, address, and port with the values used by your installation.

When troubleshooting, verify that:

  • The client uses the expected server name.
  • The host resolves to the correct address.
  • The configured protocol matches the intended connection method.
  • The server is listening on the configured port.
  • Firewall rules allow the connection when connecting remotely.

localhost does not automatically mean a connection will fail. Check the actual sqlhosts configuration and connection error before changing it.

Q3: Can I change the character set after installation?

Answer: It depends on which character set or locale setting you need to change.

GBase Database(GBase 8s) environments may use settings such as DB_LOCALE and CLIENT_LOCALE to control database and client character handling. These settings serve different purposes, and changing a client environment variable does not convert existing database data.

Before making changes:

  1. Identify the database's current locale and the application's expected encoding.
  2. Check the requirements for the specific database and client version.
  3. Test Chinese text insertion and retrieval in a non-production environment.
  4. Back up important data before performing any migration or conversion.

If an existing database must use a different database locale, creating a new database with the intended configuration and migrating the data may be necessary. Confirm the supported migration procedure first.

Do not assume that changing DB_LOCALE or CLIENT_LOCALE alone will convert an existing database. Choose the locale based on the application's requirements and the character sets supported by the installation.

Q4: Why does oninit produce no obvious output?

Answer: Limited terminal output does not necessarily mean that startup has failed.

Start by checking the instance status:

onstat -

Then inspect the relevant environment variables:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"

If the expected environment is configured, inspect the message log. For example, some installations use a log under the database installation's temporary directory:

tail -50 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"

The actual log location depends on the configuration. Check the configured message-log path if this file does not exist.

Also verify that you are using the correct database account and configuration file. Avoid repeatedly running initialization commands to troubleshoot a startup problem; first determine the instance's current state and read the error messages.

Q5: What is the default port for GBase Database(GBase 8s)?

Answer: Port 9088 is commonly seen in GBase 8s examples, but the actual port depends on the instance configuration.

Check the configured service or port in sqlhosts and the corresponding network configuration. You can inspect listening TCP ports with:

ss -lntp

If you need to change the port, follow the configuration procedure for your version and ensure the client connection settings match the server.

Changing a port may also require updates to firewall rules, monitoring systems, and application connection strings. Do not assume that every installation uses the same port.

Q6: What should I do if dependency installation fails?

Answer: First, identify the missing package or library instead of installing a large, generic list of dependencies.

On a compatible RPM-based Linux system, you can check whether package repositories are available with:

yum repolist

If the installer reports a missing library, check the exact package name and version required by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release.

Common troubleshooting steps include:

  • Confirming that the operating system version is supported.
  • Checking whether the required repositories are enabled.
  • Verifying package names for the current distribution.
  • Checking library architecture and version compatibility.
  • Using approved offline RPM packages when the environment has no internet access.

Do not assume that packages such as Java, development libraries, or terminal libraries are required for every installation. Follow the prerequisites for your specific release.

Q7: Which operating systems does GBase Database(GBase 8s) support?

Answer: Supported operating systems depend on the product release, package, CPU architecture, and vendor certification.

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8s), verify the official compatibility information for your exact version. Check:

  • Linux distribution and release
  • CPU architecture
  • Required system libraries
  • Kernel and runtime prerequisites
  • Supported deployment and maintenance configurations

Do not choose an operating system solely because an older installation guide uses it. A distribution that worked for a previous release may not be supported by a newer package.

For production systems, use a supported configuration and confirm the relevant requirements with the official product documentation or vendor support.

Q8: How can I verify that the installation succeeded?

Answer: Verify the instance state, network listener, and database connectivity separately.

Step 1: Check the instance status.

onstat -

Review the output to determine whether the instance is online and operating as expected.

Step 2: Check the network listener.

ss -lntp

Confirm that the expected port is listening. A listening port alone does not prove that database authentication and SQL queries work.

Step 3: Test a database connection.

Use the supported client for your installation, such as dbaccess where available, and connect to the intended database or a designated test database.

Verify that you can execute a simple query with the expected account and permissions.

A successful installation check should cover all three areas: instance status, network connectivity, and an actual database session.

Q9: Where can I download the GBase Database(GBase 8s) installer?

Answer: Start with the official GBase website:

https://www.gbase.cn/

Check the product documentation and download resources available for your version. Access requirements may vary.

Before downloading, confirm the following:

  • The correct GBase Database(GBase 8s) product and release
  • The target operating system
  • The CPU architecture
  • Installation prerequisites
  • Package integrity and any vendor-provided verification instructions

Keep the installer and its corresponding documentation together so that the installation procedure can be repeated consistently.

Q10: How do I configure automatic startup after installation?

Answer: Use the startup mechanism documented for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release and operating system.

On a system using systemd, database startup may be integrated with a service unit or a vendor-provided startup script. However, the correct service configuration depends on how the instance starts, the required environment variables, and the expected shutdown procedure.

Before enabling automatic startup, verify:

  1. The correct database service account.
  2. The required environment variables and configuration files.
  3. The documented startup and shutdown commands.
  4. Service dependencies and startup ordering.
  5. Behavior after a restart or unexpected shutdown.

Do not copy a generic systemd template into production without validating its ExecStart, ExecStop, process type, and environment settings. An incorrect shutdown command or service definition can interrupt database operations or cause startup failures.

Test automatic startup and shutdown in a non-production environment first, then document the verified procedure for your deployment.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation problems become easier to diagnose when you verify the environment before changing configuration. Check the database account, locale settings, sqlhosts, instance status, and message logs systematically.

For beginners, three habits are especially valuable:

  • Follow the documentation for the exact product version.
  • Verify each installation stage before moving to the next.
  • Diagnose the underlying error before reinstalling or modifying database files.

A careful installation and verification process helps reduce troubleshooting time and makes future deployments more predictable.

title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
description:
arXiv:2610.19373v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.

title: How I Shipped a Java Library to Maven Central, Solo
description:
The dual-write problem shows up wherever a service needs to update its database and notify the outside world as one atomic step. The write succeeds and the publish fails, or the reverse, and two systems that were supposed to agree quietly stop agreeing. The usual fixes are heavyweight: two-phase commit, or a CDC pipeline like Debezium reading the database's transaction log.

I built oncebox to solve it without either. The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, then polled and published separately, safely, even with several instances polling the same table at once. I started on October 11, 2025. A year later it's on Maven Central at v2.0.0, with signed releases and a test suite I'm proud of. This is what went into that.

What it does

oncebox guarantees a database write and a message-broker publish either both happen or neither does, with no two-phase commit and no CDC tooling watching the binlog. You call publish() (or annotate a method with @OutboxPublish) inside your existing @Transactional method. The event is written to an outbox table in that same transaction, and a poller picks it up and publishes it to Kafka or RabbitMQ, retrying with backoff. Anything that keeps failing moves into a dead letter queue, which has its own REST API for inspecting and replaying failed events. On the receiving side there's an inbox that dedupes on the event's id, so a redelivered message doesn't get processed twice. Postgres, MySQL, and Oracle on the write side; Kafka and RabbitMQ as brokers. You pick one of each.

A year, alone

As of today it's 13 Maven modules and 602 Java files, more than half of them tests. Five released versions so far: v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.1.1, v1.1.2 and v2.0.0.

There was no team to split this with, which meant no one to unblock me either. Every dialect quirk, every CI failure, every "why does this pass on Postgres and hang on MySQL" moment was just me and the logs. The upside of solo is that nothing shipped that I didn't fully understand. The downside is that everything took longer than it would have with a second set of eyes to catch the mistake I was too close to see.

Shipping is its own project

The polling logic was one job. Getting it onto Maven Central as something a stranger could <dependency> into their pom.xml and trust was another: GPG signing so releases are verifiable, the Sonatype/Central publishing flow, javadoc.io rendering usable docs instead of a wall of bare method signatures, and Codecov and CodeFactor wired up so the README badges report something real.

None of that touches the outbox logic, but it's what separates a repo I pushed from a library someone can depend on in production. The config is split into oncebox.outbox.* and oncebox.inbox.*, so a service can run only the side it needs. There are ready-made Grafana dashboards and a Postman collection for the DLQ API, because "read the source to figure out the metrics" is not documentation. Each of those was a small decision on its own.

Where the engineering lived

The core trick is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. It lets several instances poll the same outbox table in parallel, each locking a disjoint batch of rows without blocking the others. Event IDs are UUIDv7 instead of random UUIDs, so inserts land at the tail of the primary-key index instead of scattering writes across it under load. Polling is adaptive: exponential backoff toward a max delay while the table is empty, back to a fast poll as soon as events show up, so idle instances don't hammer the database. Event types are polled independently, in parallel, on a library-managed thread pool.

Supporting three databases with one concurrency primitive turned out to be a project of its own. Postgres and Oracle behave. On MySQL, InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ makes that same locking clause take gap locks, so concurrent pollers deadlock instead of grabbing disjoint batches, unless the outbox datasource runs at READ COMMITTED. That one deserves its own post. Oracle diverges differently: it can't express FETCH FIRST ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED the way Postgres batches it in a CTE, so the batch size is capped at the JDBC level with PreparedStatement#setMaxRows. One concurrency primitive, three implementations.

The failure paths got the same attention as the happy path. If an instance dies mid-publish, its events are left IN_PROCESS. A separate recovery worker sweeps those back to PENDING without touching the retry count, so a crash doesn't cost an event its remaining retries. Anything that exhausts its retries moves to the dead letter queue in one transaction (lock the batch, insert into the DLQ table, delete from the outbox, commit) instead of two separate writes that could disagree if the process dies in between.

v2.0.0 is a breaking release. The structure is now named by mechanism, outbox and inbox, rather than by the role of the service. Every timestamp is set by the database clock instead of the JVM, so instances in different time zones agree on it. And each captured batch now carries a lock token, which fences it against a poller that no longer owns it.

Why I went overboard on tests

With no one reviewing my PRs, tests were the only thing between me and shipping a race condition to users I'd never meet. 346 of the 602 Java files in the repo are test sources, split across tiers that each catch a different kind of failure. Unit tests cover logic, integration tests run against real databases, and a concurrent tier hammers the SKIP LOCKED polling path with multiple real threads to catch races a mock never would. A classpath-isolation job checks the library still works when only one database dialect's jar is on the classpath, catching accidental hard dependencies between modules that should be independent. End-to-end tests run across a 3-database × 2-broker matrix, and Gatling load tests run against dockerized infrastructure on every release tag.

For a library one person maintains, that's a lot of test infrastructure. It's also the only way I could say with any confidence that a release won't deadlock someone's production database.

Try it

oncebox is Apache 2.0, on Maven Central as io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-*, and the source is at github.com/dmitriy-iliyov/oncebox. If you have a dual-write problem and don't want to stand up a CDC pipeline to solve it, I'd like to know whether this works for you. Issues, PRs, and stars all help when it's one person deciding whether to keep going.

Written 2026-10-15, against oncebox v2.0.0. Repo stats are current as of this post; check the README for anything that has moved since.

title: Diagnosing Low-Confidence Patient Profiles via Localized Harmful Covariate Shift Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.19178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Before deploying clinical prediction models, their reliability must be assessed to ensure safe use. Errors may arise from distribution shifts between training and deployment or from heterogeneous performance where the model systematically underperforms for certain patient subgroups. Yet most post-hoc diagnostic methods evaluate reliability only at the population level, checking whether the deployment data resemble the training data and whether the model performs well on average, without accounting for heterogeneity that may cause some patients to be disproportionately affected. We propose a unified diagnostic pipeline that combines both perspectives. MED3pa first discovers interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, and Detectron is then applied within each profile to test whether its degradation is associated with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in MIMIC-IV, we find that shift detectability itself is informative. An injected age shift, undetectable at the population level, was nonetheless localized to specific degraded profiles, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and therefore offered little guidance for identifying the most affected patients.

title: Cheap Webhook Task Processing Explained — Node.js SaaS Rate-Limit Retry Backoff
description:
Short answer: for a nightly fintech reconciliation, put the delayed webhook work in a queue and make the worker idempotent. A cron trigger should enqueue a bounded batch, while retries and rate limits live at the worker boundary. That shape is cheap to reason about because the provider's rate limit cannot turn one long cron invocation into a hidden scheduler.

The bill is mostly downstream work, not the timer. Every payment lookup, webhook delivery attempt, and retained message costs attention; a cron job that fires 10,000 calls at once creates a burst of throttled retries. Controlling worker concurrency changes that dominant term. It also gives the team one place to record an idempotency key such as reconcile:2026-09-10:merchant-42:payment-981, so a duplicate delivery cannot post the same ledger adjustment twice.

Bursts hurt.

Suppose the provider allows 20 requests per second and the nightly window contains 2,400 merchants. A cron loop that launches every request immediately will spend its first minutes collecting 429 responses, then create a retry wave that is larger than the original wave. With a queue, the trigger publishes the merchant windows quickly, while workers take 20 tokens per second and attach the same reconciliation key to every attempt. Merchant 17 may fail once and return after a 30-second delay; merchant 18 may succeed on its first call. Those paths do not interfere. The audit row records the provider cursor, attempt count, and final comparison before the message is acknowledged. If the worker dies after the provider accepts the adjustment but before ack, the next delivery still carries the same key, so the database uniqueness check and provider idempotency guard converge on one ledger result. This is the operational reason I care about queue shape more than the timer brand.

There is a retention trade-off. An acknowledged queue message is deleted, and retention tops out at 30 days. I keep the reconciliation result and provider response hash in an audit table before acking; I do not pretend the queue is a replay log. When an auditor asks for a six-month trail, the table is what we query, and the queue's short retention is the deliberate cost of keeping the operational path small.

That boundary is where Infrai can fit: its queue is reachable through a plain REST API, so the nightly trigger and a Python or Node.js worker can share one HTTP contract without an SDK. I would test it for the low-complexity path below, not for workflow orchestration.

Two viable shapes for delayed webhook work

The simple shape is cron plus queue: a nightly trigger finds the reconciliation window, publishes one message per merchant or bounded page, and workers consume at a controlled concurrency. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work belongs behind the trigger. The queue's standard delivery is at-least-once; the invariant is that the consumer can safely run the same message twice.

The second shape is a durable workflow engine. Temporal or Airflow can model a multi-step reconciliation with joins, compensations, and a long-lived history. That is the right invariant when a payment run is a graph whose later steps depend on several earlier results. It is more machinery than a single provider sweep needs.

For a small SaaS, I would choose the first shape when the job is “fetch, compare, emit, retry.” Its broader backend surface can also keep storage and scheduling behind the same key, which removes a little integration bookkeeping without changing the queue invariant.

How should Node.js teams model rate limits, retries, and backoff?

Treat a rate limit as state, not as a sleep sprinkled through a cron loop. A worker should reserve a provider token, perform one idempotent operation, and requeue a failed attempt with a bounded delay. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents every merchant from retrying on the same second; Retry-After wins when the provider sends it.

Here is the core decision in Python, kept independent of a vendor client so the behavior is testable:

import requests
import json
import os
import random
import time


def retry_delay(attempt, retry_after=None):
    if retry_after is not None:
        return min(float(retry_after), 604800)
    cap = min(2 ** attempt, 3600)
    return random.uniform(cap / 2, cap)


def reconciliation_key(merchant_id, window_start):
    return f"reconcile:{merchant_id}:{window_start}"


def publish_reconciliation(queue, payload, delay_seconds=0):
    body = {"queue": queue, "message": payload,
            "delay_seconds": delay_seconds}
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
               "Idempotency-Key": payload["reconciliation_key"]}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            "POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            json=body, headers=headers, timeout=20)
        if response.status_code < 400:
            return response.json()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        time.sleep(retry_delay(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After")))
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after five attempts")

Keep delayed messages at or below 604800 seconds, and attach the reconciliation key to the payload. If a write is retried, send the same client id or idempotency key. The platform convention uses an Idempotency-Key header for operations that support it; your application still owns the provider-side idempotency check.

There is no native debounce or throttle primitive, and FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes. That is a capability boundary, not a failure mode: use a database uniqueness constraint for a longer business window. For one-to-many delivery, publish to separate queues because there is no built-in topic fan-out.

What do queue, cron, and workflow products actually trade?

Option Best fit Retry and rate-limit shape Retention or orchestration caveat
Queue plus cron trigger Delayed webhook batches and ordinary SaaS reconciliation Worker concurrency, requeue, exponential backoff At-least-once; finite retention; no joins
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers Short, publicly reachable HTTP trigger You build the queue and retry state A single invocation is capped at 900 seconds
Inngest Event-driven functions with managed retry history Function-level retry and step state More orchestration semantics than a basic queue
Temporal Long-running, branching reconciliation workflows Durable workflow timers and activities Operational and modeling overhead is substantial

The comparison is not a price contest. Cloudflare is compelling when the timer and edge execution are already your platform. Inngest is a better choice when each reconciliation has explicit steps and you want their history attached to the run. Stick with Temporal when you need DAG-like joins or compensation logic. A queue is not suitable when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement; persist an event log or select a stream system instead.

The small implementation I would ship

Create one queue per independent consumer, publish a bounded batch from the nightly trigger, then let workers claim and ack messages only after the audit row is durable. A failed provider call becomes a delayed republish, with the attempt count and next-attempt timestamp in the message. Keep payloads below 256 KB and delayed work within seven days; a later reconciliation window can be scheduled by the next cron run.

I initially thought a FIFO queue would solve duplicate payments by itself. It does not: the five-minute deduplication window is shorter than a nightly business key, and standard queues can deliver at least once. The invariant belongs in the database and in the provider request, where the same reconciliation_key produces the same result.

One operational wrinkle matters in fintech: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and run output is limited to the first 4 KB. Write a run record as soon as the trigger starts, then store detailed diagnostics in your audit system. Your mileage may vary around provider-specific quotas; confirm the live quota contract before choosing worker concurrency.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want this queue-centered shape and a plain HTTP integration, especially when the same service already needs several backend capabilities under one key. It is not the right choice for a workflow graph, Kafka-style replay, private push endpoints, or native fan-out. In those cases, use Temporal, Airflow, a stream platform, or a specialist queue that states those guarantees directly.

If this boundary matches your reconciliation job, the queue capability details and runnable examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
description:
arXiv:2610.19520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
description:
arXiv:2610.19028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.19190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

title: Verify authentication recovery before treating Configuration as the root cause
description:
A return URL containing error=Configuration suggests a configuration mistake. Yet the inspected Auth.js version also produces that destination when a PKCE cookie is missing. The user-facing classification does not identify the cause by itself.

This investigation read SquadNote's recovery implementation and reran tests against its actual Auth.js dependency. It examines rejection, retry navigation, and diagnostic evidence before drawing a causal conclusion.

The source is circle-hub at d116e8a, checked on September 11, 2026. No production authentication logs or user histories were collected. This is an account of recovery code and rerun verification, not proof of a production incident's cause or resolution.

Distinguish the internal error from Configuration

Auth.js's InvalidCheck reference covers PKCE, state, or nonce checks that cannot be performed. Unavailable cookies can produce it, as can configuration issues.

The repository regression test resolves @auth/core through the application's next-auth dependency. It does not substitute a separately installed latest release.

A synthetic callback without its PKCE cookie produced:

Observation Result
HTTP status 302
Redirect destination /sign-in/error?error=Configuration
Internal type passed to the logger InvalidCheck

The fixture deliberately omitted the cookie, so its cause is known. Seeing the same internal type in production would still require investigating why the cookie did not arrive. Expiration, another initiation, and browser behavior cannot be distinguished from that display alone.

First restore a path from failure to a fresh start

The recovery design record and history show the recovery screen in 061a5f2, repeated-submission protection in 2b88c31, and diagnostics in 7f180ad.

The recovery screen presents sign-in and public help without depending on auth() or the database. Displaying an authentication failure does not require successfully repeating the same authentication dependency.

Return destinations are restricted to safe paths on the same origin. Tests preserve invitation-page returns while rejecting external redirection and authentication-page loops. The original callback URL is not reused unconditionally.

Two new initiation requests sent to the actual Auth.js implementation produced different PKCE challenges, S256, and fresh PKCE cookies. However, the initiation fixture uses the internal CSRF-skip option. It does not verify browser CSRF protection or a round trip through the OAuth provider, and no production setting was changed to disable CSRF checks.

Reject a second start before React rerenders

Disabling a button visually can leave a window before React rerenders in which another button can be pressed. The implementation uses a synchronous guard shared by Google and Apple initiation on the same screen:

export function createSubmissionGuard() {
  let submitting = false;
  return {
    acquire() {
      if (submitting) return false;
      submitting = true;
      return true;
    },
    reset() { submitting = false; },
  };
}

Tests against the actual guard reject immediate reacquisition, allow acquisition after the reset used for failure or history restoration, and keep separate instances independent.

Its scope is repeated submission from one screen. It does not serialize initiation across tabs or browsers, nor remove every possible cause of missing cookies.

Correlate how far the flow progressed

The diagnostics investigate initiation and callback boundaries without storing authentication values. The principal events mean:

Event What it establishes
auth.sign_in_started A start request occurred
auth.authorization_redirect Initiation generated a destination
auth.callback_received A callback arrived
auth.sign_in_succeeded Auth.js emitted its signIn event
auth.server_error Failure and diagnostic information were recorded

Initiation and destination generation do not mean authentication succeeded. In particular, the server action's cookiesAfterStart observes the cookie jar at that time. Existing cookies can be present, so presence alone does not establish fresh issuance.

requestId identifies a failing request; attemptId supports correlation with initiation. The latter marker is client-originated diagnostic information and does not authorize authentication. It represents the browser's most recent initiation, so it does not prove the same OAuth transaction across multiple tabs.

Absent, expired, or provider-mismatched markers can prevent correlation. Record why correlation failed instead of rephrasing that as “no initiation happened.”

Add diagnostics without weakening authentication checks

Diagnostic tests verify that synthetic sensitive values, including cookie values, authorization codes, tokens, raw User-Agent strings, and IPs, do not appear in logs. Cookie observations retain only presence for specific names, and paths are restricted to authentication routes.

Tests also check isolation between concurrent requests, preservation of authentication responses when diagnostics or notifications fail, and preservation of the original Auth.js response cookies. The change does not obtain successful logins by relaxing PKCE, state, or nonce requirements.

Alert suppression operates within a Worker instance; it is not a delivery guarantee across all distributed instances. The diagnostic cookie is not a session replacement either. Neither mechanism belongs in the decision that authentication has succeeded.

The 47 tests and the remaining environment checks

The run passed 47 tests across 8 files copied from the fixed commit. It used Node.js v24.15.0, Vitest 4.1.4, Next.js 15.5.15, next-auth 5.0.0-beta.25, and its Auth.js core dependency 0.37.2. The runner and results are preserved.

Some tests invoke the actual Auth.js implementation; others mock route or notification dependencies. Real Google or Apple accounts, Safari or embedded browsers, multiple tabs, and manual browser-cookie deletion were not tested in this run. Historical UI verification documented in the repository is also separate from these rerun results.

Verify the failure classification, fresh initiation, safe return destination, same-screen repeat protection, and the limits of log correlation in order. While the cause remains uncertain, record the conditions for retry and the questions requiring further investigation.

title: A Unified Response Framework for Questions and Tutoring Dialogues
description:
arXiv:2610.19532v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing student models in educational applications largely focus on student responses to questions. However, as tutoring becomes more accessible at large scale, it is important to analyze dialogues between tutors and students, which may reveal fine-grained evidence on student knowledge. In this work, we propose a unified framework that models both student responses to questions and tutor-posed subtasks during dialogues on a shared item response theory (IRT) scale. We first identify mathematical subtasks in tutoring dialogues, rewrite them into self-contained questions, and identify the correctness of student responses to these subtasks. We then develop an IRT framework that estimates question/subtask difficulty from text, tracks students' evolving abilities across question-answering and dialogue interactions, and a novel method to leverages tutor moves between consecutive subtasks to regularize their difficulty values. We evaluate our framework on two real-world math education datasets containing both human- and AI-tutored dialogues. Results show that our framework outperforms strong baselines on both question difficulty prediction and response correctness prediction.

title: Filter in ASP.NET Core Web API
description:
Filters in ASP.NET Core Web API
What is a filter?
A filter is code that runs at a specific stage while ASP.NET Core processes a controller action. It can run before or after the action, check access, handle certain exceptions, or inspect the result. This helps you apply common behavior without repeating it in every action. learn.microsoft.com

Types of filters
Filter What it does Main methods
Authorization Checks whether the request can access the action. OnAuthorization
Resource Runs around most of the controller filter pipeline. OnResourceExecuting, OnResourceExecuted
Action Runs around the controller action. OnActionExecuting, OnActionExecuted
Exception Handles certain unhandled exceptions. OnException
Result Runs around execution of the action result. OnResultExecuting, OnResultExecuted
These are the five main controller filter types. ASP.NET Core also has endpoint filters, which run around endpoint handlers and can be used with API endpoints; they are separate from the five-stage controller sequence below. learn.microsoft.com

Order of execution
For a request that is authorized and completes successfully:

HTTP request
↓
Authorization filter
↓
OnResourceExecuting
↓
Model binding
↓
OnActionExecuting
↓
Controller action
↓
OnActionExecuted
↓
OnResultExecuting
↓
Result execution (for example, writing JSON)
↓
OnResultExecuted
↓
OnResourceExecuted
↓
HTTP response
The “Executing” methods run on the way toward the action or result. The “Executed” methods run as those stages finish. Model binding happens after the resource filter starts and before the action filter starts. learn.microsoft.com

Where does the exception filter fit? It is not a regular step in every request. It runs only when an applicable unhandled exception occurs; it does not catch exceptions from every stage of the pipeline. Also, a filter can stop the request early, so the full sequence above will not always run. learn.microsoft.com

Key point for interviews: Authorization → Resource → Action → Result, with the “after” methods running as their surrounding stages finish. Exception filtering is conditional.

title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
description:
arXiv:2610.19189v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.

title: Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.

title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks

title: Four pay-per-result YouTube and Google News scrapers on Apify (no API key)
description:
I built four small data tools on Apify that return YouTube and Google News data as JSON, without an API key or quota. You pay per result delivered, and nothing else. Here is what each one does and how to call it from Python.

The four tools

  1. YouTube Transcript Extractor - timestamped transcripts for videos, playlists and channels, with optional chunks sized for RAG. Videos without captions are reported and not charged. $0.004 per transcript. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch
  2. YouTube Comments Scraper - comments (and optionally replies) with author, likes, reply count and publish time. $0.0015 per comment. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-comments-scraper-fast
  3. YouTube Search Scraper - search results with title, channel, views, duration, publish date and thumbnail, with upload date and duration filters. $0.002 per video. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-search-video-scraper
  4. Google News Scraper with Full Article Text - news results for a keyword, language and country, with the full article text pulled from the publisher page when it can be extracted. $0.003 per headline, $0.01 per article with text. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/google-news-scraper-article-text

YouTube blocks datacenter IPs, so the YouTube tools run through a residential proxy by default. That cost is already in the per-result price.

Calling one from Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("xargaar_tools/youtube-comments-scraper-fast").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"],
    "maxCommentsPerVideo": 50,
})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item["likes"], item["author"], item["text"][:80])

Swap the Actor name and input to use the others. Every Actor has an input form in the Apify console if you prefer clicking to coding.

What I tested

I ran each Actor on Apify's platform before publishing. Transcripts: 11 of 12 test videos returned a transcript, a private video was reported cleanly instead of failing the run. Comments: 45 comments from one video, replies mode, and a channel URL across two videos. Search: two queries returned 80 videos, and the date and duration filters changed the results as expected. News: 10 results, 6 with full article text.

Known limits

  • Comments come back in YouTube's top-comments order. A "newest first" sort is not supported yet.
  • The search tool applies one filter per query (upload date or duration).
  • News articles behind paywalls or bot protection return the headline data without full text.

If something breaks or you need a field that is missing, open an issue on the Actor page and I will look at it.

Xargaar Tools builds small, pay-per-use data tools.

title: LAMP: 3D Source-Aware Lighting Estimation at Multiple Points
description:
arXiv:2610.19266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing illumination estimation methods primarily recover lighting distributions for rendering, but typically leave the contributions of individual physical light sources at specific scene locations implicit. We address this gap by leveraging the scene understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to connect local illumination with its physical sources. We introduce LAMP, a framework for point-conditioned, source-aware illumination reasoning from a single RGB image with marked query points. LAMP constructs a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks contributing sources for each query, and predicts their 3D query-to-source directions. We supervise these relationships using procedurally controlled indoor scenes, reusing independently rendered source responses to derive contribution targets across lighting configurations and obtaining exact directions from source and query positions. On the Infinigen test set, fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B increases dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m from 0% to 70.6%, with 94.5% of directions within 12.5 degrees of ground truth among correctly localized sources. Combined with a lightweight network predicting dense RGB irradiance, LAMP achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior lighting-estimation methods while additionally localizing individual physical sources in 3D and explicitly attributing local illumination to them.

title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.

title: Qlik QSSA Exam: Why Installation and Configuration Add Up to the 62% Pass Mark
description:
The Qlik Sense System Administrator (QSSA) exam has 50 questions, a 90-minute limit and a 62% passing score. Its two biggest domains, Installation at 30% and Configuration at 32%, add up to exactly 62%, so the pass line sits right where those two domains end.

That one fact shapes how you should study. This post works through what it means in questions, minutes and attempts, using the figures on Qlik's QSSA exam details page, checked on 15 October 2026.

What does the Qlik QSSA exam cover?

The exam tests whether you can plan, install, run and fix a client-managed Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows site. Qlik splits it into four domains:

  • Installation (30%): planning the infrastructure, installing Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows with Shared Persistence, and choosing between single-node and multi-node setups.
  • Configuration (32%): streams and apps, automated tasks with triggers, load balancing rules, Active Directory connections with user and group sync, and node settings.
  • Security and Licensing (16%): the Qlik Sense licensing model, user license access, and security rules.
  • Monitor, Troubleshoot, and Maintenance (22%): app issues, system issues and server maintenance.

Qlik states plainly that the exam covers only the client-managed edition. Nothing on it tests Qlik Cloud administration.

How many questions does each domain carry?

Qlik publishes percentages, not question counts. Applying the weights to 50 questions gives a rough split (our arithmetic, not Qlik's):

  • Installation: about 15 questions
  • Configuration: about 16 questions
  • Security and Licensing: about 8 questions
  • Monitor, Troubleshoot, and Maintenance: about 11 questions

At 62%, a pass means about 31 correct answers. Installation and Configuration together come to about 31 questions as well. That is the coincidence in the title, and it is worth reading carefully.

Can you pass on Installation and Configuration alone?

In theory, yes, but only with a perfect score on both, and nobody should plan for that. The real lesson runs the other way: the 19 questions in the two smaller domains are your safety margin.

At the published mark you can get about 19 questions wrong and still pass. If you treat Security and Licensing as a weak spot and miss most of its 8 questions, you have spent a big part of that margin before the clock reaches the halfway point. Qlik also says the passing score "is adjusted to maintain a consistent standard", so treat 31 as a guide and not a promise.

A sensible target is to aim for strong scores in all four domains, with Configuration first, because it is the largest single block.

How much time do you get per question?

Ninety minutes across 50 questions is 1.8 minutes, or 108 seconds, per question. That is enough time to read a scenario twice, but not enough to reason out a load balancing rule or a security rule from first principles.

A practical pace plan:

  1. Take a first pass at about 90 seconds per question and flag anything that needs more thought.
  2. Bank the spare time, roughly 15 minutes, for flagged items.
  3. Leave nothing blank. An unanswered question can only count as wrong, while a guess might be right.

What experience does Qlik expect before you sit it?

Qlik recommends at least six months as an administrator of a Microsoft Windows Server environment. It also lists hands-on work in the Qlik Management Console (QMC): governance, library maintenance, user and app security, server policies, rules and streams.

The less obvious part is the tool list. Qlik names Event Viewer, the Services Console, the DCOM Console and the Windows Registry, plus NSLookUp, Telnet, Ping, NetStat, Fiddler and browser developer tools. Those tools point to the troubleshooting questions in the 22% domain. If you have never traced a proxy or certificate problem with them, that is the gap to close.

For a different view of the exam's scope, the Tier 1 article on why the QSSA leaves Qlik Cloud out explains which skills the client-managed focus rules in and out.

Which installation steps should you know by heart?

The Installation domain asks about single-node and multi-node deployments. For multi-node sites, Qlik's help sets out a fixed order:

  1. Check the pre-installation items: system requirements, supported browsers, ports and licenses.
  2. Prepare the Windows server.
  3. Install Qlik Sense on the central node.
  4. Configure PostgreSQL multi-node connections on the central node.
  5. License Qlik Sense on the central node.
  6. Allocate access to users.
  7. Install the rim nodes.
  8. Connect and configure the rim nodes in the QMC.
  9. Optionally, set a failover candidate for the central node.

Questions often hinge on what has to happen before what. You can walk the same sequence step by step in Qlik's guide to installing Qlik Sense in a multi-node site, which was last updated in October 2026.

What happens if you fail the QSSA exam?

Qlik allows three attempts per exam, and each attempt needs a full payment or a new voucher. The waiting periods are fixed:

  • After a first fail, you wait 48 hours.
  • After a second fail, you wait 14 calendar days before the third and final attempt.
  • After a third fail, you cannot register for that exam again until Qlik releases a new version.

So the quickest path through all three attempts runs from day 0 to day 2 to day 16. Qlik enforces the waits and will not let you book an earlier date. All of this is set out in Qlik Learning's certificates and badges FAQ.

The third-attempt block is the rule to respect. Two fails should send you back to the training and practice work, not straight to a rebooking.

How long does the QSSA certification last?

Your result appears as soon as you finish, and Qlik sends it by email too. After a pass, Credly sends a badge invitation within 24 to 48 hours. Qlik no longer issues certificates; the badge in Credly and in your Qlik Learning history is the record.

The certification is valid for two years from the date you pass. Credly emails you six months before it expires, which is month 18. To keep it, you register for the current exam before the expiry date and pass it. Qlik usually updates its exams every three years, sooner after a major product change.

How should you prepare in the time you have?

A plan that follows the weights:

  1. Build a lab first. A single-node Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows install teaches more of the 30% Installation domain than any reading.
  2. Spend the most hours on Configuration. Create streams, tasks with triggers, load balancing rules and an AD user sync until you can do them without notes.
  3. Learn security rules and license allocation properly. Eight questions is a small block, but missing most of it eats your margin.
  4. Practise troubleshooting with the Windows tools Qlik lists. Break your lab on purpose and fix it.
  5. Check yourself under time pressure. The QSSA practice exam on AnalyticsExam runs timed sets so you can test the 108-second pace.

If you already run a Qlik Sense Enterprise site at work, you can shorten step 1, but keep the other four.

Before your first study session, the three-minute AnalyticsExam video on how to study for the QSSA exam gives a short overview of the preparation steps. It was recorded for the QSSA2022 version, so check the domain weights above against it.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. How many questions are on the Qlik QSSA exam?

The exam has 50 questions and a 90-minute time limit. Qlik notes that the number and difficulty of questions may change when the exam is updated.

2. What score do you need to pass QSSA?

Qlik lists a passing score of 62%, which works out to about 31 correct answers out of 50. Qlik adjusts the passing score to keep a consistent standard, so treat 31 as a guide.

3. Does the QSSA exam cover Qlik Cloud?

No. The exam covers only the client-managed edition of Qlik Sense, meaning Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows. It does not test Qlik Cloud administration.

4. How many times can you retake the QSSA exam?

You get three attempts, each paid in full or with a new voucher. You wait 48 hours after the first fail and 14 calendar days after the second. After a third fail, you must wait for a new version of the exam.

5. How long is the Qlik Sense System Administrator certification valid?

It is valid for two years from the date you pass. Credly sends a reminder six months before expiry, and you renew by passing the current exam before that date.

title: Your line of business web does not need a framework
description:
A new business app starts with a question: React, Vue or Angular? The question that rarely gets asked is whether it needs one at all. For a page that lists orders, edits a customer and shows a few figures, the browser now does most of what we once picked a framework for.

This article walks through what frameworks were for, what the browser has taken over, and what is still missing. Then it builds a working order page in one HTML file, with no framework and no build step.

The habit

You start a project. You pick a framework, then a component library for that framework, then a state library, a router and a form library that fit both. By the time the first page shows a table, you have five dependencies that must agree with each other, and each will ship a breaking major version on its own schedule.

None of that is wrong. A framework gives a team one way to do things, and every developer you hire has used one. But it is a choice made by reflex, and the reasons it was the right reflex ten years ago have mostly gone away.

What a framework was for

Frameworks filled holes in the browser. Look at what those holes were, and what fills them today:

You needed a framework for The browser has
Your own reusable tags Custom elements
Knowing when a component appears and disappears connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback
Modals that trap focus and close on Escape <dialog>
Dropdowns that float above everything The Popover API
Form validation Constraint validation: required, min, pattern, :invalid
Numbers, amounts and dates per locale Intl
Code split into modules ES modules, loaded straight from a URL

The big remaining selling point is reactivity: change a variable and the page follows. That solves a real problem in an app where a hundred things depend on each other. A business page is rarely that app. It shows records, lets you change one, and shows the result. The places that change are few, and you know which they are.

What is still missing

The browser has no table that sorts and pages. No tabs, no tree view, no chart. That is what a business page is made of, and it is the real reason teams reach for a framework and its component library.

So that is the gap I filled with @relax.js/components: tables, tree views, tabs, menus, dialogs, charts and meters for business pages. Not a framework. Each one is a plain custom element, and where the browser already has the part, it uses it: the table is a native <table>, menus use the Popover API, the dialog is a <dialog>.

A page with no framework

Save this as a file and open it. No npm install, no bundler:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Orders</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/dist/theme.css">
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui; background: var(--surface-bg); color: var(--text-primary); }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <r-stat-tile label="Orders"></r-stat-tile>
    <button id="add">New order</button>

    <r-table page-size="10">
        <r-column field="number" sortable>Order</r-column>
        <r-column field="customer" sortable>Customer</r-column>
        <r-column field="total" sortable>Total</r-column>
    </r-table>

    <r-dialog id="new-order" heading="New order">
        <template>
            <form method="dialog">
                <label>Customer <input name="customer" required></label>
                <label>Total <input name="total" type="number" min="1" required></label>
                <button value="save">Save</button>
            </form>
        </template>
    </r-dialog>

    <script type="module">
        import 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/+esm';

        const orders = [
            { number: 'SO-10001', customer: 'Fjällbo AB', total: 12400 },
            { number: 'SO-10002', customer: 'Kvarnen HB', total: 860 },
            { number: 'SO-10003', customer: 'Ekdahl & Son', total: 3150 },
        ];

        const table = document.querySelector('r-table');
        const tile = document.querySelector('r-stat-tile');
        const dialog = document.querySelector('#new-order');

        function show() {
            table.rows = orders;
            tile.setAttribute('value', orders.length);
        }

        dialog.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
            const form = new FormData(event.target);
            orders.push({
                number: `SO-${10001 + orders.length}`,
                customer: form.get('customer'),
                total: Number(form.get('total')),
            });
        });

        document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', async () => {
            if (await dialog.open() === 'save') {
                show();
            }
        });

        show();
    </script>
</body>
</html>

You get a figure, a sortable table with grouped numbers and a pager, and a modal form. The form refuses to save without a customer or with a total below 1. That is the browser, not my code and not a library.

Now count what is not there. No state store. No virtual DOM. No compiler. No component tree to keep in your head. The data is an array, and show() is the whole rendering strategy: when the data changed, you tell the page.

"But who keeps the page in sync?"

You do, and that is the point. A framework re-renders when it decides something changed. When it gets it wrong, you debug the framework: why did this render twice, why did that not render at all.

Each component here redraws when you change its attributes, its properties or its content, and at no other time. There is no base class, no reactivity and no hidden scheduler. The lifecycle is the one on MDN. If the table shows old rows, you forgot to set rows, and a breakpoint on that line tells you so.

One rule trips everybody up: records go in a property, not an attribute. Attributes are strings, and a list in an attribute is a JSON string the component would have to parse and keep in sync with the property. So rows, columns and chart data are set from code, and scalars like page-size are attributes.

"But it needs Relax.js core"

Yes. The components have one peer dependency, @relax.js/core, and the jsDelivr link pulls it in for you.

That does not sneak a framework back in. A framework calls your code: it owns the lifecycle, the rendering and the state. Core is a set of libraries your code calls, and you use only the parts you need: typed form reading, routing, dependency injection, translations. The components themselves call it for four things:

  • translating the words they show (No data, Next)
  • reporting errors through one channel
  • formatting values
  • letting the router open a dialog, and only for a dialog you give a name

When the page above grows into an app with several pages, those same libraries give you a router and typed forms. You add them when you need them, not on day one.

Already on React or Vue?

Then the components still work, because every framework renders HTML and a custom element is HTML. The property rule above is all you need to know. React 19 assigns rows={orders} as a property. In Vue you write :rows.prop="orders" and tell the compiler that r- tags are not Vue components. Events are plain DOM events.

It is a way out as much as a way in. The table you use in React today is the same table in the page that replaces it.

The takeaway

Frameworks were the right answer to a browser that could not do much. The browser caught up. For a page that lists, edits and summarizes records, what is missing is the business components, not a framework. Add those as plain custom elements, write the updates yourself, and you have nothing left to migrate away from.

Next in the series: server-side paging and sorting, with one async function.

title: Workflow SDK now supports inflight cancellation
description:
The Workflow SDK 5 beta now supports the standard AbortController and AbortSignal APIs across workflow and step boundaries.

Create a controller inside a workflow, pass its signal into one or more steps, and cancel in-flight operations using the same API fetch already uses.

That signal stays durable across suspensions and deterministic replay. When a step is running, it sees the cancellation, even when it's in a separate function invocation. Cancellation is also cooperative; steps have to inspect the signal or pass it to an API that supports AbortSignal.

Use it to stop a slow step when a durable timeout wins a race, cancel the remaining requests after the first successful response, thread one signal through a multi-step pipeline, or cancel parallel work when an external condition changes.

Try it with workflow@beta and read the cancellation documentation to learn more. Browser Workflow SDK resources in the Vercel Knowledge Base.
