title: Go 1.26 Lets new() Take an Expression. Delete Your Pointer Helpers
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

In April 2021, Rob Pike opened golang/go#45624, "spec: expression to create pointer to simple types", as an alternative to an older proposal, #9097. Getting a pointer to a struct was always easy: &S{a: 3}. Getting a pointer to the number 3 was not. When Alan Donovan closed the issue in October 2025, he signed off with a joke: "All done, in only eleven years since #9097. ;-)"

That fix shipped in Go 1.26, released on February 10, 2026. The built-in new now accepts an expression, not only a type. new(42) compiles. So does new(time.Now()).

If your codebase has a ptr[T], a StringPtr, an IntPtr, or a utils/pointer.go file that every package imports, you can likely delete most of it now, and go fix will do the bulk of the work.

Why every Go codebase grew a pointer helper

Go has no Optional[T]. When a field can be absent, and absent has to mean something different from zero, the usual answer is a pointer. The Go 1.26 release notes call this out directly: the feature is "particularly useful when working with serialization packages such as encoding/json or protocol buffers that use a pointer to represent an optional value."

The trouble was always the write side. You cannot take the address of a constant or of a function call's result, so &42 and &time.Now() do not compile. Teams kept writing the same one-line escape hatch, and the ecosystem shipped its own copies: proto.String and proto.Int64 in protobuf-go, ptr.To in k8s.io/utils, ToPtr in samber/lo. The protobuf ones are a single line each: func String(v string) *string { return &v }.

Here is the pattern you probably have today. A settings payload where "retries not set" and "retries set to 0" are different instructions:

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func ptr[T any](v T) *T { return &v }

type Settings struct {
    Theme   *string    `json:"theme,omitempty"`
    Retries *int       `json:"retries,omitempty"`
    Beta    *bool      `json:"beta,omitempty"`
    Updated *time.Time `json:"updated,omitempty"`
}

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   ptr("dark"),
        Retries: ptr(0),
        Beta:    ptr(false),
        Updated: ptr(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

Retries: ptr(0) is the whole reason the pointer exists. omitempty drops a nil pointer, but a non-nil pointer to 0 is kept, so the JSON says "retries":0 instead of saying nothing.


The helper was always a detour: take a value, park it in a variable, hand back the address.

The same code on Go 1.26

Delete ptr and call the built-in:

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   new("dark"),
        Retries: new(0),
        Beta:    new(false),
        Updated: new(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

The behavior is the same as the helper. The spec's Allocation section now reads: "If the argument is an expression x, then new(x) allocates a variable of the type of x initialized to the value of x." new(int) still gives you a pointer to 0. new(123) gives you a pointer to 123. Both are *int.

For this to compile, the module (or the file, through a build constraint) has to declare Go 1.26 or later. If your go.mod still says go 1.25, bump it:

go mod edit -go=1.26

That raises the minimum Go version for anyone who imports your module. For an application that is usually fine. For a library, it is a decision, and it is the first case where the old helper wins (more on that below). Go 1.27 has been out since August 19, 2026 and its release notes make no change to new(expr), so either current release works.

The sweep: go fix -newexpr

You do not have to hunt the call sites by hand. Go 1.26 also rewrote go fix into the home of Go's modernizers, built on the same analysis framework as go vet. One of them, newexpr, targets exactly this pattern. Alan Donovan's post on the Go blog shows the command to run only that fixer:

# preview first
go fix -diff -newexpr ./...

# apply
go fix -newexpr ./...

# read the analyzer's own docs
go tool fix help newexpr

What it does, according to the analyzer docs and its source:

  • It finds "new-like" functions: one non-variadic parameter, one pointer result, and a body that is a single return &param. Reading the source, a generic ptr[T] should qualify too: the match is on the parameter itself rather than its type, and the call-site check carries a comment saying it is formulated that way "to support generics."
  • It rewrites the helper's body to return new(x) and adds a //go:fix inline directive, so the source-level inliner can treat calls to it as inlinable.
  • It rewrites call sites like ptr("dark") to new("dark").
  • It only touches files that already require Go 1.26, so bump go.mod first or the diff comes back empty.
  • The helper's own body is only rewritten when its file requires Go 1.26 as well. Whether calls to helpers from other modules, like proto.String, get rewritten depends on the analyzer recognising them as new-like, so check the -diff output instead of assuming either way.

The blog also advises running go fix "more than once until it reaches a fixed point; twice is usually enough." So run the apply step twice.

Then delete the helper and run go build ./.... Whatever the fixer left behind shows up as compile errors, and that list is your manual review queue. I haven't run this sweep myself, so treat the -diff output as the source of truth for your repo.


go fix rewrites the safe calls and leaves the ones it cannot prove are equivalent.

The calls go fix leaves alone

The fixer refuses a rewrite when the new code would change the type. The check in the source compares the call's result type against a pointer to the argument's default type, and skips the call if they differ. That one rule explains most of what survives the sweep.

Untyped constants with a non-default type. The spec says an untyped constant passed to new is first converted to its default type. new(42) is *int. new(1.5) is *float64. So for a field typed *int64, new(42) does not compile, and ptr[int64](42) is not rewritten. Your hand-written version needs a conversion:

type Job struct {
    TimeoutMs *int64   `json:"timeout_ms,omitempty"`
    Ratio     *float32 `json:"ratio,omitempty"`
}

j := Job{
    TimeoutMs: new(int64(5000)),
    Ratio:     new(float32(0.25)),
}

That works, and the type is explicit. But if a protobuf message has twenty int64 fields, proto.Int64(5000) reads better than new(int64(5000)), and keeping it is a defensible call.

Shadowed new. If a package declares its own new (a constructor, a local variable), the fixer skips calls in that scope. Rename the local first.

Untyped composite literals. The analyzer's source skips arguments like {1, 2} because new({1, 2}) is a compile error. For structs you already had the better tool: &Config{Port: 8080}.

Where the helper is still the clearer choice

The fixer handles the mechanical part. These are judgment calls, and the old helper wins in each one.

You need a function value. The spec's built-in functions section says built-ins "can only appear in call expressions; they cannot be used as function values." So new cannot be passed where a func(T) *T is expected:

func mapSlice[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U {
    out := make([]U, 0, len(s))
    for _, v := range s {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

names := []string{"a", "b"}
ptrs := mapSlice(names, ptr[string]) // compiles
// mapSlice(names, new)              // does not compile

A closure works too (func(s string) *string { return new(s) }), but at that point the named helper is shorter.

Your library supports Go versions before 1.26. new(expr) is a language change, gated by the go directive. If your go.mod promises 1.24 compatibility, you keep the helper until you drop that promise.

The read side. new(expr) only helps you build pointers. Reading an optional field with a default still needs a helper, like ptr.Deref in k8s.io/utils (func Deref[T any](ptr *T, def T) T). Delete ptr[T], keep deref[T].

new(x) is not &x. It allocates a fresh variable holding a copy of x, exactly like the helper did:

n := 1
p := new(n) // copy of n
q := &n     // address of n
n = 2
// *p is 1, *q is 2

If you wanted aliasing, you still want &.

A five-minute checklist

  1. Bump go.mod to go 1.26 or later (applications only, or libraries ready to drop older versions).
  2. Run go fix -diff -newexpr ./... and read the diff.
  3. Apply with go fix -newexpr ./..., twice.
  4. Delete the helper, run go build ./..., and fix what is left by hand: add conversions like new(int64(5000)), or keep a typed helper on purpose.
  5. Keep any helper you pass as a function value, and keep your deref helper.

Run step 2 on your repo first. The diff tells you how big the job really is.

If this was useful

If the tricky part of this post was the language underneath it, The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers that ground: pointers and zero values, why built-ins like new behave differently from ordinary functions, how untyped constants pick their default type, and the standard library packages such as encoding/json that lean on pointers for "absent". It is the reference to keep open when a release like 1.26 changes a rule you thought was settled.

title: Vocab deck
description:
Vocab Deck

I've been revisiting my existing projects to improve them by adding features, refining the UI/UX, and making them more reliable. Vocab Deck is one of them.

It's a vocabulary practice app that helps users learn words through different study modes and track their progress.

Vocab Deck lets users choose a built-in or custom vocabulary deck and practice through flashcards, quizzes, typing exercises, or a matching game. The frontend validates vocabulary data and uses a pure-function game engine to generate randomized sessions, with features like answer checking, distractor generation, and real-time feedback. Built-in decks are served by the FastAPI backend, while custom decks and theme preferences are stored in the browser. Study progress stays in memory and resets when the page reloads.

FEATURES -

Four Study Modes
• 3D Flashcards - Review words and meanings.
• Multiple-Choice Quizzes - Test your understanding.
• Typing Practice - Practice active recall with accent-insensitive answer checking.
• Matching Game - Match words with their meanings

Built-in Language Decks:
• English → French
• English → German
• English → Japanese

Custom Decks:
Create and edit decks, with JSON and CSV import/export to manage and reuse vocabulary lists.

Progress Tracking:
Track study statistics, streaks, and time spent across different study modes.

TECH STACK
Backend -
Python 3.11
FastAPI 0.110+
Uvicorn
Pydantic 2

Frontend -
Node.js 18+
React 18 + TypeScript
Vite

Testing -
Vitest + Testing Library
Playwright

The project is live, and contributions are welcome! You can contribute to the codebase or open an issue to report bugs, suggest improvements, or propose new features.

Live Demo: https://vocab-deck.vercel.app/

PIYUSH-NEXTGEN / Vocab-Deck

Vocab Deck

Vocab Deck is a vocabulary practice application that helps language learners memorize words through four interactive study modes. It provides a modern React frontend backed by a FastAPI vocabulary service. Built-in decks cover English→French, English→German, and English→Japanese; users can also create, edit, import, and export custom decks entirely in the browser.

Features

  • Four study modes: Flashcards (with 3D flip), Multiple-choice Quiz, Typing (accent-insensitive option), Matching
  • Three built-in language pairs: English→French, English→German, English→Japanese (50 entries each, directly comparable)
  • Custom decks: Create, edit, import (JSON/CSV), export; validated client-side with same rules as built-in decks
  • Session tracking: Per-mode stats (correct/incorrect, streaks, time) preserved across mode switches; reset on demand
  • Theme support: Light/dark with prefers-color-scheme detection and localStorage persistence, no flash on load

title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.

title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

title: Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account
description:
Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account

A shared database account is a familiar design. An application reads its connection string from configuration, all replicas use the same username and password, and rotation means a coordinated restart across every service that depends on it. Rotation therefore happens rarely or not at all.

Why the static credential persists

The convenience is real. Connection pools assume a stable identity. Database proxies, failover, and read replicas all inherit the same secret. Introducing per-instance credentials appears to add operational risk rather than remove it.

What short-lived credentials change

Dynamic secrets are issued on request and expire on a schedule. Each application instance receives its own credential, so revocation affects one instance instead of the fleet. Auditing becomes concrete: the database log shows which instance connected when.

The lifetime should match the workload. A batch job that runs for two hours needs a credential that outlives the job. A web service that can re-authenticate on each connection can use a much shorter window.

Handling the transition

Connection pools are the practical obstacle. Pools must be configured to refresh credentials before expiry, and the refresh must be tested against database failover. Applications should handle a rejected connection by requesting a new credential rather than retrying the old one indefinitely.

Emergency access needs its own path. If the issuing service is unavailable, operators need a documented break-glass procedure, with the use of that path logged and reviewed.

Verifying the control

A credential system is only as good as what it prevents. Confirm that a revoked credential is rejected within the expected window, that a leaked credential from one instance cannot be used by another, and that the audit trail records the subject rather than a shared account.

References

  • NIST SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final
  • NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
description:
arXiv:2610.14146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Character Set Troubleshooting: Fix Chinese Garbled Text
description:
Chinese garbled text is a common issue when working with GBase Database(GBase 8s). The cause may be incorrect database locale settings, client encoding mismatches, terminal configuration, or data that was already corrupted during insertion. This guide covers practical checks to help identify and troubleshoot character encoding problems.

1. Understand Common Character Encoding Problems

Before changing any configuration, identify the symptom.

  • Chinese text displays as question marks (**????**): The original characters may have been lost during data insertion or conversion.

  • Chinese text displays as unreadable symbols: The client and database may be interpreting the same bytes differently.

  • Only one application has the problem: The issue may be related to that application's connection or encoding configuration.

  • Chinese text displays correctly in one tool but not another: Compare the client environments before changing database settings.

The key is to determine whether the problem occurs during storage, transmission, or display.

2. Check GBase Database(GBase 8s) Locale Settings

Start by checking the environment variables used by the database installation and client tools.

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$LANG"
echo "$LC_ALL"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"
echo "$DB_LOCALE"

These values help identify the current environment configuration. Their availability and expected values depend on the installation and client setup.

You can also inspect the database environment using the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8s) monitoring commands available in your version.

Before changing locale settings, verify the database's existing locale and the locale expected by the application. Do not assume that changing an environment variable will convert existing data or repair text that was stored incorrectly.

3. Check the Client and Terminal Encoding

If Chinese text looks incorrect in a command-line session, check the terminal environment first.

locale
echo "$LANG"

Confirm that the terminal, client application, and database connection use compatible character encodings.

If the problem occurs only in one terminal or database client, test the same query using another client. This helps distinguish a display issue from a database storage issue.

4. Test Chinese Data

Use a small test table in a non-production database to check whether Chinese characters can be inserted, stored, and retrieved correctly.

CREATE TABLE charset_test (
    id INTEGER,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO charset_test VALUES (1, '中文测试');

SELECT * FROM charset_test;

If the returned text is incorrect, compare the result across different database clients.

Before running this test, confirm that the target database supports the intended characters and that your session is configured appropriately. Use an existing test table if you do not have permission to create tables.

A successful test does not necessarily prove that all existing data is correct. It only helps narrow down the problem.

5. Check Application and JDBC Connections

For Java applications, review the JDBC connection configuration and the encoding settings supported by your specific GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver.

For example, a connection URL may look like this:

jdbc:gbasedbt-sqli://192.168.1.100:9088/mydb:GBASEDBTSERVER=gbase01

Verify the correct JDBC URL format, connection properties, and supported character set settings against the documentation for your installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver. Do not copy connection properties from another driver or version without verification.

If command-line clients display Chinese correctly but a Java application does not, focus on the application's connection configuration and data handling before modifying the database.

6. Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

When troubleshooting Chinese garbled text in GBase Database(GBase 8s), check these items in order:

  1. Confirm the database locale and supported character set.

  2. Review CLIENT_LOCALE, DB_LOCALE, and related environment settings where applicable.

  3. Check the terminal and client application's encoding.

  4. Compare query results across different clients.

  5. Test inserting and retrieving Chinese text in a test environment.

  6. Review application and JDBC driver configuration.

  7. Determine whether existing data was already corrupted before attempting any conversion or repair.

Avoid changing locale settings on a production system without understanding the impact and preparing a recovery plan.

Conclusion

Troubleshooting character encoding issues in GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with identifying where the problem occurs: storage, connection, or display. Check locale settings, compare client behavior, and test with a small amount of Chinese text before making changes.

A systematic approach helps isolate the cause while reducing the risk of disrupting existing data or production services.

title: CedarDB brings its new online data management service
description:
CedarDB, a startup born from the Umbra research project at the Technical University of Munich, is bringing its PostgreSQL-compatible database to the cloud.

The platform is optimized for running high-speed analytical queries alongside daily transaction processing without additional memory overhead.

The move into the cloud marks a new phase for the team as they look to help enterprises query long-term transaction data using natural language.

According to Sichert, large companies have systems with many years of transaction data, but these cannot always quickly answer analytical questions formulated in everyday language.

CedarDB has been in development for about ten years and began as a research project at the Technical University of Munich, called Umbra. It was designed to run quickly without requiring more processors, more computing power, or more memory.

It is also compatible with PostgreSQL, which means customers don't have to rebuild their applications to use it, which reduces the cost of migration, according to Sichert.

READ ALSO

Eight US states take legal action against OpenAI over minors' safety

In May 2025, the company announced the free CedarDB Community Edition and CedarDB Enterprise, which is installed on customer premises. At the same time, it announced initial funding of 5,3 million euros, approximately $6 million.

CedarDB had been testing its online service with users on a waitlist. On October 14, 2026, it announced on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt that CedarDB Cloud is available to a limited number of users. The fully managed online version is expected to help the company reach more users beyond large enterprises.

In June, Databricks introduced LTAP, an architecture that aims to combine transactional, analytics, dataflow, and day-to-day operations data using a common data copy. Sichert sees the move as a sign that there is demand for CedarDB’s approach. However, it’s not yet clear how much of an impact it will have on the market.

CedarDB currently has 14 employees and plans to serve the first users of the online service with these. Sichert estimates that the company will need a larger team if it gains more traction. In that case, it will seek a new round of funding.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It

What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

Uncertain rewards. Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

Self-regulation. In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: 6 Common GBase Database(GBase 8s) oninit Startup Failures and How to Troubleshoot Them
description:
Running oninit -ivy only to see GBase Database(GBase 8s) fail to start? Before reinstalling the database, check the environment variables, configuration files, port availability, directory permissions, shared memory settings, and disk space.

Here are six common causes of GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup failures and how to investigate them on Linux.

1. Cannot Find the onconfig File

Possible cause: ONCONFIG is unset, references the wrong configuration file, or the file is missing.

Check the environment:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"
ls "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/onconfig."*

Verify that ONCONFIG matches the intended configuration file and that the file exists in the expected directory. Correct the environment according to your installation before retrying startup.

2. Cannot Bind to the Database Port

Possible cause: The configured port is already in use or the listener configuration is incorrect.

Check the port:

ss -lntp | grep ':9088'

Replace 9088 with the port configured for your instance.

Identify the process before taking action. Do not terminate unrelated services blindly. If a port conflict exists, resolve it or select an available port and update the relevant server and client configurations consistently.

3. Permission Denied

Possible cause: The database operating system account cannot access required configuration, storage, or diagnostic directories.

Inspect directory ownership and permissions:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase_data

Check the relevant parent directories and files as well. Confirm that the database service account has the permissions required by your installation.

Avoid applying recursive ownership or permission changes to an entire directory tree without understanding its contents. Incorrect changes can introduce additional security and operational problems.

4. Not Enough Shared Memory

Possible cause: Available system resources or shared memory configuration do not meet the instance requirements.

Start by inspecting the system setting:

cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax
free -h

Review the actual startup error and compare the current system configuration with the requirements for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version and workload.

Do not apply arbitrary shared memory values from online examples. The appropriate settings depend on the operating system, database configuration, and available resources.

5. No Space Left on Device

Possible cause: A filesystem used for database storage, temporary files, or diagnostic logs has run out of space.

Check available capacity:

df -h
df -i

Check both disk space and inode availability. Review the relevant storage locations and database logs to identify the affected filesystem.

Free space only after confirming which files can safely be removed. Never delete database storage files or logs blindly to make the startup error disappear.

6. sqlhosts Configuration Problems

Possible cause: The connection configuration file is missing, unreadable, or contains an incorrect server entry.

Check the configured path and contents:

echo "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"
cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

Verify that the file exists, the database account can access it, and the server name, protocol, hostname, and port match the intended connection configuration.

A sqlhosts problem may primarily affect client connectivity rather than instance startup, so use the exact error message to determine whether it is relevant to the current failure.

Quick oninit Diagnostic Script

This basic script checks several common environment and system conditions:

#!/bin/bash

echo "=== GBase Database(GBase 8s) Startup Diagnostics ==="

echo
echo "1. Environment"
echo "GBASEDBTDIR=${GBASEDBTDIR:-unset}"
echo "ONCONFIG=${ONCONFIG:-unset}"
echo "GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS=${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-unset}"

echo
echo "2. Configuration file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -n "${ONCONFIG:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/$ONCONFIG" ]]; then
    echo "onconfig file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check ONCONFIG and the configuration path"
fi

echo
echo "3. sqlhosts file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS" ]]; then
    echo "sqlhosts file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check sqlhosts path and permissions"
fi

echo
echo "4. Disk space"
df -h

echo
echo "5. Inode availability"
df -i

echo
echo "6. Shared memory setting"
cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax 2>/dev/null ||
    echo "Unable to read shmmax"

echo
echo "7. Recent startup logs"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log" ]]; then
    tail -30 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"
else
    echo "Check the diagnostic log location for your installation"
fi

Save the script as check_oninit.sh and run it in the appropriate database environment. The diagnostic log location may differ depending on your installation.

This script identifies potential configuration issues; it does not replace reviewing the actual oninit error messages.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup investigations should begin with the exact error message and the database diagnostic logs. Check the environment and configuration first, then investigate ports, permissions, system resources, and storage.

The key takeaway: Avoid changing multiple settings at once. Identify the failing component, make one controlled change, and verify the result before proceeding.

A systematic troubleshooting process makes GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation and Linux database administration easier to maintain.

title: Building a Multi-Tenant RAG in 8GB RAM: Why I Ditched Qdrant and Kafka (Phase 0)
description:
I have 8 GB of RAM and 6 vCPUs. With those specs, I'm building and running a full production-ready RAG system.

I’m not self-hosting the LLM. I’m not spinning up Qdrant. I’m not adding Kafka.
Those aren't my personal preferences—they are constraints strictly dictated by the hardware. When you run a JVM alongside a Python AI worker on an 8 GB machine, every megabyte counts.

Today, I’m starting to build Corpus in public: a document chat platform where every answer strictly cites its sources, and each organization's data remains completely isolated from the rest (strict multi-tenancy).

The Stack (100% Dockerized)

  • Backend API: Java 21 + Spring Boot 4
  • AI & Embeddings Service: Python + FastAPI
  • Storage & Vector DB: PostgreSQL (pgvector) + Redis
  • Frontend: React

Why this architecture?

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector over Qdrant/Milvus: Maintaining a dedicated vector database alongside a relational DB in 8 GB of RAM is overkill. Keeping relational metadata and vector embeddings in the same engine simplifies transactions and saves precious memory.
  • Redis over Kafka: I need asynchronous processing for document ingestion, not a massive distributed event-streaming cluster eating up heap memory.

Current Status: Phase 0

All 5 services spin up cleanly with a single docker compose up, and the core system design is locked in the repository. There is no live demo yet.

Next step: The ingestion pipeline—turning raw PDFs into queryable vector chunks without triggering the Linux OOM killer.

I’ll be documenting every architectural trade-off and every failure along the way.

🔗 GitHub Repository: aletgdev/corpus-rag

Looking for advice from the community 👇

For those of you who have built something similar under tight resource constraints: How would you handle local embedding generation within an 8 GB RAM budget while guaranteeing strict multi-tenant isolation in pgvector? (e.g., Row-Level Security vs. schema-per-tenant vs. metadata filtering).

Any war stories or tips are more than welcome in the comments!

title: Amazon RDS Proxy now supports SQL Server 2022
description:
Amazon RDS Proxy, a fully managed, highly available database proxy for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), now supports Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances running major version 2022.

Amazon RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database to pool and share established database connections, improving database efficiency and application scalability. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ databases, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserves application connections, and helps reduce failover times by up to 83%. RDS Proxy supports standard IAM authentication for SQL Server, where your applications authenticate to the proxy using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and RDS Proxy manages database connections using credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

You can enable Amazon RDS Proxy for your SQL Server 2022 database in a few steps on the Amazon RDS console, then connect by pointing your application to the RDS Proxy endpoint. To get started, see our documentation.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Character Set Migration: From en_US.8859-1 to zh_CN.utf8
description:
Configuring the correct character set is essential when deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s) for applications that store Chinese data. If your database currently uses en_US.8859-1, you may encounter character conversion issues when inserting or retrieving Chinese text. This guide explains how to check locale settings, understand configuration limitations, and plan a safe character set migration in GBase Database(GBase 8s).

Why Does Character Set Configuration Matter?

Character set configuration affects how GBase Database(GBase 8s) stores, interprets, and exchanges text data. The single-byte encoding 8859-1 cannot represent Chinese characters directly.

For applications that require Chinese support, a compatible locale such as zh_CN.utf8 may be appropriate, provided it is supported by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version and operating system.

Before making changes, understand three important concepts:

  • DB_LOCALE: Defines the database locale and influences character data handling.
  • CLIENT_LOCALE: Controls locale-related behavior on the client side.
  • Operating system locale: Determines which locales are available to database utilities and applications.

These settings serve different purposes. Changing a client locale does not automatically convert existing database data, and modifying instance configuration does not necessarily change the locale of an existing database.

Method 1: Check the Current Locale Configuration

Before changing anything, inspect your GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment and verify which locales are available on the server.

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
locale -a
onstat -

The locale -a command lists the locales available on the operating system. Check whether a UTF-8 Chinese locale is installed and note its exact name, since naming conventions vary between Linux distributions.

Next, inspect the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8s) configuration files and identify the current locale settings.

Do not immediately modify onconfig and restart the instance. First, confirm which parameters are supported by your installed version and determine whether your goal is to change the client environment, configure a new database, or migrate an existing database.

Important: Changing DB_LOCALE in an instance configuration file should not be treated as a method for converting an existing database from en_US.8859-1 to zh_CN.utf8.

Method 2: Migrate Existing Data to a UTF-8 Database

If an existing GBase Database(GBase 8s) database uses en_US.8859-1, migration to a separately prepared target database may be necessary.

The migration process should preserve both the database structure and the original data while ensuring that Chinese characters are converted correctly.

Step 1: Back Up the Source Database

Before migration, create a complete backup using a supported backup method for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment.

Verify that the backup is usable and prepare a rollback plan. Do not perform character set migration directly on your only production copy.

Step 2: Prepare the Target Database

Prepare a target database using a locale configuration supported by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version.

Because database creation syntax and locale capabilities can differ by version, follow the applicable product documentation rather than assuming that a generic CREATE DATABASE statement can specify any desired character set.

Confirm the target database locale before proceeding.

Step 3: Export the Source Data

Where supported, use the database export utilities to export the source database schema and data.

For example:

dbexport old_db

Check the command output and exported files to confirm that the operation completed successfully. Review the export format and determine whether character conversion is required before importing the data.

Step 4: Import Data into the Target Database

Use a migration procedure supported by your installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) version to load the schema and data into the prepared target database.

Review table definitions, indexes, constraints, stored procedures, and other database objects during migration.

title: What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing
description:
Cross-Channel Message Routing for Chatbots: What We Learned Building It Across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram

Every chatbot starts simple: one channel, one webhook, one reply. Then a customer asks, "Can you also answer on Instagram?" and suddenly you're maintaining three webhook formats, three rate-limit models, and three definitions of what a "message" even is.

At Botsailors, we hit this wall while building our omnichannel automation layer. This post is a behind-the-scenes look at how to route messages across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram without turning your codebase into a pile of if (channel === ...) statements. You'll learn the architecture we settled on, the mistakes that shaped it, and code you can adapt.

Note: This is a build post, not a product pitch. Where we compare approaches, we include alternatives so you can pick what fits your stack.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • What is cross-channel message routing?
  • Lesson 1: Normalize before you route
  • Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent
  • Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters
  • Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out
  • Lesson 5: Design human handoff early
  • Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

Before you follow along, you should have:

  • [ ] Working knowledge of Node.js and TypeScript
  • [ ] Basic familiarity with webhooks and REST APIs
  • [ ] A developer account on at least one messaging platform (WhatsApp Business Platform, Meta for Instagram, or the Telegram Bot API)
  • [ ] A queue or job runner (we use Redis-backed queues, but any works)

What is cross-channel message routing?

Cross-channel message routing is the layer that receives messages from many channels, decides what should handle each one (a bot flow, an AI agent, or a human), and sends the reply back through the correct channel in the correct format.

It sits between channel-specific webhooks and your business logic:

WhatsApp ─┐
Instagram ─┼─> Adapters ─> Normalizer ─> Router ─> Handler (bot / AI / human)
Telegram ─┘                                            │
                                    Outbound queue <───┘

The goal: your business logic never knows or cares which channel a message came from, unless it explicitly needs to.

Lesson 1: Normalize before you route

Our first version routed on raw payloads. It worked for about two weeks.

Each channel describes the same event differently. A text message is messages[0].text.body on one platform and message.text on another. Routing on raw payloads means every new rule has to understand every payload.

The fix was a single internal message shape:

type Channel = "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "telegram";

interface NormalizedMessage {
  id: string;              // our internal ID
  externalId: string;      // the channel's message ID
  channel: Channel;
  contactId: string;       // channel-specific user ID
  conversationId: string;
  type: "text" | "image" | "audio" | "location" | "button_reply";
  text?: string;
  mediaUrl?: string;
  receivedAt: Date;
  raw: unknown;            // keep the original payload for debugging
}

Each channel gets a small adapter that converts into this shape:

function telegramAdapter(update: any): NormalizedMessage {
  const m = update.message;
  return {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    externalId: String(m.message_id),
    channel: "telegram",
    contactId: String(m.from.id),
    conversationId: `tg:${m.chat.id}`,
    type: m.text ? "text" : "image",
    text: m.text,
    receivedAt: new Date(m.date * 1000),
    raw: update,
  };
}

Tip: Always keep the raw payload. When a customer says "your bot ignored my message," raw payloads are the fastest way to find out why.

Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent

Webhook providers retry. If your server is slow or returns a non-200, the same message can arrive two or three times, and your bot happily replies to each one.

We deduplicate at the door using the channel's own message ID:

async function acceptOnce(msg: NormalizedMessage): Promise<boolean> {
  const key = `seen:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  // SET NX with a TTL: only the first writer wins
  const result = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 60 * 60 * 24, "NX");
  return result === "OK";
}

app.post("/webhooks/:channel", async (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(200); // acknowledge fast, process async
  const msg = adapters[req.params.channel](req.body);
  if (await acceptOnce(msg)) {
    await inboundQueue.add("route", msg);
  }
});

Two rules we now treat as non-negotiable:

  1. Acknowledge first, process later. Slow handlers cause retries.
  2. Deduplicate on the external ID, not on message content. Customers legitimately send "ok" twice.

Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters

Routing decisions (who handles this message?) should be pure functions of the normalized message plus conversation state. They should never import a channel SDK.

type Target = "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";

interface ConversationState {
  assignedTo?: "human" | "bot";
  activeFlowId?: string;
  lastIntent?: string;
}

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, state: ConversationState): Target {
  // 1. A human owns the conversation: bots stay quiet
  if (state.assignedTo === "human") return "human";

  // 2. A flow is mid-execution: continue it
  if (state.activeFlowId) return "flow";

  // 3. Explicit escalation keywords, on any channel
  if (msg.text && /\b(agent|human|representative)\b/i.test(msg.text)) {
    return "human";
  }

  // 4. Default: let the AI agent handle it
  return "ai_agent";
}

Because route is pure, we can unit test it with plain objects, no mock webhooks required:

test("human-owned conversations never reach the bot", () => {
  const msg = { text: "hello", channel: "instagram" } as NormalizedMessage;
  expect(route(msg, { assignedTo: "human" })).toBe("human");
});

Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out

Inbound is only half the problem. Outbound is where channels differ most:

Concern What varies by channel
Messaging windows Some platforms restrict free-form replies after a time window and require approved templates
Rate limits Different per-second and per-user throughput
Rich content Buttons, carousels, and quick replies differ in shape and limits
Message length Text limits vary

Check each platform's current documentation for exact numbers, because they change. Our approach is an outbound adapter per channel plus a shared queue with per-channel rate limiting:

const limiters: Record<Channel, RateLimiter> = {
  whatsapp: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 20 }),   // example values: verify against current docs
  instagram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 10 }),
  telegram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 30 }),
};

async function send(channel: Channel, contactId: string, reply: Reply) {
  await limiters[channel].acquire();
  const payload = outboundAdapters[channel](contactId, reply);
  return channelClients[channel].post(payload);
}

Heads up: The numbers above are placeholders. Always confirm current limits in each platform's official docs before relying on them.

A shared Reply type (text, buttons, media) that each outbound adapter degrades gracefully is the key. If a channel can't render a carousel, fall back to a numbered text list rather than failing silently.

Lesson 5: Design human handoff early

We treated handoff as a "later" feature. That was a mistake, because handoff changes your routing model.

Once a human can take over a conversation, you need:

  • A conversation owner field that the router checks first (see Lesson 3).
  • A way to hand back to the bot when the human is done.
  • Idle timeouts so a conversation doesn't stay "owned" by an agent who went home. 
async function handoff(conversationId: string, to: "human" | "bot") {
  await db.conversations.update(conversationId, {
    assignedTo: to,
    assignedAt: new Date(),
  });
}

Adding ownership after the fact meant rewriting every handler. Adding it up front costs one column.

Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider

Building your own router is not always the right call. Depending on your team and requirements, you could consider:

  • Open-source frameworks such as Botpress or Rasa if you want self-hosting and full control.
  • Managed omnichannel platforms if you'd rather not maintain webhooks, templates, and compliance yourself.
  • Direct platform APIs (as in this post) when you need custom routing logic or tight integration with your own backend.

Build your own if routing logic is core to your product. Otherwise, evaluate what already exists before writing adapters.

Conclusion

Cross-channel message routing for chatbots comes down to a few durable decisions:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one internal shape.
  • Deduplicate at the door and acknowledge webhooks fast.
  • Keep routing pure and separate from channel SDKs.
  • Treat outbound limits as first-class, with a per-channel queue and graceful degradation.
  • Plan human handoff from day one.

None of this is exotic, but skipping any one of them creates bugs that only show up in production, usually on a Friday evening.

If you're building something similar, I'd love to hear how you handle routing across channels. What did you wish you'd known earlier? Share it in the comments.

title: Why don't Graph Transformers attend to the same token?
description:
arXiv:2610.19324v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token. This 'attention sink' is believed to protect deep models against over-mixing. Even though graph transformers face a related pressure, we find that a SoTA graph transformer, GRIT, rarely forms sinks on molecules, and that it sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the opposite of the trend in LLMs. In principle, a graph can prevent sinks: we prove and show empirically that its symmetry and locality limit the attention any node can receive. On molecules, however, with distinguishable atoms and global attention, neither limit prevents sinks; what stops them lies in the model. We find that the attention scoring function is the main cause. Replacing GRIT's gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs. In Graph Transformers using dot-product attention, removing the sink gives about the same error as removing a random node, while GRIT's most-attended nodes matter to its predictions. Attention sinks are therefore a property of dot-product attention rather than of Transformers. In our experiments, they form when dot-product scoring has a distinguishable node to concentrate on.

title: Add S3 uploads to Vercel apps without storing long-lived AWS keys
description:
A Vercel app can accept a file upload and store the object in Amazon S3 without putting a long-lived AWS access key in source code or deployment variables. Vercel’s Amazon S3 Marketplace integration now connects an S3 resource to a Vercel project, supplies connection details as environment variables, and authenticates with short-lived OIDC credentials. The practical work remains yours: authorize the uploader, choose the object key, validate the file, and decide who can read it.

This guide walks through the setup boundary, the server-side upload path, and the security decisions that still matter after credentials are handled. It is for a team adding file uploads to a Vercel-hosted application, especially one that already uses AWS and wants its storage flow near the project configuration.

Choose the integration for the workflow you have

Amazon S3 and Vercel Blob solve overlapping but different setup problems. Vercel Blob is a storage service for files in a Vercel app, with Vercel-managed delivery features. The S3 Marketplace integration is a fit when the application already depends on AWS, when the team wants S3 resources visible beside its Vercel project, or when its storage workflow uses S3-specific services such as S3 Tables or S3 Vectors.

The Marketplace path keeps project setup together: create or connect the resource in the Vercel dashboard, then use the values made available to the project. A linked AWS account has an important constraint: the Vercel flow supports buckets created through Vercel, rather than attaching an arbitrary pre-existing bucket. If an application already writes to a bucket that was created elsewhere, check the current setup path before planning a migration. Do not assume “connect an AWS account” means every bucket in that account is selectable.

The integration also does not remove the need to understand AWS permissions. OIDC changes how the application obtains credentials; the IAM role still determines which AWS actions those credentials can perform. Treat the role policy, project environment, and upload route as separate controls.

Connect the S3 resource to the project

Start in the Vercel Marketplace from the project that will run the upload route. Create an S3 resource through the guided flow or link the AWS account you intend to use. Review the environment variables that Vercel adds and the project environments to which the connection applies. Keep production and preview behavior deliberate; a preview deployment should not automatically inherit broader access than it needs.

Vercel’s integration uses short-lived OIDC credentials instead of storing static AWS keys in the application. That means you do not paste an IAM user’s long-lived access key into an environment variable or commit it in a local file. The application still needs ordinary configuration such as the bucket name and region, and AWS still needs a role with a trust relationship for the intended Vercel project and environment.

For new integrations, inspect the connection details and the resulting IAM access before sending real user files. Confirm the role can write only to the bucket and key prefix the application requires. If a function only stores user uploads, it should not receive broad permissions to list every bucket or alter bucket policy. Keep any administrative bucket operations outside the request path.

Build a server-side upload route

The Vercel changelog’s example uses createS3 from @vercel/aws, then sends an AWS SDK PutObjectCommand from a route handler. The outline is small:

// lib/s3.ts
import { createS3 } from "@vercel/aws";

export const s3 = createS3();

// app/api/upload/route.ts
import { PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { s3 } from "@/lib/s3";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // First authenticate the user and verify upload permission.
  const formData = await request.formData();
  const file = formData.get("file");

  if (!(file instanceof File)) {
    return Response.json({ error: "A file is required." }, { status: 400 });
  }

  // Apply application-specific size and content checks here.
  const objectKey = `uploads/${crypto.randomUUID()}`;

  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET_NAME!,
    Key: objectKey,
    Body: Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer()),
    ContentType: file.type || "application/octet-stream",
  }));

  return Response.json({ key: objectKey });
}

An existing AWS account can be linked; buckets provisioned through the Vercel connection are new buckets. The older buckets shown remain untouched.

This is a route shape, not a complete production policy. The example deliberately leaves authentication and validation as explicit steps because they depend on the application. A successful AWS write does not prove that the requester is allowed to upload for the account identified by the URL or form.

The object key should be generated on the server. Do not accept a bucket name or unrestricted key from the browser: a user could otherwise choose another tenant’s path or overwrite an object the app treats as authoritative. Use an opaque identifier for the storage key and save the original filename as display metadata after normalizing it. Scope each upload to the authenticated user or tenant, and ensure the IAM policy and application checks agree about the allowed prefix.

Set upload limits before reading an entire file into memory. Check the declared MIME type, but do not trust it as proof of file contents; inspect or decode the bytes when the file type matters. Restrict accepted formats, cap size, and rate-limit requests. For larger uploads, design a multipart or direct-to-storage flow separately, including how a client receives narrowly scoped authorization and how unfinished uploads are cleaned up.

Decide who can read each object

Storage access is a product decision. A profile image meant to be public and an invoice or user export should not share the same read path. Keep private objects behind application authorization, and return a short-lived download mechanism only after checking the caller’s access. If a file is intentionally public, make that choice explicit and avoid placing sensitive content in that bucket or prefix.

The Marketplace S3 connection uses short-lived OIDC credentials rather than static AWS keys for the upload flow; the scene is conceptual, not a Vercel or OTF integration screen.

Do not rely on an unguessable object key as the authorization rule. Random identifiers reduce accidental discovery, but the app still needs to check ownership before returning a download URL or proxying bytes. Consider whether a user can replace a file, whether each replacement should create a new version, and how deletion requests propagate to S3 and the app’s metadata store.

Think through consistency as well. An upload can succeed in S3 while a database write fails, or the reverse if the application records an object before storage confirms it. Store the object key and upload state in a way that supports retries and cleanup. Make the route safe to retry where possible, and avoid returning a success response until the application has enough proof to show the file to the user.

Test the full path before opening it to users

Use a small, non-sensitive file in a development or preview environment. Verify the route rejects an unauthenticated request, a missing file, an oversized file, and a file type the product does not accept. Then upload an allowed file and confirm that the generated key uses the intended tenant prefix and that an authorized user can retrieve it.

Test the negative cases, too: a user from another tenant should not be able to overwrite or read the object; a preview project should not gain production access by accident; and a failed metadata write should not leave a misleading success state. Check the Vercel function logs and AWS-side audit trail without logging file bytes, user credentials, or temporary tokens.

Finally, test the deployment environments that matter. A route that works locally can still fail if the project is not connected to the S3 resource in Preview or Production, if the bucket region is wrong, or if the AWS role trust policy does not match the project and environment. Keep a short runbook with the resource owner, bucket and region, allowed prefixes, expected environment variables, and a safe way to rotate or narrow permissions.

Where an app template fits

Adding S3 is a storage integration task; it does not create the rest of the product around it. If the same team also needs an editable SaaS application shell, the OTF SaaS Dashboard template is an optional $99 starting point with a Vite and Hono app, sign-in, projects, teams, and sample analytics screens. It does not include Amazon S3 or configure this Marketplace integration. Keep the storage connection in the application’s own Vercel and AWS setup.

For an example of how a small Hono backend can be deployed on Vercel’s alternative serverless platform, see our guide to running a Hono backend on AWS Lambda. Use that as a separate deployment discussion; it is not a prerequisite for the Vercel Marketplace path described here.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 joins the Vercel Marketplace — October 14, 2026. Marketplace setup, environment variables, OIDC credentials, upload example, linked-account limits, and S3 versus Blob use cases.
  • SaaS Dashboard template and pricing — checked October 15, 2026. The kit is $99 and does not include this S3 integration.

title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
description:
arXiv:2610.19064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.
