title: 1Z0-078 Lists RAC First, but Your Cluster Is Built from the Bottom Up
description:
If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid Infrastructure goes on, which brings Oracle Clusterware and Oracle Automatic Storage Management with it. Only after that does anyone install the database software, and only after that does a RAC database exist to tune, patch and connect to.

Oracle's exam page for 1Z0-078 lists the same material in the opposite order. It starts with RAC databases and architecture, moves on to Grid Infrastructure in the middle, and ends with ASM disk groups, files and the ASM Cluster File System. That is a fine way to describe a job. It is a poor way to learn one, because almost every RAC objective assumes you understand the layers underneath it.

This article follows the build order instead. It is written for the DBA or systems administrator who already looks after clustered databases and wants to know whether 1Z0-078 matches the work on their desk. Every number in it comes from Oracle's own exam page and Oracle's 19c documentation, both checked on 15 October 2026.

What Is the Oracle 1Z0-078 RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Exam?

1Z0-078 is the exam behind the Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator credential. Its full title on Oracle MyLearn is "Exam 1Z0-078: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration", and the official 1Z0-078 exam page on Oracle MyLearn is where the topic list, the format and the session rules live.

Oracle describes the audience plainly. The certification is for database production systems administrators and database administrators with 12 to 18 months of experience using RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure. The exam measures installation, configuration, backup and recovery, monitoring and tuning of those components. Read that as a description of who does well, not as an entry rule: the page states an experience profile, and it is worth being honest with yourself about whether you match it.

The three names in the title are three layers of one stack, and it helps to be precise about how they relate, because the exam is.

Grid Infrastructure: the base layer

Oracle's Introduction to Oracle Clusterware in the 19c Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide explains that Clusterware lets separate servers communicate so they appear to applications and users as one system. Since Oracle Clusterware 12c, the Clusterware and ASM binaries are installed as a single binary called Oracle Grid Infrastructure. The same guide notes that Clusterware 19c supports only ASM 19c, because ASM sits in the Grid Infrastructure home that also holds Clusterware.

Clusterware keeps two stored components besides its binaries. Voting files record node membership. The Oracle Cluster Registry, or OCR, records cluster configuration: databases, listeners, virtual IP addresses, services and any applications Clusterware manages. Both must sit on shared storage that every cluster node can reach.

ASM: the storage layer

ASM is Oracle's volume manager and file system for database files. Oracle's overview chapter of the 19c ASM Administrator's Guide describes disk groups made of disks, files and allocation units, with normal redundancy giving two-way mirroring, high redundancy three-way mirroring, and external redundancy leaving the mirroring to a RAID subsystem.

RAC: the database layer

Oracle RAC lets several instances open one database. The RAC guide says that having multiple instances access a single database prevents the server from being a single point of failure, and that applications deployed on RAC databases can operate without code changes. RAC depends on Clusterware; the guide calls Clusterware a required component that provides the infrastructure RAC runs on.

So the order on the exam page is top-down, while the order on a real system is bottom-up. Hold on to that idea. It shapes the study plan later in this article.

1Z0-078 Exam Overview and Details

The format is short to state. Everything below is from Oracle's exam page unless marked otherwise.

  • Exam code: 1Z0-078
  • Exam name: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration
  • Credential: Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator
  • Delivery: Proctored Online
  • Format: Multiple Choice
  • Duration: 120 minutes
  • Number of questions: 77
  • Passing score: 65%
  • Price: Oracle's page shows no price to a signed-out visitor. The DBExam syllabus page lists USD $245 and notes that pricing may vary by country or local currency; confirm the figure in your Oracle account at checkout.

What 77 questions in 120 minutes means at the desk

120 minutes across 77 questions is about 93 seconds a question. That is generous for a question that asks you to recognise a view name and tight for one that describes a failed node, a set of services and a client configuration, then asks what the client sees. Plan to move quickly through recall questions so the scenario questions get the time they need.

A 65% passing score on 77 questions works out to just over 50 correct answers, if every question counts the same. Oracle does not publish how it weights individual questions, so treat 51 as a planning number rather than a rule, and aim well above it.

Session rules worth knowing in advance

  • A government-issued identification is required to take the exam.
  • Check-in time is 30 minutes before the exam time.
  • Your computer must meet Oracle's minimum system requirements for online proctoring.
  • Results are shown on screen at the close of the exam, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView.
  • To reschedule, you must do it at least 24 hours before your appointment time.

None of these is unusual, but the 30-minute check-in catches people who block exactly two hours in their calendar. Block three.

Key Topics and Syllabus for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page lists 30 topics and 115 objective lines under three groupings. The first grouping has no heading of its own on the page; it is the RAC material. Then come the headings "Grid Infrastructure Administration" and "Automatic Storage Management (ASM) Administration". Counted line by line:

  • RAC administration: 12 topics, 49 objective lines
  • Grid Infrastructure administration: 11 topics, 41 objective lines
  • ASM administration: 7 topics, 25 objective lines

One caution before you use those counts: Oracle publishes no percentage weights for 1Z0-078. A line count shows where the page spends its words, not how many questions each area gets. The 1Z0-078 syllabus on DBExam sets the same topics out on one page with the exam facts beside them, which is handy as a checklist.

Here is the syllabus in the order you would build the system, bottom layer first.

Layer 1: Grid Infrastructure and Clusterware (11 topics)

The Grid Infrastructure grouping covers the life of the cluster itself:

  • Introduction to Clusterware and Oracle Clusterware architecture, including startup details and how Grid Plug and Play affects Clusterware
  • Flex Clusters and the effect of node failure in one
  • Installation planning and pre-tasks: system and network requirements, groups, users and directories
  • Grid Infrastructure installation, verifying it, configuring ASM disk groups, and the optional Grid Infrastructure Management Repository
  • Managing cluster nodes: extending a cluster, deleting a node, and adding nodes with DBCA
  • Traditional Clusterware management: day-to-day tasks, OCR backup and recovery, network settings, what-if command evaluation and secure cluster communication
  • Policy-based cluster management: server categorization, policy sets and activating a policy
  • Upgrading and patching Grid Infrastructure, including rolling patches and zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching
  • Troubleshooting Clusterware: log files, diagcollection.pl, resource and component debugging, and OCR problems
  • Making applications highly available with Clusterware: policy-managed and administrator-managed databases, application VIPs and application resources

Two documented facts from this layer tend to matter. First, Oracle recommends no more than five voting files, although Clusterware supports up to 15. Second, you can have up to five OCR locations, and you can replace a failed OCR location online as long as it is not the only one. Small numbers like these make good exam distractors, so learn them exactly.

Flex Clusters have their own rules in the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide: a Flex Cluster can have as many as 64 Hub Nodes, Hub Nodes have direct access to shared storage and host read-write instances, other nodes request data through Hub Nodes and host read-only instances, Flex Clusters require Grid Naming Service, and you can convert a standard cluster to a Flex Cluster but not the reverse.

Layer 2: ASM, ACFS and ADVM (7 topics)

The ASM grouping is the shortest, but it sits under everything else:

  • ASM architecture and components
  • ASM instances: initialization parameters, processes, and monitoring with the V$ASM dynamic performance views
  • Flex ASM: architecture, installation, configuration and management
  • Disk groups: creating, dropping, setting attributes, maintenance, and performance and scalability considerations
  • Files, directories and templates, including the format of a fully qualified ASM file name
  • Oracle CloudFS: the ASM Dynamic Volume Manager, ASM volumes, ACFS and ACFS snapshots
  • CloudFS advanced topics: ACFS auditing, encryption, replication and tagging, and High Availability NFS

The file name objective is a good example of how literal the exam can be. Oracle's chapter on ASM files, directories and templates gives the form as +diskgroup/dbname/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation in a non-multitenant database, and +diskgroup/cdb/pdb_guid/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation with multitenant. Alias names are told apart because they do not end in a dotted pair of numbers. If you can read +DATA/ORCL/DATAFILE/system.257.967544915 and name every field, that objective is done.

Flex ASM gets three objective lines. The key documented behaviour is in Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter: a small set of ASM instances serves the whole cluster, the number is set with a cardinality setting, and the default is three instances. The ASM overview adds why it matters: in a standard ASM cluster, if the ASM instance on a node fails, the database instances on that node fail too, while with Flex ASM a database instance can reach another ASM instance on another node.

Layer 3: The RAC database (12 topics)

RAC gets the most objective lines, and it is where most candidates already feel at home:

  • RAC architecture: the benefits of RAC, why global resources are needed, and global cache coordination
  • Installing and configuring RAC, creating a cluster database, and converting a single-instance database to RAC
  • Administering RAC: redo log files, undo tablespaces, starting and stopping, and initialization parameters
  • Backup and recovery: ARCHIVELOG mode, the fast recovery area, and RMAN in a RAC environment
  • Global resources: the Global Resource Directory, global enqueue and instance locks, global buffer cache management, and affinity
  • Monitoring and tuning: RAC wait events, AWR and ADDM in RAC, the Cluster Database Performance pages, and SGA runtime management
  • High availability of services, and high availability for connections and applications: load balancing, the Load Balancing Advisory, FAN, TAF, Transparent Application Continuity and Dynamic Services Fallback
  • Upgrading and patching RAC with OUI and opatch
  • RAC One Node conversions in both directions
  • Quality of Service Management
  • Multitenant in RAC: CDBs, PDBs, PDB services and server pools, and automated PDB patching and relocation

The connections topic is the largest single topic on the page, with eight objective lines. That fits what happens on the job: users rarely notice a cluster until a node goes away and their session either survives or does not.

1Z0-078 Preparation Guide

The practitioner's advantage on this exam is that you can study it the way you would build it. A bottom-up plan means every new topic rests on one you have already worked through, and it keeps you from memorising RAC behaviour that you cannot explain.

Step 1: Build or borrow a lab you can break

Reading alone will not carry you through 77 questions on clustered systems. You need a two-node lab, or access to one, where you can stop Clusterware, pull a node, fill a disk group and watch what happens. Keep a log of each test. When a question later describes a symptom, you will have seen it.

Step 2: Start with Grid Infrastructure

Begin with the installation planning topics, because the exam asks about them directly and because they force you to understand the networks a cluster needs. Then install Grid Infrastructure and walk the startup sequence until you can explain what starts before what.

Spend real time on the OCR and voting files. Oracle's 19c documentation has a detail worth noticing here. The Clusterware guide says Clusterware files must be stored on ASM, yet the 19c changes page of the RAC Administration and Deployment Guide records that, starting with Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of direct placement of OCR and voting files on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Know both statements and which cluster type each applies to; that is exactly the kind of distinction a question can turn on.

Finish the layer with OCR backup and recovery, node addition and deletion, and policy-based management. Server pools come back later in the RAC topics, so understanding them here saves time.

Step 3: Move to ASM

Create disk groups at each redundancy level and look at the result. Oracle's ASM overview gives you rules you can test in a lab:

  • Normal redundancy disk groups require at least two failure groups, and high redundancy disk groups at least three.
  • If you omit the failure group specification, ASM places each disk in its own failure group (Exadata cells excepted).
  • You cannot alter the redundancy level of a disk group after it is created.
  • Allocation unit sizes can be 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 MB, depending on the disk group compatibility level.
  • ASM starts a rebalance automatically after you add, drop or resize disks, the power setting controls its speed, and databases can stay operational while it runs.

Then set up Flex ASM, change its cardinality, and work through ACFS: a volume, a file system on it, a snapshot, and at least one of the advanced features. The CloudFS topics hold nine objective lines between them, which is more than many candidates expect from the storage side.

Step 4: Finish with RAC

Now the RAC topics read as consequences of what sits underneath. Oracle's Introduction to Oracle RAC in the 19c RAC guide covers the ideas the exam builds on:

  • Cache Fusion uses the private interconnect for communication between instances, which is why the guide tells you not to use the interconnect for user traffic.
  • The Global Cache Service and the Global Enqueue Service coordinate buffer cache blocks and enqueues in the Global Resource Directory.
  • SCAN is a single network name, in DNS or Grid Naming Service, that round-robins to three IP addresses, and Oracle recommends that all client connections use it.
  • DBCA creates one default database service, which Oracle says should be reserved for maintenance; you create dynamic services for application connections.
  • RAC One Node runs a single instance of a RAC-enabled database on one node under normal operations, can relocate online with no downtime for users, and needs at least one dynamic database service.

Work the connection topics in the lab with a real client. Configure services, kill an instance, and watch what FAN, TAF and Application Continuity do. Then cover backup and recovery, tuning with AWR and ADDM, patching, and the multitenant topics.

Step 5: Read the objectives back as questions

In the last week, go through all 115 objective lines and turn each into a question you could answer out loud. "Explain the scope and capabilities of what-if command evaluation" becomes "what does SRVCTL evaluate mode report, and when would I run it?" Any line you cannot answer goes back to the lab.

Benefits and Career Scope of the 1Z0-078 Certification

The honest benefit of 1Z0-078 is that it names, in an employer's language, work that is otherwise hard to show on paper. A résumé line that says "supported RAC" can mean anything from running one SRVCTL command to rebuilding a cluster after a failed patch. An Oracle Certified Professional credential for RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure tells a reader that you were tested on the whole stack, including the storage and cluster layers that many database administrators never touch directly.

It also changes the work you get asked to do. Teams that run clustered Oracle databases need people who can plan an installation, patch Grid Infrastructure with minimal downtime, recover the OCR, and explain to an application team why their sessions dropped during a node failure. Those tasks map directly onto the exam topics, so preparing for the exam and becoming the person who handles those tickets are the same project.

There are limits worth stating. The credential is tied to Oracle Database 19c, and this article quotes no salary figures, because none comes from an official source. Oracle's exam page carried no retirement notice on 15 October 2026; check it again before you book, because Oracle updates its catalog.

The study itself has value even if you never sit the exam. Working through every objective line usually turns up at least one area, often ACFS, QoS Management or policy-based cluster management, that your current environment does not use and that you would otherwise meet for the first time during an incident.

Practice Test and Preparation Resources for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page links its recommended training. Three Oracle University courses on MyLearn line up with the three groupings of the syllabus, and their course pages show the module count and running time:

  • Oracle Database 19c: Clusterware Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 12 h 18 min, covering Clusterware architecture, cluster configuration options, preinstallation and installation, node management, policy-based management, patching, troubleshooting and application high availability.
  • Oracle Database 19c: ASM Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 8 h 7 min, covering ASM instances, Flex ASM, disk groups, files and templates, and ACFS with ADVM.
  • Oracle Database 19c: RAC Administration Workshop: 14 modules, 20 h 11 min, covering installation, administration, patching, backup and recovery, tuning, services, connection high availability, RAC One Node, multitenant and QoS in RAC.

Together that is about 40 hours of video before any lab time. Taken in the order listed, Clusterware first and RAC last, the courses follow the same bottom-up path as this article.

Oracle's documentation

The 19c guides are free and they are the source the exam objectives are written against. Keep three open while you study: the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide, the Automatic Storage Management Administrator's Guide, and the Real Application Clusters Administration and Deployment Guide. When a course and a guide seem to disagree, the guide for your exact release wins.

Practice questions

Once each layer is done, test it. The free 1Z0-078 sample questions on DBExam show the multiple-choice style and make a quick check after a study block. A full timed practice exam is the better rehearsal for the 93-second pace, and DBExam offers one for 1Z0-078 alongside the free set. Use the score report to send you back to specific topics rather than retaking until the number looks good.

A short video on working through answer options

The DBExam YouTube channel has no 1Z0-078 video yet. The walk-through below is about a different Oracle exam, 1Z0-149 on PL/SQL programming, but its method carries over: read every option, rule out the ones that contradict a documented fact, and only then choose.

Conclusion

1Z0-078 lists its 30 topics with RAC first, Grid Infrastructure second and ASM last. A working cluster is built the other way round, and the most reliable way to prepare is to follow the build: Clusterware and the OCR and voting files, then ASM disk groups, Flex ASM and ACFS, then the RAC database, its services and its clients.

The format is fixed and published: 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes, a 65% passing score, delivered online with a proctor. The topic list is long but concrete, and almost every line can be practised in a two-node lab. If the work it describes is the work on your desk, the exam mostly asks you to prove you understand why that work is done the way it is.

FAQs

How many questions are on the 1Z0-078 exam, and how long do I get?

Oracle's exam page lists 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes and a 65% passing score. That is about 93 seconds a question. The exam is delivered as Proctored Online.

Does Oracle publish topic weights for 1Z0-078?

No. The exam page lists 30 topics with 115 objective lines: 49 for RAC, 41 for Grid Infrastructure and 25 for ASM. Those are line counts, not percentages, so use them to judge coverage, not to predict how many questions each area will get.

Where can the OCR and voting files live in Grid Infrastructure 19c?

Oracle's Clusterware guide says both must sit on shared storage reachable by every node, and that Clusterware files must be stored on ASM. The 19c changes page of the RAC guide adds that, from Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of placing OCR and voting files directly on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Learn both statements and the cluster type each one covers.

What is the default number of ASM instances in Flex ASM?

Three. Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter says the number of ASM instances is set with a cardinality setting and that the default is three instances. You can change it with SRVCTL.

Do I have to take Oracle's training before I book 1Z0-078?

The exam page offers recommended training: the Clusterware, ASM and RAC administration workshops on MyLearn, about 40 hours combined. The page does not state a course requirement. Check Oracle's Certification Program Guidelines for the credential before you book.

What should I bring to the online 1Z0-078 session?

A government-issued identification, a computer that meets Oracle's minimum system requirements, and a testing space that meets Oracle's rules. Check in 30 minutes before the exam time. Your result appears on screen at the end, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView. If you need to reschedule, do it at least 24 hours before your appointment.

title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.14277v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.

title: Do You Want Your Web App to Feel Like a Native App?
description:
You can give your Codename One web app the same desktop theme family as your users' operating system: Aqua on macOS, Fluent on Windows, or Adwaita on Linux. Menus can sit above the app in HTML, with commands such as File and View visible instead of tucked into a mobile overflow menu.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

That gives you a browser version of your app that fits more comfortably on a desktop. The JavaScript port now supports both choices, and the same theme work reaches the Certificate Wizard you use to sign your apps.

Follow the operating system, or choose a theme

Set these in the Settings app's Build Hints:

nativeTheme=native
javascript.titleBar=html

In codenameone_settings.properties, use codename1.arg.nativeTheme and codename1.arg.javascript.titleBar instead. Desktop browsers select Fluent for Windows, Aqua for macOS, and Adwaita for Linux and the remaining desktop systems. Phones and tablets keep the mobile theme selection. The browser detection treats an iPad as a tablet even when it reports a Mac browser.

These are Codename One themes drawing the controls. They are not the operating system's native widget toolkit embedded in the page.

The Settings app demonstrates the three desktop theme families now available to browser apps. Click to compare the controls at full size.

You can pin a desktop theme when the application's design calls for it:

javascript.desktopTheme=fluent

The other explicit choices are aqua, adwaita and none. none keeps mobile themes on desktop browsers. Leave the value at auto to follow the operating system. The broader nativeTheme=modern setting has different behavior: it selects the modern mobile families, including on desktop browsers. Use native when desktop family selection is what you want.

Put commands above the app

The default javascript.titleBar=toolbar keeps the themed Toolbar inside the app. With html, the page supplies title and menu bars instead. The title follows the current form; commands group into menus using the same Command.setDesktopMenu() hint used on the desktop ports.

For example, inside an initialized app:

com.codename1.ui.Form form = new com.codename1.ui.Form("Notes");
com.codename1.ui.Command refresh = new com.codename1.ui.Command("Refresh") {
    public void actionPerformed(com.codename1.ui.events.ActionEvent event) {
        form.setTitle("Notes refreshed");
    }
};
refresh.setDesktopMenu("View");
form.getToolbar().addCommandToOverflowMenu(refresh);
form.show();

Commands without a menu hint go into a Commands menu. The HTML bars follow the selected appearance and the browser's light or dark preference. They do not have fake minimize, maximize or close buttons: the page does not own the browser window. The browser tab title remains the application's display name.

The source is in JavaScriptDesktopChrome, with build-hint and page behavior documented in the JavaScript guide.

Keep navigation inside your browser app

We do not support additional native Window surfaces in the JavaScript port. Popup blockers and the browser's window ownership make that a different promise from drawing a menu inside the current page. Windows browsers are supported; extra OS windows are the unsupported feature. Dialogs and navigation within the app remain the appropriate model.

There are renderer limits too. For example, the full lifted-lens optics from Sunday's iOS article are not implemented in the browser. Try the actual controls and effects your app uses rather than assuming a theme name proves complete renderer parity.

The build prunes theme resources it can prove the app will not reach. If your code constructs resource names dynamically, set javascript.pruneThemes=false; otherwise a theme loaded only through that constructed name may be missing.

Use the same desktop styling when you sign your app

A gallery of buttons cannot tell us whether an application works comfortably with a desktop theme. The Certificate Wizard has longer forms, tables, dialogs and instructions that people must actually read to finish a task.

PR #5916 adopts the native desktop themes there, continuing the work we did in Settings. Its current source uses @DesktopBuild(themeMode = "native", titleBar = DesktopTitleBar.NATIVE, ...), with interactive scrollbars. Fluent, Aqua and Adwaita now provide the surrounding control styles instead of a separate wizard-specific desktop imitation.

The same change fixes handling of an App ID's team prefix. That is a separate functional repair, not a consequence of adopting a theme. The wizard's current source keeps both changes visible.

Try the browser theme with a form that has real commands and enough content to scroll. Switch appearances, open its menus and check keyboard navigation. That will teach you more than another screenshot of an isolated button.

The weekly overview links the rest of the release. It also includes this week's smaller map-label improvement.

title: Historical-Feature Residual Adaptation for Sequential Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.19315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sequential screening policies must use acquired feedback effectively under a fixed experiment budget. We study acquisition-time residual adaptation: a small ranking correction built from fixed historical features and anchored to base scores recorded before feedback is revealed. The interface accepts a history-conditioned scorer and a candidate feature table; its primary instantiation augments AssayFormer's ten-dimensional representation with 64 historical directions while retaining the pretrained model. In retrospective evaluation on 20 official-test screens from 15 recorded sources, a comparison fixed before target-outcome access increased source-macro fraction of hits recovered from 22.58% to 28.61%, exceeding all six prespecified comparators. A same-feature ordinary ranking head achieved 25.73%. Supplementary strong logistic, rank-fusion, and unprojected controls achieved 26.42%, 26.02%, and 26.78%, respectively. A separate model-independent pilot on 13 reused development screens reconstructs the features without AssayFormer assets. Across three seeds, residual adaptation improves random-forest hit recovery from 28.87% to 31.27%, while logistic recovery changes from 30.22% to 29.78%. The results show effective pretrained-policy adaptation and useful transfer to an independent nonlinear base, with gains that depend on the base model.

title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
description:
arXiv:2610.19330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

title: Java Data Types in AI Applications
description:
Introduction

Java data types define the kind of data a variable can store.

They help developers organize and process information correctly.

In AI applications, data types manage user prompts, AI responses, scores, and processing results.

Choosing the correct data type makes code easier to understand and maintain.

What Are Java Data Types?

Java data types specify the type of value a variable can hold, such as text, numbers, or Boolean values.

Syntax / Example 

String prompt = "Explain Artificial Intelligence";
int tokenCount = 100;
double confidenceScore = 0.95;
boolean responseGenerated = true;

System.out.println(prompt);
System.out.println(tokenCount);
System.out.println(confidenceScore);
System.out.println(responseGenerated);

Practical Example

In an AI chatbot, String stores the user's prompt, int stores a token count, double stores a numerical score, and boolean indicates whether a response was generated.

Key Takeaways

  • String stores text.
  • int stores whole numbers.
  • double stores decimal numbers.
  • boolean stores true or false.
  • Choosing suitable data types improves code clarity.

Conclusion

Java data types are the foundation of data handling in AI applications. They help developers manage different kinds of information efficiently. Understanding them is an important step toward building Java-based GenAI projects.

Question: Which Java data type would you use to store an AI-generated response?

title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications
description:
Authors: Divya Gadde, Ko-Jen Hsiao, Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya

The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models.

The previous two blog posts(1, 2) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model.

In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches.

Embeddings from Foundation model

Transformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings.

Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store.

An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique (paper). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features.

This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online.

This approach is often the initial and most straightforward way for applications to interact with the Foundation Model. Embeddings can serve as powerful features for other models or for candidate generation, helping to retrieve appealing titles for a user or facilitate title-to-title recommendations. Integrating embeddings as features into existing pipelines is generally well-supported and offers a low barrier to entry. Compared to other integration approaches, using embeddings from the Embedding Store is expected to have a relatively smaller impact on training and inference costs.

However, this approach also has some cons. The time gap between embedding computation and downstream model inference can lead to staleness, impacting the freshness of recommendations. This may prevent applications from fully unlocking the benefit of the Foundation Model, especially for use cases requiring real-time adaptability.

Overall, the default starting point for leveraging the Foundation Model is through its profile and item embeddings via the Embedding Store, provided that the embeddings’ freshness and stability meet application-specific needs. While embeddings may not leverage the full power of the Foundation Model, they offer a good initial step.

Our biggest learning from working on this approach is that embeddings are a low cost and high leverage way of using the Foundation Model. A resilient embedding generation framework and embedding store are essential for updating the embeddings daily and serving them to application models. We found this infrastructure to be so valuable that we stepped up our investment here to build a near-realtime embedding generation framework. This new framework also enables us to update the embeddings based on user actions during the session, making the embeddings and our downstream models more adaptive. Although the near-real time framework cannot be used for very large models, it represents an important direction for addressing embedding staleness and adaptiveness of recommendations.

Foundation Model as a Subgraph

This approach involves using the Foundation Model as an input to the downstream model i.e. the Foundation Model decoder stack is a subgraph of the application model’s full model graph and hence the name “subgraph integration”. The Foundation Model subgraph processes raw user interaction sequences and outputs representations that are then fed into the downstream model graph.

Applications can fine-tune the Foundation Model subgraph as part of their own training process, potentially leading to better performance than just using static embeddings. In this approach, there is no time gap or staleness between the Foundation Model inference and the application model’s inference, ensuring that the most up-to-date learnings are used. This approach also allows applications to leverage specific layers from the Foundation Model that may not be exposed through the Embedding Store, uncovering more application-specific value.

However, the subgraph approach comes with some complexities and trade-offs. To use the Foundation Model as a subgraph, application models need to generate all the features necessary for the subgraph as part of their feature generation process. This can add time, compute and complexity to their feature gen jobs. Merging the Foundation Model as a subgraph also increases the application model size and inference time. To alleviate some of these complexities, the Foundation Model team provides some reusable code and jobs that make the feature generation more compute efficient. To optimize the inference performance, we split the subgraph and ensure it only runs once per profile per request and is shared by all items in the request.

Overall, the subgraph approach allows for a deeper integration and enables the applications to harness the full power of the Foundation Model. But it can also make the application’s training code more complex, requiring a trade-off between metric improvement, compute cost, and time. Therefore, we would reserve this approach for high impact use cases where the increase in metric wins compensate for the cost and complexity.

Fine-tuning Foundation Model and use directly

This approach is similar to fine-tuning LLMs with domain specific data. In the previous blog post, we described how the Foundation Model is trained on a next-token prediction objective, with the tokens being different user interactions. Different interactions are of different importance to various surfaces on the Netflix website. For example, for the ‘Trending now’ row, recent interactions on trending titles might be more important than old interactions. Hence, the Foundation Model can be fine-tuned on more product specific data and then the fine-tuned model can be used to directly power the product. During fine-tuning, application teams can choose to do full parameter fine-tuning or freeze some layers. They can also choose to add a different output head with a different objective. We built a fine-tuning framework to make it easy for application teams to develop their own custom fine-tuned versions of the Foundation Model.

This approach offers the ability to adapt the Foundation Model to application’s specific data and objectives, making it optimized for their use case. A side benefit of this integration approach is that it provides a de facto baseline for new models/applications. Instead of coming up with a new model stack and spending months on feature engineering, new applications can directly utilize fine-tuned foundation models. However, this approach can lead to more models and pipelines to maintain across the organization.The latency and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of the fine-tuned model must be carefully optimized for the specific application use case.

Conclusion

We are continuing to innovate on these integration approaches over time. For example, the Machine Learning Platform team is working on near-real time embedding inference capabilities to address the staleness issues with the embedding approach. We are also working on a smaller distilled version of the Foundation Model to reduce the inference latency of the subgraph approach. We also provide a fine-tuning framework to make it easy to fine-tune and leverage the Foundation Model. We also continue to refine and standardize the APIs used in these approaches to make it easy for application teams to use them. Overall, these three integration patterns provide a comprehensive framework for how Netflix applications can interact with and extract value from the Foundation Model.

Acknowledgements

We thank our stunning colleagues in the Foundation Model team for developing and continuing to innovate on the Foundation Model. We thank our colleagues in the AIMS applications teams for driving the integrations and their valuable feedback and discussions. We also thank our Machine Learning Platform team for building and supporting the infra components to get these approaches up and running in production.

Contributors to this work (name in alphabetical order): Davis Shepherd Inbar Naor Jin Wang Jonathan Indig Kevin Zielnicki Luke Wang Mario Garcia-Armas Maryam Esmaeli Michael Tu Nicholas Hortiguera Qiuling Xu Robbie Greuner Roger Menezes Sejoon Oh Trung Nguyen Vito Ostuni Yesu Feng.

Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Vercel Connect: Secure access to external services for your agents
description:
Vercel Connect lets your apps and agents access external services like Slack, GitHub, Salesforce, and your own custom APIs without storing a long-lived provider secret in your environment. You register a connector once, and your code requests scoped, short-lived tokens at runtime, only when it needs them.

You can create a connector from your dashboard or the Vercel CLI:

Your agent can then request a token from it at runtime, only when it needs it. The SDK fetches and refreshes that token automatically, so there is no secret for you to store or rotate by hand:

Scoped tokens

Each token is scoped to the task in front of it, with granularity that depends on the provider. A GitHub token can be limited to a single repository and read-only, instead of your whole organization. An agent gets exactly the access a task needs, never broad standing access to everything.

A token can also be tied to a specific user instead of the app. It then acts with that user's identity and inherits their permissions, so the agent can do only what that user is allowed to do:

Isolation and revocation

A connector only works in the environments you attach it to, so you can run separate connectors for development, preview, and production. This means if a token leaks in development, it cannot be used against production:

Because access is issued as tokens, you can revoke it with a single command, either your own or every token a connector has issued across all users and installations:

Triggers

Events can also flow from a provider to your app. With triggers enabled on a connector, Vercel Connect verifies the provider's incoming webhooks and forwards them to the projects you choose, so a new Slack message can reach an agent that acts on it. Triggers support Slack, GitHub, and Linear in Beta, and a connector can forward to up to three projects:

Connectors and adapters

Dedicated connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Discord, Notion, Salesforce, Figma, and Snowflake are available from the dashboard, along with generic OAuth and API key connectors, and you can create connectors for other services from the CLI, including MCP servers like mcp.linear.app. Vercel Connect also ships adapters for Better Auth, Auth.js, eve, the AI SDK, and MCP clients, so it works with the auth library and agent tooling you already use.

Get started

Pricing is based on token requests. Hobby includes 5,000 per month at no additional cost, and Pro and Enterprise are billed at $3 per 10,000.

Vercel Connect is now available in Public Beta. Read the documentation, or have your coding agent set it up by installing the vercel-connect skill with npx skills add vercel/vercel-plugin --skill vercel-connect.

Deploy a software factory template with Vercel Connect or browse the source.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
description:
arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

title: 5 Common Reasons Why GBase Database(GBase 8s) Cannot Connect After Installation
description:
Your GBase Database(GBase 8s) instance is online, but dbaccess or a remote client still cannot connect. Before reinstalling the database, check these five common causes: incorrect sqlhosts configuration, firewall restrictions, port conflicts, server name mismatches, and client connection settings.

This troubleshooting guide explains what to check first and how to narrow down GBase Database(GBase 8s) connectivity issues efficiently.

1. Incorrect Hostname in sqlhosts

Typical symptom: Local connections work, but remote connections fail.

The sqlhosts file defines connection information for a database server, including its server name, connection protocol, host, and port.

For example:

gbase01 onsoctcp 192.168.1.100 9088

If the configuration uses localhost or 127.0.0.1, remote clients may be unable to reach the intended network endpoint.

What to check:

  • Verify the hostname or IP address in the relevant sqlhosts entry.
  • Confirm that the address is reachable from the client machine.
  • Check that the server is listening on the expected interface and port.

Use the actual network address and connection settings for your environment. Avoid changing configuration or restarting the instance until you have identified the cause.

2. Firewall Blocking the Database Port

Typical symptom: The GBase Database(GBase 8s) instance is online, but remote connections time out.

A running database does not guarantee that network traffic can reach it. The operating system firewall, network firewall, or cloud security rules may block the database listener port.

Check the firewall status and test connectivity from the remote client:

systemctl status firewalld

nc -vz 192.168.1.100 9088

Replace the example IP address and port with your actual server settings.

If the connection is blocked, review the applicable firewall rules and allow only the required source addresses and destination port. Avoid disabling the firewall as a troubleshooting shortcut.

3. Database Port Conflict

Typical symptom: The instance fails to start correctly, or the expected database port is unavailable.

Another service may already be using the configured port.

Check which process is listening:

ss -lntp | grep ':9088'

Alternatively, use lsof if it is installed.

If a conflict exists, identify the process before taking action. Do not stop an unrelated service simply because it occupies the port.

Depending on your environment, you may need to resolve the conflict or configure GBase Database(GBase 8s) to use an available port. Ensure that the server configuration and client connection entries remain consistent.

4. Server Name Mismatch Between onconfig and sqlhosts

Typical symptom: The instance appears to be running, but client connections fail with a server name or connection configuration error.

GBase Database(GBase 8s) uses instance configuration and connection definitions that must agree with the intended server name.

Review the relevant settings:

grep -E 'DBSERVERNAME|DBSERVERALIASES' \
  "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/onconfig.gbase01"

cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

The exact configuration file names depend on your installation.

Verify that the server name requested by the client corresponds to a valid server configuration and that the associated connection protocol, host, and port are correct.

Do not change instance identifiers blindly. Confirm the active configuration before making adjustments.

5. Client-Side sqlhosts Misconfiguration

Typical symptom: The database is accessible from the server itself, but a remote application or client cannot connect.

The client may be using a different sqlhosts file or an outdated connection definition.

Check the active environment and client configuration:

echo "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

Then inspect the file referenced by that variable and verify the server entry.

For remote connections, confirm that:

  • The client uses the correct database server name.
  • The hostname or IP address is reachable.
  • The protocol and port match the server configuration.
  • Client environment variables and driver settings are appropriate for the installed version.

A correct server-side configuration cannot compensate for an incorrect client connection definition.

Quick GBase Database(GBase 8s) Diagnostic Script

This basic script checks instance status, the expected listening port, and the configured sqlhosts file.

#!/bin/bash

echo "=== GBase Database(GBase 8s) Diagnostics ==="

echo
echo "1. Instance status"
if command -v onstat >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    onstat - 2>&1 | head -5
else
    echo "onstat not found; check the database environment."
fi

echo
echo "2. Listening port"
if command -v ss >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    ss -lnt | grep ':9088' || echo "Expected port not found."
else
    echo "ss command unavailable."
fi

echo
echo "3. sqlhosts configuration"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS" ]]; then
    cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"
else
    echo "sqlhosts path is unset or file is unreadable."
fi

echo
echo "4. Firewall status"
if command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    systemctl is-active firewalld 2>/dev/null ||
        echo "firewalld inactive or unavailable."
fi

echo
echo "5. Next step"
echo "Test connectivity from the actual client."
echo "Review database and client logs for detailed errors."

Save the script as check_gbase_connection.sh and run it under an account with the appropriate permissions.

This is a preliminary diagnostic tool, not a complete connection test. Replace port 9088 with the actual configured port. A listening port alone does not prove that database authentication or SQL queries will succeed.

Final Thoughts

When GBase Database(GBase 8s) cannot connect after installation, start with the instance state, then check the listener, network connectivity, sqlhosts, and client configuration. Use the exact error message to narrow down the cause before changing settings.

The key takeaway: An online database instance is only the first step. Reliable connectivity requires consistent server configuration, an accessible network endpoint, and correctly configured clients.

Systematic troubleshooting is usually more effective than reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s) without identifying the underlying problem.

title: Stop Waiting for the Backend: A Frontend Developer's Guide to API Prototyping
description:
I spent years stuck in the same frustrating cycle during sprint planning.

Every Monday morning, our product manager would introduce an exciting new feature — say, a customer analytics dashboard with interactive filters, CRUD management, and real-time updates.

The backend engineers would estimate their database migrations and API endpoints at 4–5 days. And as a frontend engineer, I'd get hit with that dreaded phrase:

"You can start building and integrating the UI once our backend endpoints are deployed to staging on Friday."

That meant Monday through Thursday was spent twiddling thumbs or building static mockups, followed by a frantic weekend scramble when the backend was finally delivered (often with slight payload mismatches).

I hated feeling blocked. I wanted to build fully functional, interactive frontend interfaces on Monday morning — with real pagination, stateful CRUD, and error handling — without having to wait on a backend team.

That exact bottleneck inspired me to create Playground API, giving frontend engineers an instant, stateful cloud sandbox so they could prototype against a live API contract from day one.

In this guide, I'll walk you through the Contract-First workflow that completely changed how I build software and eliminated the backend bottleneck forever.

The Waterfall Trap vs. Parallel Track Development

When teams develop sequentially, every delay in the backend blocks the frontend. When teams develop in parallel, both teams agree on a shared API Contract on day one:

gantt
    title Sequential vs Parallel Development
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    section Sequential (Waterfall)
    Backend API Development     :a1, 2026-09-01, 5d
    Frontend Blocked Waiting    :crit, a2, 2026-09-01, 5d
    Frontend Rushed Dev         :a3, after a1, 3d
    section Parallel (Contract-First)
    Define API Contract (Day 1) :done, b1, 2026-09-01, 1d
    Backend Development         :b2, after b1, 4d
    Frontend Prototyping Sandbox:active, b3, after b1, 4d
    Seamless Integration & QA   :b4, after b2, 1d

By decoupling the frontend from the physical backend implementation, frontend engineers can:

  1. Validate user experience and design assumptions early.
  2. Build realistic error and loading states.
  3. Share interactive staging demos with product managers and stakeholders days ahead of schedule.

The 4 Steps to Successful Frontend API Prototyping

Step 1: Agree on the API Contract

Before writing code, both teams establish the endpoint paths, HTTP verbs, payload shapes, and status codes. For example:

  • GET /api/v1/posts?_page=1&_limit=10 → Returns paginated posts.
  • POST /api/v1/posts → Body: { title: string, body: string, user_id: number }.
  • DELETE /api/v1/posts/:id → Returns 200 OK.

Step 2: Connect to a Zero-Config Stateful Sandbox

Instead of building a temporary Node.js Express server on your machine that only you can access, use a hosted stateful sandbox like Playground API by Niles Labs.

Playground API provides pre-seeded datasets (users, posts, comments, todos) with full support for:

  • CRUD mutations that persist per session
  • Sorting (?_sort=title&_order=asc)
  • Pagination (?_page=1&_limit=10)
  • Latency injection (?_delay=1000)
  • Error simulation (?_status=500)

Step 3: Abstract Your API Layer with an Environment Variable

Always isolate your base API URL in an environment configuration file:

// src/config/api.ts
export const API_BASE_URL = 
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL || 'https://playground.nileslabs.com/api/v1';

// src/services/postService.ts
import { API_BASE_URL } from '../config/api';

export interface Post {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  body: string;
  user_id: number;
}

export async function getPosts(page = 1, limit = 10): Promise<Post[]> {
  const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}/posts?_page=${page}&_limit=${limit}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP error ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

export async function createPost(payload: Omit<Post, 'id'>): Promise<Post> {
  const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}/posts`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Failed to create post');
  return res.json();
}

Step 4: The Zero-Friction Switch to Production

When Friday arrives and the backend team deploys their service, you don’t need to rewrite your React components or modify fetch hooks.

You simply update your .env.production file:

# Before (Prototyping Sandbox)
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://playground.nileslabs.com/api/v1

# After (Production Backend Ready)
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com/v1

Because your frontend was developed and tested against real HTTP requests, headers, and status codes, the switch is seamless.

Concrete Example: Building an Interactive Admin Panel

Here is how straightforward it is to prototype an interactive user list with real-time deletion against a sandbox:

// src/components/AdminUserList.jsx
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

const API_URL = 'https://playground.nileslabs.com/api/v1';

export default function AdminUserList() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  const fetchUsers = async () => {
    setLoading(true);
    const res = await fetch(`${API_URL}/users?_limit=5`);
    const data = await res.json();
    setUsers(data);
    setLoading(false);
  };

  const handleDeleteUser = async (id) => {
    // Delete against sandbox overlay
    await fetch(`${API_URL}/users/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
    // Re-fetch or filter locally: the deleted user is gone from the session!
    setUsers(users.filter(u => u.id !== id));
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchUsers();
  }, []);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading team members...</p>;

  return (
    <div style={{ maxWidth: '600px', margin: '2rem auto', fontFamily: 'sans-serif' }}>
      <h2>👥 Team Members (Prototype)</h2>
      <table style={{ width: '100%', borderCollapse: 'collapse' }}>
        <thead>
          <tr style={{ background: '#f1f5f9', textAlign: 'left' }}>
            <th style={{ padding: '8px' }}>Name</th>
            <th style={{ padding: '8px' }}>Email</th>
            <th style={{ padding: '8px' }}>Action</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {users.map(user => (
            <tr key={user.id} style={{ borderBottom: '1px solid #e2e8f0' }}>
              <td style={{ padding: '8px' }}>{user.name}</td>
              <td style={{ padding: '8px' }}>{user.email}</td>
              <td style={{ padding: '8px' }}>
                <button 
                  onClick={() => handleDeleteUser(user.id)}
                  style={{ color: '#ef4444', background: 'none', border: 'none', cursor: 'pointer' }}
                >
                  Remove
                </button>
              </td>
            </tr>
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  );
}

Summary

Waiting for backend APIs creates unnecessary friction and delays project delivery. By establishing early API contracts and developing against a stateful sandbox, frontend engineers gain the autonomy to build polished, fully-tested user interfaces from day one.

Unblock your frontend team today with Playground API by Niles Labs.

title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.14525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.19129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
